title: DRA-SAM: Disagreement-Driven Referential Active SAM for Low-Altitude Drone Referring Segmentation
summary: Referring segmentation in low-altitude drone imagery requires distinguishing small, visually similar instances under complex linguistic and spatial constraints. Global inference may yield multiple plausible masks or leave the intended referent insufficiently represented, motivating selective local re-inference. We propose DRA-SAM, a disagreement-driven framework that allocates an additional inference pass according to competing referential hypotheses and an unresolved state. A lightweight EvidenceScorer estimates beliefs over existing candidates and the unresolved state. A training-free Referential Disagreement LOOK policy balances belief-weighted candidate competition and unresolved-region coverage to select a crop for local re-inference. The same benchmark-adapted SAM3-I backbone processes the selected region, and the resulting evidence updates existing hypotheses and introduces new candidates. Among the compared methods, DRA-SAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on six of seven test metrics on both RIS-LAD and UAVid-RIS, including mIoU and P@0.5-P@0.9, and on all seven RIS-LAD validation metrics. On RIS-LAD, DRA-SAM improves the matched global SAM3-I baseline from 49.55 to 52.34 mIoU and from 46.80 to 58.05 P@0.5. On UAVid-RIS, the independently adapted DRA-SAM achieves 73.26 mIoU and 86.86 P@0.5. Controlled crop-policy comparisons demonstrate the effectiveness of disagreement-guided crop selection, while target-size analysis reveals particularly pronounced gains for aerial targets occupying less than 1% of an image. These results establish referential disagreement as an effective criterion for allocating local inference. Code is available at https://github.com/phy709/DRA-SAM.

Referring image segmentation, low-altitude drone imagery, active inference, referential uncertainty, adaptive local re-inference. Introduction eferring image segmentation (RIS) identifies the pixels of an object specified by a natural-language expression~ hu2016segmentation . Beyond recognizing object categories, RIS must resolve attributes and spatial relations among individual instances. Low-altitude drone imagery is challenging because global resizing often makes targets small and visually similar objects crowd the scene. RIS-LAD~ ye2026rislad exemplifies these conditions. A query describing a vehicle relative to its neighbors may correspond visually to several candidate masks, although only one is the intended referent. Prior work advances RIS through cross-modal interaction and instance-aware reasoning~ ye2019cmsa,ding2021vlt,liu2023isfp,cho2024crossvlt,liu2023m3att , refined word--pixel alignment~ zhang2022coupalign , and scale-aware remote-sensing representations~ yuan2024rrsis,liu2024rmsin . Uncertainty-guided approaches such as CroBIM-U~ sun2026crobimu additionally regulate fusion and local refinement in spatially unreliable regions. Complementing these advances, we investigate where to allocate a new inference pass to distinguish competing referents. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro , the global prediction gives rise to two complementary forms of referential ambiguity. Competition occurs when several existing masks remain plausible and additional spatial detail can distinguish them. Discovery concerns a referent that is insufficiently represented among the initial proposals and may become identifiable after local re-inference. These situations call for hypothesis-conditioned crop placement rather than reliance on a single global uncertainty score. By processing a selected image region at the backbone's input resolution, local re-inference increases the effective representation of small targets while preserving the context needed to interpret relational expressions. The added pass reprocesses pixels from the original image. These two cases motivate a unified decision process. Candidate evidence identifies actionable disagreement, while the unresolved hypothesis reserves belief mass for potentially missing referents. Combining both signals allows one local prediction to refine an existing choice or introduce a missing candidate. Hypothesis-conditioned inference allocation is therefore central to referent resolution. Therefore, we propose , a disagreement-guided local re-inference framework based on SAM3-I~ li2026sam3i . A 382,920-parameter EvidenceScorer assigns beliefs to concrete mask candidates and an unresolved hypothesis. A parameter-free policy chooses a crop using belief-weighted mask disagreement (competition) and unresolved-region coverage (discovery). The same benchmark-adapted SAM3-I checkpoint predicts masks in this crop; these predictions update existing evidence and can introduce new candidates. We evaluate DRA-SAM on RIS-LAD and UAVid-RIS with separate backbone adaptation. The benchmark comparisons show leading test-set mIoU and referring precision across both datasets, as well as the highest values on all seven RIS-LAD validation metrics. Beyond these cross-method comparisons, the matched-backbone experiment raises RIS-LAD mIoU from 49.55 to 52.34 and from 46.80 to 58.05. Controlled crop-policy comparisons isolate the benefit of disagreement-driven selection. A target-size breakdown further shows gains of 11.70--15.70 points for RIS-LAD objects covering less than 1 of the image, directly connecting spatially selective inference with the small-object setting. Our contributions are threefold: We formulate active local re-inference over explicit mask hypotheses and an unresolved state, covering both candidate competition and potential target discovery. We develop a training-free disagreement-guided crop utility and a local-evidence update that re-ranks existing candidates and incorporates newly predicted masks. We validate on two UAV referring benchmarks using matched-backbone controls, crop-policy and utility ablations, and target-size analysis. Related Work Cross-Modal and Instance-Aware Referring Segmentation RIS has evolved from recurrent language-conditioned segmentation~ hu2016segmentation,li2018rrn to long-range cross-modal attention~ ye2019cmsa , Transformer-based referring~ ding2021vlt,yang2022lavt,kim2022restr , and CLIP-assisted alignment~ radford2021clip,wang2022cris . CrossVLT~ cho2024crossvlt integrates stage-wise vision--language interactions, while multi-modal mutual attention~ liu2023m3att promotes iterative feature exchange. Instance-specific propagation~ liu2023isfp , multi-level language--mask alignment~ zhang2022coupalign , and multi-modal instance reasoning~ hu2023dmmi further improve referent discrimination. Compositional referring~ xu2023meta and instruction-guided segmentation~ lai2024lisa,chen2024sam4mllm broaden the task setting. Rather than redesigning these representations, DRA-SAM allocates an additional prediction to locations identified by disagreements among concrete mask hypotheses. Remote-Sensing and Drone Referring Segmentation Aerial visual grounding~ sun2022vg and RRSIS~ yuan2024rrsis established the importance of language-conditioned localization under small-object scale, crowded layouts, and diverse viewpoints. Subsequent work explores dual-modality alignment~ pan2024dual , rotated multi-scale interaction~ liu2024rmsin , fine-grained correspondence~ lei2025fianet , adaptive feature selection~ yue2024asda , and scale-aware prompting~ lv2026resap . RIS-LAD~ ye2026rislad focuses on low-altitude referring scenes, and UAVid-RIS~ li2025aeroreformer offers a complementary aerial benchmark. Our approach complements these representation-oriented advances by choosing the location of an additional inference pass after the global candidate set is available. This distinction is relevant to low-altitude imagery, where changing the processing scale of a particular region can be as useful as refining the global feature representation. Uncertainty, Prediction Correction, and Adaptive Computation Uncertainty modeling~ kendall2017uncertainties can identify unreliable predictions. UniA~ yang2025unia uses uncertainty inference and affinity diversification in weakly supervised segmentation, whereas CroBIM-U~ sun2026crobimu guides cross-modal fusion and local refinement with spatial referring uncertainty. DRA-SAM operates at a different level: it measures disagreement between complete candidate masks, chooses an explicit crop, and integrates the resulting local proposals. Iterative prediction correction~ shi2021qrn and selective visual computation~ mnih2014ram,jaderberg2015stn,rao2021dynamicvit provide complementary motivations. Our LOOK criterion converts normalized hypothesis beliefs and spatial overlap into an analytical action utility, complementing learned attention and risk maps. Temperature scaling also controls the sharpness of hypothesis beliefs~ guo2017calibration . We select the belief temperature on internal validation to support candidate selection. Promptable and Foundation Segmentation Mask2Former~ cheng2022mask2former , SAM~ kirillov2023sam , and SAM 2~ ravi2025sam2 have advanced general-purpose mask prediction, while Grounding DINO~ liu2024groundingdino and ReferFormer~ wu2022referformer connect language with object-level understanding. SAM 3~ carion2025sam3 and SAM3-I~ li2026sam3i extend prompt- and instruction-driven segmentation. We adapt SAM3-I separately to each benchmark and then freeze it for both global and local inference. Thus, observed improvements from the proposed stage can be studied without changing the segmentation backbone. title: A Differentiable Chassis Safety Layer for Intelligent Vehicle Motion Control
summary: Learning-based vehicle motion control requires coordination between diverse task objectives and state-dependent chassis safety constraints. Conventional cascaded architectures may compromise task performance when safety filters modify nominal commands independently of policy learning. This article proposes a differentiable chassis safety layer that modularly integrates task-oriented control with explicit physical constraints. Actuator limits, individual-tire force constraints, and vehicle handling envelopes are incorporated into sequential quadratic programs. Each projected command propagates the predicted vehicle dynamics and updates subsequent constraints, enabling temporal gradient coupling through implicit differentiation. A two-stage learning strategy combines expert imitation with risk-guided supervision and conditional intervention guidance to coordinate nominal control decisions with chassis safety constraints. Closed-loop evaluations under unseen scenarios, emergency maneuvers, and ablation studies demonstrate that the proposed method improves safety-performance coordination and exploits vehicle dynamic potential while maintaining handling stability.

Introduction Intelligent vehicle motion control involves multiple objectives, including trajectory tracking, energy efficiency, ride comfort, and actuator performance iotj_zhao2026_path,11701498,11175236 . Achieving these objectives requires coordination with physical constraints imposed by vehicle dynamics, tire--road interaction, and actuator capabilities. In multi-actuator chassis systems, these constraints are coupled through vehicle motion and vary with operating conditions Bobier-Tiu02092019,9837329 . Therefore, integrating task optimization with chassis physical constraints remains a fundamental challenge. Model predictive control (MPC) explicitly incorporates physical constraints into task optimization, while learning-based extensions improve adaptation through data-driven models and parameters 2020Learning,NingyuanGuo2022rea1 . Nevertheless, their effectiveness depends on prediction accuracy, particularly under nonlinear tire behavior, uncertain adhesion, and model mismatch 9638389,lorenzen2017adaptive . Alternatively, control barrier functions (CBFs) enforce state-dependent constraints through constrained optimization 7782377 . High-order and predictive formulations extend this approach to more complex system dynamics 9516971,zeng2021safety,10644741 . However, independently applied constraint projections may modify task-oriented commands without considering the resulting performance degradation hsu2023safety . Learning-based controllers provide flexibility in optimizing complex motion tasks 9772321,10005026 . Recent applications include autonomous navigation, networked suspension control, and risk-aware decision-making iotj_yao2025_nsgvf,iotj_zhu2025_suspension,iotj_zhang2026_eirm . To incorporate explicit constraints into neural learning, OptNet introduced differentiable optimization layers amos2021optnetdifferentiableoptimizationlayer,agrawal2019differentiable . Adaptive CBF methods further enabled parameterized safety conditions 9410332,9129764 , while BarrierNet integrated differentiable CBF-constrained QPs into neural controllers xiao2023barriernet . However, optimization-layer gradients may become uninformative under certain active-constraint configurations pmlr-v235-paulus24a . For chassis motion control, the central difficulty lies in the dynamic coupling of heterogeneous physical constraints. Unlike geometric motion constraints, tire-force capacity depends on longitudinal and lateral force demands, vertical loads, and road adhesion, while handling limits depend on the evolving sideslip and yaw states. These state--control dependencies are particularly important during high-dynamic maneuvers. Moreover, each constrained control command changes subsequent vehicle states and constraint conditions. Consequently, independent single-step projections cannot explicitly represent the temporal interaction between successive chassis constraints within the learning process. This motivates a dynamics-coupled differentiable optimization architecture tailored to chassis motion control. To address this challenge, this article proposes ChassisOptNet, a differentiable chassis optimization network for joint task--constraint learning. The network integrates actuator limits, tire-force constraints, and vehicle handling envelopes into state-dependent quadratic programming (QP) layers. Successive QPs are coupled through predictive vehicle dynamics, enabling constraint corrections and their temporal sensitivities to influence task-oriented learning. A two-stage training strategy combines expert imitation with risk-guided supervision and conditional intervention guidance. The framework is demonstrated on four-wheel-steering (4WS) vehicle motion control, using trajectory tracking as a representative task. The main contributions are summarized as follows: Chassis-specific differentiable safety layer: A modular safety layer integrates actuator limits, individual-tire friction constraints, and CBF-based handling envelopes into a unified control-space QP formulation, accounting for their coupling with vehicle dynamics. Dynamics-unrolled safety projection: Sequential differentiable QPs are coupled through predictive vehicle dynamics, allowing each projected control action to update subsequent states and safety constraints. Implicit differentiation provides temporal projection sensitivities for upstream learning. Safety-guarded task learning: A two-stage learning strategy combines expert imitation with expert-relative risk supervision and conditional safety-intervention guidance, coordinating task-oriented control with chassis safety projection. Closed-loop simulations validate the framework under unseen and near-limit operating conditions. The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section~ sec:idcbf develops the 4WS vehicle dynamics, handling-stability constraints, and dynamics-unrolled differentiable safety projection. Section~ sec:Safety-Guaranteed Bi-Level Policy Optimization Framework introduces the joint policy-learning framework and two-stage training procedure. Section~ sec:Training and Online Testing Experiments reports the closed-loop simulation results and ablation studies. Section~ sec:discussion discusses the findings and limitations. Section~ sec:conclusion concludes this article. title: MDPO: Multi-constraint Dexterous Policy Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Dexterous manipulation requires high-dimensional control policies to accomplish complex contact-rich tasks while simultaneously satisfying multiple safety requirements, such as joint limits, unsafe finger configurations, arm collisions, and unstable object interactions. Constrained reinforcement learning (RL) provides a principled framework for incorporating these requirements into dexterous manipulation policy learning. However, existing constrained RL methods for dexterous manipulation primarily focus on cumulative cost constraints and struggle to simultaneously handle multiple heterogeneous constraints during dexterous policy learning. In this work, we propose Multi-constraint Dexterous Policy Optimization (MDPO) for safe dexterous manipulation. We first formulate dexterous manipulation as a multi-constraint policy optimization problem involving both cumulative cost constraints and state-wise cost constraints. Based on this formulation, we integrate multi-constraint projection into the dexterous manipulation policy optimization process. Specifically, we employ constraint-specific policy projections to map the intermediate policy that maximizes task performance onto the feasible regions defined by the cumulative cost constraint and the state-wise cost constraint. Extensive experiments on ReDMan, including safe joint control, finger safety, and grasping tasks, demonstrate that MDPO achieves superior constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive task performance compared with the baselines. Our code is available at this link.

Based on this formulation, we integrate multi-constraint projection into the dexterous manipulation policy optimization process. Specifically, we employ constraint-specific policy projections to map the intermediate policy that maximizes task performance onto the feasible regions defined by the cumulative cost constraint and the state-wise cost constraint. INTRODUCTION Dexterous manipulation is a fundamental capability for embodied robots, enabling them to perform complex tasks that require high-dimensional coordination, precise contact control, and flexible interactions with objects~ nagabandi2020deep . Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have demonstrated considerable potential for learning dexterous manipulation policies directly through interactions with the environment~ yuan2025cross . Unlike conventional model-based approaches that rely on accurate dynamics models and manually designed controllers~ hess2025sampling , RL provides a data-driven paradigm that optimizes manipulation strategies directly from environmental feedback~ ye2023reinforcement . This characteristic makes RL particularly attractive for high-dimensional dexterous manipulation tasks involving complex contact dynamics and nonlinear interactions. However, applying RL to real-world dexterous manipulation remains challenging due to the presence of multiple physical cost constraints. For example, excessive joint motions and repeated unsafe interactions should remain within tolerable limits throughout the manipulation process, whereas critical unsafe states, such as severe violations of joint limits or hazardous finger and arm configurations, should be strictly avoided~ geng2025redman . Therefore, simultaneously considering dexterous manipulation performance, cumulative safety constraints, and state-wise safety constraints is crucial for achieving reliable dexterous manipulation. Constrained RL provides a principled framework for incorporating safety requirements into policy optimization through Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDP)~ altman2021constrained . Although constrained RL has improved the safety of dexterous manipulation policies~ geng2025redman , existing methods mainly focus on a single cumulative cost constraint and rarely consider the simultaneous regulation of cumulative and state-wise safety requirements~ zhao2023state . Conventional penalty or Lagrangian approaches handle constraints by introducing manually designed or adaptively learned coefficients~ wu2024off,zhang2022penalized . However, extending such methods to heterogeneous constraints requires multiple penalty factors, increasing optimization difficulty and potentially leading to unstable or overly conservative policy updates. Projection-based methods provide an alternative by mapping updated policies back into feasible constraint regions~ lin2024projection,yang2022constrained,yang2020projection , but are still primarily developed for the single constraint settings. Moreover, cumulative and state-wise constraints exhibit different temporal characteristics and may interact during dexterous manipulation: improving task performance by relaxing cumulative safety can increase instantaneous safety risks. Therefore, an effective multi-constraint RL algorithm is needed to jointly regulate long-term cumulative risks and state-wise safety violations while preserving manipulation performance. In this work, we propose Multi-constraint Dexterous Policy Optimization~(MDPO), a RL algorithm for multi-constraint safe dexterous manipulation. We first formulate dexterous manipulation as a multi-constraint policy optimization problem involving both cumulative cost constraints and state-wise cost constraints, allowing different safety requirements to be explicitly represented according to their physical characteristics. Based on this formulation, MDPO performs a regularized policy improvement step to obtain an intermediate policy that improves manipulation performance. The intermediate policy is then projected back into the joint safe feasible region defined by both cumulative and state-wise cost constraints. Specifically, MDPO simultaneously regulates long-term cumulative safety violations over an episode and state-wise safety-critical behaviors during individual interactions, ensuring that the updated policy satisfies both types of safety requirements. Finally, we evaluate the proposed method on the ReDMan~ geng2025redman benchmark, which contains diverse dexterous manipulation scenarios with challenging physical constraints. Experiments on safe joint control, finger-level safety, and grasping tasks demonstrate that MDPO consistently achieves better constraint satisfaction and competitive manipulation performance compared with baselines. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to formulate dexterous manipulation as a multi-constraint RL problem, enabling simultaneous optimization of manipulation objectives, cumulative cost constraints, and state-wise cost constraints. The intermediate policy is then projected back into the joint safe feasible region defined by both cumulative and state-wise cost constraints. Specifically, MDPO simultaneously regulates long-term cumulative safety violations over an episode and state-wise safety-critical behaviors during individual interactions, ensuring that the updated policy satisfies both types of safety requirements. Extensive experiments on the ReDMan benchmark demonstrate that MDPO achieves superior constraint satisfaction and competitive manipulation performance across various dexterous manipulation tasks. RELATED WORK In this section, we review the literature most relevant to our work, including RL for dexterous manipulation and constrained RL for safe policy optimization. RL for Dexterous Manipulation Dexterous manipulation requires coordinated control of high-dimensional joints and contacts for complex object interactions~ yang2024anyrotate . RL has become an effective paradigm for learning such skills through direct interaction with environments~ yuan2025cross . Early studies demonstrated successful policy learning in simulation~ rajeswaran2017learning and transfer to physical robots through improved exploration and sim-to-real techniques~ andrychowicz2020learning . Recent advances have further enabled challenging tasks including grasping, object reorientation~ mandi2025dexmachina , and in-hand manipulation~ khandate2023sampling . However, most methods still emphasize task success and manipulation performance~ ze2023h , while safety is typically handled through reward penalties~ hu2023causal or early termination~ khandate2023sampling . ReDMan~ geng2025redman explicitly introduces safety costs for dexterous manipulation, but mainly considers a single cumulative constraint. Consequently, existing methods remain insufficient for manipulation scenarios involving multiple heterogeneous safety requirements~ gu2025safe . Constrained RL Constrained RL incorporates safety requirements into policy optimization through CMDP formulations~ altman2021constrained . A widely used approach is Lagrangian optimization~ stooke2020responsive , which introduces adaptive multipliers to balance reward maximization and constraint satisfaction. Other representative directions include interior-point optimization~ liu2020ipo , CVaR-based formulations~ chow2015risk , penalty-based methods~ zhang2022penalized , state augmentation~ sootla2022saute , and world-model-based safe RL~ huang2024safedreamer . Projection-based methods~ yang2022constrained instead decouple performance improvement from safety correction by projecting an intermediate policy back into the feasible region. Primal-dual approaches provide another important paradigm by jointly optimizing policies and dual variables, with representative methods including PDO~ chow2018risk and CVPO~ liu2022constrained . Despite these advances, most existing methods are developed primarily for cumulative constraints, motivating more effective optimization for heterogeneous safety requirements. Although constrained RL has achieved considerable success in safety-critical control, existing safe dexterous manipulation studies remain largely limited to single cumulative cost constraints. A straightforward extension to multiple safety requirements is to introduce additional Lagrange multipliers or penalty coefficients, which increases the number of constraint-related hyperparameters and may lead to unstable or overly conservative policy optimization. In particular, cumulative and state-wise safety constraints in dexterous manipulation are inherently coupled: relaxing the cumulative cost constraint may improve task performance, but can simultaneously increase the likelihood of violating the state-wise cost constraint. These limitations highlight the need for more effective multi-constraint formulations for safe dexterous manipulation. title: Learning Dexterous Manipulation: Hands, Simulators, Training, and Evaluation
comment: 36 pages, 14 figures, 7 tables. Survey of 113 learning-based dexterous manipulation methods, with a comparison of each paper's stated reward against its released code
summary: A dexterous hand can change an object's pose without setting it down. This survey covers 113 learning-based methods that attempt it, the hands they run on, the simulators they train in, and how they report results. The field has largely converged on one recipe: reinforcement learning on privileged state in a GPU simulator, distilled into a vision-only student for transfer to hardware. Almost half the corpus trains that way, nearly all of it in one simulator, whose own successors are barely used. A second and faster-growing branch learns from teleoperated demonstration instead, through vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, and systems whose contribution is the collection rig itself. Published work has tripled since 2022. Grasping remains the largest task family and bimanual coordination the fastest-rising, and almost every experiment runs on one of four hands. What the survey adds comes from reading released code and vendor specifications beside the papers. Eight hands that can be bought or built from published designs appear in no method paper here. Where the depth a hand sinks into the object it holds is reported at all, it is not measured in the physics that produced the motion. Section VII proposes a protocol for the unreported quantities; the body gives the counts behind every claim above.
full_text: Learning Dexterous Manipulation:\\ Hands, Simulators, Training, and Evaluation Luai Abuelsamen\\[2pt] Independent Researcher\\[2pt] abuelsamen@berkeley.edu Abuelsamen: Learning Dexterous Manipulation A dexterous hand can change an object's pose without setting it down. This survey covers 113 learning-based methods that attempt it, the hands they run on, the simulators they train in, and how they report results. The field has largely converged on one recipe: reinforcement learning on privileged state in a GPU simulator, distilled into a vision-only student for transfer to hardware. Almost half the corpus trains that way, nearly all of it in one simulator, whose own successors are barely used. A second and faster-growing branch learns from teleoperated demonstration instead, through vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, and systems whose contribution is the collection rig itself. Published work has tripled since 2022. Grasping remains the largest task family and bimanual coordination the fastest-rising, and almost every experiment runs on one of four hands. What the survey adds comes from reading released code and vendor specifications beside the papers. Eight hands that can be bought or built from published designs appear in no method paper here. Where the depth a hand sinks into the object it holds is reported at all, it is not measured in the physics that produced the motion. Section VII proposes a protocol for the unreported quantities; the body gives the counts behind every claim above. Dexterous manipulation, multi-fingered hands, bimanual manipulation, reinforcement learning, imitation learning, physics simulation, contact modeling, benchmarking, reproducibility. Introduction sec:intro \@ifundefined fnLoaded 113 63 39 8 31 14 8 5 4 97 12 5 7 0 39 15 10 16 24 12 750 7 A hand is dexterous when it can change an object's pose without putting the object down. That property, and not the finger count, is what separates a hand from a gripper. Bicchi bicchi_grasping_chapter_2001 draws the same line in Sec.~1.1 between restraining an object and manipulating it with the fingers: restraint is a static question about whether the contacts prevent motion, while in-hand manipulation is a dynamic one about whether contacts can be broken and remade while the object stays held. A parallel-jaw gripper can hold almost anything and reorient almost nothing. The classical theory of grasping is about holding, and it is good at it. Given a set of contact points and an assumption about friction, it can decide whether an object is immobilized, and what force each finger has to apply to keep it that way. What it cannot do is say what the fingers should do next. Contact is what makes that hard: a finger is either touching or it is not, and it can push but not pull, so the equations of motion change form every time a contact is made or broken. The standard treatment says as much about its own results, that immobilizing an object ``does not guarantee stability'', and that ``the nonsmooth nature of grasp dynamics, because of the unilateral constraints on displacements and forces, has made a thorough analysis very difficult'' ( bicchi_grasping_chapter_2001 ). The tradition produced tests. You can check a candidate grasp against them; you cannot run them on a robot. Learning changed what a practitioner has to produce. The old deliverable was a proof that a configuration holds. The new one is a policy that scores well over many simulated attempts, which means the simulator now stands in for the analysis and the score stands in for the proof. That is why the field moved, and it is also why this survey is organized as it is. It shifts two burdens onto the author. The simulator has to be faithful where fidelity matters. The measurement has to mean something. Much of what follows asks how well this literature carries those two. One recipe now carries most of the field. Train a policy with reinforcement learning on privileged state, the object pose, velocities and physical parameters the robot cannot sense, in a GPU simulator running thousands of environments in parallel; distill that teacher into a student that sees only what a camera and joint encoders provide; transfer the student. Fifty-four of the 113 method papers here train this way, most of them in one simulator, and about half of those add the distillation stage. In-hand cube reorientation is the recipe's benchmark, inherited from openai_dexterity_2018 and still the task a new method is expected to show. A second branch is growing underneath it and inverts the dependency. Instead of a simulator and a reward it takes human demonstrations through a teleoperation rig and fits a policy directly, as a vision-language-action model, a diffusion policy, or a data-collection rig whose design is itself the contribution. Section~ sec:training counts them, and ~ fig:field shows how fast they have arrived. It is the newer literature, most of it from the last two years, and it trades the reward-design problem for a data-collection problem. Which of the two branches ends up feeding the other is not settled here, but the growth is the clearest trend in the corpus. Both branches run on remarkably little hardware. Four hands carry almost every experiment in this corpus, led by the Allegro at 35 of the 113 papers; ~ fig:hands gives the rest of the distribution. Eight further hands can be bought today or built from published designs and appear in the experiments of none of them. The hardware exists and is purchasable, so this is not a manufacturing lag, and Section~ sec:hands takes it up: a field whose results rest on four platforms is more fragile than its publication volume suggests. What this literature cannot currently do is compare its own results. Nearly every paper states a success criterion, but they are not the same criterion, and only 70 of the 113 say how many trials a reported rate rests on. The criteria run from never dropping the object to reaching a pose within a tolerance each paper picks for itself. Two success rates from two papers on nominally the same task are usually not measuring the same event, and none of the surveys preceding this one supplies a protocol that would make them comparable. Section~ sec:evaluation derives one, with the trial counts a stated confidence interval actually requires. Every number in this survey is traceable to a stated source. Appendix~ app:method says how the papers were selected, read and coded, what the method cannot do, and why each coverage figure here is a lower bound. One part of that method is unusual enough to flag now. Where a paper published a repository, its reward was read from the repository as well as from the paper, so the two can be compared. Reading an implementation against its own description is established practice outside robotics, in repeatability and reproducibility studies collberg_repeatability_2016, raff_reproducibility_2019 , in audits of how implementation detail moves reinforcement-learning results engstrom_implementation_matters_2020 , in reward-design review knox_reward_misdesign_2023 , in benchmark re-releases metaworld_plus_2025 , and most directly in recent work on paper--code alignment scicoqa_2026, biocon_2026 . We are aware of none that does it for a robotics field's released reward functions. Section~ sec:train:code reports what this one found. The scope is single-hand and bimanual multi-fingered manipulation under learned control. Parallel-jaw work enters as a comparison and not as a subject. Two limits apply to every number here. The corpus is of the learned era, which is a selection and not a verdict on the analytic tradition; and where this survey failed to extract a value, the counts look the same as if the source had never stated one. How to read this survey subsec:howtoread ~ fig:field puts the field on one page, and the sections work outward from the task. Section~ sec:taxonomy sets out the task families, what makes each one hard, and the handful of terms this survey uses precisely. Section~ sec:hands covers the hands and their sensing, Section~ sec:simulators the simulators and what they expose about contact, Section~ sec:training how policies are actually trained, Section~ sec:bimanual what changes when there are two hands, and Section~ sec:evaluation how any of it is evaluated. Section~ sec:gaps says what the corpus supports and what it does not. The appendices hold the method and the full tabulation: app:method the method and its limits, app:tables the hardware and engine tables, app:rewards every paper-against-code comparison, app:surveys the surveys that precede this one, app:protocol the derivation behind the protocol. If you are new to the field, read Section~ sec:taxonomy for the vocabulary, then the first half of Section~ sec:training for the two ways a dexterous policy gets trained, then Section~ sec:hands to see what hardware any of it runs on. Those three give the shape of the field in about half an hour. Section~ sec:evaluation is the one to read before designing an experiment, because it is about what the field's numbers do and do not mean. If you already work here, the parts likely to tell you something you did not know are Section~ sec:sim:engines on what simulators expose about contact, Section~ sec:train:code on papers against their own released code, Section~ sec:bimanual on bimanual work as its own problem, and Section~ subsec:protocol on what a success rate at twenty trials can support. If you want the data, the tables carry it: Tables~ tab:hands-available and~ tab:hands-announced for the hands, Table~ tab:simulators for the simulators, Table~ tab:codegap for the paper-against-code comparisons and Table~ tab:protocol for the proposed protocol. The full per-paper tabulation is available from the author on request. Three things to carry while reading. The corpus is of the learned era, which is a selection and not a verdict on the analytic tradition that preceded it. Every coverage figure is a floor: when a paper is silent and when this survey failed to extract a value, the counts look the same, and Appendix~ app:method says which direction that bias runs. And a success rate in this literature is rarely comparable across two papers, for reasons Section~ sec:evaluation sets out, so prefer the sections that explain mechanisms to any ranking assembled from the numbers. A taxonomy of the problem sec:taxonomy Task families sec:taxonomy:tasks Dexterous manipulation is not one task, and what separates its tasks is what makes some of them hard: what is held, what moves, which way gravity points, and what counts as failure. Six families cover most of the corpus, and the last paragraph here says what they miss. Grasping is the largest, with 58 of the 113 papers carrying the label; the labels are not exclusive, so one paper can sit in several families. Success is a lift that survives a hold, and the thresholds differ by more than an order of magnitude: one paper requires the object ``held 10 cm above the table for 20 s'' dexgraspvla_2025 , another ``held at least 0.5 s in simulation'' omnigrasp_2024 . What makes grasping hard at scale is the continuum of starting configurations. UniDexGrasp++ unidexgrasp_pp_2023 states it in Sec.~4.3, that ``we are dealing with an infinite number of tasks considering the initial object pose can change continuously''. Functional and tool use is second with 45 papers. It is the family where a stable grasp can still be the wrong answer. Dexterous Functional Grasping dexterous_functional_grasping_2023 gives the case in Sec.~2.1, that ``grabbing a hammer from the head or handle are both equally valid ways of using it'', and only one of the two lets the tool be used. Success is defined against the tool's function, and the field has no shared way to state it. In-hand reorientation has 31 papers and the most settled criteria, because the community inherited one number: OpenAI declared the goal achieved below 0.4 rad of orien

title: AGQ: Action-Guided Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and experimental results: https://github.com/Qiuxu00/AGQ
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform tasks specified through natural-language instructions, but their large weight footprint challenges deployment on memory-constrained onboard platforms. Ultra-low-bit quantization reduces this footprint, yet preserving task performance and controlling weight recovery costs remain challenging. We propose Action-Guided Quantization, which combines action sensitivity with a measured proxy for weight recovery cost to allocate matrix bitwidths under storage budgets. Per-channel calibration compensates for quantization error, while a uniform bitwidth within each matrix preserves regular layouts. Bit-dependent grouped lossless coding reduces resident weight storage, and block-wise recovery limits temporary buffers. On LIBERO, AGQ achieves 92.7% task success at W3, exceeding AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively, and retains 70.5% success at W2.5. An asymmetric configuration, denoted W1.5$^{*}$, uses W4 vision weights and a parameter-weighted average of 1.5 bits for language weights. With lossless coding, it achieves $6.10\times$ complete-model compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/Qiuxu00/AGQ

We propose Action-Guided Quantization, which combines action sensitivity with a measured proxy for weight recovery cost to allocate matrix bitwidths under storage budgets. Per-channel calibration compensates for quantization error, while a uniform bitwidth within each matrix preserves regular layouts. Bit-dependent grouped lossless coding reduces resident weight storage, and block-wise recovery limits temporary buffers. On LIBERO, AGQ achieves 92.7 task success at W3, exceeding AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively, and retains 70.5 success at W2.5. An asymmetric configuration, denoted W1.5 , uses W4 vision weights and a parameter-weighted average of 1.5 bits for language weights. With lossless coding, it achieves 6.10 complete-model compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5 task success. Code and experimental results are available at . vision-language-action model, mixed-precision quantization, per-channel calibration, lossless coding, hardware-aware inference. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action prediction, enabling robots to perform tasks specified through natural-language instructions~ openvla, oft . Running these models locally is attractive for robots that operate with limited connectivity or require autonomous execution. However, their large weight footprint poses a challenge for resource-constrained onboard computing platforms. Ultra-low-bit weight quantization offers a way to reduce model storage and make VLA inference feasible under tighter memory budgets. These savings come at the risk of degraded action prediction: in closed-loop control, quantization-induced action errors can affect subsequent observations and task outcomes. Therefore, preserving task performance under aggressive compression remains a central challenge. Post-training quantization (PTQ) provides a practical approach to compressing pretrained models using a small calibration set~ nagel . AWQ uses activation statistics to protect salient weights~ awq , while GPTQ uses second-order information to compensate for quantization error~ gptq . For VLA models, QVLA and ActQuant further incorporate action-related information into quantization~ qvla,actquant . Beyond calibrating quantized weights, mixed precision allows different layers or matrices to use different bitwidths according to their sensitivity~ mixedint,hawq . Hardware-aware approaches such as HAQ additionally incorporate latency and energy feedback into precision selection~ haq . Recent low-bit schemes also use structured mixed precision~ huang2024slim , lattice codebooks~ tseng2024quip , and dense-and-sparse quantization~ kim2023squeezellm . Ultra-low-bit VLA deployment requires allocating limited precision across matrices with different effects on action prediction. Our analysis reveals sensitivity differences even within the same layer, motivating matrix-wise allocation. The deployment cost also extends beyond average bitwidth: metadata and padding increase storage, while weight recovery requires computation and temporary buffers. Entropy-based weight compression supports memory-efficient deployment~ hao2024neuzip,zhang202670 , while recovered BF16 weights still require temporary buffers. To address these issues, we propose Action-Guided Quantization (AGQ). AGQ selects a bitwidth for each weight matrix based on action sensitivity and a measured estimate of weight recovery cost under storage constraints. Per-channel calibration reduces quantization error while keeping a uniform bitwidth within each matrix. Grouped lossless coding reduces weight storage, and block-wise recovery reduces temporary buffer requirements. As shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , AGQ achieves a better tradeoff between task success and target-weight compression than the baseline quantization method. In summary, we make the following contributions: We design Action-Guided Quantization (AGQ), a matrix-wise allocation method that combines an action-sensitivity prior from a common W4 probe with measured weight recovery cost under explicit storage budgets. We propose a calibration and execution pipeline that combines per-channel quantizer learning, grouped lossless coding, and block-wise recovery to reduce quantization error and resident and temporary weight storage. We evaluate AGQ in closed-loop tasks on LIBERO and measure its deployment performance on an RTX 3090. AGQ achieves 92.7 and 70.5 overall success at W3 and W2.5, respectively. An asymmetric W4-vision/W1.5-language configuration achieves 25.5 success with complete-model compression relative to BF16. Proposed Method sec:method Overview Fig.~ fig:framework separates preparation from compressed inference. Starting from a BF16 policy, calibration observations, and backbone storage budgets, stage (b) assigns matrix bitwidths using action sensitivity and execution overhead. Stage (c) fixes this allocation and learns channel quantizers through block reconstruction. Stage (d) encodes the resulting integer weights for deployment. During inference, encoded weights remain GPU-resident; decoding and fused unpacking/dequantization recover the active block's BF16 weights, which are released on exit. Allocation and parameter learning remain offline. Action-Guided Bit Allocation We assign one bitwidth per matrix to preserve regular decoding. A common W4 perturbation provides a lower-bit allocation prior, assuming some consistency in relative sensitivity across precisions. One probe per matrix replaces separate sensitivity scans at every candidate bitwidth, reducing preparation work without assuming identical rankings. For matrix , we quantize only that matrix to W4 and retain all other parameters in BF16. Its sensitivity is the same-input action deviation: Each vector contains six normalized components: three for position and three for rotation, excluding the gripper. With predicted actions, averages over all components and steps. Tasks and their trajectories receive equal weight, preventing longer trajectories from dominating. Same-input W4 timing provides a measured proxy for weight-recovery overhead. We normalize sensitivity and cost separately within each backbone: Here controls the overhead contribution. Under separate vision and language budgets, we solve where accounts for candidate-format storage, including metadata and padding, and is the backbone budget. The quadratic penalty implements a conservative allocation rule: matrices with greater action sensitivity or measured recovery overhead receive stronger protection from aggressive bitwidth reduction. W4 timing sets this priority; it does not predict latency at each candidate precision. Reported compression ratios use actual exported bytes. Per-Channel Calibration for Regular Execution Per-channel scale sets the quantization step, and integer zero point locates real zero. Sharing them limits metadata and preserves regular access during dequantization. We floor at a positive constant and round it to BF16 before computing . Weights and bitwidths remain fixed; W1 learns channel amplitudes with signs fixed. Frozen BF16 block outputs provide reconstruction targets~ li2021brecq : Here is the teacher input and comes from preceding quantized blocks. AdamW updates the clipping coefficients by backpropagation; the resulting channel bounds determine and , which regenerate quantized weights. Each configuration starts independently from BF16, with a larger calibration share for long-horizon tasks. Deployment uses these parameters in a GPU kernel that fuses unpacking and per-channel dequantization, followed by BF16 matrix multiplication. Bit-Dependent Grouped Coding and Execution Entropy coding further compresses quantized weights~ han2015deep . Our bit-dependent grouping balances codebook size and values recovered per symbol. Four adjacent W2 values or two W3/W4 values form a joint Huffman symbol~ huffman , while W1 retains raw packing. These six- or eight-bit symbols capture joint distributions with at most 256 symbols, recovering multiple values per decode operation. To reduce decoding dependencies~ sitaridi2016massively , we partition fixed-size coding blocks into independently decodable segments and use prefix lookup to reduce bit-by-bit traversal. Per-matrix encoding selects the smaller representation, including codebooks and block indexes, with raw packing as fallback. Scales and zero points remain unchanged, ensuring no additional quantization error from lossless decoding. Encoded weights and metadata remain GPU-resident. On block entry, decoding restores packed codes for fused unpacking/dequantization. Temporary BF16 weights for seven language or four vision matrices are released on block exit, reducing resident storage and bounding temporary dense weights by the largest active block. =10000 Evaluation sec:evaluation Experimental Setup Following ActQuant~ actquant , we evaluate OpenVLA-OFT on four LIBERO suites~ libero . Some weights are calibrated on A100; all evaluations use RTX3090. Ten configurations each run 600 closed-loop episodes (150 per suite), totaling 6,000. Metrics include overall and per-suite success, complete-model storage, peak GPU memory, and mean latency over ten fixed inputs. Each call predicts eight actions; timing excludes observation preprocessing and action postprocessing. title: MOON: Learning When to Forget and How to Move On in Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policies act on their visual history, and an incorrect action can take them off the instructed route. Paired interventions on four VLN policies show that clearing the history doubles pooled success at the onset of a deviation but lowers it on route, while later in a deviation, removing only the off-route frames helps much less. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed, which we call behavioral inertia. We propose MOON, a framework that equips a frozen VLN policy with two lightweight modules, adding less than 1% of its parameters. A deviation judge decides when to forget, raising an alarm that clears the history when it predicts that the agent is off route. A recovery policy, trained with GRPO from alarm states, learns how to move on, turning more of the successes found only by sampling into a single greedy rollout. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show that MOON reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and raises the success rate of its frozen base by 5.2 and 6.0 points, and an ablation with a random trigger indicates that this gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON. Together, these results suggest that deviation recovery depends on knowing when to forget, not only how to act. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/MOON.
full_text: Introduction Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions and reach a target location in a 3D environment using egocentric visual observations anderson2018vln,krantz2020vlnce . Recent VLN policies leverage pretrained vision-language models to predict navigation actions from the instruction, the current observation, and the visual history zhu2026navida,cheng2024navila,wei2025streamvln,zhang2024uninavid . Yet long-horizon navigation remains vulnerable to action errors. An incorrect action can take the agent off the instructed route, causing a deviation. Unless corrected promptly, the agent must continue from an off-route state, where later errors can compound into task failure ross2011reduction . Beyond avoiding deviations, reliable VLN thus requires correcting course and resuming the instructed route after a deviation, which we refer to as deviation recovery. Existing approaches to deviation recovery primarily improve the policy itself. They expose the policy to off-route states and teach it to return to the instructed route, either by continuing training on corrective trajectories from failed episodes yu2025correctnav,xin2026decovln or by reinforcement learning navgrpo2026 . These approaches improve overall success, but because they change the policy and evaluate it over complete episodes, which mix on-route and off-route states, they do not isolate the effect of retaining the visual history during recovery. Appendix~ app:related reviews related work, including detectors that hand control to a separate controller~ jeong2026navheads . Work on human memory suggests that retaining everything is not always useful: forgetting reduces the influence of outdated information on decisions in changing environments richards2017persistence , and people segment their experience into a new event when their predictions fail zacks2007event . In VLN, visual history may help before a deviation, when it records progress along the instructed route. Once the agent deviates, however, newly accumulated observations begin to describe an off-route trajectory that no longer corresponds to the instruction ke2019tactical . The policy must therefore learn to recover while still conditioning on a history increasingly shaped by its own mistakes. This history could provide useful context for retracing the route or reinforce the deviation. We ask: To answer this question, we run paired interventions in the Habitat simulator savva2019habitat on R2R-CE with four VLN policies (NaVIDA, NaVILA, StreamVLN and Uni-NaVid) that realize three kinds of visual memory, without modifying their parameters. Following prior work yu2025correctnav,xin2026decovln , a deviation occurs when the agent's distance from the reference route exceeds a threshold; from each deviation onset, we run the policy twice, once with its accumulated visual history and once with the history cleared, leaving only the instruction and the current frame. Clearing the history raises the success rate from 13.7 to 28.6 across 915 onset states from the four policies and lowers it from 76.0 to 48.3 on route; both effects hold for every policy. A natural explanation for the harm is that the accumulated off-route frames mislead the policy. We test this explanation at states ten or more steps after the deviation by retaining only the history up to the onset, which removes the later off-route frames while keeping the agent's on-route context. On these states, doing so raises the success rate only from 13.1 to 16.3 , well below the 26.3 that clearing reaches (Figure~ fig:teaser , left). The harm therefore does not come mainly from the off-route frames. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where the new state calls for a turn. We call this behavioral inertia. At the deviation onset, after a forward step, a shortest-path expert at the same pose continues without a turn in only 2 of states. The four policies continue without a turn through their next decision in 48 of states, and in 11 once their history is cleared. Further interventions on the visual content of a full-length retained history, shuffling it or swapping in one from another scene, lower the success rate on route but barely change it after a deviation. These findings are consistent with a known failure mode of policies trained on expert demonstrations. During training, features associated with expert histories reliably predict expert actions, leading the policy to depend on them. After the policy leaves the expert distribution, these associations may no longer hold, but the policy continues acting on them and compounds its errors dehaan2019causal,codevilla2019exploring,wen2020fighting,sobolmark2026bpp . We hypothesize that, in our setting, the history itself becomes such a feature through its presence and length more than its content: histories filled with current-frame copies or noise still cause most of the harm, and the harm grows with the retained length (Sections~ sec:analysis:history and~ sec:analysis:inertia ). Clearing the history reduces this inertia and doubles the recovery success rate. It does not reveal how to return to the route, however, and most deviations still end in failure. Yet among onset states where the retained greedy rollout fails, at least one of eight sampled rollouts after clearing succeeds in , against with the history retained (Section~ sec:analysis:recovery ), so there exist many recoveries that a single greedy rollout misses. Building on these insights, we propose (Figure~ fig:teaser , middle), whose two components answer, respectively, when to clear the visual history and how to make recovery succeed after clearing. Both are added to a frozen policy and together amount to less than 1 of its parameters. The first component, a deviation judge, clears the visual history when it predicts that the agent is off route, because clearing on route is harmful. The second component, a recovery policy, takes over after clearing. Because reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is effective at making behaviors that a policy can already sample more reliable yue2025does , we train it with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shao2024deepseekmath on cleared rollouts from alarm states. We evaluate on R2R-CE and RxR-CE (Figure~ fig:teaser , right). On R2R-CE it reaches the highest success rate among the compared methods, points above the next best, Qwen-RobotNav-4B~ qwenrobotnav , and it raises the success rate of its frozen base by points on R2R-CE and on RxR-CE. A random trigger with as many alarms lowers success below the base, so the gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, the same components improve zero-shot open-vocabulary object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON yokoyama2024hm3dovon . Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=3pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt] Analysis. On four frozen VLN policies, paired interventions show that the visual history is beneficial on route and harmful after a deviation, that removing the off-route frames recovers only a small part of this harm, that the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed (behavioral inertia), and that after clearing, sampling finds successes that a single greedy rollout misses (Section~ sec:analysis ). Method. We propose , two lightweight modules on a frozen policy: a deviation judge that learns when to clear the history and a recovery policy that learns how to recover (Section~ sec:method ). Experiments. reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and competitive results on RxR-CE; its gain depends on when the history is cleared, and without retraining it improves zero-shot object-goal navigation (Section~ sec:experiments ). Motivation and Analysis sec:analysis Preliminaries sec:analysis:prelim Problem Formulation. We study vision-and-language navigation in continuous 3D environments. title: HARP: Handoff-Aware Recovery Planning for Active Target Acquisition in Multi-UAV Handoff
summary: Continuous aerial tracking often requires multiple drones to maintain target coverage over long periods. During handoff, the receiving UAV may lack prior target observations and must actively acquire a usable view without disrupting the sender's ongoing coverage. This work introduces HARP, a handoff-aware recovery planner that registers bounded sender predictions in the receiver's local map, distinguishes field-of-view failure from physical occlusion, and generates failure-specific yaw, translation, and parallax viewpoints. Candidate motions are checked for receiver clearance, sender-fiducial observability, protected sender--target visibility, temporal validity, and deadline compliance. When a complete trajectory cannot be admitted, HARP may execute a sampled admissible nonzero prefix and replan from updated evidence. In simulation, HARP acquired the target in all 49 standard trials and in 15 of 16 stress trials. Field trials validated HARP's recovery geometry under field-of-view limitation and environmental occlusions.

During handoff, the receiving UAV may lack prior target observations and must actively acquire a usable view without disrupting the sender’s ongoing coverage. This work introduces HARP, a handoff-aware recovery planner that registers bounded sender predictions in the receiver’s local map, distinguishes field-of-view failure from physical occlusion, and generates failure-specific yaw, translation, and parallax viewpoints. Candidate motions are checked for receiver clearance, sender-fiducial observability, protected sender--target visibility, temporal validity, and deadline compliance. When a complete trajectory cannot be admitted, HARP may execute a sampled admissible nonzero prefix and replan from updated evidence. In simulation, HARP acquired the target in all 49 standard trials and in 15 of 16 stress trials. Field trials validated HARP's recovery geometry under field-of-view limitation and environmental occlusions. Introduction Persistent aerial target tracking requires maintaining a usable view as the target moves through the environment~ bhagat2020uav, feng2025deep,sun2024moving . For long duration monitoring, limited flight endurance creates an additional challenge~ brommer2018long,zhang2025distributed . Transferring tracking responsibility between UAVs provides a way to extend target observation beyond a single UAV's flight time~ kim2025continuous,leong2021intelligent . During this handoff, the current tracker can continue to observe the target while the receiver prepares to take over. However, the transfer cannot complete until obtains a usable view of the target from its own viewpoint. This creates a receiver-side acquisition failure. The target may lie outside 's Field of View (FoV) or may be physically occluded by the environment, even though continues to track it successfully. In such cases, the sender's target track remains available, but the handoff is stalled because cannot establish the observation required for transfer. Active receiver side visibility recovery can provide the observation needed for handoff while continues tracking the target. Fig.~ fig:rep illustrates this asymmetric handoff condition in a representative physical setup, where continues tracking the target while the target is occluded from 's view point. This problem differs from conventional visibility-aware aerial tracking. Existing planners maintain visibility of an observed or predicted target while accounting for FoV limits, occlusion, collision avoidance, and target motion~ jeon2019online,wang2021visibility,jeon2020integrated,lee2025qpchaser,hu2025improved . Recent methods further incorporate active viewpoint adjustment and uncertainty-aware visibility reasoning~ wang2023svpto,gao2024probabilistic , while interception planners evaluate dynamically feasible motion against predicted target arrival times~ ryou2026Real . Eva-Tracker addresses reacquisition after temporary visibility loss using the tracking UAV's previous observations~ lin2026evatracker , while ASPIRe plans informative search trajectories over a maintained target belief when the target is not currently observed~ zhou2024aspire . Multi-UAV planners coordinate agents to preserve visibility and avoid inter-agent interference~ lee2025dmvc,yin2026visibility . Perception-side approaches instead address occlusion through robust visual representations and redetection~ wu2025learning,xue2024handling . Most closely related, Rao et al.~ rao2025multi use shared teammate visual information for collaborative tracking under occlusion. In the handoff setting considered here, however, the receiver has not yet observed the target in the current episode and therefore has no local target history on which to base its recovery. It must instead plan its first acquisition using information supplied by the sender, which continues to track the target throughout the handoff interval. This creates an asymmetric planning problem: one UAV retains a valid target track, whereas the receiver must actively obtain its first observation without disrupting the sender's continuing coverage. To our knowledge, existing aerial visibility aware tracking, target reacquisition, and multi UAV tracking methods do not directly address this sender-guided first acquisition regime, in which the receiver has no local target observation history and must recover a usable view from time bounded information supplied by the sender. We address this problem with HARP, an active visibility recovery framework for visual target handoff between two UAVs. The sender periodically provides a bounded target motion model, which registers into its persistent local map frame and evaluates at candidate arrival times. HARP distinguishes FoV failure from mapped physical occlusion. For FoV recovery, it first searches yaw at the current position and considers translation when no yaw-only endpoint satisfies the configured requirements. For physical occlusion, it uses target--blocker parallax geometry to propose recovery viewpoints. Candidate trajectories undergo sampled checks for receiver clearance, sender-fiducial observability, and interference with the sender--target view, together with motion limits, model validity, and the acquisition deadline. New sender information and local depth observations support revalidation and replanning from the receiver's current state. Actual acquisition is confirmed by a held sequence of fresh receiver detections. The main contributions of this work are: A motion-planning formulation for sender-guided first acquisition, enabling a receiver UAV with no prior target observations to acquire the target using information from the sending UAV. HARP generates recovery viewpoints for field-of-view and occlusion failures, checks handoff constraints under target uncertainty, and executes sampled-admissible trajectory prefixes when the complete motion artifact cannot be admitted. Validation of HARP through closed-loop simulations, controlled replays, and field trials, demonstrating HARP's recovery behavior under simulated and sensing conditions.
