title: EXE: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Pretraining via Factorized Latent Actions for VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation in a single architecture, enabling robots to follow open-ended instructions across diverse manipulation tasks~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,octo2024 . Their success, however, is tightly coupled to the scale of robot demonstration data. Curating large manipulation datasets requires physical teleoperation or scripted policies on real hardware, a process that is expensive, slow, and inherently limited in scene and task diversity~ openxembodiment2024 . This data bottleneck restricts VLA generalization and has motivated a search for alternative, scalable supervision sources. Egocentric human videos offer a compelling alternative. Datasets such as Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d , Epic-Kitchens~ damen2022epickitchens , EgoDex~ hoque2026egodex , VITRA-1M~ li2025scalable , and EgoLive~ li2026egolive,zhang2026joyai capture thousands of hours of first-person hand manipulation with rich task semantics, diverse objects, and natural language annotations. Because these videos share the egocentric perspective of a robot's wrist or head camera, they natively encode manipulation intent. Several works exploit this connection: GR-1~ wu2024gr1 and GR-2~ cheang2025gr2 pretrain video-generation backbones on human video before fine-tuning for robot control, and HPT~ wang2024hpt maps heterogeneous embodiment streams through a shared transformer trunk. Yet these approaches consume visual features only and do not attempt to transfer the action information embedded in human hand motions. The open question is how to convert action-level knowledge in egocentric video into a form that a VLA can absorb during pretraining and later translate into executable robot actions. From the perspective of action execution, humans and robots share analogous manipulation primitives such as reaching, grasping, and placing, yet realize them with distinct kinematics---human hands parameterized by MANO finger joints~ romero2017mano versus robot end-effector poses with gripper or dexterous-hand configurations---making direct alignment across the two action spaces difficult. Two strategies have been tried to bridge this gap, each with a fundamental limitation. The first, exemplified by UniT~ chen2026unit , forces the entire action into a single shared codebook, so the shared codes inevitably absorb embodiment-specific geometry that obscures the transferable task semantics. The second, exemplified by LAPA~ ye2025lapa , learns latent actions from visual frame transitions, but raw observations entangle the action signal with task-irrelevant content such as background and lighting---leading CLAP~ zhang2026clap to note that such latent actions encode visual noise rather than manipulation skill. These limitations reveal two questions at the heart of cross-embodiment transfer: which parts of an action are worth sharing, and how shared actions should be aligned across embodiments. Our work starts from two observations that address them respectively. Observation~1: Certain dimensions of the action transfer better across embodiments, while others are inherently difficult to transfer. Specifically, the 3D position of the wrist (for humans) or end-effector (for robots) encodes spatial task intent---reaching, trajectory following, target approaching, which is shared across embodiments regardless of kinematic structure. Finger joint configurations and gripper geometry, by contrast, are embodiment-specific and do not generalize across domains. This motivates our feature-group routing design: rather than unifying the entire action, which inevitably introduces noise, we factorize it into a shareable positional subspace that captures cross-embodiment task semantics and an embodiment-specific kinematic subspace kept private to each domain. Observation~2: Given a shared positional subspace, the next question is how to align representations across embodiments within it. Actions should not only be aligned when their spatial trajectories are similar, but also when they carry the same task semantics despite dissimilar trajectories. A contrastive objective such as InfoNCE~ oord2018representation naturally handles the first case: it pulls together cross-domain samples with similar spatial trajectories and pushes apart those with dissimilar ones. However, spatial similarity does not imply semantic equivalence---actions that share the same task semantics may still follow substantially different trajectories, and InfoNCE would wrongly drive such pairs apart. For example, a human grasping a cup from above with five fingers and a robot clamping the same cup from the side with a parallel gripper both execute ``grasp the cup,'' yet their spatial trajectories differ substantially. These are exactly the pairs a cross-embodiment representation should unite. This motivates our language-guided relational distillation: language provides an external semantic signal invariant to embodiment geometry, supplying pairwise similarity as a soft target to align semantically equivalent but spatially dissimilar actions in the shared space, complementing the contrastive spatial alignment. We present EXE, Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment Pretraining via Factorized Latent Actions, a framework that turns these observations into a practical VLA pretraining pipeline. EXE introduces three components: A feature group-routed action tokenizer that factorizes each action into a shareable positional subspace (3D wrist/end-effector position) and an embodiment-specific kinematic subspace (finger joints or gripper). The shareable subspace is quantized through a shared codebook trained jointly on human and robot data, while each domain maintains its own codebook for embodiment-specific features. This isolates transferable task semantics from domain-specific geometry within a single quantization framework. A dual cross-domain alignment scheme for the shared codebook that combines contrastive learning with language-guided relational distillation. Contrastive learning pulls together cross-domain actions with similar spatial trajectories, while frozen language embeddings~ zhang2025qwen3 supply pairwise semantic similarity as a soft target to further align semantically equivalent yet spatially dissimilar actions, which contrastive learning alone would drive apart. A three-stage pipeline: (1)~training the factorized tokenizer on combined human and robot action data to establish shared and private codebooks; (2)~training the VLM models with variable egocentric human video and robot data, supervising the action head with discrete tokens from the shared vocabulary so that the model absorbs cross-embodiment manipulation knowledge; (3)~fine-tuning on downstream robot tasks, where pretrained knowledge transfers directly through the shared action codes. Since the shared knowledge can be constructed across embodiments with different kinematic structures, EXE benefits both gripper (RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 ) and dexterous-hand (RoboCasa GR1~ nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation ), as well as real-world tasks, consistently improving success rates over baselines without pretraining. Ablation studies confirm that feature-group factorization and language-guided alignment each contribute independently. Related Work Egocentric human video Egocentric video captures manipulation from the operator's own viewpoint, providing first-person hand--object interactions at a scale and diversity unreachable by robot teleoperation. Large-scale datasets~ grauman2022ego4d,grauman2024ego,damen2022epickitchens,goyal2017something,buildaiegocentric10k2025,hoque2026egodex, cai2026barbiegait accumulate thousands of hours of daily activities with dense annotations spanning ego/exo views, action labels, and hand-pose tracking, driving progress in action recognition, hand--object interaction, and affordance learning. Notably, the egocentric viewpoint aligns naturally with a robot's wrist or head camera and inherently encodes manipulation intent, making it an increasingly attractive supervision source for robot learning. Egocentric video for VLA pretraining A growing line of work pretrains VLA models on egocentric human video before robot fine-tuning. The key distinction among methods lies in how human motion is converted into a robot-executable action signal. Explicit approaches recover 3D poses and map them to robot actions via kinematic retargeting or inverse kinematics~ yang2025egovla,mu2026deximit,zheng2026egoscale,zhang2026unidex,zhong2026egosteer,zou2026activeglasses,punamiya2026egoverse, chen2026egohumanoid, allshire2025visual, cai2024disentangled, weng2025hdmi,cai2025fastddhpose,lang2025beyond . They require accurate pose estimation and hand-designed embodiment mappings. Implicit approaches bypass pose recovery and instead learn a shared representation that bridges human and robot domains. Representative strategies include using human video as a large-scale VLM pretraining corpus~ li2025scalable,lin2025physbrain,fu2025metis , building unified human--robot token spaces through cross-modal reconstruction~ chen2026unit,li2026ace,wang2026mmgait,yin2026mivla , and deriving latent-action vocabularies from video~ ye2025lapa,zhang2026clap,xu2026motion . However, these methods either share the full action in a single space or entangle it with visual information. The kinematic discrepancy between embodiments and the task-irrelevant noise in raw visual signals both obscure the shared manipulation intent, limiting transferable knowledge extraction. EXE addresses this by factorizing the action into a cross-embodiment positional subspace and an embodiment-specific complement, aligning only the former with an explicit language signal. This avoids pose retargeting and paired demonstrations while preventing domain-specific geometry from contaminating the shared representation. Method EXE transfers manipulation knowledge from egocentric human video to robot control through three stages (Figure~ fig:framework ). Stage~1 trains a factorized action tokenizer ( sec:tokenizer ) that splits each action into a shareable positional subspace and an embodiment-specific kinematic subspace, quantized by separate codebooks, so that motions with the same semantics from different embodiments map to the same shared code. title: Gaussian Episodic Memory for Long-Term Spatiotemporal Reasoning
summary: Real-world environments undergo continual semi-static changes, requiring a memory representation that captures both the spatial and temporal evolution of a scene. Existing spatio-temporal memories for robots typically rely either on structured representations, which are limited to the entities and attributes captured during construction, or on image-based memories, which are constrained to previously observed viewpoints. We introduce GEMS, a framework that combines a persistent spatio-temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) map with an agentic reasoning pipeline. The 3DGS map is reconstructed once and subsequently updated only in regions where the scene changes, storing only these modifications while preserving visual detail across time. The agentic pipeline leverages this map to render novel views on demand, iteratively accumulating evidence to answer spatio-temporal questions and ground objects from natural-language queries. To advance future research, we introduce GEMS-Bench, a spatiotemporal question-answering benchmark focused on semi-static environments. It comprises 3 real-world and 12 synthetic environments, spanning 473 question-answer pairs. We evaluate GEMS on novel-view synthesis quality across scene updates, 3D object grounding, spatiotemporal question answering, and storage efficiency. GEMS outperforms recent baselines in 3D object grounding and spatiotemporal question answering, while achieving rendering quality on par with dedicated scene-update methods. Code and data: https://abwerby.github.io/GEMS/

Introduction sec:introduction Robots operating for long periods in human-centered environments must model not only the geometry and semantics of their surroundings but also how those surroundings evolve over time. Real-world environments, such as homes and offices, experience frequent semi-static changes in which objects are moved, furniture is rearranged, and equipment may appear, disappear, or change state. Modeling these changes and building episodic memory that captures when and where they occurred enables robots to reason about the environment's history and answer spatial, semantic, and temporal questions, such as where an object was previously located, when a change occurred, or how the current state of a scene differs from an earlier one. 3D scene graphs (3DSGs)~ rotondi2026survey,werby2024hierarchical,werby2025keysg have emerged as compact, structured representations that organize spatial-semantic concepts. However, typical 3DSGs represent a single snapshot of the environment. More recent 3DSG approaches incorporate temporal information into scene representations to model semi-static changes~ schmid2024khronos,behrens2025lost,saxena2025grapheqa,gorlo2026describe . However, they either preserve only object-level states and textual descriptions, precommitting to objects segmented at construction time, or preserve observations only from fixed viewpoints, limiting access to the underlying visual evidence. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d has emerged as a high-fidelity representation that preserves fine-grained visual details, supports novel-view synthesis, and enables localized updates~ galappaththige2026changes,yugay2026gaussian , making it well suited for long-term embodied reasoning. Existing 3DGS-based mapping and reasoning methods, however, either address static scenes~ lu2026gsmem,yu2026splatreasoner or maintain only the latest scene state~ fu2025gs . To this end, we present , a persistent spatiotemporal episodic memory based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), coupled with an agentic reasoning pipeline. construct an initial 3DGS map, then detect changes from observations collected during each subsequent scene revisit and locally update the Gaussian primitives in affected regions. Unchanged Gaussians are shared across temporal states, while additions, removals, and modifications are stored as temporal deltas. As a result, storage grows with environmental changes rather than the number of revisits. Given a query, the agentic pipeline can select informative viewpoints for reconstructed regions rather than being restricted to a fixed set of viewpoints. The 3DGS-based memory enables the agent to render the map from a consistent virtual camera pose across different timesteps. This controlled alignment supports cross-temporal visual comparison and reasoning about object motion and state changes. Moreover, photorealistic novel-view rendering enables the agent to perform on-demand segmentation of target objects from informative, query-dependent viewpoints. To foster future research, we introduce , a multi-revisit spatiotemporal embodied question-answering benchmark. It comprises 12 synthetic household scenes and 3 real-world scenes, each with at least 3 revisits. spans 473 question-answer pairs categorized into 5 types, as well as posed RGB-D for each revisit. In summary, we make the following contributions: We introduce , a 3DGS-based episodic memory framework that maintains long-term scene history via efficient, localized updates, enabling high-fidelity novel-view rendering over time. We develop an agentic EQA pipeline that utilizes spatiotemporal novel-view synthesis for query-dependent viewpoint selection, visual alignment across time, and on-demand object grounding. We introduce a new multi-visit spatiotemporal question-answering benchmark, , comprising semi-static environmental changes across 15 scenes and 473 question-answer pairs. We evaluate across four dimensions: novel-view synthesis quality under scene updates, 3D object grounding from natural-language queries, spatiotemporal question answering, and storage requirements. Code and benchmark will be released upon acceptance. Subsequent works~ mccormac2017semanticfusion, huang2023visual augmented such 3D geometric maps with semantic and open-vocabulary language features, enabling object retrieval and language-guided navigation. Structured representations, such as 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs)~ armeni20193d, hughes2022hydra, gu2024conceptgraphs, werby2024hierarchical, werby2025keysg, linok2025beyondbarequeries , have emerged as more efficient representations that encode both geometric and semantic information in a topological graph; however, they only maintain a single snapshot of the scene state. To extend robotics maps to also capture the temporal aspect of the environment, Khronos~ schmid2024khronos performs spatio-temporal metric-semantic SLAM that jointly captures short-term dynamics and long-term changes and can be queried for the estimated scene state at any past timestamp. However, its metric-semantic map does not preserve photorealistic appearance, so visual evidence beyond that abstraction cannot be re-examined. Other methods maintain a persistent object- or point-level representation and revise it as the scene changes~ yan2025dynamic, liu2025dynamem , whereas~ behrens2025lost, gorlo2026describe additionally retain temporal traces in the form of object trajectories and timestamped descriptions, respectively. The former keep only the current state and therefore cannot answer questions about earlier configurations, while all of them precommit to the objects and attributes instantiated at construction time and discard the underlying visual details. 3DGS-based Maps 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d is an explicit representation for 3D scene reconstruction that enables photorealistic rendering while preserving fine-grained visual details. Because it stores explicit primitives, 3DGS also supports cheap local updates, unlike implicit representations such as NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf . Recent extensions~ yu2024language further enrich the Gaussian primitives with high-dimensional semantic attributes for semantic tasks. For long-term scene updates, O-SCD~ galappaththige2026changes localizes changes by directly comparing new observations against views rendered from the previous map, and others~ ackermann2025cl, yugay2026gaussian further show the gain in time and storage from updating only the changed area. A third line of work uses 3DGS as the map representation for embodied reasoning. SplatReasoner~ yu2026splatreasoner synthesizes query-conditioned viewpoints that reveal evidence missing from fixed-view memories, and GSMem~ lu2026gsmem renders informative viewpoints on demand for exploration; both reason over a single static capture. GS-LTS~ fu2025gs instead keeps the map current across revisits, yet stores only the latest state and discards the scene's history. renders query-conditioned views over a memory spanning visits, so the agent can hold a viewpoint fixed while varying the time. Embodied Question Answering and Episodic Memory Introduced by OpenEQA~ majumdar2024openeqa , Episodic Memory EQA (EM-EQA) evaluates an agent's capability to answer questions based on past multimodal experiences. In this task, a key requirement for the agent is to correctly retrieve historical contexts during querying. ReMEmbR~ anwar2025remembr retrieves by embedding similarity over textual descriptions of video segments, and so discards the visual and geometric evidence entirely; DAAAM~ gorlo2026describe retrieves by matching per-node descriptions, GraphEQA~ saxena2025grapheqa by traversing a semantic scene graph, and STaR~ yuan2026star by task-conditioned retrieval over saved keyframes, textual descriptions, and object point clouds. In all cases the information granularity is fixed when the memory is built. 3D-Mem~ yang20253d and Enter the Mind Palace~ ginting2025enter retain raw images, are constrained to pre-recorded views, and segment objects in advance, which makes queries about off-list objects unanswerable. Our method runs object segmentation only upon receiving a query, which makes it easy to adjust object granularity without being fixed to predefined lists, utilizing the photorealistic novel view synthesis capabilities of 3DGS. Beyond memory representations, existing works also diverge in their evaluation benchmarks. EM-EQA benchmarks~ majumdar2024openeqa predominantly assume single-session explorations of static scenes, overlooking temporal evolution entirely. Other temporal benchmarks, such as NaVQA~ anwar2025remembr , assess reasoning over continuous navigation videos, focusing on when and where an event was observed along a continuous trajectory rather than how the environment altered between visits. While recent efforts begin to investigate dynamic environments, Situat3DChange~ liu2026situat3dchange is confined to change understanding between paired static 3D point scans, whereas Enter the Mind Palace~ ginting2025enter focuses on multi-episode navigation in simulated settings with limited scene scale and question diversity. title: RoboJev: An Open Vision-Language Judge for Robot Success Detection
summary: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro An important ingredient for review queues, learned terminal rewards, or aggregate evaluation is knowing which episodes succeeded. Such labels are often not machine readable and cannot be easily derived from low-level heuristics (e.g. trajectory length, data origin, or smoothness). We therefore fine-tune an episode judge from JEV-27B-VL jev_model,robojev_model into RoboJev, an open-weight success detector for robot manipulation videos. Given a task instruction, ten evenly spaced frames from the primary camera, and the final frame from any auxiliary cameras, RoboJev outputs a calibrated success probability. Rather than building a different classifier for every task and environment, RoboJev can be used in a plug-and-play fashion. Rather than generating an explanation, RoboJev scores true / false tokens at a designated position. RoboJev is reusable across tasks and environments thanks to its well-defined inputs, consistent prompting protocol, and verifiable error logs. We test RoboJev on held-out SO-101 rollouts, on lab/robot domains not included in the robot-specific fine-tuning, and on community videos that have clear labels. Community videos with ambiguous labels can still be inspected, but are not used for binary metrics. While the SO-101 split contains rollouts from the same physical environment as some of the training data, we leave out two entire tasks, as well as individual recording sessions. On this split, RoboJev-27B achieves 95.2 balanced accuracy. On the unseen-domain data, it achieves 0.890 AUROC, just under the 0.900 AUROC of the unadapted JEV-27B-VL run with the same input protocol. Alongside our released predictions, protocols, and a pinned checkpoint, this indicates that RoboJev is a useful and inspectable tool for policy evaluation, rather than indicating that fine-tuning yields generalizable improvements. Related work sec:related SuccessVQA formulates robot outcomes as visual questions and measures how well the model generalizes to unseen instructions and environments successvqa . RoboCLIP produces trajectory rewards from a text instruction or video demonstration via a frozen representation roboclip . Video-Language Critic trains a transferable reward signal from a dataset of observations using contrastive loss and temporal-ranking loss videolanguagecritic . RoboJev uses a supervised label of success/failure for each trajectory and reports a detector that has been publicly released but does not evaluate its use in downstream policy learning. RoboReward trains general reward models using various robot data, counterfactual instructions, and temporal clips roboreward . Robometer employs frame-progress loss, trajectory preference supervision, and releases the RBM-1M dataset robometer . Both of these objectives and methods are different from a terminal two-token prediction. Here, we evaluate Robometer-4B using its full video version. We do use the converted data of RoboReward during our training process, but we do not evaluate its model as a direct baseline. ViFailback includes failure trajectories that were originally collected for diagnosis and later correction vifailback . We source data from Open X-Embodiment oxe and DROID droid , which include demonstration data for diverse tasks and embodiments. Datasets from the community are accessed through the shared format and collection of tools offered by LeRobot lerobot . While these datasets allow us to access demonstrations from different embodiments and performing different tasks, they have different viewpoints, success/failure labels, and sources. In Appendix app:data , we clearly identify the processed datasets we use in our work, separately from the original datasets. Our model is based on a pre-trained vision-language model, with low-rank adaptation of the language model component, and a frozen pre-trained vision encoder. We do not propose a novel architecture for vision-language models, but instead leverage off-the-shelf components to build our system. In addition to architectural choices, we use a KL penalty towards the initial model for some data sources, and temperature scaling. Our contributions are an open-weight judge, the full training and inference recipe, and an evaluation artifact describing the trade-offs between specialization, use of visual evidence, and deployment cost. A task-conditioned episode judge sec:method Input and decision readout Let be a task instruction, and a video captured by the primary camera. Our release samples evenly spaced frames from the beginning to the end of the attempt, and includes the last image from each available auxiliary camera. The prompt specifies the task instruction, chronological order, and all other available views. Success requires completing the instruction by the end of the attempt; a dropped object, incorrect placement, unfinished attempt, or wrong task is negative. The vision-language model then consumes all this information in one pass, generating the logits at the answer location for the tokens false and true. We employ the following calibrated readout where the release preserves the token IDs, additive biases , and the temperature in decision.json. In the release, we set . This output provides a measure of the likelihood that the task was successfully completed at the end of the episode; it is not a continuous quantity reflecting the progress made by the agent toward completion of the task, nor does it describe the result in natural language. Training data Our model is fit on 52,598 episodes. The data used to fit our model is a mixture of policy failures (from real robots), demonstrations, and simulation interaction data. Specifically, there are 28,170 episodes from RBM-1M sources, 1,388 episodes from ArmnetBench, 10,216 teacher labelled community episodes, 3,718 community demonstration episodes, 4,962 episodes from ViFailback, and 4,144 successful episodes from DROID. These are the number of records used for fitting after the train/valid/test split, and do not necessarily correspond to the number of records in each dataset before the split. We do not claim that these counts are independently de-duplicated. We hold out entire validation datasets, and hold out community data from users that we evaluate on from our training mix. We leave a description of the exact composition of our training set in Appendix app:data . There is a small number of records that do not match up with the number returned by the community loader, the cause of which we could not determine. In total, the community loader reports 11,415 records were accepted, although a subset of these are discarded during validation. We start with annotations that have high-confidence agreement between GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol (probability or ) on the four primary-camera frames. If a Claude Opus 5.5 annotation exists, we discard all annotations it disagrees with on the binary outcome. We then average over all teacher-model annotations to obtain a soft target and discard any examples where the mean is not or . This process yields a consensus annotation file with 11,387 unique targets. After removing validation examples and those involving held-out robots, 10,216 examples remain for training. To avoid information leakage between training and test labels, we also discard training examples from all 106 owners that appear in the human-labeled community check. The student model still depends on teacher models, which we also use as baselines. We employ inverse-frequency class balancing for the success/failure examples for each source, clamping weights to , and if a source contains only one type of example, we assign weight 1. For data augmentation we use truncated positive episodes and episodes with mismatched instructions as heuristic negatives. This may introduce label noise because a truncated episode might fulfill a shorter instruction. We also resize, recompress using JPEG, and perturb the colour of images. Eligible episodes with ten-frame evidence use the ten-frame protocol with probability 0.6. The other branches of augmentation preserve the four-frame and final-view examples. In total, we obtain 102,172 training examples in the epoch through data augmentation and repetition. Adaptation and calibration We start with JEV-27B-VL, merging in the decision adapter weights before doing any robot-specific adaptation. To adapt LM, we freeze the vision encoder and visual merger, and train LM with rank-32 LoRA lora using a learning rate of for one epoch. Denote and the two-way softmax outputs of the adapted and original models (before fitted temperature scaling), respectively. Our per-example objective is The source-specific balancing factor only affects the cross-entropy term, the target distribution of the KL term is still the output distribution of the starting model. For , we assign an example weight for each training example: (i) for synthetic negative examples we use a fixed value ; (ii) for the original examples, we use source-balanced weights. We apply the anchoring method ( , ) for training with the RBM/research sources (ViFailback and DROID), but not for community-sourced records or ArmnetBench. We perform both adapter scaling and calibration on held-out validation sources. Motivated by weight-interpolation wiseft , we evaluate the set of scales on validation data, and select the nonzero scale that gives the highest held-out community AUROC score, while also staying no more than 0.005 AUROC below the base model on each specified validation source. These sources are AutoEval, FINO-Net, the RoboArena 0825 validation split, and the community Koch robots. All of the nonzero DA scales pass this constraint, and scale 1 has the highest community validation AUROC. In this work, AutoEval and FINO-Net are used only for validation; a different split of RoboArena provides training data. For temperature scaling temperature , we minimize the negative log-likelihood on validation data for the final-view, four-frame, and ten-frame protocols. Note that multiple protocols can be run on the same episode. It is also worth noting that our published test sets were inspected while creating the released models, so they are not a fully one-shot blind test. Evaluation protocol sec:eval Three complementary test settings There are 927 labelled episodes in the evaluation artifact robojev_evals , of which 862 yield a binary success or failure and thus contribute to our reported metrics. The remaining 65 episodes correspond to community videos for which the success or failure is ambiguous. These sets are summarized in Table tab:splits . SO-101. ArmnetBench armnetbench contains policy rollouts of 8 tasks and 7 policies. Training and testing recordings are split by session. The tasks cable unclip and ring insert do not appear in the robot-specific training set at all, and they account for 40 test episodes each. We also report results on the reduced set of held-out tasks, as well as on all 268 test runs, but our overall score is not on entirely unseen tasks. Unseen lab/robot domains. The RBM-1M OOD set rbm_ood consists of rollouts from domains not present in the robot-specific training set. There are 8 different OOD domains with a total of 459 rollouts. These domains are identified by a combination of the institution, robot (Franka, Koch, Trossen, xArm, SO-101), camera perspective and/or scene condition. The domain sizes range from 16 to 218 rollouts. Community videos. The episodes here are from public LeRobot evaluation datasets. One individual labeled each of the 200 episodes, one per dataset. We provide metrics for the 135 episodes with a definite success or failure, and leave the other 65 ambiguous in the artifact. The evaluation is on outcomes visible to human viewers in community videos; we did not evaluate inter-annotator agreement. title: POD-RoPE: Rotary Position Encoding over Physical Observation Distributions for Embodied AI
summary: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of $1.91\times$ over P-RoPE and $5.34\times$ over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.

Introduction sec:intro Perception and interaction in the physical world require embodied systems to establish physically meaningful spatial and temporal relationships between observations. Standard RoPE~ su2021roformer , however, typically defines relative positions using sequence indices or spatiotemporal grid coordinates: identical pixel offsets can correspond to different viewing angles, and identical frame-index offsets can represent different elapsed times. Positional encoding therefore needs to extend beyond discrete index differences to represent observation geometry and actual spatial and temporal scales. Geometric positional encodings such as P-RoPE and RayRoPE incorporate camera and ray information into relative relationship modeling~ li2025cameras,wu2026rayrope , but incur substantially higher latency than Standard RoPE in our model-block benchmarks. Meanwhile, an image token aggregates information over a pixel region, and a temporally compressed video token combines observations from multiple times. A single center address cannot fully describe these observation footprints. Our central view is that positional encoding should represent not only where and when a token is observed, but also the spatial and temporal extent of its observations. We investigate how to encode these physical observation distributions and their relative relationships at low computational overhead. We propose , which maps camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times into a shared physical address space and represents each token's observation footprint as an address distribution. Averaging address-dependent rotations yields a token-level positional operator; under independent sampling, the pairwise Q/K operator equals the expected rotation over the relative-address distribution (Eq.~ ). When each distribution concentrates at a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE at the corresponding addresses. The full method reuses these statistics for V/O transformations, allowing geometry to guide both matching and aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids extra tokens and pairwise processing of observation nodes, limiting computational overhead. We evaluate across four robot policy architectures, three visual-geometry tasks, and two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, full integration into Fast-WAM raises mean success from 91.83 to 92.88 ; on Sharpa North, it raises mean success from 32.5 to 52.5 . Visual-geometry experiments show task-dependent gains, and controlled ablations isolate the two design components. In H20 microbenchmarks, the full method achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of over P-RoPE and over RayRoPE, with 17.4 median overhead over Standard RoPE. Our contributions are: 2pt 0pt 4pt Physical observation distribution encoding. We represent token footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Expected rotations encode relative-address interactions and recover pointwise RoPE for singleton distributions. Efficient matching and aggregation. Per-token rotation statistics are shared by Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, avoiding additional tokens and pairwise observation-node processing. Cross-domain validation. Tests across four robot policy architectures and three visual-geometry tasks show improved aggregate manipulation success and task-dependent geometry gains. Ablations support both components; model-block benchmarks show lower latency than P-RoPE and RayRoPE. Related Work Rotary positional encoding and geometry-aware attention. RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to queries and keys so that positional interactions in attention depend on their relative displacement~ su2021roformer . For multi-view vision, GTA applies group transformations associated with camera geometry to attention matching and value-feature aggregation~ miyato2024gta . P-RoPE (denoted PRoPE in the original paper) further unifies intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters through projective transformations, incorporating complete view-frustum relationships into relative positional representations~ li2025cameras . RayRoPE constructs projective ray coordinates in the query-camera frame and predicts depth and its uncertainty. It uses expected RoPE to encode position distributions along rays and applies the transformations to Q/K/V/O~ wu2026rayrope . addresses the observation footprints induced by tokenization. It jointly encodes camera centers, unit viewing directions, and actual time in a shared reference frame, averaging over the address distributions covered by pixels and source frames. Rotation statistics can be pre-aggregated per token and reused across attention interactions. The full method further uses rotation coherence to modulate V/O content transformations with an identity branch. Observation footprints and spatiotemporal positional representations. Extending positional encoding from points to regions allows representations to retain observation scale. Mip-NeRF approximates conical frustums with Gaussian distributions and averages sinusoidal positional features to obtain scale-aware integrated positional encoding~ barron2021mipnerf . RayRoPE applies expected rotations to uncertainty intervals of predicted depth~ wu2026rayrope . Meanwhile, DiT performs diffusion modeling on image-latent patches~ peebles2023dit , and Wan compresses spatial and temporal dimensions through a causal video autoencoder~ wan2025 , so one visual token corresponds to multiple pixels and potentially multiple source frames. We map these nominal footprints into physical observation distributions, using camera calibration and timestamps to determine their addresses and the phase and magnitude of average rotations to retain the observation composition. This applies regional integration to relative matching and content aggregation between compressed visual tokens, with one construction shared by static multi-view and video observations. Vision-action policies and world-action models. ACT predicts action chunks~ zhao2023act , RDT uses a multimodal diffusion Transformer~ liu2024rdt , and combines a pretrained vision-language model with flow-matching action generation~ black2024pi0 . Fast-WAM jointly models video and actions during training but omits explicit future-video generation at inference~ yuan2026fastwam . We study observation geometry and footprints as positional inputs across these policy architectures; Section~ sec:embodied_control specifies their integrations. We evaluate manipulation on RoboTwin 2.0~ mu2024robotwin,chen2025robotwin2 and Sharpa North, and reconstruction using RoboTwin, AgiBot World~ bu2025agibot , and collected Sharpa North observations. Complementary geometry tasks use UniMatch~ xu2023unimatch with the DeMoN depth protocol~ ummenhofer2017demon , and LVSM~ jin2025lvsm for novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K~ zhou2018stereo . title: RoboReason: Boosting Robotics-Relevant VLM Reasoning Through Scalable Data Generation
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.

Introduction Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been adapted for diverse roles in robot manipulation pipelines as their capabilities have increased, serving as task planner components~ yang2025guiding , reward models~ rocamonde2023vision , action annotators~ hancock2025actions , and code policy generators~ liang2022code . Effectively performing these tasks requires sophisticated reasoning over large collections of images. Consider using a VLM to predict task progress based on recent observations; the VLM must be able to reason about spatial relationships between objects both within a frame and across frames---e.g., to measure whether the gripper moved closer to a target object to be grasped. Correspondence to co-first author: sanupam<at>engineering.upenn.edu. Equal authorship is indicated with while indicates equal advising. Code and data available at . As a consequence, there is an urgent need to study and improve the fundamental capabilities of VLMs at spatiotemporal reasoning. While there has been significant recent interest in this problem~ wang2025spatial457 , much of it focuses on general settings that do not capture the specific challenges that arise in robotics settings: (1) cluttered scenes from robot-centric viewpoints, (2) reasoning about object relationships across time, and (3) integrating information across multiple viewpoints. We first conduct a systematic evaluation of multiple large VLMs on realistic spatiotemporal ordering tasks under a variety of settings, like having access to computer vision model outputs or having structured test-time compute. Our ordering problems are constructed from robot demonstration videos in the DROID dataset khazatsky2024droid (examples in Figure fig:example_tasks ). Our results indicate that leading VLMs underperform on our dataset of real-world robotics images when compared to previously reported results. To address this performance gap, we present RoboReason, a scalable data generation pipeline for generating spatiotemporal reasoning training data from robot manipulation trajectories. We train much smaller models on a small amount (700 samples) of pipeline-generated data using Supervised Finetuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shao2024deepseekmath and show that model performance increases significantly, even matching the performance of much larger models on some tasks. We also train small models on larger pipeline-generated training datasets of 8.8K samples and find that model performance also improves on downstream spatial and robotics reasoning tasks, demonstrating the potential for our approach to improve the efficacy of VLMs targeting robotics tasks. Our main findings are as follows: [leftmargin=*] VLMs that perform well on existing spatial reasoning benchmarks struggle on multi-object ordering tasks in real-world robot manipulation images. We evaluate state-of-the-art embodied reasoning VLMs like Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5, GPT-5, and Qwen3-VL-235B on our tasks and discover that their performance decreases sharply as we increase the number of items to order. Additionally, GPT-5 and Gemini-ER-1.5 are unable to achieve more than 80 accuracy on the easiest base setting of ordering two objects in any of our spatiotemporal tasks, despite reporting higher results in several other spatial reasoning benchmarks ray2024sat, tong2024cambrian, gemini2025geminirobotics15 . VLMs improve their performance in spatial ordering tasks with outputs from computer vision models. We show that using a specialized vision model to predict segmentation maps or bounding boxes and then providing this information to the VLM mostly improves its accuracy on our left-to-right and depth-wise spatial ordering tasks. These results suggest that VLMs struggle with basic capabilities such as identifying objects in cluttered environments, compared to specialized vision models. VLMs do not improve performance on temporal ordering tasks when provided with structured test-time compute, but do improve performance on spatial ordering tasks when provided with the same compute. We study if explicitly structuring test-time compute by applying merge sort over VLM-generated pairwise comparisons aids performance in high reasoning settings. Our results show that merge sort performs worse or at a comparable level to providing all set elements to the VLM at once on temporal ordering tasks, but does improve spatial ordering performance. These results suggest that VLMs successfully reason over more than two frames to solve our temporal ordering tasks. Both reinforcement learning and supervised finetuning (SFT) on pipeline-generated data improve small model performance on downstream reasoning tasks. We scale our data construction pipeline to construct 8857 training samples for each ordering task, and finetune Qwen3VL-8B-Instruct on generated data. We observe that training on generated data improves performance on multiple downstream tasks. However, no single approach improves performance across all downstream tasks, and, in some cases, performance degrades after training on generated data. Reinforcement learning yields limited benefits on temporal ordering but offers large boosts on spatial ordering on training with a small set of generated data. We perform reinforcement-learning finetuning experiments on Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct using GRPO to maximize ordering performance on our tasks can improve its performance. Performance improves significantly on both 2D and depth spatial ordering tasks (with Qwen2-VL outperforming all larger VLMs on some tasks), while we observe more limited performance improvements on our temporal ordering task. Small model performance also increases proportional to the size of the RoboReason-generated training dataset. Related work. While several large-scale robot manipulation datasets have been released with associated robot camera images 10611477, khazatsky2024droid , attempts to utilize such trajectories for evaluating VLM reasoning have focused on trajectory-specific spatial orientation and robot-object interactions chen2025robo2vlm . Alternatively, most approaches to evaluation VLM spatiotemporal reasoning use question-answer benchmarks with high-resolution images and answer options hudson2019gqa, antol2015vqa, wang2025spatial457 , which means VLM reasoning results can be influenced by guesswork, selection bias, and lack of visual noise or cluttered scenes balepur2024artifacts, zheng2023large, song2025robospatial . Our approach instead leverages tasks using real-world robot camera images and trains models on multi-object spatiotemporal ordering tasks, decreasing the evaluation bias. We discuss related work in detail in Appendix app:rel_works . RoboReason Our pipeline comprises of methods to construct three ordering tasks. In each task, the VLM is provided with a shuffled set of items alongside any task-specific context, and is tasked with reproducing the original ordering of the items. After providing only the frames and the language description to the VLM, we ask the VLM to output a permutation of the frames such that . In the canonical task setting, each video frame comprises three images (left, right, and wrist camera) stitched into a single image. Depth ordering: This task provides a single video frame alongside a list of the names of objects present in specified via their names. We denote the list of objects as , and their associated distances from the camera . The VLM is then prompted to output a permutation of the objects such that . title: RoboLongR: Causally Consistent Rewards Teach Robots to Progressively Master Long-Horizon Manipulation
comment: 11 pages including appendices, 8 figures, 6 tables. Project website: https://chenzixuan99.github.io/RoboLongR-public/
summary: Long-horizon manipulation requires actions whose validity depends on earlier interactions, yet visual progress can conceal missing task prerequisites. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. Stage-shuffle supervision encourages execution-order sensitivity, recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, and two-round training refines trajectory segments using predicted progress. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. Sparse terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by triggering correction for repeated high-scoring failures. Pretrained on demonstrations from 88 RLBench tasks and Open-X data, RoboLongR achieves 31.8 average success on 18 long-horizon tasks excluded from reward pretraining, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. Across four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5 success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. Reward-level controls probe sensitivity to synthetic order perturbations, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components to policy improvement. Project website: . Long-horizon manipulation, causally consistent rewards, reinforcement learning, learning from demonstration. Introduction Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to coordinate subtasks whose outcomes depend on earlier interactions~ chen2026deco . Demonstrations initialize behavior, while learned visual rewards supply dense feedback for further improvement through reinforcement learning (RL)~ ma2023liv,sontakke2023roboclip,zhang2025rewind,luo2025hilserl,lei2025rl . Transferable rewards extend this guidance to new tasks, allowing policies to improve beyond their demonstrations~ zhang2025rewind,chen2026sarm,chen2026sarm2 . Reliable progress assessment is therefore central to expanding a robot's task repertoire through interaction. However, recognizing a later task state does not establish that its prerequisites are satisfied. Drawer storage requires opening, object placement, and closing. Closing an empty drawer produces a goal-like image without completing the task (Fig.~ fig:teaser , left). Rewarding this apparent progress may reinforce skipped prerequisites. This ambiguity arises because identical observations can correspond to different outcomes depending on execution history. Rewards must therefore retain earlier interaction evidence, especially when online exploration leaves the demonstration distribution~ pan2022misspecification,skalse2022defining . We call agreement between rewarded progress and task prerequisites supported by execution history causal consistency. These prerequisites can form a partial order, allowing multiple valid sequences, and unsuccessful attempts can admit recovery. Learning such rewards poses two challenges: successful demonstrations provide little supervision for prerequisite violations, and adapting policies can encounter reward errors absent from training. This raises our central question: How can demonstrations and sparse interaction feedback yield rewards that guide adaptation to new tasks while remaining sensitive to task prerequisites? We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide progressive policy adaptation to new long-horizon tasks (Fig.~ fig:teaser , right). RoboLongR consists of three key components. First, to promote causal consistency, stage-shuffle reorders intact demonstration segments, providing execution-order supervision as a proxy for prerequisite sensitivity. Recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, while a second training round refines segment boundaries using predicted progress. Second, RoboLongR uses the learned rewards to guide policy refinement beyond demonstrations. Target-task demonstrations initialize the policy through behavior cloning (BC), followed by reward-guided online RL. Coarse stages, defined independently of reward segmentation, condition both BC and scheduled RL. Every RL episode starts from a standard initial state and attempts the full task. Finally, to address reward errors encountered during policy adaptation, RoboLongR uses sparse terminal feedback to identify repeated high-scoring failures and trigger reward correction. This feedback loop allows the reward to guide policy learning while policy experience informs subsequent reward updates. We pretrain the reward on demonstrations from 88 RLBench~ james2020rlbench tasks and Open-X Embodiment~ oneill2024openx , then evaluate policy adaptation on 18 disjoint long-horizon RLBench tasks. Target-task demonstrations initialize BC, and interaction supports policy refinement and reward correction. RoboLongR achieves 31.8 average success, compared with 7.8 for BC alone, and exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. On four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5 success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. In summary, our contributions are threefold. (1) We combine stage-order supervision and recurrent memory to learn progress rewards sensitive to execution history and task prerequisites. (2) We develop a reward-guided BC-to-RL framework that separates reward segmentation from policy conditioning and uses sparse terminal feedback to correct recurring reward errors. (3) We evaluate policy adaptation on tasks excluded from reward pretraining and on real robots, supported by reward-level controls and component ablations. Related Work for Robot Learning. Learning rewards from demonstrations has been studied through inverse reinforcement learning and adversarial imitation learning~ abbeel2004irl,ho2016gail . Recent methods use visual and language representations to estimate progress, value, or similarity for robot control, including LIV~ ma2023liv , VLC~ alakuijala2024vlc , GVL~ ma2024gvl , and RoboCLIP~ sontakke2023roboclip . ReWiND~ zhang2025rewind learns transferable progress rewards from rewound trajectories for offline-to-online policy adaptation. General-purpose reward models further explore trajectory comparisons~ liang2026robometer , outcome assessment~ lee2026roboreward , and dense process supervision~ zhai2025vision . These approaches broaden the signals available for policy learning, but estimated progress alone does not establish that earlier prerequisites were satisfied. RoboLongR focuses on this distinction, combining stage-order supervision with recurrent execution memory to encourage prerequisite-sensitive reward learning. -Aware Rewards and Policy Refinement. Stage modeling structures reward estimation in long-horizon tasks. SARM~ chen2026sarm jointly predicts stages and fine-grained progress, while SARM2~ chen2026sarm2 extends stage-aware rewards to multiple tasks and improvement from autonomous rollouts. RoboHorizon~ chen2025robohorizon combines LLM-generated subtask rewards with a multi-view world model. As policies improve through interaction~ luo2025hilserl,lei2025rl,yang2026rise,liu2026lifelongrft,zhang2025robustvla , changing behavior can expose unreliable reward estimates. RARM~ yang2026rarm addresses this issue through confidence gating. RoboLongR combines distinct stage representations with feedback-driven correction: adaptive segments construct order supervision, coarse stages condition the policy, and sparse terminal outcomes identify repeated high-scoring failures. Correcting the reward on these failures connects subsequent guidance to evidence gathered during policy execution. Method sec:method RoboLongR learns a reward from multitask demonstrations to guide downstream policy adaptation. The framework comprises four stages (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ): causally consistent reward learning, demonstration stage annotation, stage-conditioned initialization, and stage-scheduled online RL. Terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by identifying recurring high-scoring failures. Problem Formulation Given a task instruction , let denote an execution, where , , and are RGB observations, robot states, and actions. The environment provides binary terminal success . Our goal is to learn a dense progress reward that supports policy improvement beyond the demonstrations. Causal consistency aligns rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by the observed history. These prerequisites may form a partial order. Without annotated prerequisite graphs, we pursue this objective through stage-order supervision and terminal-feedback correction. Causally Consistent Reward Learning sec:reward_learning -shuffle supervision. Successful demonstrations rarely show familiar actions executed without their prerequisites. To create order mismatches, we partition each demonstration into contiguous segments and sample a shuffled counterpart with probability . For three consecutive segments, stage-shuffle replaces with . Each segment retains its visual content and internal ordering in a different execution context. For example, opening--closing--placement violates the demonstrated drawer sequence. Let be the first displaced step. We preserve the positive progress target before and set the remaining targets to zero: Padding-masked MSE supervises original and sampled shuffled prefixes using and , respectively. Original positives remain in training even when no shuffle is sampled. Order-preserving splices provide training positives and a control on disjoint held-out demonstrations (Sec.~ sec:q2 ). Their boundary statistics are not exactly matched to shuffles, and zero-suffix supervision can penalize valid alternative orders or recoveries. execution memory. Order-sensitive prediction requires evidence of interactions that may no longer be visible. Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14~ oquab2024dinov2 encodes two RGB views, and frozen all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encodes the instruction. Projected features pass through an autoregressive Transformer, a recurrent module, and an MLP progress head. Attention spans 100 frames. Longer sequences use causal chunks, carrying recurrent state across chunks and detaching it during training. Memory resets between episodes. Each prediction uses only its observed prefix, while recurrent memory carries information beyond the attention window. Appendix~ app:reward_inputs details view aggregation and recurrent-state initialization. -adaptive segmentation. To adapt shuffles to progress changes, we refine segments in two rounds. Round 1 uses uniform partitions and targets . Round 2 continues from the first-round checkpoint, adapting segments to progress changes and using per-demonstration min-max normalized predictions as targets. For adaptive partitioning, we smooth each predicted curve with an 11-frame, degree-three Savitzky--Golay filter. Boundaries are local maxima of the absolute second derivative that exceed one standard deviation of curvature magnitude and are separated by at least five frames. If no boundary qualifies, we use five uniform segments. Stage-shuffle requires at least three segments. These partitions follow predicted progress and need not coincide with semantic subtasks.
