title: Sybil-Resilient Multi-Drone Exploration of Indoor and Confined Spaces
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, and 8 tables. Code, worlds and mission results: https://github.com/IDZTPHKKKS/Sybil4Drones
summary: When a team of drones explores a building together, each drone tells the others which frontier it is going to and shares the map it has built. This avoids duplicated effort, but it also means that the team trusts every identity from which it receives messages. In a Sybil attack, one compromised drone creates fake identities, and these fake teammates claim frontiers and send fabricated scans, so the real drones leave parts of the building unexplored and end up with walls in their maps that do not exist. We study five such attackers, including one that seals off the openings between floors, and five levels of defence that need no security infrastructure, only the drones' own sensors and maps: an audit of received map data against what a drone sees itself, a check that a body is present where an identity claims to be, trust only for identities whose body has been seen, a quarantine for identities that no drone has observed, and a rule that binds each observed body to one identity. Tests in simulation cover 70 maps of seven kinds, from offices and tunnels to three-storey buildings and caves. Without a defence, one compromised drone leaves on average up to 25% of a map unexplored (45% in offices), and the floor-sealing attacker cuts the explored part of a three-storey building to 82.3%, or 34.6% on the worst map. The quarantine brings exploration back to the level of an unattacked team in every setting, and in most settings it also brings the false data back to that level. The exceptions are two colluding attackers, fakes placed next to real drones, three of the ten caves and a team of 16 drones, and binding bodies to identities fixes the last three. Over 2,350 missions, an honest drone was revoked by a teammate only twice.
full_text: Sybil-Resilient Multi-Drone Exploration\\ of Indoor and Confined Spaces Shyaam Mahesh, Aditya B Prakash, Rubal Sagwal, and Avinash Gautam The simulator, the worlds and the result of every mission are available at . When a team of drones explores a building together, each drone tells the others which frontier it is going to and shares the map it has built. This avoids duplicated effort, but it also means that the team trusts every identity from which it receives messages. In a Sybil attack, one compromised drone creates fake identities, and these fake teammates claim frontiers and send fabricated scans, so the real drones leave parts of the building unexplored and end up with walls in their maps that do not exist. We study five such attackers, including one that seals off the openings between floors, and five levels of defence that need no security infrastructure, only the drones' own sensors and maps: an audit of received map data against what a drone sees itself, a check that a body is present where an identity claims to be, trust only for identities whose body has been seen, a quarantine for identities that no drone has observed, and a rule that binds each observed body to one identity. Tests in simulation cover 70 maps of seven kinds, from offices and tunnels to three-storey buildings and caves. Without a defence, one compromised drone leaves on average up to 25 of a map unexplored (45 in offices), and the floor-sealing attacker cuts the explored part of a three-storey building to 82.3 , or 34.6 on the worst map. The quarantine brings exploration back to the level of an unattacked team in every setting, and in most settings it also brings the false data back to that level. The exceptions are two colluding attackers, fakes placed next to real drones, three of the ten caves and a team of 16 drones, and binding bodies to identities fixes the last three. Over 2 , 350 missions, an honest drone was revoked by a teammate only twice. Multi-robot systems, aerial systems: perception and autonomy, security, mapping. mall drones are a natural fit for exploring buildings, mines and other places where a person cannot easily follow. A team covers such a space faster than a single drone, provided that the drones do not explore the same regions. Most coordinated exploration methods achieve this in two ways~ burgard2005coordinated,zhou2022swarm . Each drone announces the frontier it is heading for, so the others pick different ones. In addition, each drone shares the map it has built, so that no region is explored twice. Both mechanisms rest on an implicit assumption: every identity on the network is a real drone, and the information it sends is true. A Sybil attack violates exactly this assumption~ douceur2002sybil,newsome2004sybil . A single compromised drone communicates under several identities. When these fake teammates claim frontiers, the honest drones stay away from those regions, and when they send fabricated scans, the honest drones mark unexplored space as explored or plan around walls that are not there. No drone collides and no message is lost; the mission simply ends early, with part of the building never seen and with false walls in every honest map. Signing every message would stop new identities from appearing. However, it requires keys and a trusted authority before the mission starts, and it does nothing about a compromised drone that lies under its own, valid name. So we look at defences built only from what an exploring drone already has: its own sensors and its own map. This paper makes three contributions. The first is a threat model for Sybil attacks on coordinated 3D exploration, with five attackers of increasing skill, one of which sends its fakes to the openings between floors and seals them with fake walls. The second is a series of five defence levels that use only onboard sensing, ending with a rule that binds each observed body to a single identity. The third is an evaluation on 70 maps of seven kinds, which shows how much the damage depends on the shape of the space, why auditing map content alone is not enough, and where the stronger defences still fall short. Section~ sec:related covers related work. Section~ sec:system describes the exploration system, Section~ sec:threat the attacks and Section~ sec:defence the defences. Results follow in Section~ sec:results , and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper with its limitations. sec:related Multi-robot exploration and mapping: Frontier-based exploration was introduced by Yamauchi~ yamauchi1997frontier , and Burgard et al.~ burgard2005coordinated extended it to teams. It is still the basis of most multi-robot exploration systems, recent aerial swarms included~ zhou2022swarm . The maps are usually probabilistic occupancy grids~ hornung2013octomap . Robust multi-robot mapping methods reject measurements and loop closures that disagree with each other~ mangelson2018pcm,lajoie2020door,tian2022kimera , which works well against perceptual aliasing and sensor outliers. These methods were not designed for an adversary who controls several identities and deliberately makes its data look consistent. Sybil and Byzantine robots: The Sybil attack was first described for peer-to-peer systems~ douceur2002sybil , and Newsome et al.~ newsome2004sybil studied it in sensor networks. We follow their distinction between identities that act at the same time and identities that appear one after another. Gil et al.~ gil2017spoof detect spoofed robots from the physical signature of their wireless signals. The closest work to ours is IsoRank~ sagwal2026isorank , which finds Sybil identities in multi-robot exploration from the geometry of their broadcast positions; it shares two authors with this paper. Our evidence is different: we compare the map data and claims an identity sends with what the receiving drone sees for itself. The two approaches use different signals and could be combined, but we have not run IsoRank on our missions, so this paper makes no quantitative comparison with it. For robot swarms, Strobel et al.~ strobel2018byzantine limit Byzantine robots through blockchain voting, Wardega et al.~ wardega2023blocklist build a decentralized blocklist from accusations based on observed behaviour, and Luo et al.~ luo2025robotobchain store neighbour observations on a distributed ledger. Our presence check is a simpler form of neighbour observation that requires no ledger. A large body of work makes multi-robot consensus resilient to malicious agents, either by discarding extreme values received from neighbours~ saldana2017resilient or by weighting neighbours with trust values extracted from their wireless signals~ yemini2022trust,cavorsi2023trust . These methods protect a scalar or low-dimensional quantity that the team agrees on. A shared 3D map is far richer, and every honest drone can check part of it with its own sensors, which is the property our audit relies on. Trust models: We use the Beta reputation system of J sang and Ismail~ josang2002beta . The evidence is not ratings but first-hand contradictions between what a drone was told and what it later saw. sec:system Worlds: The main study uses four procedural families of \,m worlds with 0.2\,m voxels (Fig.~ fig:worlds ): offices with rooms, corridors and furniture (3.2\,m high), warehouses with shelves (6\,m), forests with trunks and canopy (4.8\,m), and tunnel networks (4\,m). Seeds 0--9 of each family give the 40 maps of the main study. Seeds 100--104 are kept aside for calibration and never appear in the results. Three more families test vertical and confined exploration (Fig.~ fig:worlds3d ). Three-storey buildings stack three office floors to 9.6\,m, joined by two 2\,m shafts through each slab. Atrium buildings have three floors of 3.6\,m around a central void with galleries and shops. Caves are 8\,m high, carved from smoothed random noise around one connected passage. We use ten seeds of each. Drones: Each of the eight drones carries a forward-looking depth camera ( , 6\,m range, 1.5 range noise, 2 dropouts) and two range sensors pointing up and down. Top speed is 1.5\,m/s. Every drone keeps its own voxel map in log-odds form, picks frontiers by their size per distance on a 0.4\,m planning grid, plans with breadth-first search and follows the path by pure pursuit, with a safety guard. They take off one second apart. We assume each drone knows its own pose. In the main study a drone moves as a point that reaches the commanded velocity within the 3\,m/s acceleration limit; Section~ sec:results repeats the key conditions with quadrotor dynamics. Communication: Two drones can communicate within 25\,m, and every wall between them halves that range. A drone sends its map updates to its neighbours under a bandwidth limit and resends lost packets. It also broadcasts a short message with its identity and position, and a claim with the frontier it is heading for. A drone will not pick a frontier that another identity claimed within 6\,m during the last 15\,s~ burgard2005coordinated . Each map cell remembers which identity reported it, so it can be checked or rolled back later. Identities: An identity is a number carried in each message. Messages are not signed, so any drone can start sending under a new number. The team is open, meaning that drones may join or leave during the mission, so no drone knows how many teammates to expect and a Sybil attack cannot be caught by counting. In our experiments, all honest drones take off at the start and stay for the whole mission; only the fake identities join later. We do assume that an identity already used by an honest drone cannot be taken over, for instance because that drone would receive messages carrying its own number. Impersonation is outside the scope of this paper. sec:threat One drone in the team is compromised (two in the collusion test). It explores and shares its own map honestly, so the team keeps trusting its real identity. We therefore do not test a compromised drone that lies under its own identity; D1 would audit such a drone like any other identity, but we leave this case to future work. In addition, it poses as up to additional drones at a time. These fake identities have no body; they exist only as messages. What the attacker knows and controls: The attacker has its own map and receives every message sent within its radio range: map updates, position messages and frontier claims. We also assume it knows exactly how the defences work. It does not know what the other drones have seen but not yet shared. For each fake it decides three things: where the fake says it is, which frontier the fake claims, and what the fake reports seeing. It derives all three from its own map and from the messages it has received. We consider five attackers of increasing sophistication. Weak: All fakes appear at the start, close to the attacker, and move openly. Their scans are random, with walls reported at random distances. This attacker is the easiest to detect, but it causes considerable damage before it is revoked. Strong: This attacker is more careful. Its fakes join one at a time, the first after 8\,s and then one every 4\,s, each within 10\,m of the attacker. Instead of random walls, each fake reports a plausible room around itself, 8 to 14\,m across. The attacker also relabels 80 of the real map data it forwards with the names of its fakes, so the fakes look honest most of the time. Once most of the team has revoked a fake, the attacker replaces it with a new one. Stealth: The same as the strong attacker, except that the fakes only go to places that no honest drone can see at that moment. Consequently, no drone can ever observe that the claimed position is empty. Targeted: The same as the strong attacker, except that the fakes are directed to the most valuable frontiers. Each fake picks the frontier with the most unexplored space behind it, such as a shaft leading to another floor or a doorway into a large unexplored a

title: I Won't Know Until I Try: Interactive Information Gathering for Long-Horizon Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances.
full_text: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances. Introduction sec:introduction Long-horizon manipulation requires a robot to determine not only how to act, but also what it needs to know before acting. While passive perception can often identify objects and estimate their poses, some task-relevant properties cannot be reliably observed from appearance alone, such as whether an object is movable, a drawer is unlocked, a non-transparent container is empty, or a pen has ink (Fig.~ fig:pen_draw_interaction ). To resolve this missing information, the robot must employ interactive perception: using physical interactions and their observed outcomes to reveal these object properties~ interactive_perception . For example, testing whether an object is movable may require pushing it slightly. While the push reveals the object's movability, it may also displace the object by an uncertain offset. Such an interaction can therefore both resolve uncertainty and alter the physical state for subsequent actions. Consequently, information gathering must be integrated into planning to determine which properties need to be revealed to accomplish the task while also accounting for the physical effects that require downstream adaptation. Plan repair and adaptive execution provide established mechanisms for revising plans when observations and changes disrupt the initial plan~ online_replanning,tamper . Adopting this perspective, we address how execution can recover when interactive observations contradict initial assumptions. Rather than replanning globally from scratch after every interaction, our approach identifies and retains valid plan suffixes and constructs minimal local connections only when needed; a process we refer to as recovery replanning. We frame this problem of multi-step manipulation under uncertainty as an instance of Task and Motion Planning (TAMP). TAMP addresses the action selection problem by jointly searching over discrete action choices and continuous parameters, such as grasps and trajectories, that satisfy geometric, kinematic, and physical constraints~ tamp_review,pddlstream . Building on the TAMP framework PDDLStream, we incorporate interactive, information-gathering actions, execution monitoring, and recovery replanning. Our framework models task-relevant properties as initially unknown, using optimistic interactive action models that are verified during execution. Observations update the state, while execution monitoring identifies when interaction outcomes or physical side effects render planned actions inapplicable or infeasible---for example, when a pick cannot be completed because an object is immovable, or when a previously planned motion is no longer collision-free. Rather than discarding the entire remaining plan, our framework retains its reusable portions and uses recovery replanning to reconnect the current state to a valid plan suffix. This allows execution to adapt to interaction outcomes and state changes while preserving prior planning effort whenever possible. Our work makes the following contributions: Augmented an existing TAMP framework with optimistic, task-directed, interactive information-gathering actions for manipulation under uncertainty. Formulated an interleaved planning and execution method that leverages recovery replanning. Evaluated across 4 interaction domains (whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer openable, and a container empty) in simulation and on a real robot. Related Work sec:related-work Our work builds on TAMP under partial observability, task-directed information gathering through interaction, and adaptive execution and online replanning. We study settings where physical interactions both reveal task-relevant properties and alter the world, requiring state updates and recovery that reuses applicable portions of the original plan. Task and Motion Planning under Partial Observability Task and motion planning (TAMP) frames multi-step manipulation as a joint search of the sequence of actions for the robot to execute and the constrained discrete and continuous values, such as grasps, paths, objects, etc., that parameterize those actions~ tamp_review . While it is common to assume a fully known environmental state, real-world manipulation often depends on properties or outcomes that can only be uncovered during execution. To address partial observability, prior approaches incorporate perception and state estimation into the planning and execution process. For example, belief-space TAMP frameworks reason over probability distributions in the context of hierarchical planning~ belief_tamp or via probabilistic abstractions of closed-loop controllers to enable information gathering and risk-aware decision-making~ tampura . Other methods infer models for unknown objects directly from RGB-D observations and estimated affordances~ estimated_affordances . While these works establish mechanisms for planning under uncertainty, our framework takes a complementary, execution-oriented approach. Rather than tracking continuous belief distributions, we maintain explicit predicates for property knowledge, dynamically adapting the plan as observations update both these property predicates and the geometric relationships. Our representation builds on established symbolic encodings of known and unknown facts~ classical_replanning,seeing_believing , rather than introducing a new epistemic formalism. Task-Directed Information Gathering through Interaction When visual information is insufficient to determine object properties or states, interactive perception uses physical actions to elicit informative sensory observations~ interactive_perception . Rather than performing unguided exploration or generating data to train perceptual models~ property_learning , active information-gathering in TAMP problems are explicitly directed by the task. In the context of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), this perspective guides the search to reduce task-relevant uncertainty rather than reducing uncertainty indiscriminately. Similarly, the recent framework Seeing is Believing uses foundation models to ground beliefs and plan information-gathering actions under property uncertainty~ seeing_believing . These frameworks often assume a strict decoupling between the information-gathering actions and actions that interact with the world, thus assuming that perception leaves the physical world unaffected. In contrast, we explicitly account for interactions that have coupled physical and informational outcomes: a push can reveal movability and alter object pose, while lifting a bottle can reveal whether it is empty and change the robot's grasp state. Consequently, our execution must account for both uncovered information and changes to the physical state. Adaptive Execution and Online Replanning When the execution of a plan deviates from expectation, due to unexpected physical dynamics or unobserved properties, the na\"ive approach is to re-generate an entirely new plan, i.e. to replan from scratch. To avoid this, planning repair seeks to reuse some components of the existing solution, ranging from the action sequence to the continuous trajectories to the closed-loop behaviors. Van der Krogt and de Weerdt formulated planning repair as removing obstructing actions or constraints and adding actions needed to restore a valid plan~ plan_repair . Approaches such as SS-Replan~ online_replanning initially constrain online replanning to reuse the unexecuted plan tail, preserving action sequencing, object selections and grasps while recomputing only observation-dependent poses, configurations, and trajectories. This constraint is relaxed if no suitable plan is found within a timeout. Alternatively, the action space of TAMPER~ tamper includes closed-loop actions that cannot be fully ground prior to execution. Once executed, an online motion repair connects the resulting configuration to the next planned action. Other frameworks achieve adaptive execution by limiting the planning horizon~ receding_horizon or by expressing motions relative to objects~ object_centric . LESAMPLE~ lesample samples scene hypotheses from low-entropy perceptual beliefs and replans when observations invalidate the current plan, while Levihn et al.~ foresight use belief monitoring and selective hierarchical replanning. Robust logical-dynamical systems~ rlds govern behavior activation and continuation through logical conditions, supporting reactive plan execution. Learning-based approaches adapt execution by updating failure probability models across tasks~ failure_option or training reinforcement learning bridge policies to handle state discrepancies~ bridge_policy . For the latter, the policy learns when to return control to the planner, without requiring reconnection to a specified original-plan suffix. Prior work provides complementary strategies for adapting execution and reusing prior planning effort. Our framework retains validated, potentially reusable, instantiated action suffixes and only generates new actions when execution encounters a gap. Problem Formulation sec:background We define our problem using the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL)~ mcdermott1998pddl . In PDDL, a predicate is a Boolean-valued expression capturing a relationship between state variables. Grounding a predicate's arguments produces a fact and the state of the world is defined by a set of these facts. For example, (Mat m) denotes that m as a mat, (IsMovable o) that object o can be moved, and (On o m) that object o is on mat m. Actions are defined as controllers parameterized by discrete and continuous variables. An action is characterized by its preconditions, , the set of facts that must hold for the controller to execute, and its effects, , the set of facts true upon execution. All of our domains share a basic set of actions (move free, pick, move holding, place), supplemented with domain-specific manipulation and information-gathering actions. Given an initial state , a action set , our objective is to find a plan that achieve the goal state , specified as a set of target facts. We cast this as a task and motion planning (TAMP) problem, where we must solve for the sequence of actions and their corresponding discrete and continuous parameters~ tamp_review . We specifically use PDDLStream, a state-of-the-art TAMP framework that reduces the hybrid discrete/continuous planning problem to a sequence of discrete planning problems via focused sampling of the continuous and discrete parameters~ pddlstream . We write if the state satisfies all of the goal facts , and otherwise. In each of our settings, the initial state specifies object types, object poses and the robot configuration. Crucially, certain task-relevant binary properties, such as whether an object is movable or whether a pen has ink remaining, are initially unknown. title: TAD: Distilling Vision-Language-Action Policies from Teacher Trajectories Alone
summary: Online distillation of vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly relies on teacher action scores that an inference-only interface may not expose. Trajectory-only Adversarial Distillation (\gad{}) instead turns a fixed bank of teacher joint-position features into adaptive feedback: a discriminator compares feature marginals from teacher and student rollouts and supplies rewards for on-policy learning. The student interacts with the environment without online teacher queries or environment task rewards. On ManiSkill \texttt{PutOnPlateInScene25Main}, \gad{} improves OpenVLA-OFT (7B) from $26.2\%$ to $76.6\%$ \successonce{} ($+50.4$ percentage points) and from $20.3\%$ to $58.6\%$ \successend{}. It trails white-box on-policy distillation (OPD) at $81.6\%$ / $59.4\%$ by $5.0$ / $0.8$ percentage points ($n{=}256$ evaluation trajectories per checkpoint). The tested four-epoch continuation achieves the highest \gad{} result without additional teacher data. This best run uses $5\times$ OPD's student interaction budget and $12.5\times$ its complete-rollout batch-passes. The comparison demonstrates online VLA improvement without teacher scoring while quantifying unequal interaction and optimization budgets.

Trajectory-only Adversarial Distillation ( ) instead turns a fixed bank of teacher joint-position features into adaptive feedback: a discriminator compares feature marginals from teacher and student rollouts and supplies rewards for on-policy learning. The student interacts with the environment without online teacher queries or environment task rewards. It trails white-box on-policy distillation (OPD) at / by / percentage points ( evaluation trajectories per checkpoint). The tested four-epoch continuation achieves the highest result without additional teacher data. This best run uses OPD's student interaction budget and its complete-rollout batch-passes. The comparison demonstrates online VLA improvement without teacher scoring while quantifying unequal interaction and optimization budgets. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, allowing pretrained representations to support manipulation across tasks. OpenVLA and OpenVLA-OFT illustrate the potential of this approach and of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for adapting a large policy to robot demonstrations~ kim2024openvla,kim2025openvlaoft . Demonstration-based training nevertheless exposes the policy primarily to states visited by the data-collection policy. At deployment, small action errors can change subsequent observations and move execution away from that distribution. Improving behavior on the student's own visited states is therefore an important complement to fitting demonstration actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this mismatch by obtaining teacher supervision on student-generated behavior~ agarwal2024gkd,opd2025 . In the score-based setting considered here, a fixed teacher evaluates the likelihood of action components selected by the student, supplying a direction for online optimization. This access is stronger than the ability to request a demonstration or execute a teacher policy. An inference-only API or proprietary robot stack may return actions without exposing their likelihoods, model weights, or internal representations. Consequently, a capable teacher may be available for collecting successful behavior but unavailable for scoring arbitrary student actions during training. We separate two resources that are often coupled in online distillation: student environment interaction and continuing teacher access. Our setting permits the student to generate new rollouts throughout optimization, but permits teacher supervision only through an initially collected trajectory bank. The bank remains fixed even as the student changes. This restriction is not offline learning: the student still encounters the consequences of its own actions and can improve through closed-loop interaction. Nor does it provide corrective teacher labels at the student's newly visited states. Trajectory-only Adversarial Distillation ( ) implements this setting with a state-feature discriminator. Teacher rollouts provide a fixed bank of normalized eight-dimensional joint-position features; recent student rollouts provide the comparison distribution. The discriminator produces dense logit rewards for group-relative policy optimization in RLinf~ shao2024deepseekmath,rlinf2025 . Its feedback adapts to the student although the teacher data do not change. The VLA policy itself receives visual-language input, while proprioception supplies the discriminator features. The method matches feature marginals rather than complete temporal trajectories, and the main and best runs use no environment task reward. A central empirical diagnostic is the distinction between discriminating behavior and improving it. Early configurations separate teacher and student features accurately without raising deterministic task success. Subsequent diagnostics examine discriminator inputs, reward construction, and actor optimization; continuations from a shared checkpoint examine regularization, update epochs, and reward mixing. The tested four-epoch continuation achieves the highest evaluation with the unchanged teacher bank. These observations motivate examining optimization alongside reward design, rather than interpreting either discriminator accuracy or a sampled training plateau as a direct measure of the supervision's usefulness. On OpenVLA-OFT (7B) and ManiSkill, raises from to and from to , compared with OPD's / . The comparison shares student initialization, teacher, task, and actor learning rate, but not the training objective or budget. The best run uses as many student rollout trajectories and as many complete-rollout optimization batch-passes. These results quantify the trade-off between teacher access and student-side training effort. The paper develops three contributions: [leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt] A trajectory-only distillation method coupling a fixed teacher feature bank, adaptive state rewards, and online optimization of a large VLA. Training diagnostics and continuation ablations that distinguish classification quality, sampled rollout behavior, and deterministic policy evaluation. A quantified comparison with white-box OPD, reporting task performance together with the unequal interaction and optimization budgets required by the tested runs. Related Work sec:related VLA learning and online distillation OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaoft provide the model family underlying our experiments. Supervised adaptation transfers demonstration behavior into a visual-language policy, but its training distribution need not cover the states induced by the deployed student. DAgger~ ross2011dagger addresses this issue by gathering expert action labels on learner-visited states and aggregating them into the training set. Its corrective-label access differs from ours: collects teacher trajectories before student optimization and makes no subsequent queries at student states. Student interaction alone does not imply access to an expert who can correct each rollout. Distillation methods also differ in the supervision they request. Knowledge distillation~ hinton2015distilling transfers teacher output distributions, whereas sequence-level distillation (SeqKD)~ kim2016seqkd trains on teacher-generated sequences. Generalized knowledge distillation (GKD)~ agarwal2024gkd evaluates teacher distributions on student-generated samples, bringing supervision closer to the student's current behavior. VLA-OPD~ opd2025 applies on-policy teacher scoring to embodied policies and supplies our white-box comparison. We retain online student rollouts but replace likelihood-based teacher feedback with a discriminator learned from a fixed feature bank. This is a change in supervision access and actor objective, not simply a different estimator of the same OPD loss. Adversarial imitation and observation-based supervision GAIL~ ho2016gail formulates imitation through adversarial discrimination between expert and learner behavior. AIRL~ fu2018airl develops an adversarial reward-learning formulation, while DAC~ kostrikov2019dac studies sample efficiency and reward bias with off-policy learning. These works motivate learning a reward from demonstrations rather than specifying a task reward by hand. uses a logit transformation of discriminator probabilities, but not AIRL's full reward-recovery architecture. Its discriminator replay should likewise not be confused with off-policy actor learning: the actor updates from the current rollout batch with fixed rewards. Observation-based imitation removes the need for demonstrated action labels, but does not necessarily remove temporal structure. GAIfO~ torabi2018gaifo discriminates state transitions, and AMP~ peng2021amp uses transition pairs to learn motion priors. Our main experiments instead discriminate single-frame joint-position features, so they compare a feature marginal rather than a transition distribution. This narrower representation cannot directly encode object relations or temporal progress. EF-GAIfO~ efgaifo2026 further studies observation-based imitation under embodiment mismatch, including real-robot validation of policies trained in simulation. Our experiments instead retain the same robot embodiment for teacher and student. Design studies of adversarial imitation~ orsini2021ail motivate examining inputs, reward transformations, and optimization together; gradient-penalty regularization~ gulrajani2017wgan motivates one continuation ablation. The distinction between a learned proxy and the intended task objective~ skalse2022reward is especially relevant when discriminator accuracy and task success diverge. Black-box generative distillation Black-box language-model distillation offers related ways to replace unavailable teacher likelihoods. GAD~ gad2024llm trains a text discriminator on teacher and student outputs, using student SeqKD warmup and separate discriminator warmup before adversarial online learning. Our student instead starts from SFT on a different demonstration dataset, and our recipe has no separate discriminator warmup. This difference matters when interpreting early discriminator separation: the initial student need not already approximate the teacher bank. ROPD~ ropd2026 derives prompt-specific rubrics from teacher--student contrasts and uses those rubrics to score student outputs. does not induce semantic evaluation criteria; it learns a reward directly from observed robot features. Adversarial objectives also appear in generative-model acceleration. ADD~ sauer2023add combines adversarial learning with teacher distillation to accelerate diffusion sampling; an adversarial loss alone therefore does not establish trajectory-only or black-box teacher access. AFD~ afd2026 studies black-box adversarial flow distillation for video generation, but its teacher-access and update protocol should not be identified with our fixed-bank embodied setting. These methods share the use of learned comparisons while differing in available supervision and optimization. Our analysis concerns the interaction between feature-based rewards and online control, where student actions change the future observations used for learning. Concurrent embodied adversarial distillation FA-OPD~ faopd2026 is closely related embodied work that learns a flow-matching teacher from demonstrations and co-trains it with lightweight MLP students. Its distillation combines adversarial and mean-squared-error objectives, rather than relying on adversarial rewards alone. In contrast, our teacher is pre-existing and supplies a fixed bank before optimization of an OpenVLA-OFT (7B) student. No teacher model is co-trained, and no teacher action scores or additional demonstrations are requested during student training. The distinction concerns teacher construction, student scale, supervision availability, and the actor loss. Our evaluation focuses on transferring behavior from a fixed external teacher into a large VLA. Score-based OPD provides a reference for measuring the performance and student-side training budgets associated with replacing online teacher scores by a fixed trajectory bank. Method sec:method Problem formulation sec:formulation We consider an episodic manipulation process . The environment observation includes camera images, a task instruction, and proprioception . The student receives only the visual-language input , not joint positions, and produces an action chunk . Here indexes chunk decisions. title: Behavior Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
summary: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.

For manipulation, we primarily use soft success as a proxy for target-selection intention. It credits completed correct interactions as well as non-committed episodes that exhibit correct intention for target approaching under task-specific rules and timeout budgets. We also report strict success for task completion rate, and the wrong-target rate measuring wrong commitments to non-instructed candidates or locations. All three rates report percentage over all evaluated episodes. Task-family rules and exceptions are detailed in Table~ tab:success-criteria . Navigation uses the recorded binary goal result: the robot must satisfy the instructed region-entry or object-proximity criterion within the episode timeout budget. We report per-task and pooled success, without the strict/soft distinction. VLM Evaluation on and sec:vlm-vqa-ir-eval How well do VLMs answer spatial questions? Table~ tab:vlm-vqa evaluates 14 VLMs, comprising five proprietary -- GPT-6~Astra~ openai2026gpt6astra , Gemini~3~ google2025gemini3pro , Fable5.1~ anthropic2026fable51card , GPT-5~ singh2026openaigpt5card , and Gemini~2.5~ comanici2025gemini25pushingfrontier -- and nine open-weight models spanning Qwen~ qwen3.5 , Molmo~ deitke2024molmopixmoopenweights , Gemma~ gemmateam2025gemma3 , and DeepSeek~ wu2024deepseekvl2mixtureofexpertsvisionlanguagemodels families. VQA evaluation prompts, including spatial conventions and multi-frame context instructions, are provided in Appendix~ app:vqa-prompts . The highest single-frame accuracy is 82.1 , compared with 51.8 for the strongest open-weight model. Multi-frame performance varies substantially across models, with several open-weight models at or below the random-guess baseline on direction questions. Spatial VQA thus remains challenging, especially across multiple views. Extracted VLA backbones also score poorly (Appendix~ app:backbone-vqa-diagnostic ). Does general VQA performance transfer to task-grounded questions? We evaluate the best open-source models from the general VQA comparison on task-grounded questions from the manipulation suite (Table~ tab:task-perception ); only open-source models are evaluated, as only these can serve as our VLA backbones. Qwen3.5-9B achieves the highest accuracy at 57.2 , followed by Molmo2-4B at 53.0 and Molmo2-8B at 50.0 . Even Qwen3.5-9B attains 56.3 on direction and 61.4 on distance, but only 47.3 on locate sub-types of direction questions. Strong general VQA thus does not guarantee task-grounded perception, motivating task-grounded evaluation of candidate backbones. How accurately can VLMs ground the instructed target? The IR evaluation asks models to predict a target point directly from the instruction and head-camera view (Table~ tab:task-perception ), using the prompts provided in Appendix~ app:ir-prompts . Qwen3.5-9B achieves the highest strict accuracy at 51.4 , followed by Molmo2-8B at 46.7 and Qwen3.5-4B at 43.3 . Under tolerant scoring, these accuracies increase to 59.7 , 58.4 , and 56.2 , respectively. Molmo2-4B and Molmo2-8B reverse order between VQA and pointing, so answer selection and localization probe different aspects of perception. We relate these task scores to policy behavior in sec:perception-success ; qualitative examples appear in Appendix~ app:perception-examples . VLA evaluation on robot tasks sec:exp-findings We evaluate the policy variants of sec:policy-var on the manipulation and navigation tasks of (Tables~ tab:main-results and~ tab_nav-results ). Checkpoints are selected around similar training steps for fair comparisons. The policy predicts 32-step action chunks using 10 flow-matching denoising steps per inference. Execution uses asynchronous receding-horizon control with a 10-step replanning threshold measured from the committed plan's input-observation timestamp. Actions are temporally ensembled over up to three committed plans, with gripper commands taken from the newest plan. Details are in Appendix~ app:execution-settings . Pooled across manipulation tasks, on held-out instances the baseline achieves 41.6 soft and 27.9 strict success, with 38.2 wrong targets. The baseline's per-task results (Appendix~ app:failure-analysis ) reveal distinct bottlenecks. For place carving knife, 70.8 soft success versus 29.2 strict success suggests execution difficulty despite frequent target-directed progress. Bowl placement achieves only 15.0 on both measures, with a 77.5 wrong-target rate, indicating that target selection itself is difficult. Both target selection and execution thus limit completion. =-1 Do policies follow changed instructions in training layouts? The baseline often fails to redirect its behavior toward a newly requested target, even in training layouts. On prompt-probe episodes, it achieves only 16.1 soft and 10.0 strict success, while 70.0 of episodes commit to a non-instructed target. The policy relies on scene--action associations rather than the instruction. In the failed probe example in Figure~ fig:vla-samples , the instruction requests the largest food item, but the policy reaches the chip bag associated with the original training instruction rather than the indicated oatmeal box. Held-out target-directed behavior thus does not imply reliable instruction following. Does VLM adaptation or robot-data pretraining improve instruction following? LoRA adaptation increases held-out soft success from 41.6 to 43.5 , but yields only a small change on prompt-probe episodes (16.1 to 17.9 ), with 68.1 wrong-target commitments remaining. DROID initialization achieves 40.1 held-out and 16.6 prompt-probe soft success. Neither recipe improves strict probe success over the baseline (9.6 and 8.9 , respectively, versus 10.0 ). Does explicit target grounding improve policy performance? Oracle IR produces substantially larger gains: dot-IR conditioning raises soft success from 41.6 to 60.3 on held-out set and from 16.1 to 38.0 on the prompt probe. Across the three IR variants, probe wrong-target commitments decrease from 70.0 to 42.4--46.0 . Strict success also improves, reaching 44.8 held-out and 24.9 on the probe for the strongest variant with dot IR. Explicit grounding thus redirects policy behavior and improves completion. title: Extended LASMP: Language Aided Subset Sampling Based Motion Planner for Drone Navigation
summary: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems. Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.
full_text: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems. Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners. Introduction sec:introduction Autonomous aerial navigation in cluttered three-dimensional environments remains a fundamental challenge in robotics. Quadcopters operating in indoor and semi-structured environments must reason over higher-dimensional state spaces, handle limited sensing, and generate dynamically feasible trajectories while avoiding obstacles. Sampling-based planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT)~ lavalle1998rapidly,kuffner2000rrt and its optimal variant RRT ~ karaman2011sampling have been widely adopted for such problems due to their probabilistic completeness and scalability to high-dimensional spaces. However, uniform sampling over large configuration spaces often results in poor sample efficiency, particularly in cluttered environments. Several works have attempted to improve sampling efficiency through heuristic or informed sampling strategies, including Informed RRT and related approaches~ gammell2014informed,gammell2015batch,kuo2018deep . Although these approaches bias exploration using geometric cost-to-go heuristics, they fail to incorporate structured task-level instructions into sampling, leading to inefficient exploration and wasted computation. In many real-world applications, aerial robots are required to follow high-level human commands, such as go left, move up, or turn back and proceed forward. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled robots to interpret natural language instructions and map them to control or planning actions~ ahn2022can,xie2023language,wu2024vision . However, most existing approaches either rely on end-to-end learned policies or treat language as an external high-level planner, leaving the underlying sampling-based motion planner unchanged. In contrast, classical sampling-based planners ignore the directional intent embedded in commands, leading to unnecessary exploration of irrelevant regions of the planning space. This work addresses the problem of command-aware sampling for quadcopter navigation. Building upon the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner (LASMP) bhattacharjee2025lasmp developed for ground robots, we extend the framework to aerial platforms to plan in . Unlike planar robots, quadcopters introduce an additional translational degree of freedom, requiring a transition from planar subset sampling to command-aligned three-dimensional subset sampling. Each navigation command is interpreted as a yaw update followed by directional translation or vertical motion, and the sampling distribution is dynamically restricted to subsets aligned with the commanded direction. This structured restriction concentrates exploration in more meaningful regions while preserving probabilistic completeness. To robustly ground natural language instructions into geometric planning constraints, we integrate an LLM-based named entity recognition (NER) pipeline. Using few-shot prompt-based extraction, the system identifies task-relevant motion entities without requiring task-specific model retraining. The extracted entities are converted into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware constraints that directly shape the sampling subsets. Additionally, the LLM is employed to detect inconsistencies or ambiguities in user instructions and request corrective input, enhancing interaction reliability. An illustration of our work is shown in Fig. fig:fig_1 where a user can give the instruction and based on that instruction, our planner computes a feasible path. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: A unified command-aware sampling framework that integrates directional navigation commands into the sampling distribution of a sampling-based planner together with a ray-guided switching strategy for consistent sequential command execution. Comprehensive empirical validation demonstrating improved sample efficiency, reduced computational cost, faster convergence compared to uniform sampling planners across diverse 3D environments. A complete ROS2–PX4–Gazebo integration of the framework, enabling physics-based execution and validating the real-time feasibility of command-aware subset sampling on a quadcopter flight stack. A probabilistic completeness analysis for command-restricted sampling, extending classical RRT guarantees to structured subset sampling. Related Work sec:related_works Sampling-Based Motion Planning Sampling-based motion planning methods such as Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT)~ lavalle1998rapidly and its bidirectional variant RRT-Connect~ kuffner2000rrt have been widely adopted for high-dimensional planning problems due to their probabilistic completeness and computational efficiency. Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM)~ kavraki2002probabilistic provide a multi-query alternative with similar theoretical guarantees. Karaman and Frazzoli~ karaman2011sampling later introduced RRT and PRM , establishing asymptotic optimality within the sampling-based planning framework. Additional planners such as FMT ~ janson2015fast and BIT ~ gammell2015batch further improve efficiency through graph-based search and batch sampling. Despite these advances, classical sampling-based planners typically rely on uniform sampling over the configuration space, which can lead to poor sample efficiency in large or cluttered environments. Informed and Biased Sampling To improve exploration efficiency, several works restrict sampling to heuristically defined subsets of the planning space. Informed RRT ~ gammell2014informed samples from a prolate hyperspheroid around a feasible solution, focusing search on regions that can improve path cost. Dynamic-domain RRT~ yershova2005dynamic reduces sampling near obstacles to improve convergence in cluttered spaces. While these methods bias sampling using geometric or cost-to-go heuristics, they do not incorporate structured task instructions or semantic constraints to draw samples. Our approach restricts sampling based on command-induced directional constraints. Rather than relying on cost heuristics or solution refinement, we align sampling subsets with yaw-updated motion commands before finding a feasible solution. This enables semantically guided exploration and preserves probabilistic completeness. Kinodynamic and UAV Motion Planning For aerial robots, kinodynamic constraints must be considered during planning. Closed-loop RRT (CL-RRT)~ luders2010bounds integrates system dynamics into the planning loop and provides tracking guarantees. Other works address quadrotor motion planning in 3D environments using trajectory optimization or motion primitives~ mellinger2011minimum,richter2016polynomial . While these approaches account for dynamic feasibility, they typically sample uniformly in the state space or rely on optimization-based methods, without incorporating structured navigation commands into the sampling strategy. Our work focuses on the geometric planning layer in , introducing command-aware subset sampling as a lightweight yet theoretically grounded mechanism for improving exploration efficiency in aerial navigation tasks. Instruction-Conditioned Planning Recent research has explored grounding natural language instructions into robotic decision-making. Approaches such as SayCan~ ahn2022can,chen2024spatialvlm and language-conditioned path planning frameworks~ xie2023language, anderson2018vision, tellex2011understanding, hu2019safe use large language models to map instructions to feasible actions. Vision-language navigation methods~ wu2024vision,shah2021ving further integrate perception and language for navigation. However, many of these methods rely on learned policies or treat language as an external task planner. In this work, we preserve a classical sampling-based planning backbone that integrates language-derived constraints directly into the geometric sampling distribution. This allows us to maintain theoretical guarantees such as probabilistic completeness while enabling structured exploration for the navigation. title: Power-of-Two Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Neurons for Event-Driven Vision-Language-Action Inference
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on dense, continuous-valued computation presents a fundamental challenge for energy-constrained deployment. Inspired by the sparse, event-driven signaling and temporal integration mechanisms of biological neurons, a promising alternative is to introduce spiking computation into VLA models. However, enabling such computation without restructuring pretrained policies or compromising closed-loop control remains an open challenge. To address this challenge, we introduce the Power-of-Two Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (PoT-LIF) neuron, which emits signed spikes with power-of-two amplitudes. By combining magnitude-coded spike events with residual-preserving membrane dynamics, PoT-LIF enables continuous information to be progressively represented through discrete spikes. The Heartbeat formulation further localizes this process within weighted projections, bridging biologically inspired spiking computation and pretrained VLA architectures without modifying their external inference interfaces. We integrate PoT-LIF into the vision projection, vision-language projection, and action projection of $π_{0.5}$ and evaluate both operating modes over 2,000 paired closed-loop LIBERO episodes per configuration. Standard-mode PoT-LIF VLA achieves success rates of 96.90% and 96.35% at $T = 1$ and $T = 2$, respectively, while Heartbeat mode achieves 97.25% and 96.90% at $T = 2$ and $T = 4$, compared with 96.70% for the original continuous-activation $π_{0.5}$ baseline. At $T = 1$ with a 60.01% firing rate, PoT-LIF uses approximately 1/7.67 of the dense-reference arithmetic energy, corresponding to a modeled reduction of 86.95%.

Keywords: spiking neural networks, vision-language-action, robot learning, neuromorphic computing Introduction sec:1 Vision--language--action (VLA) models couple pretrained vision--language backbones with action generation modules to enable closed-loop robotic manipulation in open environments~ black2024pi0 . Systems such as physicalintelligence2025pi05 , Robotics Transformer 2 (RT-2) brohan2023rt2 , and OpenVLA kim2024openvla have demonstrated strong cross-task generalization. However, VLA inference repeatedly executes dense weighted projections across vision, language, and action modules, resulting in high energy consumption on edge platforms. This motivates an alternative computational interface that preserves representational capacity while reducing arithmetic cost. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer an event-driven computational paradigm~ gerstner2014 . Leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons are widely adopted in SNNs. They convert continuous membrane potentials into sparse binary spikes, allowing synaptic computation to occur only when spikes are emitted.~ lapicque1907,brunel2007lapicque . However, a single binary spike does not explicitly encode the magnitude of the underlying membrane potential. To represent fine-grained continuous values, binary SNNs often accumulate information over multiple time steps, increasing computation and scheduling overhead. Recent studies, such as Spike-driven VLA and DS-VLA, have demonstrated the potential of SNNs for embodied control wang2026spikedriven,lyu2026dsvla . Their integration strategies include directly trained spiking architectures and dendritic spiking action modules. However, these strategies can spread temporal processing across multiple modules, complicating integration into pretrained VLA architectures. These limitations motivate two key design goals for integrating spiking computation into pretrained VLA models: (1) representing continuous values with a limited number of events, and (2) confining temporal processing to selected projections without altering token layout, residual connections, or key-value (KV) cache organization. To address the representation requirement, we draw inspiration from biological observations of exponential computation and graded signaling. Gabbiani et al. gabbiani2002 reported a nearly exponential mapping from membrane potential to firing rate in a locust visual neuron, consistent with multiplication through logarithmic input encoding and exponentiation by active membrane conductances. In cortical circuits, presynaptic membrane potential can also modulate axonal action potentials and the synaptic responses they evoke shu2006 . Motivated by these mechanisms, we use an exponent-based event representation: the amplitude takes the form where and is an integer. Successive exponent values specify multiplicative amplitude changes rather than equally spaced integer levels. We choose to align this representation with binary digital arithmetic. Residual retention then allows successive events to refine the represented value under a bounded emission budget. We therefore propose a power-of-two leaky integrate-and-fire (PoT-LIF) neuron. A signed event has the form , where and is an integer. For a floating-point weight , an event contribution is evaluated through scaling--accumulation (SAC), formally defined in Sec.~ sec:3.1 . For normal values whose scaled results remain normal and representable, scaling adjusts the weight exponent and combines the signs without a general significand multiplication. A residual membrane state retains the portion not represented by the current event, making the event budget an explicit control over precision and computational work. The same PoT-LIF recurrence supports two operating modes: standard mode and Heartbeat. In standard mode, the neuron receives successive inputs and retains its membrane state across input calls. Heartbeat instead applies the recurrence locally within each VLA projection: each projection invocation injects its input once and accumulates the weighted contributions of a bounded event sequence. The residual is retained across internal extraction steps, and the local state is reset at the end of the invocation. This confines the event-time dimension to individual projections while preserving the original token count, residual connections, and KV caches. Standard mode remains available for processing successive inputs and may support future integration with event-based sensors. We evaluate PoT-LIF in the vision projection, vision--language projection, and action projection of using a fixed paired closed-loop protocol on LIBERO liu2023libero . Across both the main and supplementary evaluations, all tested PoT-LIF configurations of differ from the dense baseline by no more than 0.80 percentage points in success rate. We also estimate the arithmetic energy of PoT-LIF projection computation under a matched FP32 accumulation model, while excluding system-level overheads. This paper makes three contributions: A unified PoT-LIF formulation with reconstruction guarantees. We define a unified PoT-LIF recurrence with signed power-of-two emissions and residual retention, describe its standard mode, and formulate Heartbeat as a specific input schedule. We establish residual reconstruction guarantees under leak-free dynamics and exact arithmetic, with the geometric error bound requiring inactive exponent clipping (Sec.~ sec:3 ). We integrate PoT-LIF into the vision projection, vision--language projection, and action projection of and evaluate standard mode followed by Heartbeat mode. Across both the main and supplementary evaluations, all tested PoT-LIF configurations differ from the 96.70 dense baseline by no more than 0.80 percentage points in success rate (Sec.~ sec:5 ; paired statistical analyses are provided in Appendix~ app:G ). We then survey related work on event representations, efficient arithmetic, and spiking VLA models. Spiking neural networks and LIF dynamics sec:2.1 SNNs compute with discrete events rather than dense continuous-valued activations. A leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron integrates input into its membrane potential, exhibits passive leakage in the absence of input, emits a spike at threshold, and resets after emission ( gerstner2014 , lapicque1907 , brunel2007lapicque ). Consequently, SNNs represent continuous quantities through rate coding, in which firing frequency carries the value, or temporal coding, in which spike timing carries the value gerstner2014,cao2015spiking,sengupta2019going . Such representations generally require multiple time steps. Surrogate-gradient training sec:2.2 Binary spike generation is modeled by the Heaviside step function, whose derivative is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the threshold. Consequently, direct backpropagation provides no useful gradients for learning. Surrogate-gradient methods enable gradient-based training through discontinuous spike-generation functions neftci2019surrogate . The forward pass retains the binary spike, while the backward pass uses the derivative of a smooth substitute in place of the step-function derivative. Event representations and efficient arithmetic sec:2.3 Biological neurons exhibit a nearly exponential relationship between membrane potential and firing rate. Presynaptic membrane potential also modulates axonal action potentials and postsynaptic response amplitudes. These observations motivate introducing exponentially spaced firing levels and amplitude-bearing events into LIF dynamics. Theoretical analyses of neural coding under metabolic constraints levy1996 and experiments on energy-efficient synaptic transmission harris2015 further motivate considering the information conveyed by each event alongside its computational cost. title: Dynamic Query as Budgeting for Tiny Object Detection
summary: Recent DETR-based tiny object detectors adopt dynamic query mechanisms to handle severe density imbalance. However, existing designs entangle two effects: how many and which queries are decoded. This entanglement obscures what drives the gains and complicates dynamic-query design; additional learned predictors and heuristic filtering also introduce overhead and potential selection errors. We disentangle these effects and show that dynamic query primarily acts as \emph{budgeting}---allocating decoder query capacity according to object density---rather than intricate query selection.Motivated by this view, we formulate a monotonic and conservative budgeting principle and propose a budgeting-based DETR (BUTR), a streamlined framework that uses a lightweight, non-learned budgeter to estimate an input-dependent query budget $K(x)$ from encoder confidences. BUTR retains standard Top-$K(x)$ query initialization without additional learned modules or heuristic filtering in the budgeter.At $800\times800$ resolution, BUTR-L achieves 35.7 AP at 47.8 FPS on AI-TOD-v2 and 29.8 AP at 42.1 FPS on VisDrone on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Inference-time integration on COCO further demonstrates its applicability to general scenario detection. Code is available at https://github.com/zhangyi-magic/BUTR.
full_text: Recent DETR-based tiny object detectors adopt dynamic query mechanisms to handle severe density imbalance. However, existing designs entangle two effects: how many and which queries are decoded. This entanglement obscures what drives the gains and complicates dynamic-query design; additional learned predictors and heuristic filtering also introduce overhead and potential selection errors. We disentangle these effects and show that dynamic query primarily acts as budgeting---allocating decoder query capacity according to object density---rather than intricate query selection. Motivated by this view, we formulate a monotonic and conservative budgeting principle and propose a budgeting-based DETR (BUTR), a streamlined framework that uses a lightweight, non-learned budgeter to estimate an input-dependent query budget from encoder confidences. BUTR retains standard Top- query initialization without additional learned modules or heuristic filtering in the budgeter. At resolution, BUTR-L achieves 35.7 AP at 47.8 FPS on AI-TOD-v2 and 29.8 AP at 42.1 FPS on VisDrone on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Inference-time integration on COCO further demonstrates its applicability to general scenario detection. Code is available at . Introduction sec:intro DETR-based detectors frame object detection as set prediction, simplifying the pipeline by reducing hand-crafted heuristics~ carion2020end, zhu2020deformable . Recent advances have improved convergence and efficiency, making this paradigm increasingly practical~ zhao2024detrs, peng2024d, huang2025deim . Detecting tiny objects, however, remains challenging. Tiny objects occupy only a few pixels, suffer from severe ambiguity, and are easily confused by background clutter. In aerial imagery, this challenge is amplified by density imbalance: most images are sparsely populated, while a tiny fraction contains crowded scenes with hundreds (or more) instances~ wang2021tiny, xu2022detecting, yang2022querydet, cheng2023towards . This creates a tension in DETR design: a fixed decoder query budget is efficient for the majority of images but may be insufficient for crowded cases, whereas uniformly increasing the budget imposes unnecessary overhead and can increase false positive detections in sparse scenes. To address this, recent works introduce dynamic query mechanisms that adapt decoder capacity to each input. DQ-DETR~ huang2024dq first predicts a density map and then uses a classifier to assign each image to a preset budget bin. This two-stage discretized design is prone to error propagation, which can lead to unstable budget assignment across density scales. In contrast, Dome-DETR~ hu2025dome adopts a selection-heavy procedure (Progressive Adaptive Query Initialization, PAQI) that combines a learned window-mask predictor with heuristic filtering, introducing sample-dependent control flow and multiple thresholds. Although effective on challenging dense cases, these methods introduce extra predictors or heuristic operators, increasing complexity and reducing practicality without always improving accuracy. More importantly, selection-heavy designs entangle query budgeting with query selection, obscuring the true source of improvement. In this paper, we revisit dynamic query from a mechanism-first perspective. Existing designs conflate two effects: changing how many queries are decoded, and changing which queries survive. To disentangle them, we analyze Dome-DETR~ hu2025dome through controlled inference-time analysis. This leads to two key observations. First, density-stratified evaluation reveals that, on AI-TOD-v2, PAQI's advantage over a fixed budget sufficient for the majority of images is concentrated on the rare high-density tail and largely obscured by overall AP. Second, a simple confidence-ranked Top- initializer closely reproduces PAQI's accuracy not only in overall AP but also within density subsets when its fixed budget is adjusted to provide comparable query capacity; in particular, increasing also closes the gap on the high-density tail. A qualitative example is shown in Fig.~ fig:examples . Supplementary experiments with DDQ-style initialization~ zhang2023dense further support this interpretation: when the query count is held fixed, replacing confidence-ranked Top- with spatially distinct query selection yields the same overall AP on both AI-TOD-v2 and VisDrone (App.~ app:ddq_style ). Together, these findings suggest that dynamic query primarily acts as adaptive budgeting---determining how many queries to decode---rather than intricate selection of which queries to keep. Motivated by this budgeting perspective, we propose a budgeting-based DETR (BUTR), a streamlined framework that realizes dynamic query through a lightweight, non-learned budgeter that estimates a per-image query budget from a simple density proxy over encoder proposals, while retaining standard Top- initialization of two-stage DETRs. Compared with prior dynamic-query detectors, BUTR delivers higher accuracy with lower overhead, faster training, and lower T4 deployment latency; as a drop-in modification for modern two-stage DETRs, it also makes dynamic query easier to implement, reproduce, and extend. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=0.2em,topsep=0.2em] Perspective. We disentangle how many and which queries are decoded, showing that dynamic query mainly performs adaptive decoder budgeting, with gains concentrated on the rare high density tail revealed by density-stratified evaluation. Method. We formulate a budgeting principle for dynamic query and instantiate it as BUTR, which estimates a per-image decoder query budget with a lightweight, non-learned budgeter to enable standard Top- query initialization, avoiding extra selection machinery. Results. On AI-TOD-v2 and VisDrone, BUTR achieves higher AP over prior dynamic-query detectors with lower overhead, and markedly faster training and lower T4 deployment latency; additional COCO results further indicate its applicability beyond tiny object detection. Related Work sec:related_work Fixed-Query DETRs DETR~ carion2020end formulates detection as end-to-end set prediction with a fixed set of object queries. Subsequent variants have greatly improved convergence and efficiency, including deformable attention~ zhu2020deformable , query design and anchor-based query formulations~ meng2021conditional,wang2022anchor,liu2022dab , denoising or hybrid matching strategies~ li2022dn,zhang2022dino,chen2023group,jia2023detrs , and recent real-time architectures~ zhao2024detrs,peng2024d,huang2025deim,zhang2023dense , while retaining a fixed query budget (typically 300--900 queries). On aerial tiny-object benchmarks such as VisDrone~ zhu2021detection and AI-TOD-v2~ wang2021tiny, xu2022detecting , fixed-query DETR-style detectors, together with related transformer-augmented two-stage baselines such as DNTR~ liu2024denoising , achieve strong performance. However, under severe density imbalance, a fixed global query budget creates a natural trade-off: it is efficient for the majority of sparse images, but may become insufficient for rare crowded scenes. This tension motivates recent efforts toward input-adaptive query allocation. Dynamic-Query DETRs To address this tension, recent works introduce dynamic queries that adapt decoder capacity to each input. DQ-DETR~ huang2024dq adopts a learned strategy by predicting an image-level density signal and selecting among preset budget buckets. title: RoboDuo: Attempt, Check and Atomic Recovery through Code for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map a language instruction and the current observation directly to actions, without checking whether the instruction has been completed. For long-horizon tasks, a single failed step therefore goes unnoticed and leaves the whole task unfinished. Such failed episodes, however, often end with the task partially complete. Moreover, the unfinished steps are reusable atomic skills that recur across demonstrations. A failed attempt can thus be recovered by composing with atomic skills. We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual-system framework that uses code as the interface between a coding agent and two VLAs. The agent writes a program that lets a full-task VLA attempt the whole task and checks whether it is complete; on failure, an atomic VLA finishes the remaining steps. Since the agent emits no actions and only decides which VLA for execution, RoboDuo wraps an existing full-task VLA without updating its weights. To train the atomic VLA and the coding agent with the completion-checking ability, we build LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from a single set of LIBERO demonstrations. RoboDuo consistently improves X-VLA and $π_{0.5}$ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks, and recovers failed rollouts of a frozen full-task VLA on a real robot.
