For long-horizon tasks, a single failed step therefore goes unnoticed and leaves the whole task unfinished. Such failed episodes, however, often end with the task partially complete. Moreover, the unfinished steps are reusable atomic skills that recur across demonstrations. A failed attempt can thus be recovered by composing with atomic skills. We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual-system framework that uses code as the interface between a coding agent and two VLAs. The agent writes a program that lets a full-task VLA attempt the whole task and checks whether it is complete; on failure, an atomic VLA finishes the remaining steps. Since the agent emits no actions and only decides which VLA for execution, RoboDuo wraps an existing full-task VLA without updating its weights. To train the atomic VLA and the coding agent with the completion-checking ability, we build LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from a single set of LIBERO demonstrations. RoboDuo consistently improves X-VLA and on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks, and recovers failed rollouts of a frozen full-task VLA on a real robot. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,zheng2025xvla,zhao2023act map a language instruction and the current observation directly to low-level actions, and have become a standard approach to language-conditioned manipulation. The policy is re-queried on each new observation, yet nothing checks whether the current observation satisfies the intended goal. Execution therefore continues under the same instruction even after a step has failed. Consider an object that slips from the gripper during transport. The post-slip state is rare in the demonstrations, so the policy rarely re-grasps and may instead continue its learned trajectory, for example by placing with an empty gripper. On a long-horizon task, that unnoticed failure leaves the remaining steps unfinished, and the episode fails even though earlier progress was correct. One route is to place this decision-making functionality inside the action model. Systems built on GPT-6-Astra~ openai2026astra use one large model to generate numerical robot actions, judge the outcome during execution, and emit a correction within the same forward pass~ galbot2026astra . However, the scale that enables such judgment and correction also slows every inference step. Even steps that a fast policy could execute unchanged must wait on the large model, and the resulting latency falls short of the control rate required for physical deployment. Dual-system architectures instead place the decision model outside the action model. In Helix and related systems, a high-level model passes a language command, a token, or a latent vector to a single low-level policy~ figure2025helix,intelligence2025pi05,shi2025hirobot,bjorck2025gr00t,bu2024robodual,zhang2024hirt,cui2025openhelix,shentu2024lcb . This interface changes what the low-level policy is conditioned on, but it cannot express a failed attempt, a retry, or a switch to a different executor. Code-as-policy methods provide exactly this control flow, in which an agent writes a program that tests the outcome of each skill and retries it on failure~ liang2023cap,huang2023voxposer,singh2023progprompt,huang2024rekep,liang2026robofoundry . Because these programs call primitives or VLA skills from the first step, they largely discard the long-horizon competence of a full-task VLA. Code is therefore better used to wrap one attempt by that VLA, and to close the loop only after the attempt fails. Building on this principle, we propose RoboDuo, a dual-system framework in which a coding agent uses code as the interface to two frozen VLAs (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). The agent serves as an orchestrator and writes a task program. The program first assigns the task to the full-task VLA for one attempt, after which is task complete evaluates the new observation. If the task fails, the agent plans the unfinished steps from the current observation as atomic instructions. An atomic VLA then executes these instructions to the end of the task, with at most three attempts per step, and the control does not return to the full-task VLA. We employ a separate atomic VLA since each atomic instruction describes a short segment already present in the demonstrations, whereas the full-task VLA is trained only on full-task instructions. We construct LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from the same demonstrations to train the atomic VLA, the coding agent, and the completion check, respectively. We instantiate RoboDuo on X-VLA and without updating the weights of either full-task VLA. On LIBERO-Long, RoboDuo raises the success rate of X-VLA from 87.4 to 91.6 and that of from 93.6 to 96.2 . On LIBERO-PRO, RoboDuo raises the mean success of from 32.05 to 39.33 , with the largest gain on Object-T ( ). On a real robot, RoboDuo raises success from 36.7 to 53.3 over three fruit-arrangement layouts, without updating the frozen full-task VLA. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual system that uses code, rather than a token or a latent vector, as its interface. When the full-task VLA fails, an atomic VLA executes the remaining steps. We construct LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from the same successful demonstrations to train the atomic VLA, the coding agent, and the completion check, respectively. We instantiate RoboDuo on X-VLA and and evaluate it on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and a real robot. The gains concentrate on long-horizon tasks that fail because a single subtask fails. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models. VLA models learn end-to-end mappings from language instructions and visual observations to low-level actions, and existing approaches differ mainly in how they represent actions. Autoregressive models discretize actions into tokens and predict them sequentially with a vision-language backbone~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla . Continuous-control models instead attach an action expert or decoder that regresses or denoises future actions~ zhao2023act,octo2024,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,zheng2025xvla . Subsequent work inserts intermediate reasoning before action generation, including textual chain-of-thought, visual subgoals, motion foresight, and retrieved trajectory memory~ zawalski2024ecot,zhao2025cotvla,lin2026hifvla,li2026optimusvla . These methods improve the quality of a single attempt within the action model. RoboDuo is complementary to them: it uses such a model, without modification, as the frozen full-task VLA. Dual Systems and Code as Policies. Dual-system architectures place a slow vision-language model above a fast policy. In Helix and related systems, the upper model passes a language command, a token, or a latent vector to that policy~ figure2025helix,intelligence2025pi05,shi2025hirobot,bjorck2025gr00t,zhang2024hirt,bu2024robodual,shentu2024lcb,cui2025openhelix . This interface changes only the conditioning of the same executor, and these systems typically lack an explicit completion check. By contrast, systems built on GPT-6-Astra let one large model emit the actions directly, so every control step incurs the inference latency of that model~ galbot2026astra . Code-as-policy methods write programs over control primitives, situated plans, value maps, or keypoint constraints~ liang2023cap,singh2023progprompt,huang2023voxposer,huang2024rekep . More recent agents also call frozen VLA policies as skills~ liang2026robofoundry . In these systems, the program serves as the plan from the first step, so no full-task policy ever attempts the task as a whole. RoboDuo also uses code as the interface, but its coding agent emits no actions. The full-task VLA first attempts the whole task, and the atomic VLA takes over only after the completion check fails. Failure Correction and Recovery. Several methods intervene around a failure and then let the original policy continue. FPC-VLA corrects the direction and magnitude of the current action when the gripper state changes~ yang2025fpcvla . Spotter repairs a confirmed error with motion primitives before returning control to the original policy~ li2026spotter . RoboFAC appends a recovery subtask or an end-effector direction to the prompt, while the original VLA still produces the actions~ ye2025robofac . Recova learns a recovery policy from failed scenes and human demonstrations, and likewise returns control once the scene becomes workable again~ liu2026recova . In all of these methods, the original policy ultimately executes the remaining steps. Embodied-R1.5 instead plans and corrects within a single model, without separating the decision model from the executor~ yuan2026embodiedr . RoboDuo plans the remaining steps as atomic instructions and executes them with an atomic VLA trained only on short segments of successful demonstrations. Both VLAs stay frozen at test time, and control does not return to the full-task VLA. Method sec:method RoboDuo turns a single VLA rollout into a verified attempt. A coding agent writes a program that gives a frozen full-task VLA one attempt on the original instruction and then tests the resulting observation with a completion check. If the test fails, the program executes the remaining subtasks with an atomic VLA, which is trained on short clips that each contain a single complete skill. The two VLAs produce every action, whereas the coding agent and the completion check only decide which VLA to query and which instruction to give it. Sec.~ sec:problem formalizes the setting, and Sec.~ sec:roboduo presents the dual-system execution. Sec.~ sec:atomic describes the segmentation of demonstrations into effect-complete clips, and Sec.~ sec:components describes how the atomic VLA, the coding agent, and the completion check are trained. title: Semantic-Coupled Perception Framework for Autonomous Laparoscope Control
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L) for possible publication
summary: In minimally invasive surgery (MIS), maintaining an appropriate field of view (FoV) is essential for surgical safety and efficiency. However, conventional autonomous laparoscope control methods often treat visual tracking and surgical phase recognition independently, limiting robustness under occlusion, entity overlap, and camera motion. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous laparoscope control framework that couples real-time surgical phase recognition with camera-motion-compensated visual perception. By exploiting phase-dependent relationships among surgical entities, the framework improves target state estimation under challenging visual conditions, supporting task-aware autonomous FoV control. Experiments on benchmark datasets evaluate the proposed framework in surgical phase recognition and target tracking, including scenarios involving occlusion and entity overlap. Phantom experiments further demonstrate the feasibility of autonomous FoV control, showing improved target visibility and task execution performance compared with fixed-FoV control. These results highlight the potential of incorporating task-level semantics into visual state estimation for autonomous laparoscope guidance.

(e-mail: endowzhao@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn; \ lifz21, zhuyj24, lusc23\ @mails.tsinghua.edu.cn; malongfei@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn.) Enduo Zhao : Semantic-Coupled Perception Framework for Autonomous Laparoscope Control In minimally invasive surgery (MIS), maintaining an appropriate field of view (FoV) is essential for surgical safety and efficiency. However, conventional autonomous laparoscope control methods often treat visual tracking and surgical phase recognition independently, limiting robustness under occlusion, entity overlap, and camera motion. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous laparoscope control framework that couples real-time surgical phase recognition with camera-motion-compensated visual perception. By exploiting phase-dependent relationships among surgical entities, the framework improves target state estimation under challenging visual conditions, supporting task-aware autonomous FoV control. Experiments on benchmark datasets evaluate the proposed framework in surgical phase recognition and target tracking, including scenarios involving occlusion and entity overlap. Phantom experiments further demonstrate the feasibility of autonomous FoV control, showing improved target visibility and task execution performance compared with fixed-FoV control. These results highlight the potential of incorporating task-level semantics into visual state estimation for autonomous laparoscope guidance. Robotic laparoscopy, field-of-view (FoV) control, visual servoing, computer vision for medical robotics. Introduction inimally invasive surgery (MIS) offers significant advantages over traditional open surgery, including reduced surgical trauma and faster postoperative recovery buia2015laparoscopic . However, the limited access and indirect visualization inherent to MIS require the operative field to be visualized through a laparoscope, whose positioning is typically handled by a camera-holder assistant while the surgeon operates other instruments jarc2017viewpoint . This arrangement introduces additional coordination demands between the surgeon and assistant and may lead to suboptimal visualization due to communication errors and involuntary camera movements gruijthuijsen2022robotic . Ergonomic studies have further reported substantial physical burden and fatigue among camera-holder assistants during laparoscopic procedures liu2023physical . These limitations have motivated the development of robotic autonomous laparoscope control systems that can automatically adjust the camera field of view (FoV) according to the surgical task shi2025hands . Current strategies for autonomous laparoscopic FoV control can be broadly categorized into direct control, instrument-based control, and task-aware approaches. Direct interfaces, such as voice commands hamza2023user , head movements sapalidis2017laparoscopic , or gaze-contingent control fujii2013gaze , allow the surgeon to directly specify camera movements, but may introduce additional cognitive or operational burden by requiring explicit user commands and context switching between surgical manipulation and camera control. Instrument-based approaches instead infer camera motion from surgical tool movements observed in the laparoscopic image. Early methods relied on color markers gruijthuijsen2022robotic or visual servoing osa2010framework , while more recent approaches employ deep learning for instrument detection and tracking cheng2021deep,huang2022surgeon . However, these methods often rely on predefined rules, such as following a single instrument or the midpoint between two instruments, without explicitly considering the surgical phase and the corresponding camera view requirements. Task-aware approaches have therefore been developed to adapt laparoscope behavior according to the current surgical phase. Li et al. li2024gmm used a Gaussian mixture model to derive phase-specific FoV requirements from instrument distributions. Sun et al. sun2025sgr proposed SGR-AutoLap, which adjusts the FoV based on recognized surgical gestures. More recently, Zhou et al. zhou2026surglat introduced SurgLAT, which models surgical attention as a temporally evolving latent state to infer the operative region. However, these methods primarily use task information to guide camera behavior, leaving target detection and tracking largely decoupled from the surgical phase and entity states. Beyond determining where the camera should look, the surgical phase may also constrain which entities should be tracked and how their states relate. This opportunity arises because surgical scenes are inherently organized by the task workflow twinanda2016endonet . During a manipulation phase, the manipulated object is spatially and semantically associated with the active instrument nwoye2022rendezvous,sharma2023surgical , while other objects are generally uninvolved in the ongoing action. These phase-dependent relationships provide cues beyond visual appearance and short-term image motion. However, reliable target tracking remains challenging under severe occlusion chen2025research and camera-induced image motion, which can disrupt spatial association and motion prediction. Exploiting task-dependent relational constraints together with camera motion awareness could therefore improve target state estimation and maintenance under these challenging conditions. To address these issues, this work proposes a semantic-coupled perception framework for autonomous laparoscope control. The framework integrates object detection and tracking with real-time surgical phase recognition, where perceived states and motion relationships support phase recognition, and the recognized phase constrains object state updating. Specifically, the manipulated object is coupled with the active instrument through phase-dependent spatial relationships, while other objects are treated as non-active and semantically static. These non-active entities are used to estimate camera motion and compensate for laparoscope-induced image motion. These constraints support state maintenance, observation correction, and tracking re-initialization upon reliable detections. The resulting states are organized into a structured surgical state to determine the FoV target. Rather than replacing detection or tracking models, the framework couples their outputs with task dynamics to improve perception robustness. The framework is evaluated through ablation studies and benchmark comparisons, followed by phantom experiments on a robotic laparoscope platform using Peg Transfer and Suturing tasks to assess autonomous FoV control. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: A semantic-coupled perception framework integrates surgical phase recognition with object detection, point tracking, and camera-motion compensation to constrain target state estimation using phase-dependent semantics. A phase-dependent state update mechanism exploits static and instrument-object binding relationships to maintain state consistency under ambiguous observations and temporary occlusions. A task-aware control representation aggregates entity states according to the surgical phase for autonomous laparoscope FoV control, validated through phantom Peg Transfer and Suturing tasks. title: HuGe: Scaling Humanoid Generalist Vision-Language-Action Models with Egocentric Experience
summary: Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios. Although egocentric human demonstrations provide a complementary source of task experience, differences in visual embodiment and missing robot proprioception complicate transfer to humanoid policies. To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs pre-trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, HuGe employs three existing representative VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller, together with hand-control signals. Based on this, we introduce a three-stage training pipeline that combines egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning. To facilitate transfer across embodiments, we construct pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulation playback during pre-training and modify arm appearance in egocentric observations through re-rendering during downstream fine-tuning. With this pipeline, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art on simulation benchmark HumanoidArena. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 indicate that augmenting robot demonstrations with visually adapted egocentric demonstrations significantly increases success on a pick-and-drop task.

Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) DBLP:conf/corl/ZitkovichYXXXXW23,DBLP:conf/corl/KimPKXB0RFSVKBT24,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2410-24164,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-14734,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2602-15922,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2601-21998 fueled by Vision-Language Models (VLMs) DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2407-07726,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2511-21631 and World Models (WMs) DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-20314,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2506-09985 have enabled language-conditioned manipulation across a wide range of tabletop tasks. Building on this progress, extending VLAs to humanoid robots offers the potential to perform diverse tasks in human environments by combining manipulation with whole-body mobility. Despite this potential, adapting VLAs to humanoid robots remains challenging because task execution requires coordinated whole-body motion while maintaining balance and stability. To meet these control requirements, existing humanoid loco-manipulation approaches commonly employ hierarchical architectures that combine high-level policies with reinforcement learning (RL)-based controllers jiang2026wholebodyvla,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2603-12263,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2604-07993 . To this end, a central research question is how to train generalist VLAs that translate language instructions into coordinated whole-body behaviors across diverse tasks. Realizing this goal requires addressing two key challenges. First, the high-dimensional action spaces and complex dynamics of humanoid robots make it difficult to directly transfer VLA policies developed for robotic manipulators to whole-body control. In particular, arm movements must be coordinated with the torso and lower body to accomplish manipulation objectives while maintaining balance and stability. Consequently, VLA-based humanoid control requires an action interface that connects task-level predictions to coordinated whole-body execution. Second, beyond these control challenges, learning generalist humanoid behaviors requires diverse whole-body demonstrations, yet collecting such data on real-world robots is costly and time-consuming. To alleviate this data bottleneck, egocentric human demonstrations offer a complementary source of task experience for large-scale training. However, differences in visual embodiment and the absence of robot proprioceptive observations complicate the direct use of these demonstrations for humanoid policy learning. These challenges motivate an approach that integrates VLA policies with whole-body control and supports effective transfer from egocentric human experience to humanoid robots through a scalable training pipeline. To address these challenges, we introduce , a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs that operate through a whole-body controller and learn from a large-scale mixture of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, builds on existing representative VLA architectures and follows a three-stage training pipeline that sequentially incorporates egocentric human data, humanoid teleoperation data, and a mixture of downstream demonstrations. To support this pipeline, we assemble a training corpus comprising over 2,000 hours of egocentric and robot data. Furthermore, we prepare egocentric data for humanoid policy learning during both pre-training and downstream fine-tuning. In particular, during pre-training, we use simulation playback to construct pseudo-proprioceptive states for egocentric data that lack robot proprioceptive observations. Building on this pre-training stage, we re-render and replace arm regions in egocentric observations during downstream fine-tuning. To assess the effectiveness of this approach, we compare with baseline methods on the HumanoidArena simulation benchmark and further evaluate its performance on real-world humanoid tasks. Overall, achieves the state-of-the-art performance on HumanoidArena, demonstrating its capability for humanoid whole-body control, while comprehensive real-world experiments and solid analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of the training recipe. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: \\ We introduce , a family of humanoid generalist VLAs, trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data through a three-stage training pipeline. \\ We develop data adaptation methods that facilitate the transfer of egocentric human experience to humanoid policy learning. \\ achieves the state-of-the-art performance against baselines on HumanoidArena, while comprehensive real-world experiments and analyses validate our design choices and training paradigm. title: ScheNav: Schematic-Guided Object Goal Navigation
summary: Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach target objects in complex environments. Humans often rely on low-cost yet informative schematic maps, such as rough sketches or directional annotations. We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework. Our lightweight data-generation pipeline turns 2D floorplans into navigation training environments, yielding Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes and noise-controllable schematic maps. ScheNav turns rough schematic guidance into exploration and stopping decisions by using SchemaField, a learned spatial module that fuses the guidance with accumulated observations and predicts spatial value fields. The framework updates these fields as exploration proceeds, with trajectory-based training and a cross-frame consistency objective supporting coherent guidance across changing viewpoints. ScheNav learns to use schematic guidance entirely from simulated floorplans and transfers this ability to unseen embodied environments. Experiments show improved navigation success and path efficiency across schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, together with tolerance to the tested schematic perturbations and omissions. Together, these results demonstrate that rough schematic guidance offers a practical way to improve embodied navigation.
full_text: Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach target objects in complex environments. Humans often rely on low-cost yet informative schematic maps, such as rough sketches or directional annotations. We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework. Our lightweight data-generation pipeline turns 2D floorplans into navigation training environments, yielding Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes and noise-controllable schematic maps. ScheNav turns rough schematic guidance into exploration and stopping decisions by using SchemaField, a learned spatial module that fuses the guidance with accumulated observations and predicts spatial value fields. The framework updates these fields as exploration proceeds, with trajectory-based training and a cross-frame consistency objective supporting coherent guidance across changing viewpoints. ScheNav learns to use schematic guidance entirely from simulated floorplans and transfers this ability to unseen embodied environments. Experiments show improved navigation success and path efficiency across schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, together with tolerance to the tested schematic perturbations and omissions. Together, these results demonstrate that rough schematic guidance offers a practical way to improve embodied navigation. Introduction Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach an instance of a specified object category in an unseen environment batra2020objectnav, zhu2017target . Recent map-free approaches, from modular semantic exploration to zero-shot agents built on large language and vision-language models chaplot2020object, gadre2023cows, zhou2023esc, yokoyama2024vlfm, yin2025unigoal , accomplish this from egocentric observations alone and generalize encouragingly to novel scenes. Meanwhile, map-based methods that plan on accurate global maps reach goals with high reliability, since a faithful map reduces navigation to well-understood localization and path planning thrun2005probabilistic, cadena2016past . Each line of work thus holds an advantage the other lacks. Map-free agents pay no cost for map acquisition, while map-based agents enjoy strong global guidance about where to go. We explore whether rough schematic guidance can help embodied agents navigate without requiring an accurate global map. Humans routinely provide and use exactly this kind of guidance tversky1993cognitive . When searching for a room in an unfamiliar building, we rarely demand a precise map. A rough sketch of the layout or a pointed direction is usually enough to focus the search. Such schematic guidance can be produced with little effort and can convey useful layout and goal cues despite distortion and omission. For example, marking a destination on a rough floorplan can help someone find a room without specifying an exact route. Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates this setting, where the agent, given a rough sketch and local observations, is steered toward the goal. Can the agent reliably convert such imperfect schematic guidance into effective closed-loop navigation decisions? We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework. The workflow starts with 2D floorplans, from which we generate environments for learning how to use schematic guidance. A vision-language model furnishes RPLAN floorplans wu2019data and extracts machine-readable furniture layouts, which are processed against the original floorplan geometry. From these layouts, we generate navigation episodes, simulated local observations, ground-truth spatial fields, and paired schematic maps with controllable noise and incompleteness. Environment generation and navigation training take place entirely in 2D, without constructing 3D scenes or collecting embodied training trajectories. This lightweight pipeline produces Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts, and supports both training and controlled evaluation of schematic-guided navigation. ScheNav turns the resulting training resources into a framework for using schematic guidance during navigation. In each episode, the agent receives a goal category and guidance in the form of a schematic map, goal ellipses, or a pointed direction. As the agent moves, its observations accumulate into a map of the area explored so far, which serves as its map memory. SchemaField, the only learned model in the framework, fuses the guidance with this observed map and predicts two spatial value fields. The distance field scores locations by their navigable proximity to the goal, while the corridor field highlights efficient routes toward it. The schematic is treated as a coarse prior to be interpreted alongside observations, rather than an accurate map on which to plan directly. Fixed rules read the fields to guide exploration and verify goal candidates. During exploration, the agent selects the frontier with the highest corridor score yamauchi1997frontier . The Goal Verification module checks whether a detected instance of the goal category maintains a high distance-field value over consecutive steps. When this condition is met, the agent commits to a final approach and stops on arrival. A single SchemaField supports the different guidance forms without retraining. ScheNav attaches to an existing navigation system as a guidance layer, leaving perception, mapping, and low-level motion to its host. Effective schematic guidance must remain coherent as the agent moves and new observations become available. In our initial implementation, adding a field predictor trained on individual observation snapshots did not improve closed-loop navigation, despite producing plausible per-frame predictions. Snapshot supervision, commonly used in learned spatial prediction for navigation ramakrishnan2022poni, georgakis2022learning , does not by itself enforce agreement across viewpoints. We observed that predictions for the same place could disagree after transformation into the world frame, causing successive frontier decisions to undo earlier progress; we call this failure cross-frame inconsistency. SchemaField is therefore trained on simulated navigation trajectories, with a cross-frame consistency objective that aligns predictions across viewpoints. The corridor field further concentrates value along near-shortest paths, turning small differences in goal proximity into clearer frontier choices. These designs allow the framework to update its guidance as exploration proceeds while maintaining coherent decisions across changing viewpoints. We evaluate this workflow by training ScheNav entirely on simulated floorplans and deploying it in unseen embodied environments without embodied training data. Integrated into UniGoal yin2025unigoal , ScheNav uses schematic guidance to improve navigation success and path efficiency on the instance-level HM3D benchmark. Experiments cover schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, examining how different forms of guidance support navigation. Controlled perturbations on Furnished-RPLAN further test tolerance to schematic noise and missing information. Component ablations examine how trajectory-based training, cross-frame consistency, corridor prediction, and Goal Verification contribute to closed-loop performance. A supplementary demonstration uses a genuinely hand-drawn map as input to the navigation pipeline. Together, these experiments examine both the practical value of schematic guidance and the framework designs needed to use it effectively. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation that connects lightweight 2D training-data generation with a closed-loop navigation framework, providing a practical route for incorporating rough schematic guidance into embodied navigation. We construct Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes, ground-truth spatial fields, and noise-controllable schematic maps, through a pipeline that operates entirely in 2D without requiring 3D scene construction or embodied trajectory collection. We introduce ScheNav, a framework that converts schematic guidance and accumulated observations into exploration and goal-verification decisions. Trajectory-based training and cross-frame consistency support coherent guidance, and experiments evaluate transfer to embodied navigation across multiple guidance forms and controlled perturbations. Related Work Goal Navigation. Object goal navigation asks an embodied agent to find and reach an instance of a given object category in a previously unseen environment batra2020objectnav, zhu2017target . Modular approaches build a semantic map online and select exploration targets on it chaplot2020learning, chaplot2020object, ramakrishnan2022poni , end-to-end policies learn navigation directly from raw observations at scale wijmans2020ddppo, mezghani2021memory , and zero-shot methods score exploration directions with the commonsense knowledge of large language and vision-language models majumdar2022zson, gadre2023cows, zhou2023esc, yu2023l3mvn, yokoyama2024vlfm, yin2025unigoal , with general-purpose frameworks unifying multiple goal modalities larsson2024goat, shah2023gnm, shah2023vint . These methods must infer where to search from egocentric observations or general-purpose priors. Our workflow complements this setting by introducing low-cost, human-provided spatial guidance and grounding it in the observations accumulated by the agent. with Human Spatial Guidance. Using human-provided spatial guidance, such as sketches, route maps, and verbal cues, is a long-standing goal in robot navigation skubic2004sketch, tellex2011understanding . Early work localizes and navigates directly in hand-drawn sketches with unknown local metric distortions boniardi2015ecmr, boniardi2016icra . Language-based guidance has also proven effective, ranging from dialogue-based clarification thomason2020vision to Vision-and-Language Navigation with sequential instructions anderson2018vision, fried2018speaker, ku2020room . More recently, HAM-Nav tan2025mobile interprets hand-drawn maps with a vision-language model under scale distortions and missing landmarks, and FloNa li2025flona shows that accurate architectural floorplans provide strong navigation priors. This line of work, from sketch localization to floorplan priors, generally treats the provided map as the geometric space in which the agent localizes, plans, or reasons. We instead use the schematic as a weak spatial prior that is fused with the agent's observations. ScheNav encodes diverse schematic forms into a shared representation and grounds them in the partial map the agent has actually built, allowing the same framework to support schematic maps, ellipses, pointed directions, and no schematic input. A hand-drawn sketch can enter this interface after conversion, while its effect is continuously modulated by the quality of the guidance and the evidence accumulated during navigation. Priors and Value Prediction for Navigation. Semantic priors learned from large-scale 3D environments, such as room layouts and object co-occurrences, improve navigation in unseen scenes yang2018visual, mousavian2019visual, mayo2021visual , supported by simulators and datasets including Gibson xia2018gibson , Matterport3D chang2017matterport3d , HM3D ramakrishnan2021hm3d , and Habitat savva2019habitat, szot2021habitat . Closest to our formulation, active exploration methods predict potential functions or semantic maps from the partial map and score frontiers accordingly chaplot2020learning, ramakrishnan2022poni, savinov2018semi, georgakis2022learning . title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions
summary: Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present RynnVLA-Latent, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core, RynnLAM learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark. It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.
full_text: Introduction Large-scale pretraining has enabled broad capabilities in language and vision-language models~ brown2020language,hoffmann2022training,kaplan2020scaling,achiam2023gpt,chen2022pali,bai2025qwen3,li2026rynnbrain . Recent vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models extend this approach to robot control~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,wu2026pragmatic,li2026causal,ye2026world,yuan2026fast,bi2026motus,zhao2026towards . Scaling policy learning, however, requires supervision that connects visual observations and task instructions to actions across diverse embodiments~ zhao2026high,zhao2025physsplat . Robot demonstrations are expensive to collect, and their native controls differ in dimensions, coordinate frames, and semantics~ zhao2026rynnworld,zhao2026rynnworld_teleop . Human and web videos provide much broader interaction coverage but lack corresponding robot commands. These sources cannot simply be pooled under one native-action prediction objective. A shared supervision interface is needed to exploit their visual transitions before adapting a policy to a particular robot. Latent actions provide such an interface by encoding changes between observations without native control labels~ ye2025latent,chen2025moto,bu2025univla,gao2026dreamdojo,gao2025adaworld,schmidt2024learning,chen2024igor . Existing approaches demonstrate the value of transition reconstruction and feature-space prediction, but visual change can include camera motion, static appearance, and effects unrelated to the agent's control. A representation that reconstructs images well therefore need not be equally useful for predicting low-level manipulation actions. We address this through geometric supervision and explicit camera-motion separation. We introduce , which encodes a frame pair into motion tokens, a global action latent, and a camera latent. Residual future-feature prediction preserves transition information through the bottleneck, while camera-compensated 3D-flow pseudo-labels and contrastive feature warping encourage motion-sensitive representations. Camera-pose prediction and gradient reversal further encourage separation of ego-motion from manipulation-related cues. These objectives provide geometric grounding without requiring manually annotated robot actions; they encourage camera decoupling rather than guaranteeing exact viewpoint invariance or physical identifiability. Using as an offline labeler, we construct shared latent-action supervision for 25 video sources spanning human interaction, real robots, and simulation. The corpus contains approximately 30.1K hours and 3.057B frames and yields 745.52M latent-action descriptors. We then pretrain , a Mixture-of-Transformers policy that couples a pretrained vision-language backbone with a narrow action expert. The policy predicts latent-action chunks from multi-view observations and language via flow matching, without native-action or proprioceptive supervision. In robot post-training, we reuse both the backbone and action-expert trunk, introduce proprioception, and retarget the output projection to native robot commands. This separates video-based motion supervision from embodiment-specific action alignment. Our evaluation follows the same path from representation learning to robot deployment. On LARY, frozen-representation probes test whether the descriptors predict low-level control targets, with the full descriptor achieving average relative-action MSE . After native-action post-training, the 4B policy obtains on LIBERO, on LIBERO-Plus, average success across five VLABench tracks, and average success under the RoboTwin 2.0 Native protocol. These benchmarks respectively assess task execution, perturbation robustness, semantic grounding, and bimanual manipulation. Six real-world tasks on stationary dexterous and mobile gripper platforms test the interface after adaptation to different controls. Data-scaling and component studies further characterize where the approach helps and where performance remains limited. Our contributions are as follows: [nosep, labelsep=0.6em, leftmargin=1.2em, itemindent=0em] 3D-grounded latent-action supervision. We introduce RynnLAM, which combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling to construct continuous transition representations without native robot-action labels. Scalable VLA pretraining from heterogeneous video. We develop RynnVLA-Latent, which learns shared latent-action targets from 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, and transfers the pretrained policy to native robot controls through embodiment-specific post-training. Representation and policy-level validation. We demonstrate control predictability through frozen-representation probes, competitive manipulation performance across simulation and real-world platforms, and improvements with increasing latent-action pretraining data. Related Work Latent Action Learning Latent action learning provides a way to exploit videos without native action annotations by representing the transformations between observations. LAPO~ schmidt2024learning and Genie~ bruce2024genie demonstrate that latent action spaces can support policy learning and controllable prediction from unlabeled videos. LAPA~ ye2025latent learns discrete latent actions through frame-transition reconstruction and uses them as VLA pretraining targets, while Moto~ chen2025moto learns motion tokens for autoregressive pretraining and transfers the resulting motion priors to robot control. IGOR~ chen2024igor similarly compresses image-goal transitions into shared action representations for learning across human and robot videos. These approaches establish visual transitions as a scalable source of action-like supervision beyond robot demonstrations. Subsequent work investigates how to make such representations more useful for control. UniVLA~ bu2025univla introduces language-guided, task-centric latent actions in DINO feature space, while villa-X~ chen2026villa augments visual reconstruction with a proprioceptive forward-dynamics objective to ground latent actions in robot states and actions. Latent actions also serve as transferable conditioning signals for world models: AdaWorld~ gao2025adaworld uses video-derived latent actions for adaptable future prediction, and DreamDojo~ gao2026dreamdojo learns continuous proxy actions from large-scale human videos. Garrido et al.~ garrido2026learning further investigate constrained continuous latent actions for representation-space world modeling on in-the-wild videos. Our focus is the geometric grounding of latent actions without robot-native action or proprioceptive supervision. combines residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated dynamic 3D-flow supervision, and contrastive feature warping to learn a factorized continuous transition representation. A dedicated camera-pose pathway and an adversarial objective further encourage separation of camera ego-motion from manipulation-relevant motion. Rather than relying on continuity or feature-space prediction alone, these complementary objectives encourage the latent representation to capture physical scene changes and provide shared supervision across human, simulated, and real-robot videos. Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer pretrained vision-language knowledge to robot control. OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and FAST~ pertsch2025fast explore action-token prediction, while ~ black2024pi_0 , GR00T N1~ bjorck2025gr00t , Xiaomi-Robotics-0~ cai2026xiaomi , and LingBot-VLA~ wu2026pragmatic couple vision-language backbones with continuous action generators. Open X-Embodiment and RT-X~ o2024open , together with ~ intelligence2025pi05 , demonstrate the value of cross-embodiment and heterogeneous training. To handle incompatible action spaces, UniAct~ zheng2025universal learns universal action representations with embodiment-specific decoding, X-VLA~ zheng2026x uses soft prompts and domain-specific projections, and Qwen-RobotManip~ yuan2026qwen aligns canonical state-action representations and camera-frame motion. Human videos provide additional supervision through latent-action labels in GR00T N1~ bjorck2025gr00t and reconstructed hand motion in VITRA~ li2025vitra . Our work focuses on constructing a shared supervision interface for scalable VLA pretraining, rather than aligning heterogeneous native control parameterizations. learns continuous -generated latent-action chunks from human, robot, and simulation videos through flow matching. The same descriptors also condition cross-embodiment video generation in the companion RynnWorld-Latent model. Native robot actions and proprioception are introduced only during embodiment-specific post-training, allowing large-scale video-based pretraining to be separated from executable control alignment. sec:method A central obstacle to scaling robotic manipulation is that the most abundant sources of manipulation knowledge---human videos, web videos, simulation, and heterogeneous robot datasets---do not share a common action representation. We address this problem by learning a shared latent-action space supervised by visual transitions and geometric pseudo-labels, without requiring identical native control spaces. This latent space serves both as an automatic annotation for large-scale unlabeled video and as an intermediate control representation that can later be aligned with concrete robot actions. Our framework consists of three components. We first assemble and preprocess the multi-embodiment video corpus (Sec.~ sec:data ). We then train (Sec.~ sec:lam ) with future-feature prediction, dynamic 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, and use its encoder to label the corpus offline. Finally, we train (Sec.~ sec:our_vla ), a vision-language-action policy that learns to generate these latent actions from visual observations and language via flow matching. In post-training, the same flow-matching objective is retargeted from latent actions to the target robot's action space, so that costly action-labeled demonstrations are required only for the final embodiment alignment. Pretraining Data sec:data We collect a multi-embodiment corpus from 25 video sources, covering real-world robot demonstrations, simulated rollouts, and human interaction video (egocentric and web sources) across diverse embodiments (Fig.~ fig:pretraining_data ). Every source is processed by the same pipeline without the need for action labels (Fig.~ fig:data-generation ). We process the entire dataset in parallel across shards using . Specifically, we extract latent actions from consecutive frame pairs sampled every frames, i.e., pairs , yielding one latent-action descriptor per adjacent pair in the four-frame sampling grid. The source corpus contains approximately 30.1K hours, 16.63M episodes, and 3.057B frames (Tab.~ tab:pretraining-data-statistics ). Offline labeling produces 745.52M latent actions. For policy pretraining, we form chunks containing latent-action targets from the offline annotation index. The RGB-frame stride used to extract a descriptor and the temporal spacing used to form a policy chunk are distinct indexing choices. The resulting policy training index contains 121.06M samples, corresponding to approximately 946K optimizer steps per epoch at a global batch size of . The corpus varies widely in embodiment, duration, and episode length. HowTo100M alone contributes more episodes than all real-robot sources combined, even though the human and robot groups have similar total duration. title: TRIAGE: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference Needs Both Reuse and Pruning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4 the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, \ stays within 3\,pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48 , and with only 7 of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4\,pp on LIBERO-Object. INTRODUCTION sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robotic manipulation~ rt2,openvla,oft,pi0,pi05 . At every control step, a VLA model feeds hundreds of visual tokens, together with a language instruction, into a large language model (LLM) backbone that outputs actions. However, on embedded boards such as NVIDIA Jetson, the hardware typically mounted on robots, LLM inference is too slow for tasks that demand rapid reactions such as catching a moving object. Offloading inference to a remote server is not a dependable alternative either: end-to-end latency then depends on the network as much as on the server~ vlaperf , wireless links to mobile robots suffer from fluctuating latency and intermittent outages, and a single delayed or lost response stalls the control loop. On such hardware, the prefill stage of the LLM backbone is compute-bound, so its latency grows with the number of input tokens~ onemore ; for models that decode all actions in a single forward pass, such as OpenVLA-OFT, prefill accounts for two thirds of each control step (Table~ tab:libero ). In VLA models, visual tokens account for roughly 90 of the input sequence, making them the main contributor to both computation and latency. Training-free acceleration methods therefore mainly focus on reducing the number of visual tokens the backbone computes through token pruning or reuse. Token pruning~ fastv,sparsevlm,vlapruner,specprune,adp,safe estimates each token's importance at a shallow layer and permanently discards less important tokens, directly shortening the sequence processed by subsequent layers. Because pruning is irreversible, aggressive pruning ratios tend to remove task-relevant tokens, sharply degrading accuracy. Token reuse~ vlacache,lac,gatedcache,tvcache instead identifies tokens that remain largely unchanged from the previous frame and reuses their key-value (KV) caches. However, these caches were computed in the context of the previous frame; as the scene changes, they become stale. Repeatedly reusing those stale KV caches causes errors to accumulate and severely degrades accuracy. We argue that applying a single operation uniformly to all tokens outside the recomputed set inevitably sacrifices accuracy or wastes computation (Fig.~ fig:1 ). Consider a token that is important but unchanged: pruning can only recompute it, wasting computation on information already in the cache, or discard it, losing information the model needs. Reuse, conversely, retains unimportant tokens that could have been discarded, and keeps serving cached states even after they have become stale. To our knowledge, no prior VLA acceleration method chooses between the two per token: every existing method either prunes or reuses all of the visual tokens it does not recompute (Section~ sec:related ). When, then, should a token that is not recomputed be reused, and when should it be pruned? Answering this requires a per-token signal that is available before the deep layers run, costs no extra computation, and predicts whether serving a cached state will distort the action. We use drift, the relative change in a token's shallow-layer value since its cache was last computed. Similar change measures have been used to choose which tokens to recompute~ eventful,cacheblend , but prior works have not studied whether such a signal can decide between reuse and pruning. We examine it with a token-level diagnostic (Section~ sec:diagnostic ), a controlled experiment that handles the same tokens once by reuse and once by pruning and compares each resulting action with that of full recomputation. On both backbones we tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas as drift rises beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4 the action error of pruning, regardless of token importance. The threshold depends on the backbone, and rerunning the diagnostic on a new backbone provides it. This finding separates the roles of two per-token signals. Cache validity, which requires drift below the threshold and a bounded cache age, decides whether a token that is not recomputed should be reused or pruned. Importance, the attention a token receives from the action-decoding tokens, decides where the limited recomputation budget should go: to important tokens whose caches are no longer valid, for which neither reuse nor pruning is adequate. We therefore propose a three-set structure that assigns each visual token to recomputation, reuse, or pruning based on its importance and cache validity. Within a given recomputation budget, important tokens with invalid caches are recomputed first; among the remaining tokens, those with valid caches are reused and the others are pruned. Experiments on two VLA backbones and two benchmarks, with latency measured on a Jetson AGX Orin, show that \ achieves success rates comparable to state-of-the-art pruning and reuse methods at similar compute while reducing prefill latency by up to 48 . Its advantage grows as the recomputation budget shrinks: on LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, \ stays within 3 \ of full recomputation when recomputing only 11 of the visual tokens, and at 7 it outperforms the strongest baseline by 24.4 . Our contributions are as follows: A token-level diagnostic showing that whether a non-recomputed token should be reused or pruned depends on its drift, regardless of its importance, which makes both prune-only and reuse-only methods suboptimal. , a three-set structure that assigns each visual token to recomputation, reuse, or pruning, with prune-only and reuse-only methods as its two extremes. Experiments on two backbones and two benchmarks showing that \ stays within 3 \ of full recomputation while reducing prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48 . RELATED WORK sec:related Vision-language-action models. VLA models adapt pretrained vision-language models to map camera images and a language instruction to robot actions, decoding them as discrete tokens~ openvla , as a continuous chunk in a single forward pass~ oft , or with a flow-matching action expert~ pi0,pi05 . In all of them, visual tokens dominate the backbone's input (256 per step for OpenVLA and 512 for OpenVLA-OFT), so reducing their cost benefits every decoding style. Quantization~ qvla , layer skipping~ mole,deer , compact backbones~ smolvla , and asynchronous execution~ smolvla,rtc,jetsonpi are orthogonal and can be combined with our method. Visual token pruning. VLM methods prune tokens that receive little shallow-layer attention~ fastv,sparsevlm , merge similar tokens~ tome,vidtldr , or keep compact subsets selected by attention or diversity~ pyramiddrop,visionzip,divprune . VLA methods add temporal and action cues: smoothed action-decode attention~ vlapruner , deep-layer attention from the previous step~ specprune , motion-adaptive ratios~ adp , forecast saliency~ safe , model scheduling~ spvla , or learned selection~ lightvla . FlashVLA~ flashvla and EfficientVLA~ efficientvla also reuse whole actions or action-head features, yet among visual tokens they too discard every token they do not keep, including tokens whose caches are still accurate. Temporal reuse. Video models and serving systems avoid recomputing unchanged inputs: Eventful Transformers~ eventful and D\'ej\`a Vu~ dejavu reuse per-token computation across frames, AutoGaze~ autogaze removes redundant patches before the ViT, and CacheBlend~ cacheblend , H O~ h2o , and DyCoke~ dycoke reuse, evict, or merge KV entries. For VLAs, VLA-Cache~ vlacache reuses the KV caches of static patches, and later methods learn the reuse policy~ lac , gate it by action confidence~ gatedcache , select reuse heads and layers~ tvcache , or fuse past and current tokens~ ttf . In all of these VLA methods, every visual token that is not recomputed is reused, even after its cache has become stale. Our work. Prune-only and reuse-only methods send every token outside the recomputed set to a single fate. \ instead decides per token among recomputation, reuse, and pruning: it reuses accurate caches that pruning would discard, retaining their information without computation, and prunes stale caches that reuse would keep. Both families are thus special cases of its partition. title: Dual Gradient Consensus for Adaptive Learning to Transient Out-of-Distribution Disturbances in Quadrotor Control
summary: Quadrotor trajectory tracking under unmodeled disturbances often relies on online residual adaptation, but short out-domain residuals can corrupt the learned disturbance model when constant-step updates treat every residual gradient uniformly. We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size. DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with $L_1$-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.

DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with -augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases. Introduction sec:intro Future aerial robots are expected to track planned trajectories accurately in complex and cluttered near-ground settings, including infrastructure inspection, last-mile delivery, search and rescue, precision agriculture, mapping and surveying, and urban air mobility, under unmodeled and often systematically unknown disturbances~ marshall2021survey,cohen2021urban,ahmed2025uam,tacconi2026taxonomy . In such settings, high-speed flight brings unexpected transient events---an inadvertent low-energy collision, a gust strike, brief contact with surrounding structures, leaves ingested by a rotor, or an in-flight motor fault---after which the vehicle must still be controllable rather than only regulated about the original plan~ loquercio2021learning,sun2021incremental,mao2024propeller . It is challenging to track the planned trajectory accurately while remaining controllable after such transients. Unknown, time-varying disturbances come in two forms that should not be treated alike: persistent, non-stationary domain changes---changes in aerodynamic loading, a payload that shifts the center of mass in flight, or transitions between regimes with and without ground effect---and the short-lived transients noted above~ tal2020accurate,hanover2021performance,huang2023datt . A common remedy is online adaptation of a disturbance estimate or an environment representation, allowing the controller to continuously account for the residual dynamics encountered during deployment~ slotine1991applied,krstic1995nonlinear,ioannou1996robust,wu2023mathcal,kumar2021rma,huang2023datt,zhou2025simultaneous,zhou2026efficient . That strategy, however, is itself subject to a mixed-residual issue: the adaptation stream mixes samples that characterize the current in-domain with short out-domain events, and excessive adaptation to the latter causes transient effects to be incorporated into the learned disturbance model rather than treated as temporary deviations. The remaining issue is therefore how to keep adapting when the domain truly changes, without letting short out-domain residuals rewrite the learned disturbance model. The current state of the art spans several approaches. Robust control bounds tracking error against worst-case disturbances without identifying a residual online~ zhou1998essentials,mayne2005robust,zhou2023safe,martin2024guarantees,liu2024robust . Classical adaptive control updates coefficients of prescribed basis functions~ slotine1991applied,krstic1995nonlinear,ioannou1996robust , while disturbance observers, estimators, and related schemes estimate additive residuals for feedback compensation~ tal2020accurate,wu2023mathcal,tao2024robust,das2024robust,hanover2021performance,boffi2021regret,boffi2022nonparametric,jia2023evolver,huang2023datt , typically through a low-pass frequency split rather than a test of whether the residual is a persistent domain change or a short out-domain residual. Learning-based controllers train policies over randomized environments~ tobin2017domain,ramos2019bayessim,lee2020learning,li2025reinforcement,sanchez2018real or condition them on environment encoders, as in RMA and DATT~ kumar2021rma,xue2026robust,zhang2025learning,huang2023datt,farahani2021brief,ben2006analysis . Online non-stochastic control updates sequentially under adversarial disturbances~ hazan2022introduction,agarwal2019online,zhao2022non,zhou2023safecdc,zhou2023saferal,zhou2023efficient . Predictive residual models have also been used for model-based control~ zhou2025simultaneous,tsiamis2024predictive,zhou2025adaptive : MPC~(RFF) adapts random-feature coefficients and kernel bandwidth online~ rahimi2007random,rahimi2008uniform,zhou2025simultaneous , while DAPL applies constant-step least squares to the same pair~ zhou2026efficient , so in-domain and out-domain residuals enter the update at a uniform rate. Direct online policy learning on hardware has been shown~ wu2023daydreamer,nan2025efficient,pan2026learning . However, residual adaptation typically uses a uniform step. This paper builds on the main pipeline of Domain-Adaptive Policy Learning~(DAPL)~ zhou2026efficient ---the RFF residual model, offline BPTT policy, and online least-squares loss---and develops a consensus-driven step-size adaptation for updating the RFF parameters that represent the unknown disturbance. We propose Dual Gradient Consensus~(DGC), overviewed in~ . Two residual-gradient memories, a long-term gradient representing the current domain and a short-term gradient capturing recent evolution, classify each incoming gradient into four adaptation regimes and modulate its update step without altering the gradient itself. Unlike CAdam, which gates Adam coordinates for neural recommenders when the gradient and momentum disagree~ wang2025cadam , DGC is a consensus map on the residual step length. In-domain agreement preserves the long-term memory and applies a consensus-modulated step; disagreement with both memories suppresses the update; persistent agreement with the short-term memory triggers a handoff to the new domain. Relative to MPC~(RFF)~ zhou2025simultaneous and DAPL~ zhou2026efficient , the residual features and least-squares objective remain unchanged, while the kernel parameters continue to adapt online. The resulting controller retains the same policy as DAPL while limiting the incorporation of short out-domain residuals into the kernel parameters and preserving adaptation to domain shifts. We evaluate the method in numerical quadrotor trajectory-tracking simulations under mixed in-domain and out-domain disturbances~ . Four disturbance profiles combine an in-domain component with impulsive transients: a steady level change, a zero in-domain residual with repeated impulses, a periodic shift, and a linear ramp. We compare Dual Gradient Consensus with MPC~(L1-E)~ huang2023datt , MPC~(RFF)~ zhou2025simultaneous , DAPL~ zhou2026efficient , and DAPL without and updates. Across all four cases, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE; the advantage is largest under repeated impulses, where constant-step DAPL incorporates transient disturbances into the residual model, while the MPC variants perform well on a stationary offset but degrade under domain shifts. Time histories of residual prediction error, position tracking error, and the applied step sizes are reported together with the RMSE comparison in~ . title: The German Tank Problem & Navigating by Scent
summary: A robot searching for the source of an odor must eventually answer a deceptively hard question: have I arrived? Near the source, concentration gradients flatten, turbulence makes the signal intermittent, and a small robot often lacks the positional accuracy to map the plume. Here, we describe a lightweight remedy inspired by a World War II statistics conundrum: the German tank problem. To approximate enemy armament production, Allied analysts developed an estimator based on serial numbers from captured tanks. Analogously, we use the same procedure over sampled chemical sensor readings from a robot to create estimates for the peak concentration of an odor plume, and therefore the odor's source. Treating each sensor reading as an observation, our unbiased estimator needs only a running maximum and a sample counter. An exact confidence bound turns both numbers into a principled rule that the robot or UAV can use to determine whether to keep searching for the plume source or land. We derive the estimator and its bound, demonstrate its sample efficiency, and examine its robustness even when its assumptions fail. Finally, we summarize the estimator's role as the termination criterion for olfactory navigation.

Finally, we summarize the estimator's role as the termination criterion for olfactory navigation. height 0.4pt 2pt Date:\; 23 October 2026 \\ Version:\; v2.0 \\ Companion paper:\; Chasing Ghosts \\ Correspondence:\; kordel@scentience.ai \\ Access:\; Scentience API \\ Introduction sec:intro In any navigation task, a robot must have termination criteria for knowing it has arrived at its destination. One of the most difficult problems for a robot navigating by scent is having it estimate when it is ``done''. In other words, how does the robot know when it has reached the global source of the odor, and not just a local maximum concentration of the plume? In the most simplistic perspective, this is analogous to one trying to climb a mountain in the fog without the ability to ever see the top - how would one know if they have reached it? If a robot is indeed near the source but does not yet know, it may circle around trying to maximize the gradient, in turn distorting the plume and creating more turbulence in the process. Declaring ``done'' is hard for compounding reasons. A typical undisturbed plume becomes simultaneously more concentrated and more homogeneous toward its source. Before we formalized the algorithm in this paper, our olfaction-only UAV would spend several seconds circling the source, chasing ever-smaller gradients~ france2026chasing . Many times, this distorted the plume so much that it created currents that pulled the UAV away from the source it was already near, and drained more of the battery. Coupled with the known drift of chemical sensors ~ dennler2022drift , this mandates a sense of urgency for the robot to find the odor source as fast and with as little movement as possible. Turbulent plumes arrive as whiffs separated by blanks~ celani2014odor,crimaldi2022active, schmuker2016exploiting , so no single reading can be decisive by itself. In addition, small platforms often cannot precisely indicate where a sample was taken: on our UAV, payload-induced bias in the inertial measurement unit made long-horizon position estimates unusable~ france2026chasing,france2025oiocalib , ruling out methods that fuse concentrations with sample locations. Concentration-based maps hold little utility in environments with wind or HVAC systems due to the constant change in chemistry, and a robot may also not know what concentration to expect at the source. Termination criteria are therefore warranted to help the robot know whether it has arrived at the plume source or should keep searching. There is a classic estimation procedure developed in World War II that models this well: the German tank problem. The German Tank Problem sec:tanks Beginning in 1943, the Economic Warfare Division of the U.S.\ Embassy in London studied the serial numbers on captured German equipment, from tires to tanks, trucks, guns, and rockets, to estimate total enemy production~ ruggles1947empirical . For tanks, the most useful numbers were on gearboxes, which typically ran in continuous sequences. Conventional intelligence consistently produced inaccurate predictions. Statisticians at the embassy developed an estimation procedure to help produce more reliable metrics as a result. For June 1940, this estimator put monthly tank production at 169, against a conventional intelligence estimate of 1 , 000; German records examined after the war showed there were truly 122 tanks. For June 1941, these respective figures were 244, 1 , 550, and 271, and for August 1942, there were 327, 1 , 550, and 342~ ruggles1947empirical . The estimator proved so successful that it was later carried forward by other intelligence groups among more scenarios. Leo A. Goodman formalized the estimator for the public within his 1952 paper ``Serial Number Analysis'' ~ goodman1952serial . The estimator follows from a simple argument. Suppose tanks are numbered and distinct tanks are captured at random, with representing the largest serial number among them. We can divide the serial numbers by to create gaps (counting the stretch below the smallest), which together hold the unseen serial numbers, or per gap on average. Nothing distinguishes the unseen stretch above from the others, so we add one additional gap for the average: Formally, the probability that the observed serial number is indeed the largest serial number can be calculated by for . We can then calculate the expected value, , where is unbiased. is a complete and sufficient statistic, which effectively means it is the best estimator that captures all knowledge needed to estimate the desired value. Due to this, can be considered as the minimum-variance unbiased estimator~ goodman1952serial,lehmann1998theory , with . In consequence, there is a characteristic of Equation ~ that really matters for robots navigating by scent. Everything the sample says about the estimated number of tanks can be characterized by two numbers: the maximum observed serial number and the number of captured tanks . As we will show in the next section, the requirement to maintain only two numbers to estimate ``done'' creates a very computationally efficient algorithm that can run on virtually any platform - a highly desirable feature for robotics. From Tanks to Odor Packets sec:packets Odor source localization is commonly split into three sub-problems: detecting a plume, staying in contact with it while moving upwind, and declaring that the source has been reached~ hayes2002distributed,kowadlo2008robot (we call this, the ``termination criteria''). The first two have drawn most of the attention within literature, from bio-inspired surge-and-cast controllers and bout detection~ schmuker2016exploiting,shigaki2018design to information-seeking search~ vergassola2007infotaxis , probabilistic source-term estimation~ hutchinson2017review , and learned policies~ singh2023emergent , with aerial implementations in~ burgues2019smelling,duisterhof2021sniffy (see~ francis2022gas for a recent thorough review). The termination criteria receive far less research attention, yet it decides whether a search ends in success or in a robot spending additional time and energy circling a few meters from its goal. Surprisingly, this outcome has a large reciprocal influence on the complexity of the algorithms required to perceive and navigate leading up to the termination criteria. This can result in either success or failure for the robot, which makes the problem worth solving. An odor plume is a stream of filaments, or packets, carrying a compound (or series of compounds) downwind from its emitter. At each sampling instant, a chemical sensor reports the concentration of the air packet currently passing over it.
