title: What Does World Modeling Actually Improve in Robot Action Learning?
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts. We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively. Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision. We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for $π_{0.5}$, where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%. These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.

We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision. We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for , where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94 to 89.19 . These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine vision-language pretraining with robot data to learn policies that generate actions from visual observations and language instructions~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,ghosh2024octo,black2024pi0 . Building on this foundation, World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate future visual prediction into action learning, training models to predict environmental changes alongside robot actions. Methods such as GR-1, GR-2, PAD, and InternW0 integrate these objectives through different architectures, demonstrating the potential of future prediction to support robot action learning~ wu2024gr1,cheang2024gr2,guo2024pad,cai2026internw0 . However, improvements in task success alone do not reveal which aspects of policy execution benefit from predictive supervision, nor do they establish that the model has acquired transferable understanding of its environment. Prior work provides an important starting point for understanding these effects. Fast-WAM separately examines video co-training during training and future generation at inference, finding that removing the former leads to a larger drop in action performance~ yuan2026fastwam . This finding supports the value of predictive supervision during training, but final success rates do not reveal how the gains manifest in execution behavior or to what extent they persist across models, tasks, and environments. Rather than simply revisiting whether video prediction improves task success, we investigate where the benefits of predictive supervision appear and under which conditions they persist. This distinction matters for assessing the practical value of future prediction and determining how such supervision should be used in subsequent model designs. To investigate these questions, we conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within two WAM families, FastWAM and OpenWAM. Within each family, we keep the architecture, initialization, robot training data, and number of training steps fixed, varying only whether the future-video prediction loss is included. We first evaluate execution success on seen tasks under clean conditions. We then use trajectory clustering to examine changes in the frequencies of coarse trajectory patterns and their within-cluster success rates, providing behavioral evidence beyond aggregate success. We further vary task identity and environment configuration separately to assess whether the gains persist on unseen tasks and under environmental randomization. Together, these comparisons distinguish improvements in familiar-task execution, observable changes in behavior, and the conditions under which predictive supervision remains beneficial. These analyses also raise a practical design question: if future-video prediction provides useful training supervision, does obtaining its benefits necessarily require a large pretrained video-generation model? To examine this, we introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for the existing VLA model ~ black2025pi05 . We compare the original policy with variants equipped with either a lightweight Transformer predictor or a pretrained Wan DiT video-generation branch. Both auxiliary prediction branches are used only during training and removed at inference. This comparison tests whether a lightweight predictor can improve action performance without introducing a large pretrained video DiT branch. Figure~ fig:overview summarizes our research questions, experimental design, and main findings. Our experiments reveal a clear distinction between the benefits of predictive supervision and the conditions under which they persist. Across ten seen tasks under clean conditions, adding the future-video prediction loss increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points for FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively, demonstrating substantial execution gains in both WAM families. Trajectory analysis further shows that within-cluster success rates increase for several coarse trajectory clusters even when their frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in shifts in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks depend on the model and task, while both WAMs exhibit low absolute success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, with no consistent advantage from predictive supervision. For , the training-only lightweight predictor increases success from 82.94 to 89.19 , showing that auxiliary prediction can provide positive gains in this setting without a large pretrained video DiT branch. These findings indicate that future-video prediction can provide effective supervision for action learning, but its benefits on familiar tasks, their manifestations in execution behavior, and their persistence under distribution shifts must be evaluated separately rather than inferred from aggregate success alone. The lightweight auxiliary predictor further shows that obtaining benefits from future prediction does not necessarily require a large video-generation backbone. Our results therefore provide empirical guidance for selecting training objectives in future WAMs and VLAs: predictive supervision should be evaluated in terms of its observed execution gains and the conditions under which they hold, rather than assuming that predictive capability, transfer performance, and prediction-model scale are necessarily linked. Related Work sec:related_work Future Prediction in Robot Action Learning. World Action Models (WAMs) combine future visual prediction with action generation, enabling robot policies to model future environmental changes alongside control actions. GR-1 and GR-2 integrate video pretraining with joint prediction of future visual observations and robot actions~ wu2024gr1,cheang2024gr2 , while PAD jointly models future images and actions through a denoising process~ guo2024pad . InternW0 adopts an asymmetric architecture, using a high-capacity video expert to model visual dynamics and a lighter action expert for control~ cai2026internw0 . These approaches illustrate different ways of combining future prediction with action learning, but the role of predictive information differs across systems. An important distinction is whether future prediction serves as auxiliary supervision during training or explicitly informs action generation at inference time. The former influences learning through an additional prediction objective, whereas the latter uses predicted future observations or intermediate goals to guide subsequent actions. For example, CoT-VLA generates visual subgoals at inference time and uses them as intermediate conditions for action prediction~ zhao2025cotvla . These two approaches can coexist within a single system, but their contributions to action performance should be distinguished. Our study focuses on the benefits of adding a future-video prediction loss during training, rather than planning with explicitly predicted future states at inference. Understanding the Role of Predictive Supervision. Beyond developing joint visual prediction and action generation models, recent studies have examined the specific contributions of future prediction within WAMs. Fast-WAM separately investigates video co-training during training and future generation at inference, finding that removing the former leads to a larger decline in action performance~ yuan2026fastwam . This provides direct evidence for the value of predictive supervision during training. OpenWAM systematically studies design choices involving generative backbones, visual representations, world-action interactions, and training strategies, examining how different configurations affect world-action learning~ wang2026openwam . Together, these studies highlight that WAM performance depends not only on future prediction but also on architectural choices, information exchange, and training configurations. It is therefore important to distinguish performance differences between complete systems from the contribution of a specific predictive training objective. Although Fast-WAM demonstrates that video co-training improves action performance in its system, aggregate success rates alone do not reveal how these gains manifest in execution behavior. Higher success may accompany changes in the frequencies of different trajectory patterns or arise within similar trajectory patterns. Likewise, improvements on familiar tasks do not establish whether the benefits persist under task or environmental changes. We extend this line of investigation through controlled future-video prediction loss comparisons within two WAM families, FastWAM and OpenWAM, complemented by coarse-grained trajectory analysis and evaluations under distribution shifts. Our study characterizes the execution gains, observable behavioral differences, and conditions under which predictive supervision remains beneficial, without attributing these observations to a specific internal control mechanism. Auxiliary Prediction and Model Design. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models improve robot policies through vision-language pretraining, robot data, and action generation objectives. RT-2 explores transferring vision-language knowledge to robotic control~ zitkovich2023rt2 , while OpenVLA, Open X-Embodiment, and Octo advance generalist policy learning from heterogeneous robot datasets~ kim2024openvla,openx2023,ghosh2024octo . For action generation, uses flow matching to model continuous actions, while further combines heterogeneous co-training with high-level semantic prediction to improve performance in open-world settings~ black2024pi0,black2025pi05 . The high-level semantic prediction in differs in its supervision target from the future-video prediction studied here. We investigate whether adding future visual prediction to an existing VLA training setup can provide useful auxiliary supervision for action learning. Future prediction need not involve direct RGB video generation. title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
summary: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs. Furthermore, RAB enables systematic comparisons of standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures under a unified planning-execution-verification framework. Extensive experiments reveal substantial gaps between manipulation and autonomy, demonstrate the advantages of agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and highlight the remaining challenges toward open-world robot autonomy.
full_text: Introduction intro Embodied AI has advanced rapidly in recent years, with vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) demonstrating increasingly strong manipulation capabilities across diverse tasks and environments~ intelligence2025pi_, ye2026world, team2026xiaomi, wu2026foundation, cai2026internvla, xu2026causalwm, shao2026causalwam . These advances raise a fundamental question: How far are we from deploying robots in the open world? Unlike predefined manipulation tasks, the real world involves numerous mundane yet complex challenges, often characterized by ambiguity, uncertainty, and constantly changing circumstances~ liu2025robopilot, pchelintsev2025lera, gong2026replan . Consider a household robot preparing for guests: it must identify what needs to be cleaned, select appropriate food based on user preferences, coordinate multiple activities, and recover when manipulation attempts fail~ mao2026cris0 . Such challenges are not exceptional, but intrinsic to everyday physical environments. Addressing them is essential for transforming robots into broadly useful assistants in human environments. Operating in the open world demands a transition from robot manipulation to robot autonomy. Beyond executing explicit instructions, robots must autonomously discover relevant tasks, reason about environmental and user context, plan physical interactions, and adapt to unexpected outcomes. Robot agents provide a natural framework for this transition, integrating high-level reasoning and planning with physical execution and feedback-driven verification into a closed loop~ team2026systematically, shi2025hi, ahn2022can, huang2022inner . Such agents must determine not only how to execute, but also what to do and how to adapt. Meanwhile, advances in multimodal foundation models, including GPT-6-Astra, and emerging agentic embodied systems~ team2025gemini, yang2025agentic, bjorck2026vesta, chen2026eta are creating new opportunities to realize this integration. Together, these developments suggest that embodied AI is entering a new stage, shifting from standalone manipulation models toward autonomous robot agents capable of handling complex, dynamic physical environments. However, existing benchmarks remain largely designed for robot manipulation rather than autonomy. Widely adopted benchmarks~ rlbench, metaworld, maniskill2, libero, robocasa, mu2024robotwin, robotwin2 primarily evaluate predefined tasks with explicit goals, overlooking autonomous task discovery and context-dependent decision-making. Recent efforts extend evaluation toward reasoning~ chen2026robodojo and long-horizon planning~ alfred, alfworld, realfred, embodiedbench, mao2025deliverybench , but often rely on stylized problems or abstracted physical interactions. More importantly, reasoning, planning, and manipulation are frequently evaluated in isolation, without capturing their interdependence during real-world operation. A robot capable of individual tasks may still struggle to determine what needs to be done, recover from failures, or adapt to human interventions. Evaluating open-world robot autonomy therefore requires moving beyond isolated capabilities toward a comprehensive assessment of the entire autonomous interaction loop. To bridge this gap, we introduce RobotAgentBench~(RAB), a benchmark for evaluating open-world robot autonomy in realistic household environments. We develop an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline to reconstruct real-world scenes and expand them into 50 diverse layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks. At its core, RAB provides 90 atomic tasks that can be flexibly composed into a wide range of household tasks, from which we construct 18 short-horizon and 8 long-horizon manipulation tasks as the foundation of our evaluation. Building upon these tasks, we introduce diverse variants and evaluation settings to systematically assess five complementary dimensions of robot autonomy: (1) task discovery, identifying what needs to be done; (2) context reasoning, interpreting implicit requirements; (3) manipulation, executing physical actions; (4) failure recovery, detecting and correcting execution errors; and (5) robustness, adapting to environmental disturbances. Beyond these task-level assessments, we introduce four open-ended household scenarios that require robot agents to integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs, enabling an end-to-end evaluation of open-world robot autonomy. Using RobotAgentBench, we systematically evaluate standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures, revealing five key findings: 0pt 0pt Standalone policies struggle with task discovery and contextual reasoning despite their manipulation capabilities, highlighting the gap between manipulation and autonomy; Coding-agent harnesses substantially improve performance, particularly through hybrid code-based and learned-policy execution; Both planner capabilities and executor instruction-following abilities critically influence agent performance; Harness-level recursive self-improvement (RSI) progressively improves task- and scenario-level performance through reusable tool refinement and experience accumulation; Real-world evaluations reveal performance degradation but broadly consistent relative rankings, supporting the benchmark's relevance to physical deployment. Together, these findings highlight the promise and remaining challenges of advancing from robot manipulation toward open-world robot autonomy. RobotAgentBench sec:robot_agent_arena We introduce RobotAgentBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate open-world robot autonomy beyond predefined manipulation tasks. We leverage a real-to-sim pipeline to construct diverse environments and collect data, then build the multi-level evaluation suite for systematic comparisons of diverse agent framework designs. Figure~ fig:RobotAgentBench illustrates the overview of our benchmark. Real-to-Sim Pipeline for Environment and Data Construction To enable realistic and scalable evaluation, we develop an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline that starts from a physical room in a real home, reconstructs it in simulation, expands the reconstructed scene into diverse interactive configurations, and collects demonstrations for training and evaluation. Environment Construction Starting from a physical room in a real home, we first reconstruct it in Isaac Sim and then expand it into diverse household environments. We subsequently collect real-robot demonstrations and reproduce them in simulation to generate trajectories. Household Scene Reconstruction. We reconstruct the physical household environment in Isaac Sim through an iterative pipeline comprising real-world parameter collection, similar asset retrieval, and new asset reconstruction. First, we collect photographs and measurements of the room layout, furniture arrangements, and household objects to establish real-world references. Next, a coding agent retrieves similar 3D assets from online repositories and adjusts their geometry, scale, and appearance to match these references. For objects without suitable existing assets, we leverage the agent to directly reconstruct their geometry and textures from photographs. The resulting assets are assembled into the simulated environment with appropriate collision geometry and physical properties to support realistic interactions. Throughout this iterative process, human reviewers continuously validate visual fidelity and physical interaction consistency against the real-world environment, providing feedback to the agent for refining the reconstructed scene. Environment Augmentation. Building upon the reconstructed home, we systematically diversify its spatial configurations and visual appearances. We generate 50 distinct layouts by modifying floor plans (e.g., T-shaped and L-shaped configurations), rearranging functional areas, and varying furniture positions and orientations. Each layout is manually reviewed to eliminate geometric inconsistencies and implausible arrangements. We further increase environmental diversity through variations in furniture colors, textures, materials, and interior design styles. Demonstration Collection We follow a three-stage workflow comprising real-world demonstration collection, simulation alignment, and agent-assisted trajectory expansion to generate scalable, physically grounded data. First, we adopt the AgiBot G1 as the robot embodiment, matching its camera configurations and joint settings between simulation and the physical platform, and collect teleoperated demonstrations in the real home. Second, we replay these demonstrations in simulation, iteratively refining asset geometry and physical parameters to align interaction outcomes with the real world. Finally, building upon these reference trajectories, we employ a coding agent to generate additional successful trajectories across diverse object positions, environment layouts, and initial robot configurations. With access to the full simulator state, including object poses, the agent synthesizes and executes action programs to accomplish target tasks. For challenging interactions, we provide manually implemented control functions that the agent can invoke and compose. This workflow enables scalable trajectory generation while maintaining consistency with real-world demonstrations. Detailed observation and action spaces are provided in Appendix~ app:benchmark_setup . Multi-level Evaluation of Robot Autonomy Open-world robot autonomy requires robots to determine what needs to be done, execute physical tasks, and adapt to unexpected outcomes. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, RAB adopts a multi-level evaluation suite built upon a composable household task foundation. At the task level, we introduce dedicated evaluation settings to diagnose five complementary capabilities: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness. At the scenario level, we assess whether robot agents can integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs in open-ended household environments. Together, these two levels enable both fine-grained capability assessment and end-to-end evaluation of robot autonomy. Composable Household Task Suite We construct a foundational task suite comprising 90 atomic tasks involving everyday household objects and appliances. These tasks can be flexibly composed into diverse household tasks, from which we construct 18 representative short-horizon tasks and 8 long-horizon composite tasks. The suite covers common activities, such as retrieving food from a refrigerator, heating meals in a microwave, and using an air fryer. These tasks involve diverse manipulation skills, including pushing, pulling, bimanual coordination, and mobile manipulation, across rigid objects, deformable materials (e.g., tablecloths), and granular materials (e.g., coffee beans). Short-horizon tasks combine a few atomic tasks, such as picking up a hat from a sofa and hanging it on a coat rack, while long-horizon tasks involve multiple subgoals, such as tidying an entire sofa area. Building upon this task suite, we construct diverse evaluation settings by varying task instructions, contextual requirements, initial states, and environmental disturbances. These variants enable targeted assessments of different autonomy capabilities without requiring entirely new manipulation tasks. We further compose these tasks into open-ended household scenarios, where the tasks to be performed depend on the environment and user context. For each atomic task and short-horizon task, we collect 50 training trajectories; for each long-horizon task and open-ended scenario, we provide 10 complete demonstrations. In total, the dataset comprises 101.8 hours of training data. Further details are provided in Figure~ fig:DataPipeline . Task-level Capability Evaluation We design f

title: Benchmarking Obstacle-Conditioned Safety in Household Robot Navigation
summary: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the \emph{Semantic Sensitivity Index} (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in \emph{semantic-to-motion grounding}, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
full_text: .toc main Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce , an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in semantic-to-motion grounding, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion. Introduction sec:intro As robots are moving from industrial settings into homes, they must navigate around people, pets, and objects with different safety implications~ householdrobot6,householdrobot1,householdrobot2,householdrobot7,householdrobot3,householdrobot4,iso13482 . Safe navigation around such entities requires , which goes beyond collision avoidance: a robot must adapt its motion to each obstacle's safety implications and to how closely its route passes it. As illustrated in , even when both paths are collision-free, a robot should keep more clearance and move more slowly past a child than past a trash bin, and slow down further as it gets closer. This caution must also be selective, since uniform conservatism toward every obstacle would needlessly sacrifice efficiency. Achieving this requires semantic-to-motion grounding: a policy must infer an appropriate level of caution from an obstacle's semantics and translate it into clearance, proximity-dependent speed, and executed motion. Foundation models are natural candidates: VLMs can interpret safety-relevant semantics to inform motion planning, and VLAs generate actions directly from visual observations and language instructions. Although both are widely used in robotic systems~ huang2023voxposer, nasiriany2024pivot, nvidia2025gr00tn1, nvidia2025gr00tn15, intelligence2025pi05 , it remains unclear whether their executed trajectories exhibit this capability. Existing evaluations do not answer this question. Human-aware and social-navigation benchmarks~ 24HAVLN,25HAVLN2,biswas2022socnavbench,fang2026obstaclestoetiquette measure executed motion but focus on navigation around people, not on whether motion is calibrated to the safety implications of diverse obstacles. Embodied-safety evaluations for foundation models~ zhang2025badrobot,ye2024asimov,chen2025safemind,lu2026isbench,huang2025annie instead assess task completion, constraint compliance, or refusal of hazardous instructions, not whether semantic safety distinctions appear in continuous motion. Evaluating semantic-to-motion grounding requires two components: spatially matched comparisons that isolate obstacle identity from route geometry, and a metric that tests whether motion follows the expected ordering of caution across obstacles. We introduce , an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark that provides both. Its matched comparisons vary only the obstacle type while fixing the obstacle position, surrounding layout and route, and are repeated across diverse layouts and routes. The obstacles span three caution tiers---Living, Fragile, and Robust, in descending order of expected caution---motivated by ISO risk assessment principles~ iso12100 and social navigation research~ althoff2012safety, marvel2017implementing, moller2021survey, singamaneni2023survey . We also introduce the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), a diagnostic metric that tests whether clearance, together with speed and smoothness as a function of distance to the obstacle, follows this ordering. Together, assess whether a policy adapts its motion to an obstacle's safety implications, beyond merely reaching the goal without collision. Using , we find that VLM- and VLA-based policies do not consistently exhibits this adaptation, even with explicit safety prompting. Our analysis on VLM shows that safety-relevant distinctions are accessible during isolated motion-parameter inference but weaken when task-execution code and motion parameters are jointly generated; separating the two improves motion adaptation. For VLAs, prompting and action-selection interventions provide only limited recovery, highlighting insufficient semantic-to-motion grounding across both policy families. In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce , a simulation benchmark that evaluates obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation through matched comparisons: each comparison varies only the obstacle while holding spatial conditions fixed, and is repeated across diverse layouts and routes. (2) We propose Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI) which quantifies the extent to which differences in executed motion across obstacle follow the expected caution ordering. (3) We identify insufficient semantic-to-motion grounding in the evaluated VLM- and VLA-based policies: safety-relevant knowledge is available but does not reliably guide executed motion, highlighting the need to improve how semantic safety judgments inform motion decisions. Related Works sec:related_works Safety Evaluation in Embodied Robotics. Existing evaluations examine both navigation behavior and the safety of task decisions and execution. Social-navigation frameworks evaluate executed trajectories around people~ tsoi2021sean,biswas2022socnavbench , while human-aware navigation consider dynamic human interactions and socially appropriate path selection~ 24HAVLN,25HAVLN2,fang2026obstaclestoetiquette . Complementary evaluations assess navigation-relevant visual reasoning: NaviTrace evaluates image-space navigation traces, SocialNav-SUB examines social scene understanding, and MovSafeBench tests judgments of potentially hazardous scenarios~ windecker2025navitrace,munje2025socialnavsub,taniguchi2026towards . Existing embodied-safety evaluation focus on task decisions and actions satisfy safety requirements. ASIMOV and SAFEMIND assess safety-relevant judgments and reasoning~ ye2024asimov, chen2025safemind , HomeSafe-Bench evaluates unsafe-action detection in videos~ pu2026homesafebench , and IS-Bench evaluates whether agents perform risk-mitigation actions in the appropriate procedural order~ lu2026isbench . BadRobot and ANNIE further examine adversarial robustness to harmful instructions and sensory perturbations, respectively~ zhang2025badrobot,huang2025annie . However, each evaluation paradigm captures only part of the problem: social- and human-aware navigation benchmarks focus primarily on interactions with people, embodied-safety evaluations assess safety judgments rather than executed motion, and neither provides paired comparisons that vary obstacle identity while holding the surrounding spatial configuration fixed. Foundation Models for Robot Planning and Control. Foundation models guide robot policies through different control framework. Policies built on VLM planners let the VLM reason over the scene and instruction, and convert its output into motion through a separate planner or controller. Two representative frameworks are code generation, where the VLM writes a program that sets planner parameters such as obstacle clearance and speed~ liang2023code, huang2023voxposer, huang2024rekep, yu2023language , and waypoint selection, where the VLM picks the next waypoint from candidates annotated on the image~ nasiriany2024pivot, liu2024moka, goetting2024vlmnav . VLA policies, in contrast, output control actions directly~ kim2024openvla, intelligence2025pi05, nvidia2025gr00tn1, nvidia2025gr00tn15, team2026xiaomi . However, these models' ability to adapt their executed motion to different obstacle types remains underexplored. title: Variational Cognitive Memory Abstraction for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown remarkable success in robotic manipulation, yet their ability to execute long-horizon tasks remains limited by insufficient long- term memory modeling. Existing methods either rely on implicit temporal representations within policy networks, where historical information can be gradually diluted, or maintain explicit memory buffers that suffer from redundancy, noise accumulation, and inefficient retrieval. In this paper, we propose CogMemory, a novel variational cognitive memory framework that enables VLA systems to selectively preserve and reuse task-relevant historical information. Our approach encodes multimodal trajectories into compact latent memory representations through a selective state- space memory encoder, multi-slot temporal abstraction, and variational information compression. During action generation, dynamic cross-attention retrieval with gated fusion adaptively incorporates relevant memories into policy prediction. With merely 3.45M additional parameters, CogMemory stays lightweight and seamlessly fits both early- and intermediate-fusion VLA backbones. Extensive experiments on long-horizon robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse VLA backbones.
full_text: Variational Cognitive Memory Abstraction for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models X. Liu, C. Tang, C. Zhang, Q Zeng, W Ju, and J. Xinyu~Liu, Daiying~Tian, Chenwei~Tang, Ruyang~Han, Chengyang~Zhang, Qingyu~Zeng, Wei~Ju, Liangli~Zhen, and~Jiancheng~Lv Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown remarkable success in robotic manipulation, yet their ability to execute long-horizon tasks remains limited by insufficient long-term memory modeling. Existing methods either rely on implicit temporal representations within policy networks, where historical information can be gradually diluted, or maintain explicit memory buffers that suffer from redundancy, noise accumulation, and inefficient retrieval. In this paper, we propose CogMemory, a novel variational cognitive memory framework that enables VLA systems to selectively preserve and reuse task-relevant historical information. Our approach encodes multimodal trajectories into compact latent memory representations through a selective state-space memory encoder, multi-slot temporal abstraction, and variational information compression. During action generation, dynamic cross-attention retrieval with gated fusion adaptively incorporates relevant memories into policy prediction. With merely 3.45M additional parameters, CogMemory stays lightweight and seamlessly fits both early‑ and intermediate‑fusion VLA backbones. Extensive experiments on long-horizon robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse VLA backbones. Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have significantly improved robotic manipulation through large-scale multimodal pretraining zhang2025pure,ma2026survey,sapkota2025vision . Existing VLA systems broadly follow two predominant fusion paradigms, as illustrated in Figure fig:motivation . Early-fusion architectures zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,mees2024octo jointly model vision, language, and actions within unified transformers, yet they lack explicit mechanisms for retaining long-range history—task-relevant cues from early steps are progressively diluted as interaction horizons grow, causing severe performance degradation in multi-stage tasks. Intermediate-fusion approaches, e.g., diffusion ho2020denoising and flow-based lipman2022flow policies black2024pi_0,li2024cogact,reuss2025flower , integrate VLM representations into continuous action generators, but they still rely on implicit temporal modeling within policy networks, where historical information is only passively aggregated through sequential updates. This implicit aggregation remains vulnerable to noise, redundancy, and the gradual decay of early critical signals, making it difficult to preserve long-term dependencies or maintain temporally consistent decisions across extended executions. To overcome these inherent limitations, recent works have introduced explicit memory mechanisms into VLA systems wang2021structured,li2025towards,shi2025memoryvla , typically via external memory banks, recurrent states, or historical token caches retrieved during inference. While these methods improve temporal reasoning, they introduce three critical shortcomings, i.e., i) , direct storage of historical observations or intermediate features incurs severe redundancy and retrieval inefficiency as horizons scale, ii) , existing memory representations lack explicit abstraction, making them susceptible to task-irrelevant or noisy history, and iii) , many such designs are tightly coupled to specific policy backbones, limiting their generality. These drawbacks motivate a lightweight, compact, and backbone-agnostic memory framework that can efficiently abstract long-term task-relevant information without compromising inference speed or architectural flexibility. To address these challenges, we propose CogMemory, a lightweight variational memory abstraction framework tailored for long-horizon VLA models. Unlike conventional memory banks or token caches, CogMemory directly compresses extended histories into compact latent slots through two core mechanisms, i.e., a selective State-Space Model (SSM) that efficiently accumulates long-range temporal information and Variational Information Compression (VIC) that distills task-relevant signals while discarding redundancy. This design directly mitigates . Instead of storing raw observations or intermediate features, we maintain only a handful of structured latent slots, drastically reducing storage and retrieval costs. The SSM’s selective gating and the VIC objective jointly filter out noisy, task-irrelevant history, thereby overcoming and ensuring that only temporally coherent and informative cues are preserved. During action generation, a dynamic cross-attention mechanism coupled with gated fusion allows the policy to query these memory slots on demand, selectively incorporating relevant context while ignoring irrelevant distractions. This further reinforces robustness against noise. Moreover, CogMemory is designed as a plug-and-play module that integrates seamlessly into both early-fusion and intermediate-fusion VLA backbones, as shown in Figure fig:motivation , effectively resolving without requiring invasive modifications to the base policy. We evaluate CogMemory on representative long-horizon robotic manipulation benchmarks across diverse task settings. Experimental results demonstrate that explicit cognitive memory abstraction consistently improves long-horizon manipulation performance across diverse VLA backbones. These results highlight the effectiveness of compact explicit memory abstraction for improving long-horizon robotic decision making. Our contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*, nosep, topsep=0pt] We propose CogMemory, a lightweight variational memory abstraction framework that compresses long-horizon interaction histories into compact latent slots via SSM for efficient temporal accumulation and VIC for redundancy filtering, enabling selective preservation of task-relevant cues while discarding irrelevant history. We design a plug-and-play memory retrieval mechanism based on dynamic cross-attention and gated fusion, which allows the policy to query memory slots on demand and selectively incorporate historical context. This module is backbone-agnostic and seamlessly integrates into both early-fusion and intermediate-fusion VLA architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CogMemory consistently and significantly improves performance across diverse VLA backbones, validating the effectiveness, generality, and lightweight nature of our approach for long-horizon sequential decision-making. Related Work sec:related work VLA models have recently advanced general robotic manipulation by combining large vision-language models radford2021learning,liu2023visual,steiner2024paligemma with large-scale robot datasets o2024open,ebert2021bridge,walke2023bridgedata . Existing VLA approaches formulate robot control as multimodal sequence modeling, where visual observations, language instructions, and robot states are jointly encoded for action prediction. Representative methods like RT-series models brohan2022rt,zitkovich2023rt , OpenVLA kim2024openvla , Octo mees2024octo , black2024pi_0 , CogACT li2024cogact , and FLOWER reuss2025flower , have explored different architectures for representation learning and continuous robot action generation. Despite their strong performance on individual manipulation tasks, long-horizon robotic control remains challenging due to the difficulty of preserving and exploiting relevant historical information over extended interactions. Recent works have introduced explicit memory mechanisms into robotic policies. RoboFlamingo li2024vision propagates compressed vision-language representations through recurrent states, while TraceVLA zheng2025tracevla and Interleave-VLA fan2025interleave encode interaction histories into visual or multimodal sequences. UniVLA bu2025univla incorporates previous actions for temporal reasoning, and MemoryVLA shi2025memoryvla introduces an external memory retrieval mechanism for cognition-guided action generation. However, existing approaches either rely on implicit temporal accumulation or directly cache historical features, which may introduce redundancy and limit scalability for long-horizon manipulation. In contrast, CogMemory explicitly abstracts interaction histories into compact variational memory representations and adaptively retrieves task-relevant information for long-horizon decision making. The abstraction stage sequentially compresses long-horizon interaction histories into compact latent memory slots through three core operations, i.e., i) selective state-space modeling (SSM) for long-range temporal encoding, ii) multi-slot temporal pooling for structured memory consolidation, and iii) variational information compression (VIC) for learning informative and noise-robust latent memory distributions. The action generation stage then retrieves task-relevant memory via cross-attention and adaptively fuses it with current representations through gated fusion, enabling temporally coherent and context-aware decision making. While this suffices for short-horizon tasks, implicit temporal modeling struggles to preserve long-range task-relevant dependencies over extended interaction horizons. title: VLA-HWBench: Where the Time Goes When VLA Models Run on Edge Hardware
summary: Vision--language--action (VLA) models increasingly run on edge devices aboard robots, where inference latency constrains closed-loop robot control. However, it remains unclear how to design VLA models, their inference software and edge hardware so that robots can run VLA inference in real time. Most VLA models report only task success, while prior studies cover limited action-generation strategies, divide inference into at most three stages, and lack comparisons of inference optimizations on the same models.benchmarking 18 open VLA models across released and alternative backends on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, with a seven-stage inference breakdown. Our study reveals three insights. First, action-generation strategy matters more than model size. It dominates 14 of 19 Jetson configurations, latency varies by $82\times$ on Jetson and $157\times$ on AMD, and parameter count explains at most 15% of latency variance. Models that generate long action chunks in a few flow-matching steps keep up with control, whereas token-by-token decoding does not. Second, kernel fusion with 4-bit weights helps most, running $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 2.6--2.9$\times$ faster than PyTorch with \texttt{torch.compile}, but it exists for only these two models and only on the Jetson. Optimization also moves the time to the stages it shortens least, as CPU preprocessing grows from 12\% to 39\% of the GR00T N1.7 call. Third, after optimization, memory bandwidth limits only the stages that process few tokens on the Jetson, such as the denoising steps, whereas software limits all other stages, from unfused kernels to serial preprocessing on the host CPU. Overall, low-latency edge VLAs should use few action-generation iterations, inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit weights to more models and platforms, and edge hardware needs high memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU.

Overall, low-latency edge VLAs should use few action-generation iterations, inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit weights to more models and platforms, and edge hardware needs high memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU. Introduction sec:intro Vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robotic control, mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,octo2024,black2024pi0,groot2025 . Unlike text or image generation, VLA inference operates within a continuously evolving physical system: the robot may continue executing previous commands while objects or obstacles change state or position~ falanga2019howfast,morrison2018ggcnn , causing observations to become stale before the corresponding actions are executed. Practical deployment therefore increasingly calls for low-latency inference close to the robot. This is particularly important when wireless connectivity is variable or intermittent, or when privacy-sensitive camera observations cannot be transmitted to remote servers. Meanwhile, advances in edge compute hardware~ jetsonthor,strixhalo are making on-robot VLA inference increasingly feasible. However, the observation-to-action characteristics of state-of-the-art VLA models on edge devices have not been systematically characterized. Recent studies have begun to characterize VLA inference through measurements on edge and datacenter GPUs crossplatform2025,vlaxpu2026 , profiling of a single architecture vishwanathan2026characterizing and analytical performance models jiang2026vlaperf , but three gaps remain. First, they cover few of the ways in which recent VLAs generate actions. Recent models differ in architecture and training and denoise action chunks by flow matching, decode them in parallel, generate them token by token or reason before acting. These choices change how much sequential work a call performs, but the measured studies cover at most five models and two of these four forms. Second, they divide a call into at most three phases, which cannot show where the time goes. CPU preprocessing, data transfer, vision encoding, prefill and action generation stress different resources, and none of these studies times CPU preprocessing. Third, they do not compare inference optimizations on the same models. None of the four studies evaluates a specialized backend and only one tests low-bit weights, while each backend is evaluated only on the models it targets tensorrt,flashrt,embodiedcpp2026,vlacpp2026 . It thus remains unclear which optimization helps most, which stages it shortens and whether its gain carries over to other models and platforms. To bridge these gaps and provide a systematic basis for practical on-robot deployment, we present , a benchmark for characterizing the complete observation-to-action path of state-of-the-art VLA models on edge devices. is designed to incorporate additional VLA models, inference backends, and edge hardware as the ecosystem evolves. First, to cover the forms of action generation, evaluates 18 widely used open VLA models spanning all four forms, selected based on Hugging Face downloads and community stars, on two architecturally distinct edge platforms, the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395. Each model runs in a common reference configuration using eager PyTorch, with optional optimizations disabled, on the same LIBERO-10 observation~ liu2023libero and timing boundary. Second, to show where the time goes, divides each call into the seven stages of Figure~ fig:stages , timed at the stage boundaries and split by kernels inside CUDA graphs. Third, to study optimizations systematically, enables compilation, specialized backends (TensorRT and FlashRT) and lower precision one at a time on two representative models and attributes each gain to stages. With , we answer three questions. (Q1) Where does the time go in VLA models, and what sets their latency? Without optional optimizations, action generation is the largest stage in 14 of the 19 configurations on the Jetson, and latency ranges from 77\,ms to 6.3\,s on the Jetson ( ) and from 114\,ms to 17.9\,s on the AMD platform ( ), with only 10 and 9 of the 19 configurations generating actions as fast as LIBERO executes them. As Figure~ fig:params shows, a least-squares fit of log latency on log parameter count explains at most 15 of the variance, and latency instead follows the number of iterations of action generation. (Q2) How much do optimizations help, and where does the time move? On the Jetson, compilation, a specialized backend and lower precision make , and faster in turn, in total, and GR00T N1.7 , and , in total. A backend with kernel fusion and 4-bit weights gives the largest gain, 2.6--2.9 over compilation, but exists only for these two models and only on the Jetson. Optimization also moves the time to the stages it shortens least, as CPU preprocessing grows from 12 to 39 of the GR00T N1.7 call. (Q3) What limits the remaining time after optimization? No single resource limits the remaining time. Action generation and other stages with few tokens are memory-bound and on the Jetson already run at more than half of the peak memory bandwidth , whereas vision encoding and long prefills reach only 6--42 of what the hardware allows because of unfused kernels and missing low-precision support, and CPU preprocessing is limited by serial Python and idle-thread wake-ups . Overall, the latency of a VLA on edge hardware is determined jointly by its action-generation method, its runtime backend and the platform rather than by its model size. For future designs, edge VLAs should therefore reduce action-generation iterations, for example through fewer denoising steps or parallel decoding, rather than simply shrink the model; inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit execution, which provide the largest gains, to more models and platforms while optimizing host preprocessing as carefully as GPU execution; and edge hardware should prioritize memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU over peak GPU compute. title: SceneAgent: An Agentic Pipeline from 3D and 4D Captures to Simulation Environments
summary: Visual captures provide detailed scene appearance, but converting them into interactive simulation environments requires object reconstruction, physical modeling, and correction of intermediate errors. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that coordinates these steps through simulator-based visual inspection and repair. The pipeline processes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), photogrammetry, LiDAR captures, AI-generated 3DGS scenes, and 4D videos of dynamic scenes, and combines object segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation. To support policy learning, SceneAgent generates diverse object variants ("digital sisters") and scripted demonstrations. On a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D, SceneAgent raises F1 at 1 cm for every coding agent with scorable outputs both with and without its skills, and its reconstructions are better than SimFoundry: all agent configurations exceed SimFoundry's F1 score, with a best of 60.75% versus 6.9%. On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09%. We further demonstrate diverse simulated interactions and preliminary policy transfer to a real robot.
full_text: SceneAgent: An Agentic Pipeline from 3D and 4D Captures to Simulation Environments Luke Hollis Tianxing Fan Heng Yang , , 0pt Simulation scenes and tasks from SceneAgent (left to right, top to bottom): a kitchen from CollectData with its doors, drawers, and appliances articulated; picking and plugging cables into a data center server rack; Sharpa hands putting sunglasses on a statue; a TeleAvatar with two Sharpa hands at a clamp in a lab space; and SceneAgent's 4DCodeBench reconstructions of a liquid dam break around rigid cylindrical pillars (B 09) and a layered watermelon breaking apart on impact (Z 12). fig:teaser Introduction sec:introduction Generalist robot policies~ brohan2023rt2,octo2024octo,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,al2025gr00t learn from large teleoperated datasets to perform a wide range of manipulation tasks specified by language instructions. Collecting these datasets is labor-intensive and can take months or years. Similarly, evaluating the resulting policies in a target environment requires physical robot trials, which are time-consuming, difficult to reproduce, and costly to scale~ atreya2025roboarena . Simulation offers a way to scale both data collection and evaluation. Reconstructed environments can generate demonstrations~ yu2025real2render2real,yang2025demonstration,wang2026exogs , support policies that transfer to physical robots~ qureshi2024splatsim,li2024robogsim,zhang2026gase , and provide estimates of real-world policy performance~ jain2025polaris,ranawaka2026simfoundry,zhang2025realtosim,luo2025sim2val,luo2026x4val . In particular, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussian reconstructs photorealistic scene appearance from images, enabling simulators to render observations grounded in a captured workspace~ qureshi2024splatsim,escontrela2025gaussgym,jia2026gsplayground . Visual reconstruction alone, however, does not provide the object geometry, physical parameters, or articulation needed for interaction. Real-to-sim systems recover these components by combining segmentation, mesh generation, pose alignment, and physical modeling~ jain2025polaris,ranawaka2026simfoundry,zhang2026gase,gao2026mirage2matter . SimFoundry, for example, supports articulated objects and estimates their physical parameters~ ranawaka2026simfoundry . A remaining challenge is to coordinate these components across diverse inputs and correct errors that arise between stages. An incorrect mask, scale, or transform can produce an unusable object even when the individual models return plausible outputs. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that converts 3D and 4D captures into interactive simulation environments (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). Agents execute reconstruction and physical modeling tools, inspect rendered outputs in the target simulator, and repair visible errors before the scene is used downstream. The resulting environments contain segmented objects with estimated physical parameters, decomposed parts, and articulation or soft-body behavior where needed. For 4D captures, which are videos of dynamic scenes, agents also fit simulated dynamics such as liquid flow, deformation, and destruction mechanics to the observed scene (Section~ sec:4d ). SceneAgent also generates digital sisters---related object variants---and combines captured objects with artist-authored environments to expand the range of training scenes. We evaluate reconstruction quality on a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D~ back2025graspclutter6d and a Messy Kitchen dataset from CollectData~ collectdataio_tidyup using coding agents with and without SceneAgent, and compare with SimFoundry. Here, a harness is the software environment in which a coding agent runs, and skills are the reusable instructions and tools that guide its conversion workflow. With SceneAgent, F1 at 1~cm improves for every harness with scorable paired outputs, and reconstruction quality is much better than SimFoundry's (Figure~ fig:harness ). On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench~ shen20264dcodebench , where agents reconstruct simulations from videos, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86 to 99.09 (Figure~ fig:4dcodebench-tokens ). We also demonstrate simulated interactions and preliminary real-world deployment after policy learning. In summary, our contributions are: [leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=2pt] An agentic scene-conversion workflow that integrates reconstruction, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, and articulation with simulator-based visual inspection and repair, and that extends from 3D captures to 4D captures by fitting simulated dynamics to the motion observed in a video. Scene augmentation through digital sisters and hybrid environments that combine captured objects with artist-authored assets, together with an automated research loop that turns failures of a policy on the real robot into simulated training data. A quantitative study of reconstruction quality across coding-agent harnesses on static captures and on dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, complemented by qualitative examples of articulated, deformable, and contact-rich interactions and preliminary real-world policy transfer. title: ISB-NMPC: Interception-Oriented Spherical-Bearing Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors
comment: 9 pages, 10 figures, and 1 table. Submitted to IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics
summary: Quadrotor interceptors equipped with strapdown cameras offer a low-cost solution for physically countering unauthorized UAVs. However, this configuration inherently couples vehicle maneuvering and camera pointing, creating a conflict between rapid closing and maintaining target visibility. We present interception-oriented spherical-bearing nonlinear model predictive control (ISB-NMPC), which couples spherical-bearing prediction with nonlinear quadrotor dynamics to jointly optimize target-directed closing motion and visibility. An attitude-compensated extended Kalman filter on S^2 estimates target bearing motion, compensates for perception delay, and predicts target bearings to guide scale-adaptive detection. Across 30 paired simulation trials, ISB-NMPC achieves an interception success rate of 86.7%, the highest among the evaluated controllers, with a mean per-trial target-visible time of 99.11%. Outdoor flights demonstrate acquisition of a 30 cm target at approximately 150 m, with interceptor speed reaching 17 m/s in the long-range flight and approximately 14 m/s while pursuing a quadrotor-towed maneuvering target. The software and hardware are open source at https://github.com/HOLYNOTBAD/ISB-NMPC and https://github.com/HOLYNOTBAD/holydrone, respectively.

Introduction The growth of low-altitude aerial applications makes shared-airspace safety increasingly important. Non-cooperative small targets create a practical need for affordable onboard interception systems~ liBearingOnlyFollowing2023,pliskaSafeMidairDrone2024 . A strapdown monocular camera offers lightweight, mechanically simple sensing, but the interceptor must acquire the target, retain visual feedback, and close to a capture region without cooperative target-state measurements. Figure~ fig:framework_overview illustrates the long-range and maneuvering-target scenarios considered here. This mounting arrangement creates a fundamental control conflict. Target-directed acceleration requires tilting the thrust vector, which rotates the camera and can push the target toward the field-of-view (FOV) boundary. Recentering the target can, in turn, restrict closing acceleration. Thus, the same thrust and attitude motion govern both closing efficiency and visibility~ bourquardezImagebasedVisualServo2009 , requiring coordination under nonlinear dynamics and actuator limits (Fig.~ fig:interception_process ). Camera rotation, detection delay, and target-scale variation further affect the supporting visual feedback. Existing approaches follow three complementary routes: target-state estimation and trajectory planning, visual servoing and line-of-sight (LOS) guidance, and perception-aware model predictive control (MPC). The first plans and tracks interception trajectories. Optimization-based planning explicitly handles engagement geometry, but its execution depends on the available target-state information~ pliskaSafeMidairDrone2024 . A second route generates motion directly from visual feedback or relative geometry. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) regulates image features, whereas position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated relative pose~ chaumetteVisualServoControl2006,xuVisualServoReview2026 ; barrier-function constraints can preserve visibility~ zhengVisibilityGuaranteed2019 . For interception, LOS guidance connects visual feedback to closing. Yang et al. developed high-speed image-based control~ yangHighSpeedInterceptionMulticopter2025a and analyzed LOS-constrained multirotor interceptability~ yangLineofSightConstrainedMulticopterInterceptability2025a . Related studies address planar-sector guidance~ liuPlanarsectorGuidanceInterception , pursuit--evasion interceptability~ zhangInterceptabilityVisionguidedUAVs2025 , and persistent interception~ yangPersistentInterception2026 . Bearing-only following also uses helical motion to improve observability while maintaining a prescribed geometry~ liBearingOnlyFollowing2023 . These methods establish useful feedback structures; rapid capture additionally requires coordinating closing demand with visibility-preserving vehicle motion. The third coordinates motion and sensing over a prediction horizon. Falanga et al.~ falangaPAMPCPerceptionawareModel2018 incorporate perception into quadrotor motion optimization. Related formulations address reactive collision and occlusion avoidance~ peninVisionBasedReactivePlanning2018 and combine visibility with actuator constraints~ dmytrukPerceptionAwareNMPC2022 , while robust visual predictive controllers address tracking and visibility constraints~ zhangRobustVisualNMPC2021 . Qin et al.~ qinPerceptionawareImagebasedVisual2023 combine quaternion-based spherical features and visibility constraints for aggressive flight, and Li et al.~ liRobocentricVisualServo2023 integrate estimation and control in a robocentric model. MPC has also been applied to non-cooperative aerial interception and impact-angle-constrained visual engagement~ srivastavaAerialInterceptionMPC2022,cetinVisualInterceptionMPC2023 . For strapdown interception, the remaining question is how to choose closing direction and speed under visibility and actuation constraints. Uncoordinated closing can lose visual feedback, whereas recentering alone can delay capture. We connect LOS guidance to spherical prediction through an optimized closing-speed state; paired simulations and flight observations examine closing and visual retention together. The supporting perception front end draws on depth-independent bearing estimation~ hamelVisualServoingUnderactuated2002,mebarkiNonlinearVisualControl2015 , small-object slicing~ akyonSlicingAided2022 , and delayed-feedback estimation~ guoDelayedVisualLanding2024 to address camera rotation, target-scale variation, and latency. We propose interception-oriented spherical-bearing nonlinear model predictive control (ISB-NMPC), predicting -lifted bearings jointly with quadrotor dynamics. LOS velocity tracking, bearing-dependent speed demand, and visual costs and constraints coordinate approach and visibility. Compensated bearings and predicted regions of interest (ROIs) support detection. The main contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*] An interception-oriented spherical-bearing NMPC that jointly optimizes desired closing speed and vehicle motion. LOS-aligned relative velocity objectives, visual costs, and soft FOV constraints coordinate rapid closing and target visibility under quadrotor dynamics and actuator limits. A spherical-bearing estimator with attitude and delay compensation that supplies current-time bearing feedback and absolute-time ROI predictions to support onboard operation during large attitude changes and target-scale variation. Paired controller comparisons over 30 simulation trials and outdoor flights involving long-range acquisition of a quasi-static small target and pursuit of a maneuvering target, evaluating controller performance and the operation of the integrated perception--control system.
