title: Behavioural Quality Is Not Learning Utility: Objective Mismatch in Human Behaviour Models for Robot Learning
summary: Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution.
full_text: Behavioural Quality Is Not Learning Utility: Objective Mismatch in Human Behaviour Models for Robot Learning Haoyang Jiang, Dana Kulic, Michael Burke, and Pamela Carreno-Medrano Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution. Human–Robot Interaction, Human Behaviour Modelling, Reinforcement Learning, Behaviour Simulation, Model Evaluation, Policy Learning. Introduction sec:introduction As robots transition from controlled industrial settings to dynamic, human-centred environments, learning from and adapting to human behaviour becomes increasingly critical for successful deployment in real-world settings Kroemer2021, Thomaz2016 . In this context, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising framework for robot training, as it enables agents to optimise long-horizon behaviour through interaction and feedback backman_ReinforcementLearningShared_2023, sen_DomainRandomizationLearning_2025 . In order to learn how to interact with human partners via RL, a robot must be exposed to interactions with humans during training. Although training robots using data collected from real-world human interactions remains the gold standard for achieving robust performance, this approach is often costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale Kober2013 . To address these challenges, the robotics community has increasingly relied on simulated or modelled human behaviour models to train robot policies chen_CrowdRobotInteractionCrowdAware_2019a, sen_DomainRandomizationLearning_2025 . These models, ranging from simple rule-based approaches Gipps1981, Krauss1997, Treiber2000 to complex data-driven generators salzmann_TrajectronDynamicallyFeasibleTrajectory_2020a, zhang2023trafficbots, zhang2024trafficbotsv15 , offer a scalable and cost-effective means of producing the large volumes of interaction data required by modern machine learning methods Mavrogiannis2023 . Consequently, human behaviour models serve not only as models of human behaviour, but also as interactive partners for robot policy training. Their value therefore depends not only on how well they reproduce human behaviour, but also on how effectively they support downstream robot learning. This creates an important distinction between behavioural quality and downstream utility. Behavioural quality concerns how closely a given model reproduces behaviours observed in real human data, whereas downstream utility concerns how effectively interactions generated by this same model support the learning of robot policies. We argue that these objectives may not be aligned. A model may accurately reproduce the distribution of behaviours observed in human data while failing to expose a robot to interactions that are important for learning an effective policy. Conversely, a model that generates behaviours that are less representative of the empirical human distribution may provide training experiences that lead to better downstream policies. =-1 This distinction reflects a broader objective-mismatch problem that has been studied in model-based RL lambert2020objective : model quality under a predictive or model-fitting objective does not necessarily imply usefulness for downstream decision making. Related work has demonstrated that models that are accurate according to conventional predictive objectives may nevertheless produce poor downstream control performance. This suggests that evaluating a model without considering the downstream task can provide an incomplete picture of its practical value. However, whether a similar mismatch arises when human behaviour models are used as training environments for HRI policy learning has not been systematically investigated. This question is increasingly relevant in simulation-based robotics, where human behaviour models are used to construct interactive environments for training and evaluating autonomous agents. Recent traffic simulation frameworks, including WOSAC, TrafficBots, Symphony, BITS, and TrafficBots V1.5, have developed increasingly sophisticated models of human road-user behaviour for autonomous driving and evaluate these models primarily according to measures of behavioural realism, such as trajectory likelihood, prediction error, collision and rule-violation rates, diversity, and distributional similarity montali2023wosac, zhang2023trafficbots, igl2022symphony, xu2023bits, zhang2024trafficbotsv15 . These measures provide valuable assessments of whether a simulator faithfully reproduces human traffic behaviour, but they do not directly establish whether models achieving higher behavioural quality are more effective for downstream policy learning. Similarly, recent work on planner evaluation in reactive traffic environments has shown that changing the human behaviour simulator can affect the resulting assessment of autonomous planners hagedorn2025planners . While this highlights the influence of the simulated humans on downstream evaluation, it does not establish whether realism-oriented evaluation metrics can predict the utility of these models for training robot policies. Thus, although existing work has made substantial progress towards evaluating the fidelity or diversity of human behaviour models, the relationship between behavioural faithfulness and downstream utility remains largely unexplored. This motivates our central research question: Can existing model evaluation metrics predict the downstream utility of human behaviour models for RL policy learning HRI scenarios? To investigate this question, we evaluate a diverse set of rule-based and data-driven human behaviour models across two representative HRI domains: highway driving and object handover. These domains represent substantially different forms of HRI, involving large-scale coordination and close-proximity physical collaboration, respectively. For each human behaviour model, we evaluate two complementary aspects: behavioural quality, measured using commonly adopted generative-model evaluation metrics across different trajectory representations, and downstream utility, measured by the performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding human behaviour model. By comparing these two evaluations, we investigate whether models that score favourably according to existing behavioural evaluation metrics also provide more useful training interactions for downstream robot learning. Our study provides the following contributions: We provide empirical evidence of a mismatch between behavioural similarity and downstream RL utility of human behaviour models. Specifically, we show that existing evaluation metrics are not a consistent predictor of downstream policy performance across both HRI domains and trajectory representations. We show that the form of this mismatch can be task-dependent, with the relationship between behavioural evaluation and downstream policy utility differing between highway driving and object handover. We demonstrate that human behaviour model evaluation is sensitive to trajectory representation, with metric scores and model rankings varying substantially across representations and, in particular, learned feature configurations. In addition to these contributions, we provide detailed formulations and parameter inference procedures for the rule-based human behaviour models used in our experiments. The parameters of these models are inferred from real human datasets highDdataset, khanna_MultimodalDataSet_2023 , with the corresponding model formulations, inference procedures, and fitted parameters provided in the Appendix, which is also included in our project page https://objective-mismatch-hri.github.io/supplementary/ . =-1 Background sec:background Reinforcement Learning (RL) in HRI subsec:reinforcementLearningInHRI RL is commonly used for training robots to operate in interactive and unstructured environments. By optimising long-horizon objectives through trial-and-error, RL enables robots to learn adaptive policies that account for both environmental dynamics and human responses Kober2013, Kroemer2021 . In HRI, RL has been applied to problems such as social navigation ahsen_HumanAwareSubgoalGeneration_2022, Xue2024, sen_DomainRandomizationLearning_2025 , assistive manipulation Chen2022 , collaborative decision-making Mehri2025 and shared autonomy backman_NoviceSkilledRLBased_2025 , where explicit supervision is difficult and optimal behaviour depends on sequential interaction with humans Thomaz2016, Mavrogiannis2023 . Despite its conceptual appeal, RL faces well-known challenges in HRI. Real-world interaction with humans is expensive, safety-critical, and often ethically constrained, making large-scale data collection infeasible. Moreover, RL algorithms are data-hungry, particularly when learning from sparse or delayed rewards Ding2020, Akalin2021 , which is often the case in HRI scenarios. These challenges have motivated the use of simulated environments and human behaviour models to generate interaction experience for training RL agents across various domains, including autonomous driving zhang_LearningRealisticTraffic_2023 , social navigation vandermeer_ComparativeStudyHuman_2025 and human–agent interaction liang_LearningCooperateHumans_2024 . Human Behaviour Modelling for Robot Training subsec:humanBehaviourModellingForRobotTraining To support scalable robot learning, a wide range of approaches have been proposed to model or simulate human behaviour. Early work relied on hand-crafted, heuristic models to encode simplified assumptions about human motion or decision-making Helbing1995, Trautman2010 . While computationally efficient, such models often fail to capture the diversity and stochasticity of real human behaviour. More recent approaches leverage data-driven techniques, including probabilistic models Trautman2013 , inverse planning Chris2009 , and deep generative models Mavrogiannis2023 , to learn human behaviour directly from data. In the context of HRI, human behaviour models, either open-loop, where human actions are generated independently of the robot's actions, or interactive, where human behaviour adapts in response to the robot's actions, are frequently used as environment components for training robot policies, particularly when using RL Abeyruwan2023, sen_DomainRandomizationLearning_2025, jiang_InfluenceBasedRewardModulation_2026, VanDerMeer2026 . These models are used to substitute real humans, producing interactions that shape the robot’s learning process. Thus, their quality has a direct impact on the learned policies. title: Physics-Informed and Data-Driven Composite Disturbance Separation and Predictive Control for Airborne Electro-Optical Gimbals with Multiple Constraints
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures. Includes supplementary derivations and proofs. Demonstration video included as an ancillary file
summary: This paper studies the constrained pointing control problem of airborne electro-optical gimbals subjected to composite periodic and aperiodic disturbances. Under carrier vibration, input delay, and actuator constraints, achieving line-of-sight stabilization and tracking is challenging. A disturbance-separated model predictive control (MPC) scheme is proposed to compensate these heterogeneous disturbances according to their physical characteristics. An adaptive periodic observer predicts multi-harmonic vibrations over the MPC horizon using linear-regression frequency estimation. A linear observer estimates the aperiodic disturbance, and a bounded long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts its change over the input delay. Embedding periodic predictions into the MPC model while applying aperiodic compensation outside the optimizer limits amplification of aperiodic estimation errors and improves pointing accuracy under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. On the stated headroom envelope, input-set tightening provides feasible commands within the prescribed limits, and a regional practical tracking bound is established under explicit input-sequence and predicted-state margin conditions. A UAV-mounted two-axis gimbal platform is assembled for comparative indoor hovering experiments, complemented by simulations under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. In the reported trials, the proposed method achieves yaw and pitch relative-angle root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 0.770 degrees and 0.350 degrees, reducing tracking errors by 25.1% and 45.9% compared with linear active disturbance rejection control.

Disturbance separation airborne electro-optical gimbals long short-term memory model predictive control periodic disturbance prediction pointing control Introduction sec:introduction Airborne electro-optical gimbals support emergency response, maritime search and rescue, and bridge crack inspection by directing imaging sensors toward targets of interest. These missions require accurate two-axis line-of-sight (LOS) control, where the gimbal operates as an inertially stabilized platform (ISP) with azimuth and elevation degrees of freedom~ rueStabilizationPrecisionElectrooptical1969, hilkertInertiallyStabilizedPlatform2008, Masten2008, ekstrandEquationsMotionTwoaxes2001 . Achieving high-accuracy pointing control for such systems is challenged by composite disturbances with distinct physical mechanisms and by multiple constraints. In typical low-to-medium altitude tracking scenarios, atmospheric turbulence and propeller vibration produce high-frequency periodic jitter~ renAngularVibrationSurvey2003, maoModelingRobustContinuous2020, yunInvestigationTwoStageVibration2020 , while rapid slewing excites state-dependent aperiodic torques including gravity, gyroscopic effects~ hilkertInertiallyStabilizedPlatform2008, dongDynamicModelControl2017 , and nonlinear friction~ congIsolationControlInertially2016 . Since these disturbances span distinct spectral bands, a separation strategy is physically motivated. Furthermore, the ISP operates within actuator saturation and field-of-view (FOV) constraints~ dongDynamicModelControl2017 . For aerial vehicles, MPC combined with disturbance observers has been applied to trajectory tracking~ tianAdaptiveModelPredictive2026, nigusieExtendedStateObserver2026 . Robust and disturbance-observer-based control (DOBC) schemes, including Extended State Observer (ESO) and Active Disturbance Rejection Control, have been extensively studied for ISP pointing~ guoDisturbanceAttenuationRejection2005, chenDisturbanceobserverbasedControlRelated2015, maoAdaptiveNonsingularFast2022, safaRobustOutputFeedback2019, golestaniDisturbanceObserverConstrained2023 . For ISPs under composite disturbances, Lei et al.~ leiCompositeControlMethod2015a combined an adaptive radial basis function neural network with an ESO, and Chang et al.~ changCompensationControlStrategy2024 compared adaptive and sliding mode observers for friction and moving-base compensation. Recent work~ zhuangMechatronicDisturbanceSuppression2026, miaoRobustObserverBasedVisual2027 applied ESO-based feedforward to electro-optical platforms and UAV-mounted cameras. However, most DOBC schemes adopt a single total-disturbance estimate, limiting accuracy when periodic and aperiodic components coexist~ guoCompositeDisturbanceFiltering2023 , and require precise disturbance models. Learning-based techniques augment estimation without explicit models. Sun et al.~ sunNeuralNetworkBasedDOBC2017 established a neural DOBC framework, and Shen and Xu~ shenAdaptiveNeuralNetworkBased2021 used adaptive radial basis functions for unmanned-helicopter disturbance rejection. For ISPs, physics-informed neural networks~ leblebiciogluPhysicsInformedDisturbanceEstimation2022 and online learning frameworks~ jiaEVOLVEROnlineLearning2024 improved adaptability, while Huang et al.~ huangLSTMMPCDeepLearning2023 combined LSTM with MPC. These methods still use aggregate estimates without structural separation and struggle with high-frequency dynamics due to spectral bias~ rahamanSpectralBiasNeural2019 . Refined disturbance separation has been proposed to decouple composite disturbances by their influence topology~ guoAntidisturbanceControlTheory2014, zhuDisturbanceSeparationBasedEnhanced2024, yangFixedTimeRefinedDisturbance2024, baoDeepCoupledSlidingMode2025, tengRefinedDisturbanceUtilization2025 , with related studies on antidisturbance controllability and fixed-time predictive control~ yuAntidisturbanceControllabilityAnalysis2021, liuFixedTimeDOBPredictive2024 . Nevertheless, aperiodic estimation in these methods still requires precise physical models. When disturbance estimates are integrated into MPC, they are commonly held constant over the prediction horizon~ Yang2012CCDC,Maeder2009Automatica . For periodic disturbances, horizon prediction using a nominal or known period~ Li2014JPC,Xie2026Automatica or learned profiles~ Ahmed2025LCSS,Zhou2026TIE has been studied. In airborne ISPs, however, vibration frequency varies with flight state, and propagating an aperiodic observer estimate through the prediction model feeds estimation error into the MPC optimization, which under unmodeled lag can drive actuator saturation (Section~ sec:res_main ). Existing gradient-type frequency adaptation laws~ yangAdaptivePeriodicdisturbanceObserver2023 are nonlinear in the unknown frequency and converge slowly after frequency switches. Motivated by the above analysis, this paper proposes a disturbance-separated MPC (MPC-DS) framework that combines physics-informed periodic prediction with data-driven delay-residual learning for airborne two-axis ISPs. The proposed disturbance separator decouples the total disturbance into periodic and aperiodic components. Periodic vibration is predicted over the MPC horizon by an APDO with a projected linear-regression frequency estimator, while the aperiodic disturbance is estimated by a biomimetic LSTM-based disturbance observer (LSTM-DO). Periodic predictions enter the MPC prediction model, whereas the aperiodic estimate and its lead correction are compensated outside the optimizer. The MPC formulation incorporates tightened input bounds together with mechanical-range and FOV constraints~ dongDynamicModelControl2017, moratoDataScienceModel2024, liSurveyControlLyapunov2023a, fuAntiWindupMethodBased2024, tengAdaptiveFixedTimeDisturbance2023, kimQuadrotorConstraints2024 . title: Localization-Uncertainty-Aware UAV Swarm Search for GNSS-Denied Maritime Surveillance
summary: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices. First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain. Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds. Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended Kalman filter in the loop. The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs. An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5 s, 20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible and containment in at least 98.97% of UAV-frames, and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence. The source code is publicly available.

UAV swarm, Control barrier functions, GNSS-denied maritime search, Position uncertainty, Formation control, Cooperative localization Introduction sec:introduction nmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms have received growing attention for search-and-rescue and surveillance because they cover large areas more efficiently than a single platform bogdanowicz2017flying . In maritime surveillance, UAV swarms are attractive for search, border monitoring, and wide-area patrol over oceans. Practical maritime operations are often challenged by Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied conditions (jamming, spoofing, interference), so UAVs must search, navigate, and coordinate with onboard sensing and inter-UAV cooperation. This paper considers a GNSS-denied maritime surveillance scenario in which a swarm systematically searches a large ocean region extending from the coastline (Fig.~ fig:gdms ). Hovering beacon UAVs (bUAVs) near the coast localize through coastal features (e.g., lidar-visual-inertial odometry shan_lvi-sam_2021 ), while searching UAVs (sUAVs) perform coverage. sUAVs carry forward-looking sensors (cameras or radar) and ranging sensors for cooperative localization; because direct ranging to coastal bUAVs cannot support long-range offshore search, references propagate from the bUAVs into the search area in a multi-hop chain. A central difficulty is that localization uncertainty accumulates along this chain: each sUAV estimates its position from noisy ranges and from the already uncertain estimates of its reference neighbors, which directly affects control design. Localization-linked distances must remain within sensing range after accounting for position errors, and collision-avoidance constraints must include uncertainty margins for both vehicles. Maritime search therefore requires an uncertainty-aware mechanism coordinating coverage, localization, and inter-UAV safety. We refer to this problem as uncertainty-aware GNSS-denied Maritime Search (uGdMS). Compared with conventional coverage control, uGdMS operates without global positioning, its uncertainty is cascading (each UAV depends on the uncertain estimates of upstream references), and its forward-looking sensors couple position control with yaw orientation; unlike our prior work under perfect localization yang2024aerial , we explicitly incorporate the cascading uncertainty into the control design. This paper develops a CBF-based framework that integrates cooperative-localization uncertainty into swarm search and safety control. The main contributions are: Cascading uncertainty modeling for cooperative localization: We develop a Fisher-information-based model approximating position covariance in range-only cooperative localization, capturing how ranging noise and reference-neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the multi-hop localization chain. Robust CBF design under localization uncertainty: We construct uncertainty-tightened CBFs for localization-connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance by incorporating a position-error envelope and its rate into the constraint design, establish a conditional invariance statement under the envelope and rate conditions, and a graceful-degradation bound quantifying the residual constraint margin when the envelope is breached, and validate the resulting distributed controller with the estimator in the loop. Hierarchical search strategy with forward-looking sensing: A task-oriented search controller lets squad leaders select targets through Voronoi partitioning while followers maintain formation, with decoupled distance and yaw objectives for forward-looking sensors. Estimator-in-the-loop validation: We validate the estimator-agnostic framework end-to-end with a standard unbiased EKF in the control loop, demonstrating complete coverage with all quadratic program (QP) rows feasible and no true-distance constraint violations across the representative run and 20 Monte Carlo deployments. The resulting framework applies to arbitrary convex polygonal search regions and varying swarm sizes. Numerical simulation with the estimator in the control loop demonstrates complete coverage of a region with 14 sUAVs and 3 bUAVs in ~s; Monte Carlo studies confirm completion repeatability, and six high-fidelity MBZIRC runs complete coverage with no constraint violations. The remainder presents related work (Section~ sec:relatedwork ), models and CBF preliminaries (Section~ sec:preliminaries ), uncertainty propagation and robust constraints (Section~ sec:constraint_satisfaction ), the search strategy (Section~ sec:search_strategy ), numerical and Gazebo results (Sections~ sec:results and~ sec:validation ), and conclusions (Section~ sec:conclusion ). Related Work sec:relatedwork This section reviews GNSS-denied cooperative localization, maritime search and coverage control, and CBF-based multi-UAV coordination. GNSS-denied Cooperative Localization and Maritime Search Cooperative localization through inter-UAV ranging is essential in GNSS-denied maritime environments cooperative_localization_survey_2025 ; vision-based tron_distributed_2016 and ultra-wideband (UWB)-based xu_decentralized_2020, zhang_agile_2022 methods are extensively studied for relative localization and formation control, along with decentralized scheduling for cooperative localization peng_decentralized_2019 and UAV position estimation with collision avoidance luo_uav_2013 , but localization methods typically do not integrate uncertainty into safety-critical control design. Maritime search and rescue has attracted considerable attention wu_maritime_rl_2024 , offshore coverage path planning is studied for autonomous surface vehicles zhao_spcpp_2026 , and multi-UAV search with connectivity maintenance is addressed in vehicular networks yanmaz_dynamic_2024 ; existing approaches usually assume reliable positioning and do not address the coupling among search effectiveness, localization connectivity, and collision avoidance under uncertain cooperative localization. Several works consider coverage control under localization uncertainty: AWGV papatheodorou2018awgv builds guaranteed Voronoi cells from known circular regions but assumes independent bounds and no connectivity maintenance; Chen et al. chen2020collision contract uncertain Voronoi cells with each agent's own uncertainty, still with independent bounds; Boldrer et al. boldrer2026uncertainty achieve communication-less flocking without modeling error accumulation along reference chains; and resilient coverage strategies rezaee_uav_coverage_2024 likewise assume bounded independent uncertainty. In contrast, this work models cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices and incorporates the resulting radii into safety-critical control design. CBF-Based UAV Swarm Control Control barrier functions provide a systematic framework for enforcing state and input constraints in safety-critical systems ames_control_2017, ames_cbf_survey_2019 . Recent advances extend CBFs to uncertain dynamics garg_robust_2021, alan_cbf_iss_2023 , safety-critical vehicular platooning bohara_adaptive_2024 , and multi-UAV applications including collision avoidance wang_multi-objective_2016 and coverage with connectivity maintenance luo2019connectivity . Existing CBF-based methods assume exact state information or externally specified, independent uncertainty bounds, ignoring uncertainty derived from cooperative localization (sensing geometry, ranging noise, and inherited upstream uncertainty), and most coverage-control formulations assume downward-looking sensors with circular footprints funada_nonsmooth_cbf_2024 , while maritime surveillance typically uses forward-looking sensors with limited fields of view, coupling translational motion with yaw alignment. Safe navigation under uncertainty has been addressed via model predictive control saccani_multi_trajectory_uav_2023 or invariant set planning greiff_invariant_set_uav_2025 , but these approaches do not combine cascading localization uncertainty with forward-looking sensing constraints. The robust CBF construction garg_robust_2021 provides the uncertainty-margin machinery we adopt; our contribution is to derive that margin online from a cascading cooperative-localization model and its rate rather than from an externally specified bound, and to embed it in a distributed QP whose rows cover every pairwise constraint. Our previous work yang2024aerial assumed perfect localization; here sUAVs localize through range-based multi-hop cooperation, and the resulting uncertainty enters localization-connectivity maintenance, collision avoidance, and search control. The differences from existing methods are summarized in Table~ tab:comparison . title: Agentic AI Orchestration Framework for Spatial Intelligence: Supply Chain Deployment
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for publication in the proceedings of GeoIndustry 2026 (5th ACM SIGSPATIAL International Workshop on Spatial Big Data and AI for Industrial Applications). In-person presentation scheduled for November 3, 2026, Riverside, California. Proceedings forthcoming in the ACM Digital Library
summary: Industrial spatial decisions are assembled across systems that share neither a reference frame nor an owner, and analysts spend substantial effort reconciling those systems rather than reasoning about space. This paper presents ANASSA, a reference architecture integrating structured reasoning, multi-agent workflow orchestration, authoritative spatial grounding, and feedback-driven execution, and reports its instantiation in an operating supply-chain deployment. The architecture places typed data contracts at agent boundaries, validates spatial claims against a certified authoritative foundation, and enforces two blocking human-in-the-loop approvals inside a six-step cognitive loop. The deployment covers multi-hazard risk assessment on an ocean-and-inland freight lane, including cold-chain excursion detection over container telemetry. Across a three-month proof of concept (POC) with three implementation iterations, three deployment outcomes are reported: 25% improvement in data quality, 50% reduction in spatial workflow runtime, and 60% lower decision latency relative to the preceding manual workflow. Absolute deployment-scale quantities and baseline counts are confidential; reported percentages are observed relative changes. These are uncontrolled deployment observations, not controlled experiments. We therefore specify instrumentation and ablation protocols for mechanism-level evaluation.

We therefore specify instrumentation and ablation protocols for mechanism-level evaluation. <ccs2012> <concept> <concept_id>10002951.10003227.10003236.10003237</concept_id> <concept_desc>Information systems~Geographic information systems</concept_desc> <concept_significance>500</concept_significance> </concept> <concept> <concept_id>10010147.10010178</concept_id> <concept_desc>Computing methodologies~Artificial intelligence</concept_desc> <concept_significance>500</concept_significance> </concept> <concept> <concept_id>10010147.10010178.10010219.10010220</concept_id> <concept_desc>Computing methodologies~Multi-agent systems</concept_desc> <concept_significance>300</concept_significance> </concept> </ccs2012> Introduction Modern geospatial operations face persistent coordination challenges across organizational boundaries. Spatial data is distributed through disconnected GIS platforms, satellite feeds, IoT sensors, field devices, cloud databases, and legacy infrastructure, each operating largely in isolation papantoniou2021enterprise . Human analysts must extract, transform, route, and reconcile data across fragmented systems, diverting effort from spatial reasoning and decision support kaza2026, mansourian2026 . Agentic AI increasingly allows coordination tasks to be delegated to systems capable of planning, memory, and tool orchestration wang2024,xi2023 . Recent work combines multi-agent architectures with retrieval-augmented generation to address the inability of text similarity alone to represent topology, proximity, and spatial dependency hu2025,liang2026,mansourian2026 . Other systems constrain reasoning with explicit workflow graphs encoding spatial entities and transformation dependencies bao2026,bhattaram2025 . Execution benchmarks show that agents can handle moderately complex workflows but degrade on multi-step tasks requiring precise parameter inference and tool sequencing hashemi2026,krechetova2025,wu2025,yu2026 . This paper introduces ANASSA (Autonomous Neural Agents for Spatial Systems Architecture), an autonomous orchestration layer for geospatial intelligence, and reports its instantiation in an operating supply-chain deployment. Building on prior research papantoniou2021enterprise , ANASSA extends the GeoBlockchain coordination model papantoniou2021geoblockchain from blockchain-based to AI-agent-based orchestration, distributing reasoning, planning, execution, and validation across autonomous agents under human-in-the-loop governance. The architecture addresses the limitations above by integrating spatial reasoning with execution-aware orchestration, embedding feedback-driven adaptation through a continuous cognitive loop, and incorporating governance for hallucination management. This paper makes three contributions. First, it specifies ANASSA as a unified architecture of eleven components across four layers, in which every boundary between agents is a typed data contract rather than an ad hoc handoff. Second, it instantiates that architecture in an operating supply-chain deployment---multi-hazard risk assessment on an ocean-and-inland freight lane, including cold-chain excursion detection over container telemetry---and reports three deployment outcomes together with an explicit account of what those observations do and do not support. Third, it specifies the instrument set and ablation protocol required to convert uncontrolled deployment observations into attributable, controlled evidence, and identifies design principles for agentic GIS that follow from the deployment. The evidentiary status of this work should be stated at the outset. The outcomes reported in Section 5 are observations from operating the platform against a pre-existing manual workflow, not controlled experiments, and they do not establish which architectural mechanism produced the improvement. Sections 5.2, 5.3, and 7 state the threats to validity, the instrument set, and the ablations that would. ANASSA Framework Agentic GIS systems improve automation, workflow generation, and natural-language interaction hu2025,liang2026,mansourian2026 , but robust spatial reasoning, execution reliability, and evaluation remain fragmented. Multi-agent architectures improve decomposition yet remain sensitive to ambiguous spatial constraints and long dependency chains liang2026,wu2025,bao2026,yu2026 ; structured reasoning approaches enforce logical consistency but do not fully integrate execution feedback bao2026,bhattaram2025 . Classifications are based on properties explicitly documented in the cited publications; the cited references provide the basis for external verification. Figure~ fig:workflows shows the progression from manual GIS to LLM/LMM-augmented GIS and then to agentic GIS, where reasoning, multi-agent execution, feedback, and validation form a closed loop. Architecture Components ANASSA is organized into eleven numbered architectural components (C1--C11) structured across four layers (Figure~ fig:arch ). The Governance and Output layer (C7, C10) validates framework outputs and governs all agent and workflow behavior. The Operational layer (C1--C4, C6) defines participants, industry sectors, deployment paths, the technical system-of-systems backbone, and multimodal spatial data. The Cognitive Engine (C5) runs the six-step Geospatial AI Cognitive Loop. The Foundation layer (C8) provides trusted authoritative data and knowledge that all other components draw from, while C9 and C11 represent the continuous downward and upward process flows that close the loop. The layer assignment is summarized in Table~ tab:layers . Two numbering schemes are kept separate throughout. Architectural layers are the four groupings of Table~ tab:layers , and each component belongs to exactly one. Infrastructure levels C4-L0 through C4-L4 are internal to Component 4: C4-L0 is the Orchestrator, C4-L1 the multi-model language gateway, C4-L2 the specialized geospatial agents, C4-L3 the GIS platform and protocol integration surface, and C4-L4 the AI infrastructure. The Orchestrator is therefore Level 0 of an Operational-layer component, not a fifth architectural layer. A third scheme, the agent coordination levels A0--A4, is introduced in Section 3.3. Each component is implemented as a coordinated set of specialized agents under C4-L0, which decomposes participant intent into agent tasks, sequences execution, monitors outputs, and synthesizes results into trusted intelligence. After each cycle, the Learning Agent may update authorized operational parameters and generate governance-rule proposals; it cannot autonomously weaken or bypass A3 controls. The ``Neural'' in the acronym refers to the LLM- and LMM-based reasoning agents at C4-L1 and C4-L2. ANASSA proposes no novel neural architecture and makes no claim about model internals; the contribution is the coordination, contract, and governance structure surrounding those models. Geospatial AI Cognitive Loop Component C5 is the core of ANASSA: a continuous six-step reasoning and action cycle that transforms spatial data into spatial intelligence and intelligence into action (Table~ tab:loop ). The six steps are S1 Sensing, S2 Reasoning, S3 Planning, S4 Decision and Hallucination Validation, S5 Execution, and S6 Learning. All six are coordinated by the Orchestrator (C4-L0) and grounded in authoritative data from C8. The cycle is feedback-driven rather than linear. Outputs from S5 do not terminate the workflow; they are captured at S6 and fed back into the system, enabling authorized operational parameters and agent capabilities to adapt while governance-policy changes remain subject to explicit approval. This closed-loop design distinguishes ANASSA from pipeline-based agentic GIS systems, which typically treat execution as a terminal stage and rely on offline retraining for adaptation liang2026,yu2026 . Two mandatory human-in-the-loop gates appear at S3 (Planning) and S4 (Decision and Hallucination Validation). At S3, participants review and approve the generated workflow before any geospatial operation is executed, preventing inappropriate model or tool selection from propagating downstream. At S4, participants approve or reject the cross-validated outputs before publication. Both gates are blocking rather than advisory in the deployment reported here, and both record approver identity and timestamp. These gates reflect the framework's position that the highest-stakes geospatial decisions must remain under explicit human accountability. Section 6 examines the cost this imposes on machine-pace orchestration, which is the subject of RQ4. Governance and Hallucination Management Component C7 functions as the governance backbone of ANASSA and is positioned as a framework-wide overlay connecting to every other component. Its design is informed by the CPMAI methodology cognilytica2019 , which structures the AI project lifecycle from problem definition through production operation. Governance is organized across seven pillars: business and problem governance (G1), data governance and sovereignty (G2), AI model and agent governance with hallucination management (G3), human-in-the-loop governance (G4), trust and auditability (G5), ethical AI and responsible use (G6), and operationalization and continuous improvement (G7). A distinctive feature of the framework is explicit management of geospatial hallucinations as a primary governance concern. Fabricated coordinates, invented boundaries, and false spatial claims can produce incorrect maps used for high-stakes decisions, generate jurisdictional disputes, and in safety-critical contexts endanger lives. The Claim Validation Agent in C7 tests every spatial claim in a candidate output against the certified ground truth maintained in C8. Claims that do not match a certified assertion are not silently dropped and not silently published: they are delivered with the output on an explicit unverified-claim list. This mechanism is specified as contract K5 and is the subject of RQ2. Research Questions and Use Case The central research question motivating this work is: how can agentic GIS systems integrate spatial reasoning, workflow orchestration, and execution feedback to enable robust and scalable geospatial analysis in real-world environments? This paper investigates that question through a single instantiated use case: multi-hazard supply-chain risk asses

title: Learning Direct Control from Optimization for Dynamic Target Tracking
summary: Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to maintain target visibility while navigating obstacles with smooth, feasible controls. Online trajectory optimization explicitly encodes these objectives but requires repeated numerical solving, whereas waypoint-based neural policies separate geometric prediction from control execution. We introduce LECO, a framework that transfers tracking optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. LECO predicts control sequences and maps them to trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model, allowing trajectory-level objectives to directly guide control learning. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum initializes effective tracking behavior and progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. At deployment, a predictive safety lock checks short-horizon obstacle clearance and invokes a classical planning and control fallback when the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO reduces root-mean-square linear jerk by 14.1--31.2\% relative to the best competing method for this metric and achieves the highest tracking success rate, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25--5.63\,ms. Experiments on two robot platforms further demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments. These results demonstrate that learning direct control from optimization enables smooth and robust dynamic target tracking.

Introduction Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to keep a moving target in view while navigating the surrounding environment~ 40,44 . In cluttered scenes, these requirements are tightly coupled: a collision-free maneuver may place an obstacle between the robot and the target, while maintaining visibility may require turning through narrow passages. The robot must therefore coordinate target distance, line of sight (LoS), obstacle clearance, and control smoothness under its own kinematic constraints. The central challenge is to translate these spatial tracking objectives into feasible control actions as both the target and the local environment change. Trajectory optimization provides an explicit way to express these objectives. Optimization-based trackers account for target motion, visibility, and obstacle avoidance when generating robot trajectories~ 5,6,47 , while model predictive control (MPC) incorporates motion constraints into control computation~ 4 . This approach requires numerical solving as observations change. Learning-based planners offer a complementary route by transferring trajectory costs into network training~ 8,10 . For example, YOPOv2-Tracker learns motion-primitive offsets from trajectory costs and converts the resulting predictions into quadrotor commands~ 8 . Kinematics-aware learning also incorporates motion models into planning~ 43,48 . These developments motivate learning tracking behavior directly in the control space of a mobile robot, so that visibility, clearance, and smoothness objectives shape the commands through the motion they produce. Our key idea is to retain the explicit objectives of tracking optimization while moving their optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. A differentiable kinematic model provides the connection: it maps a predicted control sequence to a robot trajectory and propagates trajectory-level costs back to the policy. Target visibility and obstacle clearance can then guide control learning together with control smoothness, using the platform's motion model throughout. This formulation connects what the robot should achieve in the environment with the controls it will execute. We instantiate this idea in LECO, a framework for learning direct control from optimization for dynamic target tracking (Fig.~ fig:framework ). Given local geometry, robot motion, and target-relative observations, LECO predicts a future control sequence and rolls it out through a platform-specific differentiable kinematic model. Tracking objectives evaluated along this rollout jointly encourage the desired target distance, clear lines of sight, obstacle clearance, and smooth motion. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum establishes effective tracking behavior early in training, then progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. The expert thus provides an initialization for control learning, while the final policy is refined by the quality of the motion it predicts. At deployment, LECO executes the first predicted control in a receding-horizon manner, avoiding iterative task optimization in the neural branch. A predictive safety lock checks obstacle clearance along the short-horizon rollout before execution. When the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid, it invokes a classical hybrid A*~ 3 and MPC~ 4 branch for obstacle avoidance or target reacquisition. Neural execution resumes once the target prediction and clearance checks permit it and the lock duration has elapsed. This deployment strategy combines learned direct control with explicit motion checks and a fallback that continues to serve the tracking task. Experiments validate this formulation for smooth and robust tracking. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO achieves the lowest root-mean-square linear jerk and the highest tracking success rate among the evaluated methods, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25--5.63\,ms. In the 150-obstacle setting, it achieves an 86 success rate and a 6.32 occlusion rate. Further evaluations in dense layouts and temporary obstacle disturbances show that the neural policy supplies 88.57--95.81 of control decisions. Real-world experiments with platform-specific policies on the differential-drive Unitree G1D and Ackermann-steered AgileX HUNTER 2.0 demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments (Fig.~ fig:head ). Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce LECO, a direct-control learning framework for dynamic target tracking that propagates trajectory-level tracking objectives through a differentiable kinematic rollout to the control policy. We develop a decaying expert-guidance curriculum for visibility-aware control learning and a predictive safety lock that combines neural execution with classical fallback for obstacle avoidance and target reacquisition. We demonstrate improved control smoothness and tracking success across three simulated obstacle densities, and validate the framework on two robot platforms in indoor and outdoor environments. The source code and implementation details will be made publicly available. Related Work Classical Optimization-Based Target Tracking Traditional planning methods include MPC, MPPI, ESDF-based nonlinear optimization and so on~ 23,24,35,36 . They typically encode line-of-sight maintenance and obstacle clearance as cost terms for dynamic obstacle avoidance and target tracking. However, in nonconvex scenarios involving narrow passages and tight corners, online solvers such as SQP and L-BFGS are prone to local minima and zero-velocity deadlocks~ 37 . The computational burden depends strongly on the solver, optimization horizon, and environment complexity. Online optimization is still required at every control cycle and becomes more expensive as problem complexity grows. Meanwhile, modeling and state-prediction errors can accumulate over long-horizon rollouts. Learning-Based Motion Planning and Control To avoid repeated online optimization, DRL and behavioral cloning have been widely used in robotic motion planning~ 30,31,41 . Recent cost-guided methods further train policies with trajectory-level objectives. For example, YOPOv2-Tracker~ 8 back-propagates trajectory costs for target tracking, but still predicts intermediate motion representations before execution. Such waypoint- or trajectory-based architectures separate geometric prediction from platform control~ 7,8,9 . This separation can introduce a representation mismatch between training objectives and executable controls~ 13,14,16 . LECO follows the cost-guided learning paradigm, but directly predicts control sequences and introduces explicit target-tracking and LoS objectives. Optimization Distillation and Safe Deployment Optimization-to-Policy transfers the knowledge encoded in traditional optimizers, such as MPC, into neural policies~ 26,43 . It provides a promising way to combine physical constraints with efficient inference. However, existing optimization-distillation methods typically mainly focus on generic motion planning or point-to-point navigation~ 7 . Direct cost optimization can also converge to near-zero controls during early training. Moreover, black-box policies lack deterministic safety guarantees in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios~ 11,17,22,50 . Control barrier function (CBF)-based safety filters add an online constrained safety-filtering step~ 51 . In contrast, fallback strategies, such as emergency stoppage or global replanning, can disrupt the continuity of dynamic tracking. title: JevVLA: Jev-Inspired Energy-Based Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can select among discrete candidates for pick-and-place manipulation or generate continuous action chunks for motion control. Improving both forms of decision making through a common mechanism while retaining the capabilities of a pretrained policy is an important adaptation problem. Inspired by Jev's structured, probabilistic decision interface, we propose JevVLA, a lightweight energy-based adaptation framework for VLA policies. JevVLA instantiates this inspiration by modeling the relative quality of action proposals: with the base policy frozen, it learns a differentiable scalar energy conditioned on observations, task context, and actions, using execution feedback, expert corrections, or demonstration-derived preferences. JevVLA uses this single learned action preference function in two ways: its values compare discrete candidates, while its action gradients correct continuous actions or guide their generation. Candidate selection and continuous control thus share one trainable decision core. Each benchmark uses independently trained weights and fixed input/output encodings, while retaining the same core network with approximately 80,000 trainable parameters. On the held-out test sets, JevVLA improves task success over the respective matched base-policy controls by 1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points on MetaWorld MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and CLIPort, respectively. These results support the feasibility of a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy model for adapting both discrete action selection and continuous action guidance. The JevVLA implementation will be open-sourced at https://github.com/ZJU4EmbodiedAI/JevVLA.
full_text: fig:jevvla-teaser Introduction sec:introduction Vision--language--action (VLA) models connect visual observations and task instructions to robot actions. By combining vision--language pretraining with robot demonstrations, these models learn control policies that serve multiple manipulation tasks, making the reuse and adaptation of existing models an important direction in robot learning~ pmlr-v270-kim25c,pmlr-v305-black25a . However, producing a semantically plausible action does not ensure that an operation will succeed in a particular scene: small geometric errors can change the execution outcome~ ijcai2026p569 . Further fine-tuning a pretrained policy, particularly through full-parameter updates, often entails substantial computational costs and additional task-specific data~ pmlr-v270-kim25c,yang2026_260702092 . This motivates a practical question: how can lightweight adaptation improve action decisions while retaining the action-generation capabilities of the base policy? This goal must accommodate differences in the action interfaces of robot policies. Policies that predict pick-and-place actions can be adapted by constructing a finite set of candidates and comparing their quality. Policies that control robots through continuous action sequences can also be adapted through corrections applied after action prediction or during iterative generation~ pmlr-v202-jiang23b,pmlr-v164-shridhar22a,Chi-RSS-23,black2024_241024164 . Both approaches require an assessment of relative action quality, but they place different demands on the evaluator: candidate selection requires comparable scores across actions, whereas continuous guidance requires useful local correction directions in action space. We investigate how a single lightweight evaluation architecture can support both requirements across base policies with different native action representations. Prior work has shown that scalar energies can represent implicit action policies and support robot control through action optimization~ pmlr-v164-florence22a . For policy adaptation, learned value or performance estimates can select among sampled action chunks or guide continuous action generation through gradients~ ijcai2026p569,yang2026_260702092,wang2026_260310980 . These advances establish the utility of action evaluation for improving base policies. We study how to reuse the function values and action gradients of a common scalar core to organize candidate comparison and continuous correction within one adaptation framework, while keeping the base policies frozen. Jev provides an inspiration for this design through its structured, probabilistic decision interface. Its public interface combines a state with predefined options or scoring questions, returning structured results and probability distributions that software can use for selection, ranking, and branching~ almeida2026jev,typesafe2026jevintro . This perspective motivates modeling action proposal and action evaluation as separate components: the base policy proposes actions, and an adapter represents preferences among them given the current observation and task context. JevVLA draws on Jev's public decision-interface concepts; its robotic action energy, training objectives, and gradient-guidance mechanism are developed independently. We extend explicit comparison among candidates to continuous action space, using a differentiable scalar function both to support selection and to provide local correction directions. We propose JevVLA, a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy-based adaptation framework (Figure~ fig:jevvla-teaser ). JevVLA takes observations, task context, and actions as inputs and uses a conditional quadratic term together with a scalar residual network to model action energy. Depending on the supervision available for each benchmark, it converts executed-branch outcomes, expert corrections, or demonstration-derived action preferences into ranking or gradient-learning signals. At inference time, JevVLA compares energies over a finite candidate set and incorporates the base-policy prior when available. For continuous actions, it differentiates the same energy with respect to the action and applies bounded corrections or guides action generation. The architectural contribution is one trainable preference function for these two decision interfaces: its value supports choice, and its derivative supplies the continuous update. Each benchmark has fixed input/output encodings and independently trained weights, while the energy core remains identical, with 79,817 trainable parameters per adapter. We evaluate this design on five robot manipulation benchmarks: MetaWorld MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and CLIPort~ pmlr-v100-yu20a,pmlr-v202-jiang23b,lynch2022_221006407,Fei_2026_CVPR,pmlr-v164-shridhar22a . These evaluations cover both candidate selection and continuous control. After validation-set selection, JevVLA improves held-out test success over the respective matched base-policy controls by 1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points. These results provide empirical support for applying the same lightweight energy architecture across different robot-policy interfaces. Our contributions are threefold: One action preference core for two VLA interfaces. Values of a conditional scalar energy rank discrete proposals, while gradients of that energy correct continuous actions and guide their generation. The same trainable architecture supports both uses across benchmarks, with independently learned weights. Jev-inspired structured action decisions. We make alternatives and their relative preferences explicit for frozen robot policies, connecting action proposals to a probabilistic comparison and executable selection rule. Evaluation across five robot manipulation benchmarks. Independently trained adapters with approximately 80,000 parameters improve task success over matched base-policy controls in the specified held-out test settings, providing cross-interface evidence for the common architecture. Related Work sec:related_work Vision--language--action models Vision--language robot policies connect images, task instructions, and actions, bringing semantic knowledge and interaction experience to manipulation. Early robot Transformers and subsequent VLA models demonstrate the value of multitask learning and vision--language transfer, while open models provide reusable weights and adaptation pipelines~ Brohan-RSS-23,pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a,pmlr-v270-kim25c . Cross-embodiment pretraining, flow-based action generation, and heterogeneous co-training expand policy coverage; compact vision--language backbones and asynchronous execution also explore training and deployment efficiency~ Ghosh-RSS-24,black2024_241024164,pmlr-v305-black25a,shukor2025_250601844 . These policies expose different action interfaces. Semantic--spatial decomposition, multimodal prompting, and real-time language-conditioned control support pick-and-place decisions or ongoing motion control~ pmlr-v164-shridhar22a,pmlr-v202-jiang23b,lynch2022_221006407 . Action chunking and diffusion-based sequences extend individual predictions to short-horizon generation~ Zhao-RSS-23,Chi-RSS-23 . For downstream adaptation, prior work improves action decoding and fine-tuning objectives or learns a new sampling distribution over the latent-noise space of a frozen policy~ KimM1-RSS-25,pmlr-v305-wagenmaker25a . Reusing an adapter across policies requires handling these action-interface differences: finite-candidate comparison and continuous correction require different operations, and guidance tied to a particular generator has a corresponding scope of applicability. To accommodate these differences, JevVLA extracts action evaluation into a separate conditional scalar module, connecting policies through fixed encodings and using the same core structure for candidate selection and continuous guidance. Robot preference learning Robot preference learning expresses difficult-to-specify objectives through the relative quality of behaviors. Iterative trajectory improvement and joint modeling of demonstrations, corrections, and preferences show that supervision can come from alternatives that improve on current behavior~ jain2013_13066294,mehta2022_220703395 . Reward learning from human comparisons converts segment preferences into scalar objectives, while experience relabeling, unsupervised pretraining, and data augmentation improve feedback utilization~ NIPS2017_d5e2c0ad,pmlr-v139-lee21i,park2022_220310050 . Interactive imitation learning queries experts or records human interventions at states visited by the policy, using data aggregation, sample reweighting, and intervention budgets to improve subsequent behavior~ pmlr-v15-ross11a,liu2022_221108416,pmlr-v164-hoque22a . Work on heterogeneous demonstrations and robotic action preferences learns behavior-quality evaluators or directly updates policies to favor corrected actions over unsuccessful ones~ pmlr-v229-kuhar23a,NEURIPS2025_347110fb . Trajectory quality, terminal success, and local expert corrections provide feedback at different time scales. Mismatched preference and optimization scales affect credit assignment~ taranovic2026_260611982 . JevVLA accordingly constructs ranking or gradient supervision from each data source, preserving the distinct meanings of branch outcomes, corrected actions, and demonstration distances. These signals train a separate energy adapter with a common core architecture, while the available supervision determines the loss used in each setting. Energy-based action selection Energy models represent relative action preferences or unnormalized distributions with conditional scalar functions. Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning connects action values to energy-based policies; implicit imitation learning learns complex action distributions by comparing expert actions with negative samples, with subsequent work analyzing ranking objectives and negative sampling~ pmlr-v70-haarnoja17a,pmlr-v164-florence22a,singh2023_230905803 . Implicit kinematic policies and compositional scene planning further show that energy representations can connect action coordinates or combine spatial relations, acting on control representations and target layouts, respectively~ ganapathi2022_220301983,gkanatsios2023_230414391 . Visual action-value learning, finite-candidate maximization over behavior models, and value-based reweighting of diffusion candidates provide different implementations of proposal followed by evaluation~ pmlr-v87-kalashnikov18a,pmlr-v139-ghasemipour21a,hansenestruch2023_230410573 . This approach also supports few-shot VLA adaptation through geometrically conditioned evaluation of similar action chunks with different execution outcomes~ ijcai2026p569 . However, finite-candidate selection remains limited by the proposal distribution and candidate set. Correctly ranking observed actions does not necessarily provide reliable local gradients between them. Although existing energy policies already employ sampling and optimization, directly learning a control distribution differs from adapting a frozen policy that retains its native interface. JevVLA uses ranking and gradient supervision in its respective training settings and assigns both functions to the same energy architecture, studying its use as an adapter for frozen policies. Inference-time action guidance Score matching and denoising connect probabilistic models to input gradients, while diffusion and flow matching provide different iterative paths for generating complex samples~ JMLR:v6:hyvarinen05a,Vincent_2011,song2021scorebased,NEURIPS2020_4c5bcfec,lipman2023flow . Classifier gradients and combinations of conditional and unconditional predictions modify sampling preferences in conditional generation; trajectory diffusion brings generative priors together with test-time reward guidance for decision making~ NEURIPS2021_49ad23d1,ho2022_220712598,pmlr-v162-janner22a . title: VISTA: Active Exploration for Self-Improvement in Embodied Agents
summary: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.
full_text: VISTA: Active Exploration for Self-Improvement in Embodied Agents Zhang Zhang , Shengjun Zhang , Simin Huang , Min Chen , Chong Xia , \\ Xin Fei , Yueqi Duan Tsinghua University, National University of Singapore ~~Project Page] agenticei.github.io/VISTA-page/ \\[-1.5ex] ~~GitHub Repo] github.com/AgenticEI/VISTA \\[-1.5ex] Introduction Embodied artificial intelligence has emerged as a cornerstone for enabling autonomous systems to perceive, reason, and interact seamlessly within dynamic physical environments, offering transformative potential across household assistance, healthcare logistics, and industrial automation~ brohan2022rt1,openx2023 . Catalyzed by multimodal foundation models and large-scale embodiment datasets, learning-based paradigms have demonstrated increasingly competitive capabilities in executing atomic manipulation tasks~ rt22023,octo_2023,openvla2024,pi02024,pi052025,wu2023gr1,lyu2026lda,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva . But scaling end-to-end policies to long-horizon, multi-stage tasks remains notoriously difficult. End-to-end models suffer severely from compounding execution errors over extended trajectories, out-of-distribution generalization under perturbations, and prohibitive sample complexity when attempting to fit multi-modal, long-tail action distributions across heterogeneous task phases~ ahn2022can,innermonologue2022 . To overcome these fundamental limitations, the convergence of frontier large language model (LLM) agents and robotics has established embodied agentic systems as a pivotal research frontier~ codeaspolicies2023,singh2022progprompt,voxposer2023,voyager2023,rpent2026 . By coupling high-level symbolic reasoning and stateful tool orchestration with low-level control policies, agentic embodied architectures offer decisive advantages in managing long-horizon complexity: they facilitate modular hierarchical task decomposition, support active perception to resolve visual ambiguities, and enable closed-loop error diagnosis and autonomous recovery. The performance, reliability, and long-horizon coherence of such systems depend not only on their pre-trained foundation model weights, but also fundamentally on their harness~ yang2024swe,reflexion2023 . construct harnesses , on or . To address this issue, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that unifies active environmental exploration with closed-loop harness adaptation to achieve embodied self-improvement. harness , the and evidence are , meta-agent to prior hypotheses, reuse effective mechanisms, and from earlier candidates. We evaluate VISTA on LIBERO-Pro~ and . VISTA improves task success . These results support as embodied experience into in . Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose VISTA, a framework that departs from conventional handcrafted heuristics and static memory augmentation by framing the robot's operational harness as an evolvable, executable control plane, realizing autonomous embodied self-improvement. We introduce an active exploration mechanism where the meta-agent empowers the embodied system to actively gather diagnostic physical evidence, exploratory . Furthermore, we develop a Harness Graph to track the evolutionary lineage of candidate harnesses, facilitating hypothesis retrieval, component reuse, and principled branch exploration. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on the challenging LIBERO-Pro and benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves manipulation success rates through accumulated experience, . Related Work sec:related-work Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation Low-level action policies. Foundation models for robotic manipulation can be broadly categorized according to how their semantic knowledge is connected to physical control. One line of research extends pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) into low-level policies through vision--language--action (VLA) models, which generate continuous action chunks using diffusion or flow matching pi02024,diffusionpolicy , task-space keyframes or spatial-grid actions spatialvla , and latent action codes learned from robot trajectories or videos univla,moto . Recent video--action and world--action models further couple action prediction with future visual dynamics lightwam,selfwam . Robot foundation models extend these capabilities across heterogeneous tasks and embodiments scaling,openx2023 , while subsequent studies improve action initialization, tokenization, and adaptation to new tasks and embodiments apt . Despite their strong control performance, these approaches translate general pretrained knowledge into embodiment-specific motor signals and often require additional robot trajectories when the task family or platform changes zhong2025survey . Semantic decision making and physical grounding. A complementary line of research treats foundation models as semantic decision makers rather than direct motor controllers. These models predict subgoals, keypoints, affordances, value maps, or spatial constraints, which are subsequently realized by downstream controllers palme2023,voxposer2023 . Although this preserves high-level semantic reasoning, it separates model intent from physical execution and depends on system-specific grounding pipelines matters,manipulate , as well as long-horizon planning, closed-loop feedback, and failure recovery addressing . Together, these two directions reveal a trade-off between direct physical control and semantic generalization: low-level policies offer precise execution but are closely tied to specific embodiments, whereas intermediate representations preserve semantic structure but limit physical adaptability. This trade-off motivates interfaces that combine semantic interpretability with fine-grained executable actions. Embodied Agent Systems Agentic control architectures. Building on these foundation-model paradigms, agentic embodied systems place a pretrained VLM within an iterative harness that translates model decisions into robot actions and feeds execution outcomes back to the model, thereby closing the perception--decision--execution loop lima2026agentic,guava . Existing systems mainly differ in the primitives through which decisions are executed. Some models generate programs over perception and control APIs roboscript,fu2026cap , while others select skills from predefined libraries roboclaw,sayplan , steer learned policies such as VLAs with language subgoals volo,cortex , or delegate decisions to symbolic planners and numerical optimizers autotamp,chen2025code . To support long-horizon interaction, these systems typically maintain task context and persistent memory remembr , perform feedback-based monitoring and reflection innermonologue2022 , and detect failures for replanning and recovery aha . Interfaces for embodied execution. Within agentic robot systems, interface design strongly affects control performance. While high-level, human-designed abstractions can improve reliability, composing low-level perception and control APIs remains difficult fu2026cap . Many systems therefore expose skills, controllers, or VLAs as callable primitives shi2025hi,rpent2026 , leaving the agent to decide what to do while an opaque executor determines how to perform it addressing . Although this simplifies planning, it reduces the model's role in fine-grained physical control. Similar compact action interfaces are used by computer-use and game agents showui,gameworld , simulated embodied agents behavior,humanclaw , and navigation systems zhou2026embodied . and reusable , , and . Method sec:method VISTA improves an embodied agent by evolving its harness, including the instructions, executable skills, and coordination logic through which the agent perceives, reasons, and acts. The online agent has access to a language-model planner, a VLA model, and public robot capabilities. VISTA keeps the underlying model parameters fixed and optimizes how these resources are composed into autonomous behavior. Figure~ fig:pipeline illustrates the resulting development loop. A meta-agent, implemented as a coding agent, retrieves a harness version and its execution evidence, identifies a behavior to improve, and develops a candidate. During development, it can actively investigate the environment, probe execution failures, and revise the harness in response to newly acquired evidence. It can also request autonomous tests of intermediate versions. The submitted candidate is then frozen and evaluated in fresh autonomous episodes. A host-controlled selection rule updates the incumbent, while the candidate and its evidence remain available for subsequent iterations. Improvement is thus carried forward through both executable harness versions and the experience accumulated while developing them. Harness DAG sec:method:formulation Let denote the online language model, the VLA, and the public capability interface. The interface exposes observation, perception, policy inference, and bounded robot control. A harness is a package , where specifies model-facing instructions, contains skill descriptions and executable implementations, provides hooks for request construction, tool selection, and feedback processing, stores persistent procedural knowledge, and declares tool bindings and capability dependencies. Skills may compose multiple perception or control operations, while policy hooks govern their use within the host's execution loop. Harness revisions can therefore change both the operations available to the agent and how it coordinates them. The model parameters, capability interface, and evaluation rule are fixed. For a task instance , comprising a goal and scene initialization, and execution randomness , let denote official autonomous task success. Our objective is where is the space of admissible harnesses and is the task-instance distribution within the declared search scope. A frozen harness still induces closed-loop behavior: its code and persistent knowledge remain fixed during evaluation, while episode-local state and actions depend on incoming observations. Harness development produces a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of immutable versions. We instantiate each harness as a Git-versioned package, with commits identifying snapshots and parent links defining lineage. Branches preserve alternative development directions, and explicit merges can combine histories. Execution records and development notes are linked to their corresponding versions. Each iteration begins from the incumbent by default, but the meta-agent may select another recorded base, including a previously rejected candidate, and inspect earlier implementations for reusable mechanisms. Retaining unsuccessful proposals makes their diagnostic findings available to later development. Evidence-Guided Harness Revision sec:method:evidence Each development record is tied to a frozen harness version and exact execution condition, including task initialization, repetition, randomness, and execution mode. A trajectory aligns planner decisions and tool calls with robot actions, images, and state, allowing the meta-agent to localize a failure from an aggregate outcome to a specific decision or physical execution interval. Given a base harness and these records, the meta-agent forms a concrete hypothesis and revises the implicated components, such as instructions, observation processing, skill termination, or coordination logic. The resulting version and its supporting evidence are retained for later development. When recorded trajectories are insufficient to resolve the hypothesis, VISTA acquires additional embodied evidence through active exploration.
