title: 3D-Force Estimation for Dual-arm Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects via Factor Graphs
summary: Estimating forces acting on Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is challenging due to their underactuated nature. However, reliable contact estimation is crucial to precisely control them and enable safe manipulation tasks. Differently from the various approaches presented in the literature, this work adopts a probabilistic formulation where the DLO state and sensor data are related through conditional distributions. In particular, factor graphs are used to determine the magnitude, direction, and location of a 3D force acting on a DLO, while simultaneously reconstructing its shape. Since DLOs are not actuated and are typically thin, like cables and wires, strain gauges and actuation readings are usually impractical. Therefore, to overcome this issue, this work is tested using one type of sensing information only, thus developing a generic technique suited for a wider variety of tasks. Realistic tests are performed by introducing noise into the measurements while the DLO follows a prescribed path in the presence of external forces that are accurately estimated.
full_text: 3D-Force Estimation for Dual-arm Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects via Factor Graphs Annika Delucchi, Vincenzo Di~Paola, Bruno Marco Quadrelli, Matteo Zoppi Estimating forces acting on Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is challenging due to their underactuated nature. However, reliable contact estimation is crucial to precisely control them and enable safe manipulation tasks. Differently from the various approaches presented in the literature, this work adopts a probabilistic formulation where the DLO state and sensors data are related through conditional distributions. In particular, factor graphs are used to determine magnitude, direction and location of a 3D force acting on a DLO, while simultaneously reconstructing its shape. Since DLOs are not actuated and typically thin -- like cables and wires -- strain gauges and actuation readings are usually unpractical. Therefore, to overcome this issue, this work is tested using one type of sensing information only thus developing a generic technique suited for a wider variety of tasks. Realistic tests are made by introducing noise on the measurements while the DLO follows a prescrived path in presence of external forces accurately estimated. Contact Force Estimation, Contact Estimation, Factor Graphs, Dual-arm Manipulation, Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) Introduction ual-arm manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects refers to the class of tasks where a slender flexible object --- like ropes and cables --- is guided into a desired shape by imposing a sequence of poses at its end tips. Indeed, threading, knotting and routing~ CuiralZueco2024,Caporali2024,Renda2026DualManip,Delucchi2026 are just a few of the recurring movements necessary for their application in healthcare domain~ BurgnerKahrs2015, Dupont2022, Webster2006,Orekhov2015 , search and rescue~ TognonGabellieri2018 , space applications~ Russo2023Space and so on. Beyond their impressive motion range, a primary motivation in studying DLOs lies in their intrinsic compliance making them well-suited for contact-rich tasks. In this context, although the physics of contact has been extensively studied in the past under both modelling and computational perpectives~ Kikuchi1994,Konyukhov2013,Beal2003,Chamekh2009, GayNeto2015,Tasora2020 , only recently researchers considered the contact in the field of DLOs' manipulation~ Delucchi2026Eucomes,Ferguson2026dlo . The explanation for this delay must be searched in the underactuated nature of DLOs which makes the contact estimation and thus their control highly complex. Therefore, we employ factor graphs~ DellaertBook-FactorGraphs to foresee the contact along the DLO thus addressing one of the limitations that prevent their application in the aforementioned tasks. Though actuated and then different The DLO model does not include any actuation term. , this approach has been applied in the proximal field of continuum robots which will provide the main reference for this work. In this context, early research focused on estimating loads applied at the robot's tip~ Xu2016,Wang2023Survey . As the field further evolved, several approaches were proposed to estimate external forces acting also along robot's backbone~ Lilge2023,Diezinger2022,Pourafzal2023 , combining vision-based information with other sensors, like actuation readings~ FeliuTalegon2025 , strain gauges~ Ferguson2024, Wang2026CosimoRendaLaschi , Fiber Bragg Grating~ Lilge2025 and laser scans~ FergusonRuckerWebster2024 . Among them, it is possible to distinguish two main directions. The first formulates force estimation as an inverse problem, exploiting the kinematic or mechanical model of the robot and using sensors to infer the unknown external forces. Instead, the second adopts a probabilistic formulation, where the robot's state and sensor measurements are related through conditional probability distributions, allowing force estimation even in weakly observable scenarios. For the mentioned reasons, this article leverages the Graph-based method for the estimation of 3D forces acting on DLOs. Hence, without any assumption, location, direction and magnitude of the contact force are estimated simultaneously from discrete spatial information only. During the estimation, only discrete positions along the rod are assumed to be available through camera tracking, emulating a motion capture system based on reflective markers. This minimal sensing setup is dictated by the will of a practical solution, while existing approaches typically combine multiple sensing modalities~ Caporali2024,Hu2025 . The use of a single type of information further emphasizes the challenge of estimating contact forces from limited measurements while simultaneously reconstructing the rod configuration. title: Late Breaking Results: Audio-Language-Action Models with Direct Speech Conditioning for Robotic Manipulation
comment: 2 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to DAC 2026 Late Breaking Results
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to follow instructions in typed text, limiting broader deployment in natural speech. The traditional solution by prepending a speech recognition before VLA to convert speech into texts would incur additional latency and propagate errors. To address this, we present Speech-$π_{0.5}$, which maps raw speech directly to motor commands without explicit textual transcriptions. Specifically, built on $π_{0.5}$, we use a cross-modal projection to convert voice frames directly into audio tokens with significant response latency reduction. To further improve the accuracy, we adopt split LoRA adaptation with dedicated audio and task adapters, under a two-stage training. Speech-$π_{0.5}$ achieves $3\times$ lower response latency than ASR pipeline while maintaining competitive task success on LIBERO, and generalizes robustly to unseen accents where a single adapter degrades significantly.
full_text: Late Breaking Results: Audio-Language-Action Models with Direct Speech Conditioning for Robotic Manipulation Enfu Nan , Pu Zhao , Yixiao Chen , Lin Zhao , \\ Juyi Lin , Chen Wang , Weiwei Chen , Yanzhi Wang cccc Northeastern University & EmbodyX Inc. Nan et al. Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to follow instructions in typed text, limiting broader deployment in natural speech. The traditional solution by prepending a speech recognition before VLA to convert speech into texts would incur additional latency and propagate errors. To address this, we present Speech- , which maps raw speech directly to motor commands without explicit textual transcriptions. Specifically, built on , we use a cross-modal projection to convert voice frames directly into audio tokens with significant response latency reduction. To further improve the accuracy, we adopt split LoRA adaptation with dedicated audio and task adapters, under a two-stage training. Speech- achieves lower response latency than ASR pipeline while maintaining competitive task success on LIBERO, and generalizes robustly to unseen accents where a single adapter degrades significantly. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ black2024pi0,pi05,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla have made rapid progress in enabling robots to follow natural language instructions, but they universally require typed text as input. This may limit their wide deployment in practical natural speech environments zhao-etal-2024-pruning,shen2024search,zhan2024exploring,zhan2024fast,shen2025sparse,shen2024lazydit . The traditional solution is to prepend an automatic speech recognition (ASR) such as Whisper~ radford2023whisper , which converts speech into texts first, and then feeds texts to VLA. However, it incurs large response latency to trigger robot actions due to verbose textual transcription, with potential accuracy loss from transcription errors. Although recent works~ vlas,tang2024salmonn show that speech tokens can be integrated into LLMs via projection, integrating speech into high-performance VLAs such as ~ pi05 remains largely unexplored, as their vision-language backbones present a modality gap that cannot be bridged by projection alone. To address this, we propose Speech- , with three key contributions: (i)~cross-modal projection that compresses speech into compact VLM tokens; (ii)~split LoRA that improve audio quality and accent robustness over a standard single adapter; and (iii)~two-stage training to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Our model eliminates the ASR decoder, achieving lower response latency with competitive task success on LIBERO~ liu2023libero . Method We propose Speech- , which accepts voice instructions and outputs robotic actions for robot tasks. Built on , our method has three key techniques (Figure~ fig:arch ), including (i) cross-modal projection, (ii) split LoRA adaption, and (iii) two stage training. Cross-Modal Projection We design a cross-modal projection to convert speech hidden states into VLM tokens. Specifically, given a spoken instruction, a frozen pretrained speech encoder produces frame-level hidden states ( frames). Then a two-layer MLP with GeLU activation projects these into the VLM token space ( ). A learned cross-attention pooling module with learnable query vectors then compresses the projected sequence: \[ _ = ( ,\, ( )) ^ 32 d_v . \] where is a set of 32 learnable query vectors optimized during end-to-end training. By compressing 1500 speech frames into 32 tokens via attention pooling, we bypass the autoregressive ASR decoder, reducing ASR-stage latency by 94–97 . Split LoRA Adaptation. To equip the model with audio capabilities, we adopt LoRA~ hu2022lora to finetune the VLM backbone. However, we observe that a single LoRA is easy to overfit to training voices, with sharply degrading accuracy on unseen accents ( sec:ablation ). To address this, we therefore propose to use split LoRA: each of the 18 Gemma-2B backbone layers receives two rank-16 adapters---a task LoRA ( ) active at text/action positions and an audio LoRA ( ) active at audio positions. For hidden state at position , the LoRA output is: Position-based routing keeps the two pathways separate. This separation ensures that speech adaptation does not interfere with task learning, preserving task performance while enabling robust generalization across diverse audio commands. Two-Stage Training Stage~1: Speech--Language Alignment. To effectively supervise ASR, we use the outputs of the original PaliGemma ( backbone) under the ground-truth text inputs, to distill our speech- with our projection and audio LoRA adapter. By aligning the outputs of the original model under texts and our model under audio through MSE loss distillation, our modules are enforced to extract and align linguistic content from audio tokens. Training uses robot-domain TTS covering 100k instructions across voices, mixed with task-specific vocabulary. The action expert remains frozen. ~2: Task Training. We optimize the LoRA adapters (both the task-specific and audio-specific), the action expert LoRA, and the audio projector, using the flow matching action loss on robotic demonstration data, while keeping the speech encoder and base model weights frozen. Crucially, the task and audio LoRA parameters are updated at different learning rates, with the audio LoRA assigned a smaller learning rate. This asymmetric update scheme prevents task-oriented gradients from overwriting the learned audio representations, thereby preserving speech understanding capability throughout manipulation training. The joint optimization of the projection layers and LoRA modules is essential: it enables the model to acquire task-level manipulation competence while retaining the generalization ability of the speech recognition pathway. Experiments sec:ablation We evaluate on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Object (10 tasks each, 50 episodes per task, per condition)~ liu2023libero . We use Whisper-large-v3~ radford2023whisper as the frozen speech encoder. We use Piper TTS (22 VCTK speakers) to train audios. For held-out evaluation, we use 10 Azure Neural TTS voices with accents unseen during training. Accuracy. Our method achieves higher action accuracy than single LoRA, as split LoRA adaptation mitigates interventions from audio tokens for robotic tasks. As shown in Table~ tab:main , our method reaches 89.2 on LIBERO-Spatial and 86.0 on LIBERO-Object, higher than single LoRA with non-marginal improvements. Robustness. With the proposed LoRA Adaptation and two stage training, our Speech- achieves higher accents robustness. As shown in Table~ tab:main , when our finetuned Speech- is evaluated on held out accents unseen during training, the accuracy of LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Object only drops slightly. By contrast, on LIBERO-Object, the single LoRA baseline without our split loRA adaptation suffers from significant accuracy drop from 69 to 38 due to overfitting. Differently, by isolating audio representations in a dedicated adapter, our method learns accent-invariant speech features rather than overfitting to training voices. Latency Reduction. Our method can significantly reduce the response latency for the first action, since our model directly addresses voice tokens without voice decoding into plain texts. As shown in Table~ tab:latency , traditional ASR pipeline needs to decode voice into texts with massive computations, resulting in significant latency before the first action. By contrast, our cross-modal projection converts speech features into tokens which are sent directly to following VLMs, skipping the steps of decoding into texts and then further encoding into tokens. With our method, the first action fires in 109 ms, achieving a 3 reduction in response latency. Conclusion We present Speech- , an audio-language-action model that maps speech directly to robot actions. Our end-to-end approach eliminates the ASR decoder bottleneck, achieving lower latency than the traditional ASR decoder pipeline with competitive accuracy. title: RelateGS: Reliable Semantic and Relational Evidence for 3D Scene Understanding with Gaussian Splatting
summary: Language-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has advanced language-driven 3D scene understanding by incorporating semantic and relational cues into reconstructed scenes. However, relation-aware grounding depends not only on representing such information, but also on whether the underlying scene-side evidence is reliable and sufficient. Multi-view semantic aggregation can incorporate weak observations, while object relations can remain under-observed along the available camera trajectory, leading to ambiguous evidence for target disambiguation. We present RelateGS, a structured language-aware Gaussian representation that selectively refines semantic and relational evidence for 3D visual grounding. RelateGS suppresses unreliable observations during semantic feature uplifting and consolidates multi-view object observations into a persistent 3D graph. The graph further identifies under-observed object relations and guides targeted re-querying of informative existing frames to complement their evidence. Experiments on Sr3D+ and Nr3D demonstrate competitive 3D grounding performance, improving the previous best by 7.9 and 1.7 percentage points at Acc@0.25, respectively.
full_text: Language-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has advanced language-driven 3D scene understanding by incorporating semantic and relational cues into reconstructed scenes. However, relation-aware grounding depends not only on representing such information, but also on whether the underlying scene-side evidence is reliable and sufficient. Multi-view semantic aggregation can incorporate weak observations, while object relations can remain under-observed along the available camera trajectory, leading to ambiguous evidence for target disambiguation. We present RelateGS, a structured language-aware Gaussian representation that selectively refines semantic and relational evidence for 3D visual grounding. RelateGS suppresses unreliable observations during semantic feature uplifting and consolidates multi-view object observations into a persistent 3D graph. The graph further identifies under-observed object relations and guides targeted re-querying of informative existing frames to complement their evidence. Experiments on Sr3D+ and Nr3D demonstrate competitive 3D grounding performance, improving the previous best by 7.9 and 1.7 percentage points at Acc@0.25, respectively. Introduction sec:introduction Understanding and localizing objects in 3D environments from natural language is essential for embodied applications such as navigation and manipulation. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs provides an explicit and high-fidelity scene representation with real-time rendering, and recent language-aware extensions associate Gaussian primitives with vision-language features to support open-vocabulary localization and semantic understanding~ langsplat,LEGaussian,opengaussian,occamslgs . By embedding language-aligned semantics directly into an explicit 3D representation, these approaches provide a promising foundation for grounding natural-language descriptions in reconstructed 3D scenes. Despite these advances, many referring expressions identify a target not only by what it is, but also by how it relates to surrounding objects. While language-aware 3DGS can retrieve semantically relevant objects, multiple instances may appear equally plausible, yet only one may satisfy a description such as ``the chair next to the table.'' Resolving such expressions therefore requires object-level relational context beyond semantic similarity alone. Recent approaches have extended language-aware 3D representations from dense semantics to structured relational representations by organizing reconstructed scenes into persistent object instances and modeling their pairwise relations~ gaussiangraph, reasongrounder, chainsemantics . However, constructing an object-centric relational representation does not by itself guarantee reliable relational grounding, as shown in Fig.~ fig:main_intro . The resulting representation is ultimately constrained by the quality and coverage of the visual observations from which its semantics and relations are constructed. First, semantic evidence can be unreliable because language features are aggregated from observations affected by viewpoint changes, partial occlusion, object boundaries, and limited visibility. Weak observations can therefore corrupt the semantic representation of a Gaussian and increase ambiguity among similar object candidates. Second, relational evidence can be insufficient because pairwise relations are inferred only from the object configurations exposed by the available camera views. When a grounding-relevant object pair is poorly observed, the relation needed to distinguish the target may remain weak or missing. Consequently, even an explicitly structured scene can fail to resolve relational language when its semantic evidence is unreliable or its relational evidence is under-observed. Our key insight is that relation-aware grounding benefits from selectively refining the scene-side evidence supporting the representation, rather than treating all available observations as equally informative. Specifically, weak semantic observations should be suppressed during Gaussian feature construction, while under-observed object relations should be complemented using informative existing observations. Based on this insight, we introduce RelateGS, a structured language-aware Gaussian representation that selectively refines the scene-side evidence required for relation-aware 3D grounding. Specifically, RelateGS realizes this principle through complementary semantic and relational refinement. First, confidence-aware semantic uplifting estimates the contribution of each image observation to individual Gaussians and selectively aggregates reliable language evidence, reducing semantic ambiguity introduced by weak observations. The resulting multi-view semantics are consolidated into a persistent 3D object graph that maintains object identities and spatial relationships across views. Second, graph-guided relational re-querying reasons over the current graph to identify under-observed object pairs and selects informative frames from the existing camera trajectory for targeted re-querying. The recovered relational evidence is fused back into the persistent graph, allowing RelateGS to complement missing relations rather than treating the initially constructed graph as a fixed output. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RelateGS substantially improves relation-aware 3D visual grounding. On Sr3D+ and Nr3D~ referit3d , RelateGS achieves competitive overall grounding performance, showing the effectiveness of selectively refining scene-side semantic and relational evidence. Additional semantic evaluations and controlled ablations further validate the underlying representation and the contribution of each refinement strategy. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate relation-aware 3D grounding from the perspective of scene-side evidence quality, considering both the reliability of Gaussian-level semantic evidence and the sufficiency of object-level relational evidence. We introduce RelateGS, which realizes selective evidence refinement through confidence-aware semantic uplifting and graph-guided relational re-querying over a persistent 3D object graph. RelateGS improves grounding performance on Sr3D+ and Nr3D, while complementary semantic evaluations and controlled ablations validate the proposed representation design. Related Work sec:related_work Language-Embedded 3D Gaussian Splatting Recent advances in 3DGS~ 3dgs have extended its role from photorealistic scene reconstruction to language-aware 3D understanding. Building on 2D foundation models such as SAM~ sam and CLIP~ clip , recent approaches extract object masks and language-aligned features from multi-view images and transfer this semantic evidence to Gaussian primitives. LangSplat~ langsplat and LEGaussians~ LEGaussian embed language-aligned features into Gaussian scenes for open-vocabulary localization. OpenGaussian~ opengaussian further targets point-level open-vocabulary understanding through improved semantic representation and 2D--3D association. GAGS~ gags improves multi-view semantic consistency through granularity-aware segmentation and feature distillation. Instead of optimizing additional semantic parameters, LUDVIG~ ludvig and Occam's LGS~ occamslgs transfer multi-view language features to pre-trained Gaussian primitives according to their rendering contributions. More recently, ReasonGrounder~ reasongrounder introduces hierarchical Gaussian feature fields together with large vision-language models for open-vocabulary grounding and reasoning. These methods demonstrate the effectiveness of dense language-aligned Gaussian representations for connecting natural language with reconstructed 3D scenes. However, the resulting Gaussian-level semantics ultimately depend on the multi-view observations from which they are constructed. Observations can vary substantially in reliability due to visibility, occlusion, and object boundaries, yet this variation is not always explicitly considered during semantic aggregation. RelateGS builds on language-embedded Gaussians from this perspective, focusing on how reliable semantic evidence can be selectively preserved for downstream relation-aware grounding. 3D Scene Graph Generation 3D scene graphs provide an object-centric abstraction of a scene by representing objects as nodes and their semantic or spatial relationships as edges. 3DSSG~ 3dssg establishes object and relation prediction from 3D point clouds, while SceneGraphFusion~ scenegraphfusion incrementally constructs scene graphs from RGB-D sequences. Subsequent works improve the quality and consistency of object-level representations: VL-SAT~ vlsat incorporates visual-linguistic context for 3D scene graph prediction, and SGAligner~ sgaligner exploits cross-modal alignment for object association across 3D scenes. With the emergence of 3DGS, GaussianGraph~ gaussiangraph extends this object-centric perspective to Gaussian scenes by organizing reconstructed primitives into objects with semantic attributes and spatial relationships. These works demonstrate that object-centric graphs complement dense semantic representations by explicitly modeling inter-object relationships. However, the presence of a scene graph does not guarantee sufficient observational support for relation-aware grounding. In particular, limited visibility and co-visibility along the camera trajectory can leave relational evidence incomplete, even when the corresponding objects are represented in the graph. RelateGS therefore leverages a persistent scene graph not only to represent object relationships but also to identify under-observed object pairs and guide targeted retrieval of complementary evidence from multi-view observations. 3D Visual Grounding 3D visual grounding aims to localize a target object from a natural-language referring expression. When multiple instances share the same semantic category, grounding often requires spatial and contextual relationships with surrounding objects. Point-cloud-based approaches such as CORE-3DVG~ core3dvg and ViewSRD~ viewsrd exploit contextual and relational cues to resolve such ambiguity. ConcreteNet~ concretenet improves dense 3D grounding through relation-aware attention, contrastive learning, viewpoint modeling, and multi-view ensembling. More recently, EG-3DVG~ eg3dvg introduces an expression- and geometry-aware grounding decoder that improves text--vision alignment and selectively aggregates geometry-consistent visual cues. Recent methods exploit relational scene representations to disambiguate referred objects~ reasongrounder, gaussiangraph . Chain of Semantics Programming~ chainsemantics formulates grounding as zero-shot neuro-symbolic reasoning, constructing a relationship graph and chain of semantics while leveraging multi-view 3DGS rendering for complementary semantic observations. In contrast, RelateGS focuses on whether the scene representation provides reliable and sufficient grounding evidence, rather than introducing new decoders, reasoning programs, or rendered viewpoints. It selectively preserves reliable Gaussian-level semantics and complements under-observed object-level relations before downstream reasoning. Method sec:method Overview sec:overview We present RelateGS, a structured language-aware Gaussian representation for relation-aware 3D grounding. Given posed RGB-D observations and a reconstructed 3D Gaussian scene, we construct semantic and relational evidence to disambiguate the referred object through its relations to other instances. We first construct reliable Gaussian-level semantic evidence from multi-view observations and associate object observations across views to form an initial object graph. We then identify under-observed object pairs and selectively re-query informative observations to complement missing relational evidence, yielding a refined object graph for language grounding. title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Reproducible simulation study of quadrotor controller benchmarking
summary: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.

We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing. Quadrotor trajectory tracking is inherently coupled with attitude regulation because translational motion is generated by reorienting the thrust vector, while achievable performance is constrained by motor dynamics, thrust saturation, and power limitations~ mahony2012,faessler2017 . Controller comparisons are therefore a recurring theme in the literature, from early PID/LQ, backstepping, and sliding-mode studies~ bouabdallah2004,bouabdallah2005,bouabdallah2007 to recent comparisons of linear and nonlinear MPC and differential-flatness-based control~ kamel2017,sun2022 . Surveys of multirotor, PID, and MPC control~ nascimento2019,lopez2023,nguyen2021mpc and of agile autonomous flight~ hanover2024 summarize the broad design space. The observed outcome of such a comparison, however, depends on more than the feedback law. It is also influenced by (i) the effort devoted to tuning each method, (ii) the availability of future reference information, (iii) whether motor dynamics are represented in the predictor, (iv) the command applied when the optimizer fails or returns an unacceptable solution, and (v) whether each command is available within the sampling period. The last two factors are especially important for optimization-driven controllers, since the system may receive a mix of accepted optimizer results and fallback actions, and each optimizer call has a non-negligible computation latency~ findeisen2004,wang2010 . For these reasons, simply reporting an average tracking error can hide these influences. This paper examines these effects in a controlled simulation study of cascade PID, hover LQR, BL-SMC, and LMPC-F. A preview-enabled LMPC-F and a geometric controller are included in a confirmation study using fresh realizations. All controllers are evaluated on the same nonlinear plant, with a common rotor allocator and a 50~Hz update rate, while retaining their method-specific reference construction, feedforward terms, and inner-loop structure. It addresses three questions: How does a matched candidate-count tuning protocol affect the accuracy ordering, and does the resulting ordering persist on fresh realizations and under larger candidate-count budgets? How do reference preview, motor-state prediction, fallback projection, and tilt-constraint placement individually and jointly affect LMPC-F under smooth and discontinuous references? How sensitive are the closed-loop results to measured command-call delays and missed deadlines? The main contributions of this work are as follows. A paired fixed-versus-tuned evaluation over 50 randomized realizations demonstrates that a matched candidate-count tuning protocol changes the mean-RMSE ordering of the four controllers, and that the accuracy gains are accompanied by controller-dependent changes in actuation smoothness. A factorial analysis of LMPC-F design choices shows that reference preview has a stronger effect than predictor choice during a smooth maneuver. For an abrupt step, however, fallback projection helps only in combination with preview, motor prediction, and reduced actuator authority. An analysis of LMPC-F applied-input variation shows that most of the large variation occurs within fallback intervals rather than at transitions between QP and fallback operation. A confirmation study on 50 fresh realizations extends the evaluation to a geometric controller, preview-enabled MPC, and nested tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. It reproduces the change in the mean-RMSE ordering, shows that the ordering is maintained when the candidate-count budget is quadrupled, and finds that reference preview removes the large variation in the MPC input. A replay using recorded command-call timing traces on a desktop computer and a Raspberry Pi~5 demonstrates that numerical acceptance of a control solution does not guarantee its timely delivery to the actuators, and that an iteration cap tied to the deadline removed the resulting failures in the tested nominal timing profiles. These results provide the basis for a reporting checklist in Table~ tab:checklist for future quadrotor controller comparisons. All configurations, raw logs, and timing traces are publicly released to support reproducibility (see the Data and code statement). An independent rerun reproduces every non-timing array to within , and the confirmation study reproduces the non-timing metrics of all 96 shared development episodes exactly. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related reviews related controller benchmarks. Sections~ sec:model and~ sec:ctrl describe the quadrotor model and controller implementations, respectively. Section~ sec:design presents the experimental protocol, and Section~ sec:results reports the results. Section~ sec:discussion discusses verification, practical implications, and limitations. Finally, Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper. Related Work sec:related Quadrotor Controller Comparisons Bouabdallah et al. compared PID and LQ control on an indoor micro quadrotor, where the observed differences depended on the model used for controller design~ bouabdallah2004 ; they later compared backstepping and sliding-mode control~ bouabdallah2005 and extended backstepping to full position control~ bouabdallah2007 . Geometric tracking on ~ lee2010 and differential-flatness-based control~ mellinger2011,faessler2018 provide high-performance baselines beyond hover linearization. Kamel et al.~ kamel2017 compared linear and nonlinear MPC for trajectory tracking, and Sun et al.~ sun2022 found that the relative merit of nonlinear MPC and flatness-based control depends on reference feasibility and on how the inner loop and rotor drag are handled. Time-optimal contouring MPC~ romero2022,krinner2024 and data-driven or learned aerodynamic models~ torrente2021 extend the operating envelope further. These studies motivate the present focus on implementation choices rather than on the feedback law alone. Benchmark Frameworks Martini et al.~ martini2023 evaluated seven controller architectures over six missions on a nonlinear quadrotor model with motor lag and saturation. Safe-Control-Gym~ yuan2022 provides symbolic dynamics, constraints, and repeatable disturbances for cart-pole and reduced-dimensional quadrotor tasks, and gym-pybullet-drones~ panerati2021 offers a physics-based multi-agent environment for learning-based control. Zhang et al.~ zhang2025 introduced a RotorPy-based suite for adaptive control under disturbances, uncertainty, and delayed actuation. Table~ tab:framework summarizes their documented features. Because plant models, interfaces, and objectives differ, the numerical results are not directly comparable with those reported here. MPC Implementation Issues Stability and feasibility of constrained MPC are classically analyzed under exact, timely solutions~ mayne2000,rawlings2017 . In practice, real-time MPC relies on fast QP solvers such as OSQP~ stellato2020 , qpOASES~ ferreau2014 , or acados~ verschueren2022 , with bounded iterations and early termination~ wang2010 or reduced-order prediction models~ bangura2014 . Soft state constraints preserve feasibility, and with an exact penalty the original hard constraint is still satisfied whenever it is feasible~ kerrigan2000,zeilinger2014 ; and computation delay degrades closed-loop behavior unless it is explicitly accounted for~ findeisen2004 . How fallback policies, solver acceptance rules, and measured delays jointly shape quadrotor tracking is rarely reported; this study makes these elements explicit and measurable. Related work in machine learning has highlighted the sensitivity of reported results to implementation and evaluation choices~ henderson2018 , while random and stratified sampling provide strong baselines for finite-budget hyperparameter optimization~ bergstra2012,mckay1979 . The present protocol applies related concerns to classical and optimization-based flight-control benchmarking. title: Labference: Benchmarking the Reasoning-Action Connection in Robotic Laboratories
summary: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.

Realizing this promise requires reliable handling of samples, reagents, and instruments, often around chemicals, heated vessels, and moving equipment where sustained precision and attention are essential. Laboratory automation can reduce hands-on exposure and repetitive workload while increasing throughput~ leong2025safety,zhang2025robochemist ; the longer-term goal is a laboratory that selects experiments, carries them out, and uses the resulting evidence to guide its next investigation~ tom2024selfdriving,canty2025science . For that cycle to produce meaningful scientific evidence, the robot must preserve experimental requirements throughout the physical procedure and adapt when an operation produces an unexpected result. Progress in experimental planning and robot control provides complementary foundations for this goal. For example, Coscientist has demonstrated synthesis planning, instrument programming, and experiment optimization with tool support~ boiko2023coscientist , while vision-language-action policies such as RT-2 map visual observations and instructions to robot actions across varied manipulation settings~ brohan2023rt2 . Systems also connect these capabilities directly: SayCan grounds language-based skill selection in robotic affordances, and RoboChemist combines multimodal planning, visual targets, and execution monitoring for chemical procedures~ ahn2022saycan,zhang2025robochemist . Although these advances establish routes from high-level requirements to physical action, an attempted operation can leave the scene in a state different from the one the plan assumed. As objects move and measurements change, the robot must therefore use the observed outcome to determine what remains to be done and guide its next action accordingly. The ability to execute a skill thus differs from the ability to apply it appropriately: the same grasp-and-insert motion can satisfy or violate a procedure depending on the selected tube, destination, and timing. Geometric grounding methods such as VoxPoser and ReKep translate language and visual evidence into spatial objectives or manipulation constraints~ huang2023voxposer,huang2024rekep ; when an outcome changes the required operation, the system must also revise the objective guiding those constraints. Laboratory autonomy therefore involves two coupled feedback loops: measurements guide the next experiment, while manipulation outcomes guide the next operation within it~ fakhruldeen2022archemist,dai2024autonomous . Both depend on selecting appropriate operations and executing them while maintaining sample identity, meeting geometric tolerances, and respecting instrument timing and procedural dependencies~ lan2025autobio,salazar2026adept . For instance, when loading two equal-mass tubes into opposite centrifuge slots, the destination of the second tube depends on where the first tube actually settles. If the first tube enters a different slot from the intended one, the second destination changes; if insertion fails, the robot must complete that placement before advancing. The same dependence appears in feedback weighing: for a 200\,g target, a stable reading of 150\,g calls for adding 50\,g, whereas a reading of 180\,g calls for 20\,g. Because a weight that misses the pan leaves the load unchanged, the next adjustment must follow the measured result rather than the attempted placement. In both cases, the robot must apply a procedural rule to an observed outcome and direct its manipulation skill to the resulting target. Where loading and weighing use current occupancy or readouts, sample retrieval additionally depends on an earlier observed result. For example, if a colleague or another robot moves a rack after a tube has been placed, an instruction to retrieve that tube still refers to the same sample even though its world position has changed. Among visually identical tubes, successful retrieval therefore requires remembering the sample's actual local slot and locating that slot in the rack's current pose. Since grasping a neighboring tube can succeed physically while violating the procedure, retrieval evaluation must distinguish the remembered target association, its current localization, and the execution of the grasp. Across these examples, the reasoning--action connection has a concrete meaning: commands must preserve the selected object, destination, quantity, and timing, while subsequent choices must reflect the observed result. A changed pose calls for updated motion, a failed placement calls for recovery, and confirmed progress enables the next operation. Evaluating this connection addresses a central requirement of Embodied AI for Science: turning experimental plans into physical procedures that satisfy their requirements and produce interpretable outcomes. These operational demands create a corresponding measurement problem. Chemistry3D, AutoBio, LabUtopia, Labimus, and LabDex establish foundations in scientific simulation, instrument interaction, dexterity, quantitative precision, and extended workflows~ li2024chemistry3d,lan2025autobio,li2025labutopia,wu2026labimus,tang2026labdex , while LABSHIELD examines hazard perception and safety-critical planning~ sun2026labshield . Reasoning benchmarks further study plan adaptation, history-dependent manipulation, and decision-making interfaces~ tupini2026asgard,chen2026rmbench,li2024eai . Although these evaluations characterize important aspects of laboratory competence, deployment also requires understanding how outcome interpretation, operation selection, and execution work together: does a changed physical outcome lead to the required change in choice, and does that choice guide successful manipulation? Aggregate completion scores combine wrong-target selection with failed execution, whereas isolated interface scores leave their downstream effects unresolved. Addressing this gap requires controlled changes to physical evidence and targeted support within the same procedure, so that both the adaptation of choices and their consequences can be measured. Addressing this gap calls for three connected measurements. To test evidence use, the same goal and rule must require different choices after different outcomes; controlled variations distinguish this adaptation from repetition of a predictable sequence~ jiang2026benchmarkaudit . Once a choice is identified, choice and execution must be recorded separately so that selecting the wrong slot and failing to insert into the correct slot remain distinct outcomes. To make the diagnosis actionable, matched support conditions must then test what changes when state recognition, operation selection, localization, or execution receives assistance. Common physical checkpoints connect these measurements: they fix the starting condition, identify the tested interface, and expose the consequence of support during continued manipulation. Within this evaluation, we use state-dependent reasoning to denote applying a task's rules to current evidence and relevant interaction history to select an operation, object, destination, or appropriate waiting and stopping condition. The observable relationship between evidence and choice therefore supplies the evaluation target, while physical confirmation establishes whether the resulting action fulfilled the requirement. We introduce , a benchmark for studying this relationship during robotic laboratory manipulation (Figure~ fig:state-choice ). Each task specifies the relevant evidence, the set of legal next operations, and the physical events that confirm progress. For example, a placement advances the task once the object is released, supported, and stable, while a weighing decision uses a stable measured load. By tying progress to these events, the formulation accommodates multiple valid operation orders and grounds subsequent decisions in actual outcomes. Controlled instance pairs then preserve the goal and task rule while varying the evidence that should change the choice; online evaluation separately records the first identifiable choice, its execution, and overall completion, together with subsequent correction and recovery. This structure accommodates spatial occupancy, measured quantities, equipment states, and sample-location history across laboratory procedures. Once a behavioral failure has been identified, the next question is which support helps the system make progress. addresses this question through online checkpoints that measure state recognition, operation selection, target localization, or execution from common physical starting conditions. Matched Oracle continuations then alter one registered input or interface output, allowing the subsequent choice and physical result to be compared with the base branch. For instance, observed occupancy can provide state support, a legal symbolic operation can provide decision support, and candidate coordinate frames can provide geometry support; a reference executor can also attempt the operation selected by the system. Comparing these outcomes alongside checkpoint errors helps identify targeted improvements for further testing. The framework accommodates both native vision-language-action policies and agents that combine these policies with other tools, applying compatible support at declared observation or execution interfaces. Across these system designs, evaluation asks whether behavior responds to relevant evidence, whether the selected operation is carried out successfully, and which support improves subsequent performance. The resulting measurements can guide targeted improvements to be tested on held-out instances, connecting the diagnosis of operational failures to the broader goal of sustained autono

title: TurboWAM: Learning What Matters for Fast World Action Models
summary: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.

Introduction sec:introduction World Action Models (WAMs)~ ye2026world,kim2026cosmos,li2026causal,bi2026motus,yuan2026fast,zhang2026world have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robot policy learning. Typically, WAMs integrate future visual generation with action prediction into a unified framework, allowing robots to anticipate how the physical world evolves during interaction. Despite their promising performance, the high computational cost of WAMs remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. In particular, WAMs often rely on large-scale video generative models that require iterative denoising to predict future observations, resulting in substantial computational overhead and inference latency. This limits their applicability to real-time robotic control, where efficient and responsive action prediction is essential. Recently, several methods~ yuan2026fast,ma2026faster,zhao2026faster,li2026efficient,li2026light have been proposed to improve the inference efficiency of WAMs for robot policy learning. These methods primarily address the computational bottleneck by reducing test-time future imagination, accelerating action prediction, or developing more efficient model architectures. Despite their encouraging results, several limitations remain. First, these methods often process or aggregate features from all world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to the ongoing action prediction. However, different layers may contribute unequally to action prediction, and their importance can vary across denoising timesteps. Consequently, indiscriminately processing all layers introduces redundant computation and leads to suboptimal representation utilization. Second, existing approaches typically lack explicit mechanisms to regulate how action supervision influences the optimization of different world model layers. Without such mechanisms, the learned world representations may not be sufficiently aligned with the requirements of action prediction, limiting policy performance. To resolve these limitations, in this work, we propose TurboWAM, a novel fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured In this work, ``structure'' refers to model structure rather than geometric structure. Specifically, TurboWAM employs layer-wise world representation aggregation and action supervision across world model layers. We therefore use “structured” to characterize this layer-wise design. world representations conditioned on action predictions. Following~ yuan2026fast,ma2026faster , TurboWAM preserves video co-training during training while eliminating future visual prediction during inference. Specifically, we introduce a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively aggregates representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to action prediction at each denoising timestep. Unlike existing methods that rely on fixed or action-independent representation fusion, our approach dynamically adjusts the contribution of different layers based on the current action denoising state. Furthermore, by restricting inference to a limited number of world model layers and caching reusable representations for efficient aggregation, TurboWAM substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving informative world representations for action prediction. To further improve the alignment between world representation learning and action prediction, we develop a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation. Importantly, this mechanism operates exclusively during backward propagation without introducing additional computation into the forward inference process, allowing TurboWAM to benefit from structured action supervision without compromising inference efficiency. We conduct extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks and on real-world robot manipulation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods (as illustrated in Figure~ fig:illustration ). In summary, our contributions are: We propose TurboWAM, a novel fast world action model that efficiently leverages structured world representations for action prediction, reducing inference overhead while preserving the benefits of video co-training. We develop a structured world representation aggregation module that fuses representations across different world model layers conditioned on the action denoising state. We propose a structured action supervision mechanism that modulates action-supervision gradients across different world model layers during backward propagation. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves lower inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods. Related Work sec:related_work World Action Models. World Action Models (WAMs)~ ye2026world,kim2026cosmos,zhang2026learning,zhu2025unified,zhang2026imagewam and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models~ black2024pi_0,black2025pi_05,kim2024openvla,kim2025fine have emerged as two prominent paradigms for robot policy learning. While VLA models typically predict actions directly from visual observations and language instructions, WAMs leverage visual generative models, such as video generation models~ wan2025wan , to incorporate knowledge of physical dynamics into action prediction. By jointly modeling future visual observations and robot actions, WAMs learn world representations that capture how the environment evolves during interaction~ ye2026world,kim2026cosmos,li2026causal,bi2026motus,yuan2026fast . Representative approaches, including DreamZero~ ye2026world , Motus~ bi2026motus , Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos , and LingBot-VA~ li2026causal , have demonstrated the potential of leveraging predictive world modeling for robot control. Despite their promising performance, these methods often incur substantial computational overhead due to the expensive process of future visual generation, limiting their applicability to real-time robotic control. Our work focuses on improving the inference efficiency of WAMs while maintaining competitive task success rates. Low-Latency World Action Models. Recent efforts have explored various strategies to reduce the inference latency of WAMs. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast eliminates explicit future visual generation during inference while retaining video co-training during training, enabling efficient action prediction without test-time future imagination. Faster-WAM~ ma2026faster aggregates key and value representations from all video world model layers using learned fusion weights and employs a single-DiT-block action head to reduce action prediction latency. ARPS~ gu2026right aggregates intermediate world model features into a compact state for the action expert to reduce inference overhead and employs future-representation supervision to enhance world representation learning. Other methods explore model compression and lightweight architectures~ li2026efficient,li2026light , as well as sparse video-action interactions~ zhao2026faster , to improve inference efficiency. Despite these advances, existing methods do not explicitly explore adaptive world representation learning conditioned on the evolving action denoising state and still leave room for improvement in the efficient utilization of world representations. In contrast, our TurboWAM introduces structured world representation aggregation that dynamically adjusts the contributions of different world model layers conditioned on the current action denoising state. Additionally, our structured action supervision explicitly modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers. By reducing the number of world model layers executed during inference and caching reusable representations for efficient aggregation, TurboWAM further reduces inference latency. title: VisGeo-PipeTrack: A Visual Geometric Servo Control Framework with MPC-RCAPID Control for UAV-Based Dynamic Pipes Tracking
comment: Submit to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems IEEE TITS
summary: While unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed for pipeline inspection, prevailing research predominantly assumes static pipes. In real-world industrial environments, pipes often exhibit dynamic movements, such as vibrations. This imposes more stringent requirements on UAVs' adaptive control and computational efficiency than in static scenarios. Therefore, this paper proposes a servo control framework named VisGeo-PipeTrack, which utilizes geometric constraints to enable UAV tracking of dynamic pipes. To achieve efficient UAV positioning, YOLOv5 is employed to detect labels on the pipe. The positions are derived from visual geometric constraints based on these detected labels to enable precise localization. To address tracking control challenges, a model predictive control based real-time corrected adaptive PID (MPC-RCAPID) controller is proposed. This controller employs the Recursive Least Squares method for real-time model estimation and integrates rolling horizon optimization to dynamically adjust PID parameters. Experiments conducted on both the AirSim simulator and the Tello UAV platform validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Simulation comparisons with standard PID, fractional-order PID, adaptive PID, and fuzzy PID demonstrate that MPC-RCAPID achieves the shortest settling time (3.26 s) and the lowest average tracking error (3.52%). In physical experiments on the Tello platform, compared with standard PID control, MPC-RCAPID reduces the average tracking error by 55.52%, 26.72%, and 26.52% across the three test dimensions. These results demonstrate that VisGeo-PipeTrack facilitates efficient autonomous tracking in dynamic pipe environments.

Visual Geometric, YOLOv5 Detection, MPC-RCAPID, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle, Dynamic Pipes Tracking Introduction nmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), owing to their high maneuverability and compact size, have emerged as a core technology for autonomous inspection within confined spaces, including industrial pipes and ventilation ducts Ibrahim2025 Fadl2024 . They are primarily useful in overcoming the accessibility constraints faced by human personnel and ground-based robotic systems, thereby providing critical support for industrial inspection tasks. Inspections within confined spaces present challenges intrinsic to such environments, including limited volume, poor lighting, and aerodynamic disturbances Papachristos2019 Ogai2018 . These characteristics impose stringent demands on UAV systems, particularly regarding positioning accuracy, attitude control robustness, and interference resistance Dekai2026 . Beyond these requirements, confined operational spaces often present dynamic changes, such as vibration in industrial piping systems. It imposes additional demands on system stability and adaptive control. Such dynamic changes induce variations in the pipeline's position, thereby increasing the risk of in-flight collisions for the UAV GursoyDemir2025 . However, extant research lacks effective solutions for UAV flight within dynamic pipes. Targeted technological innovation is therefore imperative to achieve breakthroughs for UAV operations in these environments. Extensive research has developed effective solutions for UAV navigation within static pipeline environments. Current systems are typically designed with the assumption of fixed positions and lack mechanisms to respond to dynamic positional changes. Wang et al. proposed an autonomous flight system integrating virtual omnidirectional perception with airflow disturbance planning Wang2025 . Their system enables navigation in static tunnels as narrow as 0.5m in diameter, including those with complex cross-sections. However, it assumes fixed tunnel geometry and position, neglecting inherent tunnel motion. Zhao et al. developed an H-shaped tilt-rotor quadcopter with a disturbance observer and fixed-time sliding mode control for stable Zhao2024 . The quadcopter performs high-angle flights in static narrow passages. It is effective for fixed environments like rubble but lacks adaptation to passage displacement. Martin et al. used a robotic platform to characterize duct aerodynamics and achieved stable hovering in a static 35cm duct via neural network localization Martin2025 , yet their work does not account for dynamic effects like duct vibration or translation. Xie et al. employed deep reinforcement learning to traverse static gaps at tilt angles up to , but the gap properties were predefined and unchanging Xie2023 . Chen et al. implemented a reinforcement learning strategy for real-time attitude adjustment in response to static gaps, with the dynamic response limited to the UAV's own pose Chen2023 . Wang et al. introduced a velocity planning method optimizing perception and aerodynamic stability in static tunnels, but the method does not incorporate mechanisms for tunnel dynamics Wang2022 . In summary, existing control strategies universally presuppose static environments. When dynamic motion occurs in pipes, current methods lack the capability to update positional references and control targets in real time. It results in accumulating state estimation errors and lagging control responses, which consequently elevate collision risk. This gap restricts the practical deployment of UAVs in dynamic confined spaces and thus underscores the necessity for an efficient control framework. To address the above challenges, this paper proposes a servo control framework, named VisGeo-PipeTrack, for UAV-based dynamic pipes tracking based on visual geometry. The structure of the control framework is shown in Fig. fig:1 , which is characterized by two technical contributions: A lightweight visual positioning system is realized through YOLOv5 label detection and geometric constraint resolution Han2024 . It employs YOLOv5 to detect labels attached to the pipe. The geometric intersections derived from these detected labels serve as target points for UAV tracking. This strategy ensures positioning accuracy while reducing computational overhead, thereby improving the UAV's dynamic response Liu2025 . A model predictive control-based real-time corrected adaptive PID (MPC-RCAPID) control strategy. It consists of three integrated components: (1) Tracking error prediction through model predictive control (MPC); (2) Real-time model parameter estimation via the recursive least squares (RLS) algorithm Lai2024 ; (3) Online PID parameter optimization in rolling time domain. This integration resolves limitations of standard PID controllers with fixed parameters and insufficient adaptability. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II introduces the basic technologies (YOLOv5 target detection algorithm, PID controller and dynamic pipes movement). Section III elaborates the pipe localization method based on visual geometric constraints. Section IV presents the design principle of the MPC-RCAPID control strategy. In Section V, the performance of the proposed framework is verified by simulation and physical experiments. Section VI concludes the paper and looks forward to future research directions. Preliminaries Problem Statement and Dynamic Pipes Movement This paper investigates the tracking of a UAV within a dynamic pipe environment. Existing UAV methods for pipe inspection are designed for static pipes and fail under dynamic pipe motion such as vibration or translation. When the pipe moves, the UAV cannot update its relative position or control target in real time, leading to error accumulation and increased collision risk. Therefore, this work solves the problem of enabling a UAV to robustly track a dynamically moving pipe using only onboard visual sensing and an adaptive control strategy. In contrast to a static pipe, a dynamic pipe is characterized by variable movement speeds and positional offsets. The experimental protocol involves imposing a movement velocity on the pipe through human intervention. This procedure is implemented to ascertain whether the proposed framework can facilitate the UAV’s accurate and timely tracking of the pipe. The movement of the dynamic pipe is shown in Fig. fig:3 . YOLOv5 Target Detection Algorithm To meet the requirement of pipe positioning, the UAV must identify and detect pipe labels. In light of this necessity, the YOLOv5 target detection algorithm is selected for this task. The reason why is that YOLOv5 remains the most stable version that achieves a favorable trade-off between detection accuracy and processing speed on embedded platforms AJayasudha2025 Ganapathy2026 . Consequently, YOLOv5 is deemed the optimal choice for this application. In this section, a lightweight tracking servo system based on visual geometric constraints is designed to enhance the performance of pipes positioning. Label Visual Localization In this study, the YOLOv5 algorithm is employed to detect labels and construct the perception of the UAV within the pipe space. Four points are selected and marked on the pipe’s side wall, forming two groups of two points each. The two groups of points are each connected to form two lines. The intersection point of these two lines represents the relative position that the UAV maintains within the pipe. (In certain scenarios, the presence of oil stains or other obstacles within the pipe may impede the UAV’s flight, necessitating that the intersection point may not correspond to the pipe’s geometric center.) The positions of the four labels within the UAV camera’s field of view are detected using YOLOv5.
