title: Explaining Navigation Decisions: Stage-Aware Visual Attribution for Vision-Language Navigation
summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly enable robots to follow language instructions, understanding their navigation decisions becomes important for reliable deployment. Existing explainability methods overlook a key challenge in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN): evidence for the current action may be distributed across historical and current observations and associated with different instruction stages. We identify instruction-stage insensitivity, where existing methods produce similar explanations despite changes across different navigation stages. To address this issue, we propose a stage-aware attribution framework for VLN. We first construct action-conditioned temporal instruction--visual attributions across observations. These attributions are projected into instruction space to estimate stage associations, which guide the aggregation of relevant historical evidence for refining the current explanation. An instruction-guided spatial filter further suppresses isolated responses while preserving compact, instruction-relevant regions. Experiments across multiple VLN policies and benchmarks show improved attribution quality over existing methods. We further demonstrate that our method acts as a diagnostic tool for analyzing failure cases, and validate its applicability to real-world navigation on a Unitree G1 robot.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments Experimental Setup sec:experimental_setup Dataset. We evaluate our method on R2R~ anderson2018vision and RxR~ ku2020room under the Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) setting~ krantz2020beyond . Both benchmarks are instantiated in Habitat, where agents follow natural-language instructions from RGB observations in continuous 3D environments. We conduct quantitative evaluations on both benchmarks and use the available semantic scene annotations to evaluate instruction-aware visual grounding. Implementation Details. We evaluate on NaVILA~ cheng2024navila , NaVid~ zhang2024navid , and StereoNav~ wang2026limits under VLN-CE. For action-conditioned attribution, we use language-model layers 8--15 with all attention heads and gradient-based sensitivity weighting. We set , , and . Input resolutions are , , and for NaVILA, NaVid, and StereoNav, respectively. At each decision step, explanations are computed over the current view and all valid model-selected historical observations. All baselines are adapted to the same selected action and evaluated on the identical policy inputs and observations. Metrics. We evaluate explanation quality from two complementary perspectives. Decision Faithfulness. A faithful explanation should identify visual evidence that actually supports the policy's selected navigation action. We therefore introduce an input-perturbation-based Action-Space Delta-NLL metric that measures how strongly the predicted action depends on the highlighted regions. Given the selected action , we mask the salient regions and compute the increase in its negative log-likelihood: Since masking itself may perturb the policy, we subtract the average effect of random masks: A larger indicates that the highlighted regions contribute more specifically to the current action decision, and thus correspond to a more faithful explanation. Semantic Alignment. We evaluate whether the highlighted regions correspond to instruction-relevant visual concepts. For each observation, semantic scene annotations are converted into binary masks for individual categories. A pretrained CLIP text encoder~ radford2021learning is used to estimate the semantic relevance between the navigation instruction and category . We then construct an instruction-conditioned soft semantic target: The explanation heatmap is binarized using OTSU thresholding: Following the spatial evaluation protocol of TAM~ li2025token , semantic alignment is measured as A higher Precision indicates stronger alignment with instruction-relevant semantic regions. Overall Score. We additionally report a harmonic-mean score that jointly considers decision faithfulness and semantic alignment: A higher score indicates better overall explanation quality. Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods sec:sota_comparison Quantitative results. As shown in Table~ tab:explanation_results , our method achieves the best overall F1-Score on both R2R and RxR. The gain mainly comes from substantially improved semantic alignment, with Precision increasing from 0.3591 to 0.4370 on R2R and from 0.2862 to 0.4241 on RxR over the strongest baselines. Meanwhile, our method also achieves the strongest decision faithfulness. On R2R, it obtains the highest (0.3198), while simultaneously achieving substantially better semantic alignment in terms of Precision and F1-Score. On RxR, it also obtains the highest faithfulness score (0.2846). Overall, these results show that our method better identifies instruction-relevant visual evidence without sacrificing fidelity to the navigation decision. Qualitative results. Fig.~ fig:sota further support the effect of our method. Across different navigation stages, our explanations consistently shift toward the visual evidence associated with the active sub-instruction, such as the staircase region in Step 1, the plant and hallway in Step 7, and the couch/fireplace area in Step 21. Moreover, our method preserves relevant evidence across historical and current observations, reflecting the temporally distributed nature of VLN decision making. In contrast, DEX-AR~ bousselham2026dex ~produces highly diffuse and noisy activations, while GradCAM~ selvaraju2017grad and TAM~ li2025token often highlight broad scene regions without clearly adapting to the current instruction stage. Together, the quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that our method produces more stage-consistent, semantically aligned, and decision-faithful explanations for VLN policies. Generalization across VLN policies. As shown in Table~ tab:agent_results , our method consistently outperforms DEX-AR across NaVid, NaVILA, and StereoNav on both R2R and RxR. The improvements are especially strong in Precision, reaching up to 34.58 on R2R and 42.03 on RxR. This consistent gain across different policies and datasets indicates that our stage-aware explanation framework generalizes beyond a specific VLN architecture. Ablation Study sec:ablation We ablate the two key components of our framework, stage-guided temporal refinement ( ) and instruction-guided spatial filtering ( ), to evaluate their individual contributions. Table~ tab:ablation reports the results of progressively enabling each module. Effect of . As reported in Table~ tab:ablation , enabling ~alone improves Precision from 0.4180 to 0.4328 and F1-Score from 0.3252 to 0.3386, indicating better alignment with instruction-relevant evidence. Figure~ fig:temporal_refinement_ablation further shows that ~reduces temporal cross-stage interference and produces cleaner, more focused current-frame attributions. After refinement, irrelevant responses from other instruction stages are suppressed, while evidence relevant to the current navigation decision is enhanced. Effect of . Table~ tab:ablation shows that enabling ~alone yields a larger gain in decision faithfulness, increasing from 0.2661 to 0.3082 and F1-Score from 0.3252 to 0.3553. Fig.~ fig:semantic_filter_ablation visualizes the effect of SF. The base rank filter~ li2025token removes isolated responses but may also suppress compact instruction-relevant evidence,~ , ``the picture on the wall". Incorporating instruction--patch associations improves target preservation, and the bidirectional variant further reduces irrelevant activations while retaining both the dining-table and wall-picture regions. Instruction-Stage Sensitivity Analysis. We further quantify whether the explanations respond to changes in the instruction stage. For each trajectory, we normalize the instruction-token attribution at each decision step and compute the Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) between different action decisions. For visual attribution, we compute the cosine similarity between flattened heatmaps across different stages. To measure spatial concentration, we stack the attribution values from the eight evaluated observations and report the fraction of total attribution mass contained in the top 10 responses. All metrics are averaged over the evaluation samples. Figure~ fig:statics further quantifies instruction-stage sensitivity. Compared with the baseline, our method produces a substantially higher instruction-attribution JSD (0.33 vs.\ 0.02) and lower cross-stage visual similarity (57.4 vs.\ 96.8 ), showing that both instruction and visual attributions change more clearly across navigation stages. Meanwhile, the higher top-10 attribution mass (43.4 vs.\ 13.5 ) indicates more concentrated visual explanations. Together, these results confirm that our method effectively alleviates instruction-stage insensitivity. Real-World Evaluation sec:real_world We further deploy our framework on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Figure~ fig:unitree shows two representative navigation trajectories, pairing egocentric action-conditioned attributions with third-person execution views. Across different decision steps, the explanations consistently highlight visual evidence relevant to the current instruction, demonstrating that the proposed attribution framework transfers from simulation to real-world navigation. Attribution as a Diagnostic Tool sec:diagnostic_tool We further use our method to diagnose failed VLN decisions. Figure~ fig:failure shows three representative cases where visual and instruction-token attributions reveal mismatches between the model's selected action and the instruction requirement: (a) Premature subgoal execution. The model should pass through the right doorway before continuing across the hallway, but instead turns left. The attribution shifts toward the later hallway clause, suggesting premature progression to a subsequent subgoal. (b) Action-phrase neglect. The instruction requires passing the stove while entering the dining room. Although the stove is correctly localized, token attribution emphasizes ``stove'' over ``passing by,'' and the model turns toward it. This indicates correct landmark grounding but insufficient attention to the action phrase. (c) Partial instruction grounding. The model should turn right at the living room and enter, but moves forward. Attribution remains concentrated on ``kitchen'' from the preceding clause, with weaker response to the turning instruction, indicating incomplete grounding of the current step. These examples demonstrate that our attributions can expose stage mismatches, action-phrase neglect, and incomplete grounding underlying erroneous VLN decisions.

title: LegoOcc++: Towards Consistent Open-Vocabulary 3D Occupancy Prediction
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction is important for embodied agents operating in complex environments whose semantic categories extend beyond fixed taxonomies. While recent studies have explored open-vocabulary occupancy in outdoor driving scenarios, indoor environments remain challenging due to dense occlusions, complex geometry, and fine-grained long-tailed semantics. To reduce the need for expensive voxel-level semantic annotations, we study a geometry-only supervision setting requiring only binary occupancy labels. We build upon Language-Embedded Gaussians as a unified representation coupling 3D geometry with language-aligned semantics. For geometry learning, we introduce an opacity-aware Poisson-based Gaussian-to-Occupancy formulation that enables stable volumetric aggregation under binary occupancy supervision. For semantic learning, we render Gaussian features into images and align them with a frozen open-vocabulary model, together with Progressive Temperature Decay to reduce feature mixing during Gaussian splatting. Building on this framework, we further introduce Instance-Level Semantic Consistency to alleviate fragmented object predictions, and Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection to provide informative and less redundant multi-view semantic supervision. We also extend our framework to outdoor driving scenarios to evaluate its generality across substantially different environments. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves strong open-vocabulary occupancy performance, validating the effectiveness and generality of our framework. Code will be available at https://github.com/JuIvyy/LegoOcc.

Introduction sec:intro Comprehensive 3D geometric and semantic understanding of surrounding environments is fundamental to embodied agents across applications such as service robotics, drones, and AR/VR systems. Among different scene representations, 3D semantic occupancy has emerged as a powerful and compact formulation that jointly models scene geometry, semantics, and free space within a unified volumetric representation, providing rich spatial information for downstream reasoning and decision-making~ volumetrivln,occvla,occllama,chen2025constraint . Vision-based occupancy prediction is particularly attractive due to the ubiquity, low cost, and rich appearance cues of cameras. Recent studies have demonstrated promising performance from both monocular inputs~ ISO,embodiedocc,embodiedocc++,yu2025shtocc,OccFormer,VoxFormer,SparseOcc,gpocc,jiang2026freeocc,gpoccpp and multi-view inputs~ surroundocc,gaussianformer,gaussianformer2,gaussrender , using architectures ranging from dense voxel networks and transformers to Gaussian-based representations. Despite this progress, most existing occupancy methods operate under a closed vocabulary, where semantic categories are predefined during training. This assumption is restrictive in real-world environments, where category distributions are highly long-tailed~ zhang2023deeplongtailsurvey,chen2025open and the semantic space is inherently open-ended~ joseph2021towards . As illustrated in~ , closed-vocabulary models cannot recognize categories beyond their training taxonomy, whereas an open-vocabulary formulation enables arbitrary semantic concepts to be queried directly in 3D space. Such capability is particularly important for embodied agents, which must recognize and reason about previously unseen objects before interacting with their surroundings. Open-vocabulary occupancy prediction has recently received increasing attention in autonomous-driving scenarios, where vision-language models and text-aligned representations are incorporated into camera-based 3D occupancy to support free-form semantic reasoning~ veon,yu2025language,boeder2024langocc,li2025ago,groundingocc . In contrast, indoor occupancy remains substantially less explored and is typically trained and evaluated under small, predefined taxonomies. For example, Occ-ScanNet~ ISO defines only 11 semantic classes, which substantially underrepresent the diversity of real indoor environments. Indoor scenes further pose two particular challenges: they contain much denser and more heavily occluded geometry, while exhibiting a substantially richer set of fine-grained and long-tailed object categories. Consequently, directly transferring existing outdoor open-vocabulary occupancy pipelines to indoor environments leads to limited performance~ embodiedocc . Early attempts such as OVO~ ovo distill 2D open-vocabulary segmentation into 3D voxels, but still rely on a predefined set of base categories during training. These observations motivate a more scalable formulation for indoor open-vocabulary occupancy prediction. A central challenge is therefore the availability of semantic supervision. Dense voxel-wise semantic annotation is particularly expensive for indoor scenes because it requires labeling a large number of fine-grained and long-tailed categories. In contrast, scene geometry can be obtained much more readily from RGB-D observations and existing reconstruction pipelines. For example, ScanNet provides RGB-D observations, while Occ-ScanNet constructs occupancy ground truth using SCFusion~ scfusion , which combines depth-based reconstruction~ supereight , scene-completion methods~ scan2cad,forknet , and aligned ShapeNet CAD models~ scan2cad . This observation suggests an attractive learning paradigm: geometry can provide reliable 3D supervision, while open-vocabulary semantic knowledge can be transferred from pretrained 2D models. We therefore consider a geometry-only supervision setting, in which training uses binary voxel occupancy labels but does not require semantic voxel annotations, and ask: How can open-vocabulary semantics be reliably transferred from images into a geometrically supervised 3D occupancy representation? To address this gap, our previous conference work, ~ legoocc , proposed Language-Embedded Gaussians (LE-Gaussians)~ shi2023legaussians,zhou2024featuregs as a unified intermediate representation for geometry and open-vocabulary semantics. Each LE-Gaussian jointly encodes geometric attributes, including position, covariance, and opacity, together with a language-aligned feature anchored at a specific 3D location. This representation allows geometry and semantics to be learned through two complementary supervision paths. For geometry learning, converts continuous Gaussian primitives into voxel occupancy using an opacity-aware Poisson-based Gaussian-to-Occupancy formulation. Unlike existing Gaussian-to-Occupancy mappings that aggregate spatial kernels independently of opacity, our formulation explicitly incorporates Gaussian opacity into volumetric aggregation, making 3D occupancy inference consistent with the opacity-aware rendering used for semantic learning. For semantic learning, LE-Gaussian features are differentiably rendered into the image plane through Gaussian splatting~ gaussiansplatting and aligned with features extracted from a frozen training-free open-vocabulary segmenter, such as Trident~ trident . Since standard -blending mixes embeddings from multiple Gaussians along each ray, further introduces Progressive Temperature Decay, which progressively sharpens Gaussian opacities during training to reduce feature mixing while preserving differentiable supervision. Together, these designs enable language-aligned 3D occupancy to be learned without semantic voxel annotations. While demonstrates the effectiveness of Language-Embedded Gaussians for indoor open-vocabulary occupancy prediction, several limitations remain. First, performs semantic alignment primarily at the pixel level. Although Progressive Temperature Decay reduces feature mixing along individual rays, pixels belonging to different regions of the same object are optimized independently. As a result, the predicted semantics can become fragmented within a single object, with different parts assigned inconsistent categories. Second, exploits additional frames for semantic supervision but selects support views without explicitly modeling geometric covisibility. Temporally nearby or visually similar frames may provide redundant observations, whereas distant frames may have insufficient shared geometry. The appropriate temporal interval also varies with video frame rate and sampling frequency, making fixed temporal selection difficult to generalize. Third, was developed and evaluated primarily on indoor embodied scenes, leaving its applicability to large-scale outdoor environments with different geometry, sensing configurations, and semantic distributions unexplored~ wei2026onebev,tan2024epmf,hong2024unified . These limitations point to two complementary requirements for a more general open-vocabulary occupancy framework: semantic consistency should be enforced at the object level, and multi-view supervision should be determined by geometric overlap rather than temporal proximity. Motivated by these observations, we further propose , a substantially enhanced framework that extends in both semantic representation learning and multi-view supervision, while broadening open-vocabulary occupancy prediction from indoor embodied environments to outdoor autonomous-driving scenarios. First, we propose Instance-Level Semantic Consistency, which complements pixel-wise language alignment with an object-level semantic constraint. Category-agnostic masks generated by a frozen SAM~ sam are used to aggregate open-vocabulary teacher features within reliable object regions into instance-level semantic prototypes. Rendered LE-Gaussian features associated with the same instance are then encouraged to agree with this shared representation. This constraint provides a direct mechanism for suppressing intra-object semantic fragmentation, complementing the ray-level feature disambiguation provided by Progressive Temperature Decay. Second, we introduce Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection for more reliable multi-view semantic supervision. Rather than relying on a fixed temporal interval, we explicitly measure geometric overlap between candidate views using their visible 3D regions. Views with insufficient overlap or nearly duplicate content are filtered out, after which pose-diverse support views are selected to provide complementary observations. This strategy improves the quality of cross-view feature alignment and makes more effective use of multi-frame language supervision. We further extend our framework from indoor embodied scenes to outdoor autonomous-driving environments. Unlike the indoor setting, where binary occupancy labels provide geometry supervision, we follow prior open-vocabulary driving methods and train on outdoor data without any occupancy annotations. This substantially different supervision setting, together with the large differences in scene scale and semantic distribution, provides a broader test of the effectiveness and generality of our approach. On Occ-ScanNet, improves from 59.50 to 61.73 IoU and from 21.05 to 24.22 mIoU. On Occ3D-nuScenes, achieves 15.14 mIoU with single-frame inference, outperforming all compared single-frame methods and nearly matching the 15.15 mIoU of the eight-frame PGOcc~ yan2025progressive . These results demonstrate that our approach generalizes effectively across substantially different scene domains and supervision settings. title: Preemptive Instruction Following with Resumption
summary: Long-horizon embodied navigation may be interrupted by a higher-priority instruction before the current task sequence is complete. The agent must finish its current atomic task, execute the inserted task, and resume the remaining sequence from the updated environment state, where its viewpoint and available navigation candidates may have changed. To evaluate this capability, we introduce PIFR benchmark, a novel task for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR includes single, repeated, and nested interruption settings,with stage-specific metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption of the original task, and completion of the full sequence. Evaluations show that recovery performance varies across interruption conditions, while aggregate success can obscure differences in interruption handling and resumption. We further propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline to improve target re-grounding after interruption. Together, PIFR and the baseline provide a systematic framework for studying interruption handling and task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.

The results show that performance changes are not uniform across datasets or interruption structures. On PIFR-OVON, PIFR-Rank achieves higher SR than MTU3D under all three interruption structures on the Unseen split, whereas its advantage on the Synonym split is small and varies by structure. On PIFR-GOAT, PIFR-Rank outperforms MTU3D on the Synonym split and under single and repeated interruption on the Unseen split, but not under nested interruption. These results indicate that robustness to synonym variation and generalization to unseen goals present different challenges, and that their effects depend on the temporal structure of the episode. The four metrics also reveal that changes in overall success do not necessarily imply corresponding changes in interruption handling or resumption. Since the source benchmarks define their Synonym and Unseen splits independently, comparisons should be made within each benchmark and split protocol. For repeated interruption (ABACA), it reports the first and second resumptions ( and ). For nested interruption (ABCBA), it reports the inner and outer resumptions ( and ). PIFR-Rank exhibits different stage-wise profiles across the three benchmarks. Under repeated interruption, its Resume SR decreases from 32.5 to 17.5 on PIFR-SG3D and from 53.8 to 38.7 on PIFR-OVON, but increases from 44.0 to 66.0 on PIFR-GOAT. Under nested interruption, its inner and outer Resume SRs are 1.9 and 24.5 on PIFR-SG3D, 50.5 and 49.5 on PIFR-OVON, and 56.0 and 64.0 on PIFR-GOAT. Thus, later or nested recovery does not produce a uniform monotonic decline. Instead, recovery performance varies with both the source benchmark and the position of the resumption within the interruption sequence. title: Robot-Aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting for Precise Reaching with Wrist-Camera VLA Policies
summary: Efficient robotic data collection remains a major bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) policy learning, especially for tasks requiring accurate end-effector positioning and camera-action alignment. This challenge is particularly severe in electronic-waste disassembly, where robots operate in cluttered assemblies of densely packed, visually similar components. Full digital-twin simulation is difficult because many parts are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level meshes and contact models difficult to obtain. In this work, we focus on pre-contact reaching and propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based data generation pipeline for wrist-camera VLA adaptation. Our method reconstructs the real workspace with 3DGS and renders diverse wrist-camera observations from robot-aligned poses. These observations are paired with smooth, structured reaching trajectories to provide robot-aligned visual-action supervision for VLA fine-tuning. We further augment the VLA policy with an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that estimates target proximity and provides reliable termination before physical interaction. Experiments in motherboard disassembly demonstrate precise VLA-based reaching using wrist-camera observations alone, without an external side-view camera. With $π$0.5, 1,500 generated trajectories achieve 80.0\% precise-reaching success across three targets, compared with 58.7\% using 150 teleoperated demonstrations, while requiring less than 10 minutes of active human capture. Project website: https://001-wang.github.io/PrecisionReach-GS/
full_text: Efficient robotic data collection remains a major bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) policy learning, especially for tasks requiring accurate end-effector positioning and camera-action alignment. This challenge is particularly severe in electronic-waste disassembly, where robots operate in cluttered assemblies of densely packed, visually similar components. Full digital-twin simulation is difficult because many parts are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level meshes and contact models difficult to obtain. In this work, we focus on pre-contact reaching and propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based data generation pipeline for wrist-camera VLA adaptation. Our method reconstructs the real workspace with 3DGS and renders diverse wrist-camera observations from robot-aligned poses. These observations are paired with smooth, structured reaching trajectories to provide robot-aligned visual-action supervision for VLA fine-tuning. We further augment the VLA policy with an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that estimates target proximity and provides reliable termination before physical interaction. Experiments in motherboard disassembly demonstrate precise VLA-based reaching using wrist-camera observations alone, without an external side-view camera. With 0.5, 1,500 generated trajectories achieve 80.0 precise-reaching success across three targets, compared with 58.7 using 150 teleoperated demonstrations, while requiring less than 10 minutes of active human capture. Project website: Data-efficient manipulation, robot learning, robotic data generation, vision-language-action models, 3D Gaussian splatting. Introduction recise reaching is a fundamental requirement for real-world robotic manipulation. Before a robot can grasp, pull, insert, place, cut, or otherwise interact with an object, it must first move its end-effector to the correct target region marwan2021comprehensive, 11288083, oguntosin2017design, robin2016multi . This requirement becomes especially challenging in robotic disassembly, where targets include small components such as screws and memory modules as well as larger but fragile components such as GPUs tian2026redefining, foo2022challenges . These components are often densely arranged and surrounded by neighboring parts, leaving little tolerance for reaching errors liu2026self, shi2025viso . Once the robot reaches the correct interaction region, subsequent actions can often be handled by task-specific controllers or skill modules, making target-oriented reaching a critical bottleneck between visual perception and successful manipulation le2025application . Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a promising framework for learning such reaching behavior directly from visual observations and task instructions zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,sapkota2025vision,intelligence2025pi05 . By mapping camera observations and language commands to robot actions, VLA policies can learn visually grounded motion generation without requiring each target or task to be manually encoded. With sufficiently large, diverse, and well-aligned demonstrations, VLA models have the potential to generate accurate and adaptive reaching actions across different target objects, viewpoints, and instructions. This makes VLA particularly attractive for manipulation tasks where the robot must understand both the semantic meaning of the target and its spatial location in the scene. Importantly, in many manipulation tasks, the pre-contact reaching stage occupies a large portion of the VLA-controlled action sequence, as the robot must progressively move from an initial pose to the target interaction region before executing the final physical skill. Therefore, improving the data efficiency and reliability of reaching behavior can substantially benefit the overall VLA manipulation pipeline. However, the effectiveness of VLA models is strongly tied to data scale and data quality pfaff2025scalable,hofer2021sim2real,mandlekar2023mimicgen,martinez2020unrealrox . To learn precise reaching behavior, the policy requires many demonstrations in which the visual observation, language instruction, robot state, and action are consistently aligned. In practice, collecting such data on real robots remains difficult. Most demonstrations are collected through human teleoperation, which is slow, expensive, and difficult to scale mandlekar2019scaling, zhang2018deep . This problem becomes more severe when robot access is limited, because data collection occupies the physical robot for long periods and reduces the time available for training, testing, and other experiments. Moreover, human-collected demonstrations often introduce noise that can directly affect VLA learning. Teleoperated trajectories may be jerky, inaccurate, or contain unnecessary corrective motions richards2025modeling, pmlr-v305-guo25a . For example, an operator may move the robot toward an approximate region, realize that the target has been missed, and then perform several small adjustments before reaching the desired position. While this behavior is natural during manual operation, it creates ambiguous supervision for the policy: the model may learn both the intended reaching motion and the accidental correction behavior. In addition, delays between camera capture, robot state recording, and action execution can cause visual observations to be paired with slightly mismatched actions. Such camera-action misalignment is especially harmful for precise reaching, where small spatial errors can determine whether the robot reaches the correct component or misses it. A natural alternative is to generate demonstrations in simulation, but building a full digital-twin simulator for electronic-waste disassembly is also challenging. Motherboards contain many densely packed components with different sizes, materials, and appearances, including small screws and connectors as well as larger but fragile parts such as GPUs, heat sinks, and memory modules. Many of these components are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level mesh reconstruction, material modeling, and contact simulation difficult. As a result, full simulation requires substantial manual modeling effort and can still introduce a large sim-to-real gap if the geometry, camera viewpoint, or physical interaction does not match the real workspace. In addition to data collection and simulation, camera configuration also affects the scalability of VLA training and deployment. Many robot-learning systems use fixed external cameras or multi-view observations, which provide useful global context but require stable placement and calibration kim2026ego, zhao2026atlasvla . In contrast, we consider a harder wrist-camera-only setting, where the viewpoint moves with the end-effector and the policy must infer both target location and motion correction from a narrow, continuously changing view. This reduces dependence on fixed side-view cameras, but also makes precise reaching more data-demanding, since the policy needs diverse and well-aligned wrist-camera observations to learn reliable corrections. In this work, we propose PrecisionReach-GS, a lightweight real-to-sim-to-real pipeline for data-efficient VLA fine-tuning in a wrist-camera-only setting. As shown in Fig.~ fig:workflow , the pipeline first reconstructs the real task environment with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), preserving the cluttered background, object layout, and visual complexity of the physical workspace. Unlike full digital-twin simulators that require object-level meshes, collision models, and contact dynamics, PrecisionReach-GS focuses on the pre-contact reaching stage, where realistic wrist-camera observations and robot-aligned action labels are the main requirements. The system samples feasible starting poses, renders diverse wrist-camera observations, generates smooth reaching trajectories toward target components, and organizes the resulting observation--action pairs for VLA fine-tuning. During deployment, the fine-tuned VLA policy predicts reaching actions from wrist-camera observations, while a lightweight verifier determines whether the robot has reached the target interaction region. As a result, the user only specifies the target task and desired data scale, and the pipeline produces structured wrist-camera training data without large-scale teleoperation or a complete physical digital twin. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose PrecisionReach-GS, a lightweight real-to-sim-to-real framework that uses 3DGS as a photorealistic workspace representation for VLA adaptation, avoiding object-level meshes, contact models, and full physics-based digital twins. We develop a robot-aligned visual-action generation method that maps the reconstructed scene into the robot frame, samples kinematically feasible starting poses, and generates synchronized wrist-camera observations, robot states, and smooth reaching actions with minimal human intervention. We introduce an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that complements the VLA policy with instruction-conditioned reach assessment, enabling more reliable stopping under the distinct geometric precision requirements of different manipulation targets. We experimentally validate the proposed pipeline in a robotic motherboard disassembly scenario, demonstrating that wrist-camera-only VLA fine-tuning, together with reach verification, can achieve precise target reaching and support successful downstream manipulation skills. Related work sec:related work Robot data collection for VLA adaptation. Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for instruction-conditioned robot control, mapping visual observations, language instructions, and robot states directly to actions. Representative models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, Octo, , and show that large vision-language backbones can be adapted for visuomotor control through action tokenization, continuous action regression, action chunking, or flow-based action generation~ zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,kim2025fine,team2024octo,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . These models are attractive for robotic disassembly because the robot must interpret component-level semantic targets while producing continuous motion toward the correct interaction region. However, adapting these models to precise, task-specific manipulation remains limited by the availability of high-quality robot action data. Existing robot data sources mainly rely on large-scale robot logs or human teleoperation~ o2024open,walke2023bridgedatav2,fang2023rh20t . Robot logs can scale with deployment but are often tied to specific embodiments and task distributions, while teleoperation provides flexible demonstrations but remains slow, labor-intensive, and noisy. This bottleneck is especially severe for component-level reaching in robotic disassembly, where small spatial errors can cause downstream manipulation to fail. Real-to-sim-to-real and 3DGS-based data generation for robot learning. To reduce real-robot data requirements, recent work has explored real-to-sim-to-real pipelines that reconstruct real scenes and use simulation, rendering, or generated demonstrations for policy learning fan2025twinaligner . Early methods reconstruct object-level meshes from real observations and place them into simulators to generate grasp or manipulation data~ wang2023real2sim2real . More recent systems extend this idea to broader policy learning, including X-SIM, which reconstructs photorealistic simulation from action-less human videos and distills privileged policies into image-conditioned policies~ dan2025xsim ; Real2Render2Real, which generates robot training data from object scans and a single human demonstration~ yu2025real2render2real ; and EmbodieDreamer, which combines physical parameter alignment with photorealistic video generation for reinforcement and im

title: Beyond Behaviour: A Stimulus-Response Safety Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Humans exhibit biological sensitivity to safety-critical stimuli that can trigger defensive action. Across three models and two video benchmarks, we investigate whether similar responses emerge in vision-language-action models by examining their internal representations and action tendencies in response to visible hazards and harmful consequences. Our findings suggest that task execution may remain the default response even when danger is internally registered.
full_text: Humans exhibit biological sensitivity to safety-critical stimuli that can trigger defensive action. Across three models and two video benchmarks, we investigate whether similar responses emerge in vision-language-action models by examining their internal representations and action tendencies in response to visible hazards and harmful consequences. Our findings suggest that task execution may remain the default response even when danger is internally registered. Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models have enabled robots to execute a wider range of manipulation tasks across different embodiments and environments~ kim2025openvla,black2025pi05 . However, successful task completion does not necessarily imply safe execution. Existing safety evaluations examine whether VLAs violate safety constraints during execution~ zhang2025safevla,lyu2026foresightsafety , refuse unsafe instructions~ yin2026roboshackles , or detect unsafe actions in videos~ pu2026homesafebench . We here approach this problem from a fundamental perspective: why are humans sensitive to danger, and how does this sensitivity shape perception and action? One biological foundation is the need to maintain physiological conditions compatible with survival. Homeostasis describes how organisms maintain internal physiological conditions within ranges necessary for survival, motivating responses to threats that could disrupt these conditions. Allostasis extends this view by emphasising anticipation of future demands and preparation for potential threats~ friston2010freeenergy,sterling2012allostasis . From an evolutionary standpoint, the smoke detector principle suggests that defensive systems may favour false alarms when failing to detect a threat is substantially more costly than an unnecessary response~ nesse2019smoke . Complementing these theories, human experiments show that unexpected events can recruit action-stopping mechanisms and transiently suppress motor output~ wessel2013unexpected . Together, these accounts connect safety to the processes that register potentially consequential stimuli and prepare an organism to respond. Inspired by these viewpoints, we investigate a limited functional analogy in VLA policies: (1) do VLA models show internal sensitivity to safety-critical visual stimuli? and (2) do their predicted actions exhibit avoidance behaviour in the presence of danger? To the first question, we measure the level of atypicality in internal representations and their changes relative to the baselines estimated from scenes in which harmful consequences are not yet visible. We examine these departures across the vision encoders, vision-language backbones, and action generation heads, comparing responses before and after the onset of harmful consequences. To the second question, we assess whether the initial predicted action moves the gripper of a robot arm towards or away from an estimated danger location. Our analysis therefore complements the existing safety evaluations by characterizing response signatures under safety-critical inputs, yet without assuming a biological equivalence or treating these signatures as evidence of danger recognition or safe behaviour. Methodology sec:method We address the two research questions through complementary analyses. The representational sensitivity study examines whether the internal representations of a VLA model depart from a calm baseline before and immediately after harmful consequences become visible. The avoidance behaviour study subsequently assesses whether the initial predicted action approaches or retreats from an estimated danger location. Videos and temporal segments. The evaluation dataset consists of videos depicting household scenarios in which a robot causes harm, for example by dropping a mug, starting a kitchen fire, or stabbing a person. We distinguish a hazard, a potential source of harm, from danger, defined here as the visible occurrence of its physical consequence. Each video contains sampled frames and has an associated harmful-consequence onset time , marking when the consequence first becomes visible. To compare responses around the danger onset, we define , which is positive before onset and negative afterwards, and suppress the clip index when unambiguous. We select three temporal groups of scenes relative to where the danger is present Here, \,s is the earliest eligible timestamp, and the calm cutoff is taken from the dataset's manual annotations. Calm frames may contain hazards but should not show their consequences. The window widths and define the near group before onset and the just-after group at and immediately after onset, respectively. Representational Sensitivity Analysis A frozen VLA policy receives one frame and a fixed instruction shared across all clips, without frame history or action feedback. At each selected layer , we extract a hidden representation . We organise these extraction sites into three groups: vision, the encoder output before language projection; language, the fused vision--language backbone; and action generation, the action head at its final denoising step. We quantify representational ``surprise'' with a transition surprise score , which measures how atypical the change in a representation is between consecutive sampled frames, relative to the changes seen during calm frames. For a clip and sampled frame time (in seconds), let denote the representation at site , i.e.\ a module output mapped to a vector. Each frame is processed independently, so depends on frame alone. For a frame with a preceding sampled frame at in the same clip, we define the time-normalized change . Let denote the calm frames across all clips, i.e.\ frames before any harm is visible. To ensure that no clip is scored by a baseline fitted on its own frames, we use -fold cross-fitting, where clips are randomly partitioned into folds . For fold , the baseline is fitted on the changes between consecutive calm frames of clips outside the fold, and is then used to score every frame of the clips in , including their calm frames. Let . For each fold and site, we estimate the mean and coordinate variances of the calm changes: and use the regularized diagonal covariance , where and is a relative ridge coefficient. The diagonal form remains well defined when is comparable to or larger than , where a full sample covariance would be rank-deficient. Finally, we define as the regularized Mahalanobis distance of a frame's change from the calm changes: where and , are those of the fold containing clip . Avoidance Behaviour Analysis sec:digital_cousin_method In response to the second question, we examine whether the initial predicted action is directed towards or away from an estimated danger location. We evaluate the onset and final frames of each video to assess responses when the harmful consequence first becomes visible and after it has occurred. The video datasets do not directly provide the 3D geometry needed to measure gripper-danger distance. We therefore construct a digital cousin: a simplified simulated scene that reproduces the gripper-danger geometry estimated from image annotations and metric depth. This reconstruction provides a common spatial frame for evaluating how the initial predicted action changes that distance. Let be the initial gripper position, the realized endpoint or predicted target, and a fixed danger anchor at the location of the visible harmful consequence. For policies that predict delta actions, the relative changes in the gripper's position or orientation, we execute the predicted command for a fixed interval of eight simulation steps ( \,s) and use the resulting gripper position as . For policies that predict absolute positions, we use the predicted position target directly. Let . The metric of interest is the net reduction in gripper-danger distance , normalized by the gripper's displacement magnitude: . For non-zero displacement, , in which positive values indicate approach and negative values indicate retreat. For zero displacement, we assign . To summarize behavioural tendencies, we group the actions into three descriptive bins: away ( ), sideways ( ), and straight at ( ). Note that these labels summarise net point-to-point distance change rather than exact motion directions. Reconstruction and execution details are provided in Appendix~ app:action_method . Results and Key Findings sec:result Experimental setup. sec:experimental_setup We use RoboShackles videos~ yin2026roboshackles and HomeSafe-Bench videos~ pu2026homesafebench in which a hazard develops into a visible harmful consequence. We sample every second frame at fps (about apart). VLA-JEPA~ sun2026vla , GR00T N1.7~ bjorck2025gr00t , and X-VLA~ zheng2026x are evaluated with LIBERO~ liu2023libero and SimplerEnv~ li24simpler fine-tuned checkpoints. Each frame is paired with the instruction ``complete the household task.'' Avoidance behaviour evaluation only involves LIBERO checkpoints and the selected onset and final frames with visible grippers. Internal sensitivity is most evident in vision and language. Compared with all calm frames (Figure~ fig:main , grey ), the transition scores in the vision and language backbones rise as the consequence approaches and peaks at its onset in all six settings and both datasets, while action generation sites respond less (Figures~ fig:hs_qtime_raw to fig:rs_qtime_same ). This raw comparison is however ambiguous as calm frames come from the first seconds of a clip, hence later frames also reflect how far the generated video has drifted from its start, and the video's own motion peaks at the same moment. Controlling for the same second into the clip removes the drift (Figure~ fig:main , blue ). In HomeSafe-Bench, the pre-impact rise flattens to the calm level, while the peak at impact remains. In RoboShackles, the two curves nearly coincide and the rise before onset persists in all six settings. However, object motion persists in the same way, so timing alone does not separate a response to harm from a response to on-screen change. Sensitivity partly reflects the visual changes over time. Such potential confounding effect motivates the additional control for object motion and appearance change in Figures~ fig:hs_qdiff and fig:rs_qdiff , which reduces the vision and language difference near the consequence to about a third. Thus, part of the measured sensitivity reflects the visual changes accompanying harmful events rather than necessarily their harmfulness. An exception is GR00T N1.7, whose language states remain significantly atypical after onset in both settings, given the same elapsed time, visual change and danger category. Initial actions predominantly move towards danger. For the second question, the dominant initial response in the evaluated scenes is movement towards danger rather than withdrawal. This holds for all three models on RoboShackles and for GR00T N1.7 and VLA-JEPA on HomeSafe-Bench (Figure~ fig:act_rs_hs ). X-VLA behaves differently on HomeSafe-Bench, moving towards, away from, or sideways relative to danger with similar frequency. GR00T N1.7 and VLA-JEPA tend to move towards danger across all categories, whereas the behaviour of X-VLA varies more with the type of danger (Figures fig:act_cat_hs and fig:act_cat_rs ). Under the shared task instruction, these patterns suggest that task execution may remain the default response even when harmful consequences are visible. Conclusion sec:conclusion This paper examined VLA responses to safety-critical videos in terms of internal sensitivity to danger and avoidance behaviour in action generation. Internal responses were more pronounced in the vision and language backbones and were also influenced by visual changes and video progression. By contrast, safety-related signals remained comparatively weak in the action generation head, while initial actions predominantly moved towards danger under a fixed task instruction

title: Differentiable Contact Dynamics for Legged Locomotion: Policy Learning and Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization
summary: This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de Saxcé-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: https://diffcontact.github.io
full_text: Differentiable Contact Dynamics for Legged Locomotion: Policy Learning and Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization Gijeong~Kim , Seungbin~Oh , Dongyun~Kang , and~Hae-Won~Park The authors are with the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Daejeon 34141, South Korea. This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de~Saxc\'e-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2~min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: Differentiable simulation, frictional contact, second-order cone complementarity, contact-implicit trajectory optimization, analytic policy gradient, quadruped locomotion. Introduction sec:intro he first-order gradient through contact in a differentiable physics simulator provides a common computational primitive for two classes of methods in contact-rich robot control. The first is policy learning, in which model-free reinforcement learning is widely used and policy-gradient estimates are computed from rollouts across thousands of parallel environments~ hwangbo2019learning,rudin2022learning, makoviychuk2021isaac . First-order policy learning~ Heess2015,degrave2019differentiable preserves the same objective but replaces the score-function (REINFORCE) estimate~ Williams1992,Sutton1999 with a typically lower-variance first-order estimate~ Mohamed2020 . This estimate can be obtained by differentiating through the simulator, with comparable policies learned from fewer samples~ Xu2022 . The second is trajectory optimization. Contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO) methods determine when and where contacts are made and broken without a prescribed contact-mode sequence~ Mordatch2012,Posa2014,Manchester2019 . Shooting-based DDP/iLQR methods~ Tassa2012,Neunert2018 use the same transition Jacobians as the policy-learning estimator and have been applied online in receding-horizon control for contact-rich locomotion~ Kim2023 . For legged robots, both tools are limited by the contact sensitivity provided by differentiable simulation. A simulator may be differentiable without providing a useful first-order direction toward a neighboring contact mode~ Suh2022,Freeman2021 . The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form~ Werling2021,LeLidec2025 , but it is evaluated with the active set, or contact-mode assignment, held fixed and therefore describes only the response within the current mode. A clamped contact is linearized as remaining clamped, providing no first-order information toward liftoff or slip, and the sensitivity changes discontinuously when the active set changes. In contact-implicit optimization, this mode-restricted sensitivity keeps the local search near the contact sequence of the nominal trajectory~ Kim2023, Werling2021, Pang2023 . In first-order policy learning, the same Jacobians enter backpropagation through time (BPTT), where they can produce fragile or ineffective optimization in contact-rich systems~ Suh2022,Freeman2021,Metz2021,Georgiev2024 . Prior work addresses contact sensitivity in policy learning and CITO in different ways. In policy learning, methods shorten the differentiation horizon~ Xu2022,Georgiev2024 , use a reduced-order model for the backward pass~ Song2024 , or smooth contact in the forward rollout~ Schwarke2024 . Shorter horizons can help with long-horizon gradient instability, but do not change the contact sensitivity within each window. In CITO, transcription methods optimize contact impulses alongside the trajectory~ Posa2014,Manchester2019,Dietz2026 , whereas shooting methods rely on transition Jacobians from the contact dynamics~ Tassa2012,Neunert2018,Kim2023 . Other approaches smooth the forward contact model~ Kurtz2025,Pang2023 , differentiate relaxed contact solutions~ Howell2022,LeCleach2024 , or estimate gradients across perturbed solves~ Suh2022rs,LeLidec2024rs . For shooting-based CITO with a hard-contact forward solve, however, the exact contact sensitivity remains tied to the current contact mode and offers limited first-order guidance toward a different mode~ Werling2021 . Relaxing only the Signorini condition during differentiation~ Kim2023 partly addresses this limitation by providing directions for contact make/break transitions, but leaves sliding and normal–tangential coupling unaddressed. We therefore propose a contact sensitivity obtained by relaxing the full frictional contact condition only in the backward pass, providing search directions toward neighboring contact modes while retaining the hard-contact forward solve. The de Saxcé correction expresses frictional contact as a single second-order-cone complementarity condition~ DeSaxce1998,LeLidec2024 . Relaxing this condition along a central path~ Acary2026 couples normal and tangential contact sensitivities across separation, clamping, and sliding. These coupled sensitivities are available in every contact mode, allowing the optimizer to change modes through gradient-based updates. We further investigate their role in guiding transitions to sliding, where a normal-only relaxation lacks the required tangential information. We test the effect of this sensitivity in two optimal-control settings using a quadruped robot: first-order policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization. In each setting, we compare the exact~ LeLidec2025 , Signorini-relaxed~ Kim2023 , and proposed sensitivities while keeping the forward contact model, objective, and initialization fixed. The policy-learning experiments ask whether single-environment BPTT can produce locomotion policies that transfer directly to hardware. The trajectory-optimization experiments ask whether the proposed sensitivity improves contact-rich motion generation and recovery from unmodeled external pulls by enabling contact-mode changes and foot repositioning. The main contributions are: [leftmargin=*] An analytic backward contact sensitivity that relaxes the complete de~Saxc\'e-corrected frictional contact law along its central path while retaining the hard-contact forward solve. It provides first-order directions toward separation, sliding, and clamping in every contact mode and recovers the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. The proposed gradient in BPTT-based first-order policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization guides contact-mode changes and yields improved policies and lower-cost contact-rich trajectories. Hardware demonstration of quadruped policy learning with the proposed gradient for trotting, pacing, and gait-free locomotion. Trotting policies obtained using 100,000 samples in under 2~min are tested on hardware without fine-tuning under pushes, debris, and low-friction surfaces. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section~ sec:related reviews related work and Section~ sec:bg the optimal control and contact dynamics background. Section~ sec:problem states the required contact sensitivity, Section~ sec:method derives the proposed gradient, and Section~ sec:impl the implementation details. Sections~ sec:apg and~ sec:cito present the policy-learning and trajectory-optimization demonstrations, and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes. Related Work sec:related Contact simulation and differentiable contact sec:related_contact Forward models. Rigid frictional contact is commonly modeled using three coupled principles~ LeLidec2024,Hwangbo2018 : the Signorini condition, Coulomb's friction-cone bound, and Moreau's maximum-dissipation principle (MDP)~ Moreau1988 . Their combination yields a nonsmooth nonlinear complementarity problem for the contact impulse, solved at each time step using iterative methods such as projected Gauss--Seidel and staggered projections~ LeLidec2024 . Linear-complementarity (LCP) models polygonalize the friction cone, allowing the use of pivoting methods~ AnitescuPotra1997 . Convex cone-complementarity (CCP) models relax strict Signorini complementarity to obtain a convex contact problem. During sliding, this can permit a nonzero normal force together with separating normal velocity, leading to artificial normal motion and, in time-stepping simulations, force across a gap~ LeLidec2024 . MuJoCo employs a related convex soft-contact formulation~ todorov2012mujoco . Compliant models use finite contact stiffness and dissipation; with suitable regularization, convex formulations can also handle near-rigid contact~ Castro2022 . In this work, the hard-contact forward model in CITO retains the three principles of the rigid nonlinear complementarity problem. We use per-contact iteration~ Hwangbo2018 , solving sliding-contact subproblems by bisection with the de~Saxc\'e correction~ LeLidec2024MDP . For BPTT policy learning, we instead use RaiSim~ Hwangbo2018 for efficient forward rollouts because training requires repeated simulations at a fine time step. This also allows us to compare BPTT with PPO in the same simulation environment, although standard RaiSim can deviate from maximum dissipation during sliding~ LeLidec2024MDP . In both settings, we derive the contact gradient from the de Saxcé representation of the rigid frictional contact law~ DeSaxce1998,Acary2018 . Differentiating contact. Finite differences estimate contact sensitivities through repeated evaluations with perturbed inputs, with the number of evaluations growing with the input dimension~ todorov2012mujoco,Tassa2012 . Near contact-mode transitions, the estimates can depend on the perturbation size. Automatic differentiation instead applies the chain rule to the operations executed by the simulator~ hu2020difftaichi,Freeman2021,degrave2019differentiable . Analytic approaches can combine derivatives of rigid-body algorithms ~ Featherstone2008,carpentier2018analytical with implicit differentiation of the contact equations at the converged contact solution~ Werling2021,LeLidec2025,BelbutePeres2018 . The proposed method follows this analytic approach, but evaluates sensitivity at a relaxed central-path point of the frictional contact condition. Differentiable simulation for policy learning sec:related_learning Model-free reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used for legged locomotion. Score-function policy-gradient methods do not require derivatives of the simulator~ Schulman2017 , and large-scale parallel simulation accelerates the collection of large sample batches for stable policy updates~ rudin2022learning . This approach has produced hardware locomotion~ hwangbo2019learning,Tan2018,Lee2020,Miki2022 and example-guided motor skills~ Peng2018 . First-order policy learning instead differentiates the rollout dynamics to estimate the policy gradient~ degrave2019differentiable,Freeman2021 , which can improve sample efficiency~ Xu2022,Zhang2025 . title: Birth-Death Structural Learning for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a standard representation for real-time novel-view synthesis. Yet, its quality-efficiency trade-off still relies heavily on adaptive density control. Existing cloning, splitting, and pruning rules use proxy signals, such as position gradients, opacity, and image-space error. Although effective in practice, these signals do not directly answer the structural question behind density control: where should new Gaussians be allocated to reduce the multi-view reconstruction loss, and which existing primitives can be pruned with minimal penalty. To address this, we propose first-variation birth-death control for 3DGS, a principled approach that replaces heuristic structural decisions with a variational score derived from the reconstruction loss. At each structural update, we freeze the current Gaussian population, attach auxiliary mass coordinates to each primitive, and differentiate the multiview loss with respect to these coordinates. We demonstrate that this score is a coordinate of the first variation of the Splat Regression Model, giving a rigorous local descent surrogate for birth-death moves: high-score Gaussians are selected as birth sites, while low-score, low-opacity Gaussians are selected for removal. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, integrating this score into 3DGS-MCMC yields state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and outperforms existing methods, delivering the most significant gains under tight Gaussian budgets. Ultimately, our work provides compelling evidence that gradient-based variational metrics offer a principled alternative to proxy heuristics in 3DGS.

Introduction sec:introduction High-quality photorealistic scene modeling from images is a fundamental task in computer vision and graphics, with applications spanning immersive rendering, robotics, digital humans, and geometric reconstruction~ ChenWang2024Survey3DGS, Zhu2024RoboticsSurvey3DGS . 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ Kerbl2023GaussianSplatting has emerged as a fast explicit radiance-field representation that models scenes as anisotropic Gaussian primitives and renders them by differentiable rasterization. Its speed and explicitness have led to rapid extensions in dynamic rendering, anti-aliasing, generative 3D content, and SLAM~ Yan2024StreetGaussians, Yu2024MipSplatting, Tang2024DreamGaussian, Qian2024GaussianAvatars, Zhu2024EndoGS, Shao2024SplattingAvatar, Keetha2024SplaTAM, Franke2025VRSplatting, Guedon2024SuGaR . Despite this progress, 3DGS training still relies on heuristic adaptive density control (ADC). Training a 3DGS model interleaves two distinct optimization mechanisms. Continuous optimization adjusts the parameters (position, covariance, color) of existing Gaussians to fit the image data. Structural control, meanwhile, changes the population itself by creating or destroying primitives. In standard 3DGS, these population updates rely on indirect proxies: high accumulated position gradients trigger cloning or splitting, while low opacity triggers pruning~ Kerbl2023GaussianSplatting . These signals correlate with regions needing refinement, but they do not directly measure how a discrete birth or death event affects the photometric objective. As a result, primitive placement is sensitive to hand-tuned thresholds. The model frequently misses high-frequency details, creates floaters or needle-like artifacts, and wastes redundant Gaussians to regions that are already well covered~ Bulo2024RevisingDensification, Zhang2024PixelGS, Grubert2025ImprovingADC . The cost is most visible under tight primitive budgets, where redundant placement directly competes with missing detail~ Baranowski2025ConeGS, Kotovenko2025EDGS, Kheradmand2024MCMC . While recent methods improve these signals through pixel-aware gradients, error-guided insertion, and budgeted densification~ Zhang2024PixelGS, Baranowski2025ConeGS, Mallick2024Taming3DGS , they remain mathematically decoupled from the empirical risk. The Splat Regression Model (SRM) framework~ DanielsRigollet2026SRM provides a rigorous lens to understand this limitation: it models splat fitting as optimization over mixing measures structured by Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry. Under this view, standard 3DGS successfully performs continuous transport (moving Gaussian parameters via gradient descent), but completely ignores the WFR mass component when deciding where to spawn or destroy primitives. Because disconnected heuristics govern these mass perturbations, a fundamental allocation problem remains unresolved: How can we identify which discrete primitives to kill, and where to spawn new ones guided by a first-order descent surrogate for the multiview reconstruction loss? Contributions. In this work, we propose reframing 3DGS structural updates from a collection of proxy heuristics into a formal component of empirical risk minimization. Motivated by the WFR geometry, we formulate structural control as a finite-particle birth--death process. At each control step, we freeze the continuous scene parameters and attach an auxiliary mass coordinate to each Gaussian. Differentiating the multiview reconstruction risk with respect to these coordinates yields a per-primitive first-variation score. This score is the negative directional derivative of the objective, evaluated at the frozen parameter state. It mathematically predicts the first-order descent achieved by applying an infinitesimal mass perturbation to that specific primitive. We then use score gaps to guide the birth-death process: capacity is reclaimed by killing low-score, low-opacity Gaussians and reborn at high-score sites. This provides a criterion for birth--death decisions. Because finite structural updates lack strict continuous descent guarantees, we execute them via the state transitions of 3DGS-MCMC~ Kheradmand2024MCMC . This work bridges the theoretical view of splat fitting as mixing-measure optimization with practical 3DGS training. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=2em] We replace heuristic proxy signals with a first-variation score for 3DGS structural control, directly tying primitive allocation to the multiview empirical risk. We theoretically justify this framework by discretizing the SRM first variation, and by proving that restricting death to low-opacity Gaussians bounds the immediate rendering disturbance. We demonstrate that variational allocation outperforms proxy heuristics when representation capacity is constrained. Across standard benchmark datasets, our method achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality against matched 3DGS-MCMC and recent budget-aware baselines. Related Work sec:related_work Adaptive density control and densification. The original 3DGS framework couples continuous photometric optimization with adaptive density control: accumulated position-gradient statistics trigger cloning or splitting, while low opacity triggers pruning~ Kerbl2023GaussianSplatting . A massive body of recent work improves this controller. Revising Densification and Pixel-GS replace or reweight the growth criterion using pixel-level error or pixel-aware gradients~ Bulo2024RevisingDensification,Zhang2024PixelGS , while AbsGS and Improved ADC refine gradient aggregation, threshold schedules, and pruning rules~ Ye2024AbsGS,Grubert2025ImprovingADC . Other methods manage the primitive budget explicitly through resource-aware schedules, progressive propagation, or high-error insertion rules~ Mallick2024Taming3DGS,Cheng2024GaussianPro,Baranowski2025ConeGS . While these methods engineer better proxy signals or insertion heuristics, our work diverges fundamentally: we abandon proxies in favor of the structural derivative. By explicitly differentiating the multiview risk with respect to Gaussian mass, we formalize capacity allocation as a direct objective rather than a heuristic byproduct. Relocation, MCMC, and compact representations. Several methods improve 3DGS efficiency by pruning redundant Gaussians or compressing attributes post-training~ Fan2024LightGaussian,Hanson2025PUP3DGS,Niedermayr2024Compressed3DGS,Lee2024Compact3DGaussianRF , while others avoid incremental growth entirely by relying on dense initializations~ Kotovenko2025EDGS . The closest backend to our method is 3DGS-MCMC~ Kheradmand2024MCMC , which rewrites densification and pruning as relocation/addition transitions. Our approach adopts these discrete transitions from 3DGS-MCMC, but completely replaces its structural selection statistic. Rather than relying on opacity-sampling to blindly select relocation targets, we use our first-variation score to predict where released capacity is most likely to reduce the reconstruction risk under a local first-order model. Variational splat models and first variation. The Splat Regression Model (SRM) formalizes splat models as optimization over mixing measures, deriving Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao gradient flows and explicit first-variation characterizations of mass rescaling~ DanielsRigollet2026SRM ; related birth--death discretizations also appear in sampling theory~ LuSlepcevWang2023BirthDeath . However, while SRM establishes the continuous, measure-level WFR geometry, it does not prescribe a finite, budget-constrained training algorithm for discrete rasterizers. Our contribution bridges this gap: we derive a concrete, renderer-level mass-coordinate score and a finite score-gap birth--death controller, making this continuous variational geometry actionable for practical 3DGS training. title: DriveUniTok: A Unified Multimodal Tokenizer for Driving World-Action Models
summary: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.
