Introduction Driving world models initially served as scene simulators and data engines, forecasting future observations for data augmentation and policy training. More recently, generative models of future observations have been integrated into policy backbones that jointly model scene evolution and ego trajectories zhang2025epona,zhao2025pwm,xia2026drivelaw,shi2026drivewam . In this setting, the latent representation is no longer merely an interface for visual reconstruction; it is the space in which the model captures the information required for both future prediction and planning. Existing world-action models, however, expose asymmetric representation interfaces. Most inherit a pretrained RGB video autoencoder whose latent primarily captures appearance, while geometry is introduced through auxiliary supervision and ego pose remains outside the latent, where it is handled by a separate conditioning stream or action head wan2025wan,kong2024hunyuanvideo,agarwal2025cosmos . Driving tokenizers fuse camera and LiDAR observations into scene-centric bird's-eye-view latents, but still leave ego pose outside the scene representation zhang2024bevworld,chen2025bevvae,zhuo2026drivetok,liao2025i2world . Cross-modal and latent-action tokenizers incorporate actions alongside observations, yet commonly retain modality-specific streams or align them through a designated anchor or intermediary representation lu2026atoken,bachmann2024fourm21,chen2025villax,fan2025xr1,chen2026unit . Figure~ fig:fusion_comparison compares these representations according to whether appearance, metric geometry, and ego pose reside in the same decodable latent. This asymmetry forces the downstream predictor to learn cross-modal correspondence together with temporal evolution, which can make future-scene and ego-trajectory predictions inconsistent. Therefore, a central question arises: Should visual appearance, metric geometry, and ego-motion be represented within a unified tokenization framework? DriveUniTok addresses this question by encoding RGB appearance, projected LiDAR geometry, and clip-relative ego pose in one jointly decodable latent. To construct such a representation, we propose DriveUniTok, a query-based multimodal tokenizer. Shared learnable queries aggregate appearance features from RGB, metric geometry features from projected LiDAR depth, and clip-relative ego-pose features into a common sequence of per-frame multimodal tokens. A causal temporal compressor then maps this sequence into a compact continuous unified latent. All three modalities are reconstructed from the shared bottleneck through modality-specific readouts, without using a privileged anchor modality. In addition, a training-only semantic decoder is supervised by representations from a vision foundation model, encouraging the unified latent to preserve high-level scene semantics alongside metric geometry and pose. To evaluate whether this representation supports joint forecasting and planning, we freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model into DriveUniWAM, using the same downstream backbone and training protocol for unified and separate representations. The Wan-initialized flow-matching transformer predicts future unified latents under block-causal attention, conditioned on DriveUniTok-encoded historical observations and clip-relative ego poses together with a navigation signal. Future RGB, depth, and ego trajectories are decoded from the same predicted latent evolution rather than generated through independent observation and action pathways. Because supervised flow matching fits recorded futures but does not directly optimize the NAVSIM planning metric, we additionally post-train DriveUniWAM with GRPO against the PDM reward while regularizing it toward the supervised reference model. Our key contributions are as follows: We propose DriveUniTok, a query-based tokenizer that encodes RGB appearance, projected LiDAR geometry, and clip-relative ego pose in a unified continuous latent. We develop DriveUniWAM, a diffusion-based WAM that forecasts this latent for joint future-scene prediction and ego-trajectory planning. We show on NAVSIM that the unified design achieves stronger prediction and planning at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream controls, with DriveUniWAM reaching state-of-the-art performance at 91.54 PDMS after reinforcement learning post-training. Related Work General and Driving Tokenizers For visual tokenizers, discrete codebooks are commonly paired with autoregressive or masked token prediction van2017neural,yu2024magvitv2 , whereas continuous latents are often used with diffusion and flow-matching models. Large video VAEs provide high-fidelity latent spaces for RGB generation wan2025wan,kong2024hunyuanvideo,yang2025cogvideox,agarwal2025cosmos , and quantization and model design materially affect representation quality luo2024openmagvit2,yu2024magvitv2,wang2024omnitokenizer,tang2024vidtok,wang2025larp,guo2026vrae . General-purpose multimodal tokenizers place vision, language, audio, and other signals in a shared token space through semantic or contrastive objectives lu2026atoken,bachmann2024fourm21,lu2023unifiedio,lu2024unifiedio2 . These tokenizers, however, are optimized for general visual generation or cross-modal alignment, and do not explicitly capture the metric geometry or ego motion required for driving scenes. Driving-specific tokenizers instead focus on scene representations. BEV-VAE and DriveTok construct tokens from multiview observations chen2025bevvae,zhuo2026drivetok , while OccWorld and -World tokenize structured 3D occupancy for world modeling and 4D forecasting zheng2024occworld,liao2025i2world . Moving beyond camera- or occupancy-centric scene tokens, BEVWorld fuses surround-view images and LiDAR into a BEV latent that can be rendered back to both modalities, but the latent still describes the scene without encoding ego pose zhang2024bevworld . These limitations motivate a unified tokenizer that keeps appearance, metric geometry, and ego pose jointly decodable. Driving Planners and World-Action Models End-to-end driving systems jointly optimize perception and planning, from feature fusion and waypoint regression chitta2022transfuser and planning-centric perception and prediction hu2023uniad to anchored trajectory sets refined by truncated diffusion liao2025diffusiondrive or autoregressive mixture-of-experts decoding feng2025artemis . World-model-assisted planners expose future-scene information through future rollouts, predicted BEV features, or world-objective constraints on the planning latent li2025wote,zhang2025seerdrive,yang2026worldrft . Vision-language-action planners add semantic priors and explicit reasoning, using either chain-of-thought reasoning with discrete action tokens or language-derived representations with diffusion planning and reward refinement zhou2025autovla,li2026recogdrive,li2026sgdrive , and recent variants further incorporate generated futures through interleaved generation, latent conditioning, iterative replanning, or auxiliary supervision liu2026uniworldvla,li2026imagidrive,zuo2026vega,sheng2026explorevla,li2026drivevlaw0,zhou2026drivedreamerpolicy . These planners use future information in different ways, but generally treat future-scene prediction and trajectory generation as separate modeling components. World-action models instead couple the two within a generative model. Existing world-action models differ primarily in how predicted future observations interact with trajectory generation. Some use parallel diffusion heads over a shared spatiotemporal latent zhang2025epona or attention over discrete future-frame tokens in an autoregressive sequence zhao2025pwm , while others condition action transformers on cached video-denoising features xia2026drivelaw , decode action chunks from a sampled future-video latent shi2026drivewam , or autoregressively interleave scene and action tokens ye2025dap,chen2026drivinggpt . While these designs couple future prediction and action generation, they do not generally provide a single decodable latent that jointly represents appearance, metric geometry, and ego motion. In contrast, DriveUniTok unifies RGB appearance, projected LiDAR geometry, and clip-relative ego pose at the tokenization stage in one jointly decodable continuous latent. DriveUniWAM forecasts this latent for joint future-scene prediction and planning. Our contribution centers on unifying appearance, metric geometry, and ego motion at the representation level for world-action modeling. Methodology Problem Setup A driving observation sequence contains consecutive frames sampled at 2\,Hz. Each observation consists of a front-camera image , a sparse depth map obtained by projecting the LiDAR sweep onto the image plane of , and an ego pose expressed relative to the first frame of the sequence, with . Given observed sequences, we predict the next sequences. Learning this mapping in observation space is expensive, and it leaves appearance, geometry, and motion in three different formats that a predictor would have to relate on its own. DriveUniTok therefore maps each sequence to a single unified latent of tokens with width , from which all three modalities are decodable. DriveUniWAM then models the evolution of across sequences, and the DriveUniTok decoder maps predicted latents back to , , and . In this division of labor, DriveUniTok determines which information the latent preserves, and DriveUniWAM determines how it evolves. We train DriveUniTok first, freeze it, and post-train DriveUniWAM against the NAVSIM PDM score. title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
summary: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/

Introduction Physical intelligence~ agarwal2025cosmos,agarwal2026cosmos3 , including autonomous driving~ survey_ad and embodied control~ fastwam , holds the promise of freeing human workers from physical tasks that are dangerous, laborious, or tedious. A general-purpose physical agent should not only act from visual observations, but also anticipate the physical consequences of their actions. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, including those standard models~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_05,li2026drivevla-w0 and specialized end-to-end ones~ liao2025diffusiondrive,chi2025diffusionpolicy_robot,li2025LaW , typically predict actions directly without explicitly modeling the future evolution of the environment. This has motivated a shift toward World Action Models (WAMs)~ fastwam,zhao2026simwam,li2026lingbot-va,liu2026driveva for physical AI, which build on pretrained video generative models wan22,lingbot-world to jointly predict future visual states and their corresponding actions. However, WAMs follow the imagine-then-execute paradigm~ bi2026motus,li2026lingbot-va and incur prohibitive inference latency, rendering them impractical for latency-critical applications such as autonomous driving. Borrowing few-step techniques from image and video generation, some methods apply step distillation~ akbari2026flashwam to reduce this latency, but often at the expense of a substantial drop in control accuracy, as illustrated in Fig.~ Fig::inference_performance . To address this issue, efforts~ fastwam,zhao2026simwam propose to switch from the imagine-then-execute paradigm to direct-policy WAMs. These methods retain video prediction as a training-time objective that shapes physically grounded representations, without synthesizing future observations at test time. This direct-policy formulation is more than faster than the imagine-then-execute paradigm. Despite this speedup, efficiently generating high-quality actions remains a key challenge for direct-policy WAMs. They require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, resulting in latency that remains too high for real-time applications such as autonomous driving. This bottleneck cannot be resolved by reducing the number of denoising steps. Specifically, as shown in Fig.~ Fig::Insight , the performance degrades as the step count decreases, dropping by on NAVSIM (autonomous driving) and on RoboTwin (embodied control) in the one-step setting. We attribute this to the lack of action structure in random noise: multiple denoising steps can gradually impose temporal and physical consistency, whereas one-step generation must recover a coherent action sequence in a single update. Existing few-step accelerations, such as step distillation~ akbari2026flashwam and trajectory rectification~ liu2022rectifiedflow , still start from Gaussian noise and, therefore, do not supply the missing action prior. This motivates introducing structured action priors at initialization, providing an informed starting point for high-quality action generation in a single denoising step. In addition, direct-policy WAMs~ fastwam,zhao2026simwam remain limited in their ability to exploit future dynamics for effective control. They use a consistent first-frame-only interface during training and inference, relying on video co-training to encode future dynamics into the current representation. However, compressing all future information into a single first-frame representation may provide insufficient temporal context for effective future-aware control. To address this limitation, subsequent methods reintroduce future features at inference and mitigate the associated rollout cost through caching, sparse interaction ~ zhao2026fasterwam_huake , or compact latent representations~ li2026efficientwam . Despite these efforts to reduce rollout cost, generating and incorporating future features at test time still incurs additional inference overhead. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose OSWAM, a world action model with one-step action generation for more effective physical control. Our key observation is that previous one-step action generation methods fail mainly because the action diffusion processing is initialized from unstructured Gaussian noise. To supply the missing action structure, we learn a compact set of imagination tokens from the video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and use them as structured start points for action denoising. These tokens are far fewer than video first-frame tokens and are obtained in a single forward pass, so they add negligible computation, yet they interact with visual features to accumulate physically grounded, action-relevant context. We then noise the imagination tokens to an intermediate timestep and decode them with the action DiT in one step, replacing the long denoising trajectory required by random initialization. To enhance future-aware control, we train these imagination tokens with privileged-information distillation. A teacher attends to visual tokens over the full future horizon, while the student imagination tokens, at test time, attend only to the first frame. By distilling the teacher's privileged representations into the imagination tokens and subsequently into the action DiT, OSWAM transfers long-horizon context without reintroducing future-dependent features at inference. This design preserves the first-frame-only interface of direct-policy WAMs, while enabling high-quality action generation in a single denoising step. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose OSWAM, a world action model that enables high-quality one-step action generation. It learns compact imagination tokens from the video DiT as structured start points for the action DiT. These tokens are obtained in a single forward pass with negligible overhead and are decoded in one denoising step. We introduce privileged-information distillation to transfer long-horizon context into the imagination tokens. A teacher attends to visual tokens over the full future horizon, while the student remains first-frame-only at test time, preserving the interface of direct-policy WAMs without future-dependent features at inference. Experiments on autonomous driving and embodied control show that OSWAM achieves competitive results with multi-step WAMs while being substantially faster. Related Work World Action Models for Autonomous Driving Autonomous driving has recently shifted from modular pipelines with separate perception~ zhang2024voxelmamba,zhang2024gga,he2024scatterformer,zhang2026bevdilation and planning~ cheng2024pluto modules toward end-to-end frameworks~ chitta2022transfuser . To further integrate future dynamics modeling, world models~ wan22,chen2026omni3dedit,chen2026fast,wang2026one2scene for autonomous driving have recently been extended into world action models (WAMs). Existing methods fall into two categories: bird's-eye view (BEV)-based and video-generation-based world models. BEV-based approaches~ li2025LaW,zheng2024occworld,li2025wote forecast occupancy evolution and ego motion, predict future latent scene features, or infer future BEV layouts for online trajectory evaluation. They are computationally efficient but do not exploit large-scale video generative priors. A complementary line of research leverages pretrained video generators and predicts the future in the image domain. These methods~ shi2026drivewam,liu2026driveva,xia2026drivelaw transfer such priors to driving, but jointly rolling out video features at test time remains inefficient. SimWAM~ zhao2026simwam follows the direct-policy design of Fast-WAM~ fastwam to avoid test-time video rollout, yet the remaining multi-step denoising is still impractical for onboard driving. In contrast, our proposed OSWAM inherits large-scale video generative priors without test-time video rollout, and reduces action generation to a single denoising step. World Action Models for Embodied Control Unlike autonomous driving, where compact BEV representations naturally encode road topology and traffic interactions, embodied control needs to model fine-grained object interactions and appearance changes in close-range scenes. As these phenomena are naturally captured in video, embodied WAMs are predominantly built on pretrained video generators for image-domain future modeling in two ways: explicit future imagination and direct-policy inference. Explicit-imagination methods~ li2026lingbot-va,bi2026motus generate future visual representations at test time to guide action prediction, incurring substantial rollout latency. Direct-policy WAMs~ fastwam retain video prediction as a training signal but generate actions directly from current observations, avoiding test-time visual rollout; however, its iterative action denoising remains a bottleneck for high-frequency closed-loop control. In contrast, OSWAM preserves large-scale video-generative priors without test-time visual rollout and reduces action generation to a single denoising step. Effective World Action Models The main deployment bottleneck for WAMs lies in the high computational cost of diffusion-based video and action generators, whose test-time latency is prohibitive for onboard driving and closed-loop manipulation. Drawing one-step distillation from video generation, Flash-WAM~ akbari2026flashwam compresses joint video-action diffusion to a single denoising step per modality, but still synthesizes future video at inference. Fast-WAM~ fastwam removes test-time video rollout by predicting actions from current observations only, yet retains iterative action denoising. Light-WAM~ li2026lightwam further replaces the generative action expert with a lightweight fusion head for single-pass action prediction, but underperforms on challenging benchmarks such as RoboTwin. SimWAM~ zhao2026simwam follows Fast-WAM to drop test-time video rollout, but its multi-step action denoising keeps inference latency well above the budget required for onboard deployment. Building on this video-rollout-free direct-policy formulation, OSWAM addresses the remaining action-generation bottleneck through one-step action denoising. title: RIDE-Splat: Reflection Removal for In-the-Wild Driving Environments
summary: Driving video captured through a windshield violates the world-space consistency assumed by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the road scene exhibits parallax while cabin reflections remain attached to the camera, causing standard 3DGS to embed reflected content into the reconstructed scene. We introduce RIDE-Splat, a pipeline for reflection-free 3D reconstruction from posed driving video without clean images, reflection masks, or pretrained networks. RIDE-Splat assigns world-consistent transmission through the windshield to a 3DGS scene and the dominant camera-attached reflection to one shared, signed RGB image. It builds the clean reconstruction in two passes. First, it learns the 3D geometry and the signed reflection image, representing both added radiance and transmission attenuation. Then, it uses the reflection-removed training images to fit a clean 3DGS model. At inference, the reflection image is discarded, preserving the standard 3DGS rendering path. We also introduce the RIDE-Splat Dataset, the first 3D reconstruction benchmark for reflection removal from driving video -- with real driving scenes, physical windshield reflections in training views, and separately captured non-reflective evaluation images. Across the RIDE-Splat Dataset, XLD, and Wayve, RIDE-Splat outperforms 3DGS, DC-Gaussian, and RobustSplat on all nine aggregate metrics, improving PSNR by up to 3.59 dB and reducing LPIPS by up to 0.0876. We achieve the highest metrics in 38 out of 42 per-scene comparisons and removes windshield reflections that remain visible in the baselines while preserving the transmitted scene.

Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time, photorealistic novel-view synthesis~ 3dgs , but its standard formulation assumes that posed images depict a coherent world-space scene. Driving video captured through a windshield violates this assumption because each frame contains the transmitted road scene and reflections of the vehicle interior. Camera motion reveals the key separation cue: the road scene exhibits parallax and remains consistent in world coordinates, while the dominant windshield reflection moves with the camera and remains approximately fixed in image coordinates. Standard 3DGS can therefore fit reflected content as scene geometry or appearance, contaminating novel views. Single-image reflection removal cannot exploit this multi-view cue, and rejecting contaminated observations discards valid transmission supervision. Conversely, a flexible per-view reflection field can mistakenly absorb road appearance that belongs in 3D. These failures motivate a constrained decomposition that assigns each signal to the coordinate system in which it remains consistent. Historical dashcam archives and consumer driving videos document diverse roads, weather, lighting, and rare events that would be costly or impossible to recapture. Yet they remain underused for 3D reconstruction because windshield reflections make them poorly suited to pipelines designed for clean, purpose-captured imagery. Recovering reflection-free 3D scenes from these recordings could support closed-loop simulation, sensor-realistic augmentation, and rare-event replay without dedicated recapture. We therefore introduce RIDE-Splat, a non-generative 3DGS formulation for reflection-free novel-view synthesis using only posed driving video with windshield reflections. It assigns world-consistent transmission through the windshield to a 3DGS scene and the dominant camera-attached reflection to one shared, signed RGB image. Because the reflection image is fixed in image coordinates and shared across views, it can represent image-stationary reflection content but cannot follow parallax-bearing road texture. Its signed values capture both added reflected radiance and transmission attenuation. The first pass uses a geometry warm-up to establish scene structure and a sparsity penalty to bias ambiguous content toward the 3D scene. Reflection self-localization then derives a fixed spatial weight from the recovered reflection image and refits both representations from scratch with the weight frozen. This second pass suppresses scene leakage without adding optimized parameters. At inference, we discard the reflection image, using standard 3DGS rasterization for rendering. Existing benchmarks force a tradeoff: datasets with exact non-reflective targets use synthetic reflections, while those with physical windshield reflections lack clean targets. The RIDE-Splat Dataset closes this gap as the first 3D reconstruction benchmark designed specifically for reflection removal from driving video. For each real driving scene, it pairs a training traversal containing physical windshield reflections with a separately captured non-reflective evaluation traversal of the same route. The paired traversals are recorded within minutes using the same rigid camera mount, with only the reflection-inducing materials removed. All methods train only on the reflective traversal, with the non-reflective images held out as evaluation targets. Across the RIDE-Splat Dataset, XLD~ xld , and Wayve~ wayve , RIDE-Splat outperforms 3DGS, DC-Gaussian~ dcgaussian , and RobustSplat~ robustsplat on every aggregate metric under both physical and synthetically added reflections. It improves PSNR by up to 3.59\,dB and LPIPS by up to 0.0876. These gains are consistent across scenes, with RIDE-Splat achieves higher performance in 38 of 42 per-scene metric comparisons. As shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , RIDE-Splat removes windshield reflections that remain visible in the baselines while better preserving the transmitted scene. In summary, we propose the following contributions: 2pt RIDE-Splat. A coordinate-based 3DGS method that separates world-consistent transmission from camera-attached windshield reflections. RIDE-Splat Dataset. The first 3D reconstruction benchmark for reflection removal from driving video. Related Work Reflection removal has primarily been studied in image space. Single-image methods separate transmission and reflection using handcrafted or learned priors~ sir2benchmark . Multi-frame methods use layered motion, low-rank structure, or temporal consistency to distinguish the two signals~ szeliski2000,nandoriya2017,liu2020obstructions . RIDE-Splat instead brings this motion cue into 3D reconstruction, assigning world-consistent transmission to the 3D scene and the dominant windshield reflection to image coordinates. Neural radiance fields~ nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs represent view-dependent radiance in world coordinates. Reflection-aware variants of these representations model glossy appearance, separate transmitted and reflected radiance, or reconstruct specular and semi-transparent surfaces~ refnerf,gaussianshader,refgaussian,nerfren,rtsplatting . Flash-Splat~ flashsplat separates transmission and reflection with Gaussian primitives but requires paired flash and no-flash captures. RIDE-Splat instead targets driving videos and learns a windshield-reflection layer fixed in image coordinates from reflective monocular video alone. In-the-wild 3D reconstruction methods suppress transient or view-inconsistent distractors through sample rejection or transient modeling~ robustnerf,spotless,hybridgs . DF3DV-1K~ lu2026df3dv benchmarks anti-distractor 3DGS methods~ t3dgs,wildgaussians,spotless,desplat,degauss,ocsplats,asymgs , but does not include reflections of the vehicle interior on the windshield. RobustSplat~ robustsplat , the strongest single-model baseline, delays Gaussian densification and bootstraps transient masks across scales. Our reflective weight maps are inspired by SplatSuRe~ splatsure which derives per-pixel weight maps from multi-view sampling fidelity, but targets multi-view-consistent super-resolution rather than reflection removal. Driving-scene methods reconstruct large environments and dynamic actors~ streetgaussians,drivinggaussian,emernerf,neurad , but do not model windshield reflections. DC-Gaussian~ dcgaussian is the only prior 3D reconstruction method designed specifically to remove windshield reflections. It predicts a per-view reflection field from camera pose using a hash grid and MLP, while a latent code modulates the field's intensity over time. RIDE-Splat instead uses one shared, signed image to impose a coordinate-based separation prior; this representation is orthogonal to DC-Gaussian's geometry enhancement. In Sec.~ sec:results , RIDE-Splat outperforms DC-Gaussian and RobustSplat across all metrics. title: DUET4D: Self-Corrective Coupled Guidance for Sparse-View 4D Reconstruction
summary: Sparse-view 4D reconstruction is highly under-constrained when only a few cameras are available. Generative priors can recover missing appearances, but video models are computationally impractical for iterative reconstruction, whereas single-view models produce temporally inconsistent pseudo-observations. Moreover, directly absorbing uncertain generative outputs into Gaussian optimization often creates redundant primitives and floating artifacts. To address these challenges, we propose DUET4D, a self-corrective coupled guidance framework for sparse-view 4D Gaussian splatting. The core of our approach is a self-corrective framework where the 4D representation guides generative prior for spatio-temporal consistent supervisions. We first construct sequential alignments from current Gaussian evidence to steer the latent restoration. Then we use Sequential Fidelity Resampling to lift generative supervisions into Gaussian space to selectively distinguish repeatedly supported primitives. The corrected representation then provides more reliable Gaussian evidence for the next restoration cycle. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET4D significantly improves rendering quality and rendering efficiency.

Introduction By extending 3D Gaussian Splatting to the temporal domain, 4D Gaussian methods can reconstruct and render dynamic scenes with high visual quality~ cai2022neural,du2021neural,fang2022fast,kratimenos2024dynmf,li2022neural . However, most existing methods rely on sufficiently dense multi-view observations~ shi2026sparse4dgs,pan2026sparsecam4d, zhou20264c4d . When the input is reduced to only a few cameras, reconstruction quality degrades severely. Many regions of the scene are never directly observed, while dynamic objects are only partially constrained across time. As a result, sparse-view 4D Gaussian reconstruction often suffers from distorted artifacts, floating Gaussians, and temporally inconsistent motion. Existing works~ shi2026sparse4dgs, zhou20264c4d introduce texture regularization and Gaussian decaying to constrain sparse-view reconstruction. However, they are insufficient to recover stable dynamic appearance under large viewpoint drifts. To introduce stronger generative priors, SparseCam4D~ pan2026sparsecam4d utilizes video diffusion models (VDM) to synthesize pseudo-observations, but iteratively querying a VDM is computationally impractical for multi-view 4D optimization. This presents the first challenge: single-view diffusion models (SDMs) provide a more efficient alternative, yet their independent predictions lack cross-view and temporal awareness, leading to temporal incoherent motions. However, temporal coherence alone does not make pseudo-supervision uniformly reliable. There remains a spatial drift between the generative supervisions and the sparse observations. Blindly densifying these locations leads to redundant primitives and floating Gaussians. A second challenge is therefore to selectively lift pseudo supervision into reliable representation-side decisions. To address these challenges, we propose , a self-corrective framework that couples a frozen single-view diffusion model with an evolving 4D Gaussian representation. Instead of relying on a computationally heavy VDM or directly using independently restored views as supervision, DUET4D exploits the current 4D Gaussians as a spatiotemporal correspondence carrier. The resulting Gaussian-derived alignments and confidence estimates construct a reliable anchor that steers the latent denoising direction of a frozen SDM, enabling temporally coherent pseudo-observations without training or invoking an additional video model. Crucially, DUET4D does not indiscriminately absorb these generated observations into the representation. The Sequential Fidelity Resampling distinguishes reliable reconstruction deficits from persistent inconsistencies by jointly considering confidence-gated pseudo supervisions and real observations, and then lifts these 2D signals to individual 3D primitives. The updated representation consequently provides cleaner correspondence evidence for the next restoration round, forming a closed self-corrective cycle that improves reconstruction fidelity while suppressing redundant Gaussians. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose , a unified framework for sparse-view 4D reconstruction, establishing a self-corrective framework where the 4D representation guides generative prior for spatio-temporal consistent supervisions. We introduce a training-free anchor-driven latent steering mechanism that uses Gaussian-derived correspondences to make a frozen SDM produce temporally coherent pseudo-supervisions. We design Sequential Fidelity Resampling to selectively lift confidence-supported pseudo-view discrepancies into Gaussian densification while pruning primitives that remain inconsistent with real observations, producing a cleaner and more compact representation. Related Work Sparse-view Dynamic Reconstruction Dynamic scene reconstruction requires temporally coherent modeling of appearance and motion. While NeRF-based methods rely on time-conditioned fields or feature factorization~ mildenhall2021nerf,pumarola2021d,park2021nerfies,park2021hypernerf,cao2023hexplane,fridovich2023k ,4DGS-based approaches significantly improve efficiency via deformation fields, tracking, or direct 4D representations~ kerbl20233d,yang2024deformable, li2024spacetime,luiten2024dynamic,lin2024gaussian,wu20244d,yang2024real,duan20244d . However, these methods typically require dense, synchronized multi-view videos and degrade heavily under sparse camera setups. To tackle the under-constrained sparse-view setting, prior works exploit category-specific priors like SMPL for humans~ peng2021animatable,peng2021neural,weng2022humannerf,hu2024gauhuman or monocular depth and tracking cues~ lei2025mosca,wang2025shape,pradeep2013monofusion . Though providing useful temporal constraints, recent methods~ shi2026sparse4dgs,zhou20264c4d still suffer from unstable appearance under large viewpoint changes. Diffusion Models for Novel-View Synthesis Diffusion models serve as powerful priors for 3D/4D generation. While object-centric models~ liu2023zero,liu2024syncdreamer,shi2024mvdream,long2024wonder3d achieve strong multi-view consistency, they cannot directly handle scene-level dynamic reconstruction. Recent camera-controlled video diffusion models~ wang2024motionctrl,he2024cameractrl,xu2024camco,yu2024viewcrafter,bai2025recammaster,wu2025cat4d synthesize novel-view dynamic observations, offering richer supervision. However, they rely on expensive multi-frame denoising and often produce cross-view or temporal inconsistencies that harm 4D optimization. To incorporate diffusion into sparse dynamic reconstruction, recent methods such as Diffuman4D~ jin2025diffuman4d and SparseCam4D~ pan2026sparsecam4d query video diffusion models for better rendering quality, which take ~40 hours for a single dynamic scene, facing a strict trade-off between consistency and efficiency. We address this through a unified framework that constructing a self-corrective coupled pipeline where the 4D representation guide generative prior for spatio-temporal consistent supervisions. title: MemVLN: Streaming Episodic Memory for Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through 3D environments. Maintaining persistent episodic memory remains a challenge for VLM-based streaming agents in long-horizon navigation. We present MEMVLN, a streaming episodic memory framework that maintains a bounded bank of compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, and produces compact memory tokens via cross-attention. We pair the proposed memory with a frozen pretrained geometry encoder. To learn the memory module, we design a masking-based trajectory summarization task with multi-granularity sub-trajectory decomposition, encouraging route reconstruction exclusively from episodic memory. Under navigation training restricted to the official R2R/RxR trajectories, MEMVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics on standard VLN-CE benchmarks. Long-horizon analyses further characterize when episodic memory is useful. For physical evaluation, we collect 30 instruction-conditioned episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, MEMVLN improves success over the VLM baseline from 17% to 40%, and post-training further raises it to 47%.

Under navigation training restricted to the official R2R/RxR trajectories, achieves performance on most reported metrics on standard VLN-CE benchmarks. Long-horizon analyses further characterize when episodic memory is useful. For physical evaluation, we collect 30 instruction-conditioned episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, improves success over the baseline from 17 to 40 , and post-training further raises it to 47 . Introduction sec:introduction is a fundamental task in embodied AI, requiring an embodied agent to follow language instructions through 3D environments~ anderson2018vision,krantz2020beyond,majumdar2023we . Recent have substantially improved navigation performance, with monocular streaming video as a prevailing formulation that is natural and practical for real-world deployment~ zhang2025uninavid,cheng2025navila,wei2026streamvln,wei2026ground . Despite rapid progress, the lack of persistent memory remains a critical constraint for real-world long-horizon navigation, where decisions depend on observations from earlier in the episode. In this paper, we address the key problem: how to design a simple yet effective episodic memory that integrates seamlessly with streaming to elevate capability ? Navigation memory has received prior attention, yet existing approaches remain insufficient along several key dimensions. Early methods encode navigation history in recurrent hidden states~ elman1990finding,hochreiter1997long,hong2021vln , compressing perceptual observations into a fixed-size representation. Explicit memory representations retain observation-level features but are often coupled to panoramic observations or topological maps, requiring adaptation to monocular streaming video in continuous environments~ chen2021history,mezghan2022memory,an2024etpnav,wang2023gridmm,yu2025mossvln . More recent works revisit navigation memory within a streaming formulation~ zeng2026janusvln,zheng2025efficient , yet the capacity limitation persists. These shortcomings motivate our approach: an episodic memory design that is expressive and natively compatible with streaming video, accompanied by a systematic study of navigation memory spanning long-horizon navigation scenarios and real-world validation. We propose , a streaming episodic memory framework that endows with persistent navigation memory. maintains dense short-term observations for immediate action while building a compact, queryable summary of the accumulated episode history. Concretely, a memory bank progressively stores perceptual features of streaming observations alongside their timestep and action-derived relative pose. For action prediction, a memory perceiver extracts latent features from the bank and encodes them with the corresponding spatio-temporal context. It then derives a fixed-size set of memory tokens via cross-attention with learnable queries grounded in the current timestep and relative pose. Memory tokens enter the 's multi-modal sequence for auto-regressive action prediction. When the bank reaches its capacity limit, a frame-merging strategy consolidates consecutive frames into a bounded episodic summary. As a complementary source of spatial features, we use a frozen pretrained StreamVGGT encoder~ zhuo2026streaming and train a lightweight adapter to fuse its features into the . Both the memory module and the geometry encoder integrate into existing for streaming video without modifying the underlying LLM architecture. To supervise memory learning, we design a dedicated auxiliary task alongside navigation. Specifically, we adopt trajectory summarization~ zheng2024towards,zhang2024navid,cheng2025navila as the supervision for the memory module, where local visual tokens are masked, leaving memory tokens as the visual evidence for describing the traversed path. To enrich the supervisory signal, we further decompose each full trajectory into hierarchically structured sub-trajectories~ hong2020sub , yielding fine-grained supervision across multiple temporal scales. Together, the memory module design, multi-granularity trajectory summarization, and masking strategy constitute a principled framework for learning navigation memory. We conduct extensive experiments in simulation and on a physical robot. On standard VLN-CE benchmarks~ anderson2018vision,ku2020room,krantz2020beyond , reaches at least 55 success on both R2R and RxR and achieves performance on most metrics among methods whose navigation fine-tuning trajectories are restricted to the official R2R/RxR training splits. Ablations isolate the contributions of memory, geometry, and auxiliary supervision, while long-horizon analyses further examine when memory is useful. For physical evaluation on the G1 robot, we collect 30 episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, improves success over the baseline from 17 to 40 , and post-training further raises it to 47 . Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language Navigation. requires an embodied agent to follow natural language instructions through 3D environments. Early works establish as a foundational task for embodied AI~ chang2017matterport3d,zhu2017target,xia2018gibson,anderson2018evaluation,savva2019habitat,anderson2018vision,chaplot2020object,qi2020reverie,ku2020room,krantz2020beyond,thomason2020vision,ramakrishnan2021habitat,krantz2023navigating,yadav2023habitat . In this paper, we focus on the fundamental task in continuous environments and study how navigation memory can be learned and leveraged without relying on massive data scaling~ anderson2018vision,ku2020room,krantz2020beyond,hong2020sub . Vision-Language Models for Navigation. Effective requires models to perceive 3D environments and comprehend natural language instructions. While early approaches trained navigation models from scratch~ fried2018speaker,nguyen2019vision,wang2019reinforced,hao2020towards , the strengths of pretrained have emerged as a more promising pathway towards general-purpose ~ majumdar2022zson,gadre2023cows,dorbala2022clip,zhou2023esc,wang2024navigating,long2024instructnav,zhou2024navgpt . This paradigm has inspired diverse approaches, including topological structure methods~ chen2021topological,krantz2021waypoint,hong2022bridging,chen2022weakly,chen2022think,yokoyama2024vlfm,an2024etpnav , explicit 3D spatial modeling~ an2023bevbert,wang2024sim,huang2024embodied,zhu2025move,wang2025dynam3d,wang2026d3d , and trajectory-level modeling~ shah2022viking,shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad,wang2025trackvla,gode2025flownav . More recently, the input formulation has been simplified to monocular streaming video, under which navigation performance has improved rapidly~ zheng2024towards,zhang2024navid,zhang2025uninavid,cheng2025navila,wei2026streamvln,zeng2026janusvln,zheng2025efficient,qi2025vln,wei2026ground,chu2026abot , with significant progress also demonstrated in real-world deployment~ gervet2023navigating,yue2024safe,yang2024pushing,qiao2025open,sun2026view,yue2026spatial,yu2026correctnav,zhang2026embodied . Despite this progress, directly retaining long visual histories in streaming policies increases input context and computation, motivating dedicated memory mechanisms. Memory for Embodied Agents. Memory mechanisms for embodied agents predate modern -based navigation and span several task formulations. Recurrent policies compress navigation history into hidden states~ elman1990finding,hochreiter1997long,hong2021vln , whereas explicit approaches retain observation histories or structured spatial representations~ chen2021history,mezghan2022memory,wang2023gridmm,yu2025mossvln . SMT appends each observation to a growing within-episode memory for visual navigation, while E.T. jointly encodes language with the full visual-action history for ALFRED~ fang2019scene,pashevich2021episodic . ESceme instead maintains a cross-episode, location-indexed scene memory for VLN~ zheng2025esceme . title: Complexity-guided Regularization for Generalizable Human Gaussian Splatting
comment: 28 pages, 11 figures, including appendix. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Recent studies on generalizable human Gaussian splatting have achieved the notable progress in synthesizing novel views of unseen human subjects from multi-view images. Despite this progress, existing methods still struggle to represent fine-grained details of human subjects, which inherently involve high geometric and textural complexity. This is because previous methods do not impose a constraint on how densely Gaussians are placed, which often leads to blurry rendering results in complex regions. To address this problem, we propose a complexity-guided regularization scheme. The key idea is to leverage a complexity prior computed via the local entropy in geometric and textural characteristics of a clothed human. This effectively prevents Gaussians from being coarsely placed in complex regions, which facilitates the faithful reconstruction of intricate structures. Furthermore, we sample local patches predominantly from complex regions according to this complexity prior, which allows the model to be sufficiently supervised by local details. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method delivers state-of-the-art performance while maintaining the real-time inference speed in generalizable human Gaussian splatting. The code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/DCVL-3D/CGR-GS_release.

Introduction Realistic 3D human reconstruction has gained the significant interest due to its wide range of applications in virtual reality, telepresence, gaming, content creation, etc. In recent literature, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs , which explicitly represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussian primitives while enabling real-time rendering, has been widely adopted for this task. Most recently, various studies~ hugs,gart,3dgsavatar,gomavatar,animatable3dgs,splattingavatar,gauhuman have begun to integrate human body templates, e.g., SMPL~ smpl , to improve the rendering performance. However, since previous methods rely on the per-subject optimization scheme, they cannot be directly applied to unseen individuals without repeating the entire training procedure, which severely restricts their practicality in real-world scenarios. To overcome the aforementioned limitation, recent studies have explored generalizable approaches, which regress Gaussian attributes for unseen human subjects in a single forward pass. Due to the absence of the iterative refinement process, the majority of generalizable methods rely on an explicit structural prior to mitigate the difficulty of directly predicting Gaussian attributes. For example, some methods~ gps-gaussian, eva-gaussian, mvsc-ghgs have exploited geometric constraints between view pairs as a structural prior to determine the spatial layout of Gaussians. A skinned human model has also been employed~ ghg, lifegom, rogsplat to enable the feed-forward model to place Gaussians directly on the body surface. Even though considerable efforts have been devoted to determining where to place Gaussians via feed-forward approaches, how densely they should be placed across different regions of the human subject has not been sufficiently explored. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for effectively handling generalizable human Gaussian splatting. Due to the inherent smoothness of Gaussian primitives, Gaussians need to be densely placed to faithfully reconstruct high-frequency details. However, previous feed-forward methods localize Gaussians based on the pixel grid~ gps-gaussian, eva-gaussian, mvsc-ghgs or vertices of the skinned mesh~ rogsplat, ghg, lifegom , whose density is highly related to the image resolution or the skinned mesh template rather than the visual properties of the target subject itself. While this may not be significant in simple regions (e.g., plain areas), it often leads to an insufficient number of Gaussians in complex regions (e.g., fingers or textured clothes), which produces blurry rendering results as shown in Figs.~ fig:fig1 (b) and (c). To deal with this problem, we propose a complexity-guided regularization scheme. The key idea is to allocate Gaussians in proportion to the local complexity of the clothed human mesh. Specifically, we define the complexity prior as the entropy of the local geometric and textural information around each vertex of the human mesh. Guided by this prior, we regularize the local density of Gaussians to be positively correlated with the complexity. This helps the model faithfully reconstruct high-frequency details with sufficient Gaussians, as shown in Fig.~ fig:fig1 (d). Moreover, we find that supervising the model with the entire image is suboptimal for reconstructing fine-grained details. This is because supervisory signals from complex regions, which often occupy only a small portion of the human-centric image, e.g., fingers, facial features, etc., are easily dominated by those from surrounding simple regions. Accordingly, during the training phase, we use the complexity prior as sampling weights to select local patches, where regions of higher complexity are more frequently sampled. This training strategy enables the model to receive sufficient supervision on fine details. The main contribution of the proposed method can be summarized as follows: We define a complexity prior as a per-vertex scalar value, which is computed via the local entropy in geometric and textural characteristics of the clothed human mesh. Leveraging this prior, we propose a novel regularization scheme to guide the model to adjust the local Gaussian density according to the complexity. This encourages the model to allocate Gaussians densely in complex regions, which enables faithful reconstruction of fine-grained details. To effectively provide sufficient supervisory signals on intricate details, we introduce a patch-based training strategy, which samples local patches with probability proportional to the complexity prior. Related work -subject optimization-based 3DGS for human rendering. Motivated by the great success of 3D Gaussian splatting~ 3dgs in novel view synthesis, several studies have begun to apply 3DGS to human rendering based on the point-based representation. For example, Gaussian points are initialized on faces of the human mesh and optimized to represent the detailed appearance while preserving the geometric structure of the target subject~ gomavatar, splattingavatar . On the other hand, other methods~ gaussianavatar, 3dgsavatar, gart, hugs, animatable3dgs, gauhuman optimize Gaussian attributes to reconstruct the human in a canonical pose, which are rendered in arbitrary poses via forward skinning. Although these approaches have demonstrated the impressive performance, they typically require the per-subject optimization, which restricts their generalizability to unseen human subjects. 3DGS for human rendering. To overcome this limitation, recent studies have explored generalizable human Gaussian splatting, which regress Gaussian attributes for unseen subjects in a single forward pass. As a pioneer, Zheng et al.~ gps-gaussian estimated per-pixel Gaussian attributes based on the depth map, which is predicted through stereo matching between adjacent views. In a similar vein, Hu et al.~ eva-gaussian improved the regression process by employing the 1D-window attention along epipolar lines between view pairs. More recently, Kim et al.~ mvsc-ghgs leveraged a foundation model~ vggt to inject the implicit 3D geometric knowledge, while recalibrating multi-view features via semantic consistency-based cross-view attention, which helps the model robustly estimate Gaussian attributes in visually complex regions. Instead of estimating per-pixel Gaussian attributes, skinned human models have been adopted as a structural prior to directly place Gaussians on the body surface. In this direction, Wen et al.~ lifegom attached Gaussians to the skinned mesh surface and iteratively refined Gaussian attributes through a feedback mechanism. Similarly, Xiao et al.~ rogsplat densified SMPL vertices to align with the actual human geometry and predicted Gaussian attributes on such densified points. Kwon et al.~ ghg regressed Gaussian attributes in the 2D UV space of the SMPL template and introduced a multi-scaffold representation to effectively mitigate the geometric discrepancy between the skinned body and clothed human. While previous efforts have focused on accurately estimating the position of Gaussians, we shift our focus to how densely Gaussians should be placed and propose an effective regularization scheme, which significantly improves the rendering performance of generalizable human Gaussian splatting. Method Architecture details The overall architecture of the proposed method is shown in Fig.~ fig:overall . Given multi-view RGB images of a clothed human subject with the corresponding Pl\" u cker ray~ plucker maps and human masks , our goal is to regress a set of Gaussian attributes in a single feed-forward pass. Following previous feed-forward approaches~ gs-lrm, grm , each input image is concatenated with the corresponding Pl\" u cker ray map along the channel dimension, which yields a per-view feature map . The resulting feature map is partitioned into non-overlapping patches, which are subsequently flattened and projected into tokens. Since the target subject only occupies a small area of the human-centric image, we discard tokens whose patch lies entirely outside the human mask , which yields foreground tokens for the -th view. This significantly reduces the number of tokens fed into transformer layers, which leads to the real-time inference. Following Long-LRM++~ longlrm++ , a Gaussian decoder regresses attributes of Gaussians from each token. Specifically, the decoder predicts depth , 3D spatial offset , scale , rotation quaternion , opacity , and color . The 3D position of each Gaussian is computed by unprojecting the predicted depth along the ray as , which is further shifted by the spatial offset . Note that and denote directional vectors of the origin and the center ray of the patch, respectively. Consequently, the model produces Gaussians, where is the total number of foreground tokens across all views, which are rasterized to synthesize the target view image. title: VidEdit3D: Flexible 3D Gaussian Editing with Video Diffusion
summary: Recent advancements in text-guided 3D editing, particularly with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have shown promise but still lag behind the flexibility of 2D editing tools. Existing methods face a critical trade-off between preserving multi-view consistency and allowing structural modifications. Image-based editors can also struggle to apply the intended edit to objects viewed from unusual angles. To address these limitations, we introduce VidEdit3D, a framework that reformulates 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. By drawing a parallel between camera movement in static 3D scenes and temporal dynamics in video, we leverage the robust spatiotemporal priors of pre-trained Video Diffusion Models (VDMs) to encourage semantic and structural coherence across views. Specifically, we propose Trajectory-Guided Rendering (TGR) to select informative keyframes and construct smooth video clips aligned with VDM input requirements. To propagate edits from an anchor view to these clips, we develop Flow-Aligned Video Editing (FAVE), a training-free framework incorporating an Editing Consistency Guidance (ECG) mechanism. ECG contrasts source and edited image conditions at a shared latent state, using scheduled source-image amplification to strengthen adherence to the edited reference while maintaining original scene context. Finally, we introduce Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement (RS-GS) to strictly confine geometric and appearance updates to target primitives, reducing background attribute leakage. Experiments demonstrate stronger instruction alignment and better multi-view consistency than the baselines.

By leveraging large-scale diffusion or transformer-based models, these systems can generate semantically aligned and visually coherent edits, such as replacing objects, altering styles, or modifying attributes, while preserving content fidelity. This paradigm has significantly democratized content creation, making intuitive visual editing accessible to non-experts. Building upon this progress, researchers have recently extended text-driven editing to the 3D domain, particularly in neural implicit representations such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)~ mildenhall2021nerf and explicit point-based representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d . Particularly, compared with NeRF, 3DGS offers greater flexibility and efficiency as an explicit 3D representation, enabling high-quality real-time rendering and fine-grained local editing. These advantages make 3DGS editing an attractive paradigm for controllable 3D content manipulation, which is the focus of our paper. However, despite the potential of 3DGS, the capabilities of existing 3D editing frameworks still lag significantly behind their 2D counterparts. 3D editing methods operations as global style transfer, texture modification, or removal. This stands in stark contrast to state-of-the-art 2D editing tools, which support highly imaginative and complex transformations with ease. A primary bottleneck restricting 3D editing flexibility is the requirement for multi-view consistency; unlike 2D editing, modifying a 3D scene requires simultaneous adjustments across multiple viewpoints while ensuring the underlying geometry remains coherent. Early attempts that naively applied 2D editors independently across different views inherently lacked cross-view coherence~ haque2023instruct, chen2024gaussianeditor, wang2024gaussianeditor , leading to severe artifacts such as ghosting and flickering. To mitigate these inconsistencies, subsequent works~ wu2024gaussctrl, wang2024view, chen2024dge introduced depth with the original images. While these constraints stabilize the optimization process, editing flexibility. This limitation becomes particularly evident in instructions that require structural changes. For instance, a simple instruction like ``make the person wear a hat'' becomes difficult to execute the required geometric addition conflicts with constraints derived from the original shape. These limitations motivate the design of a flexible 3D editing framework capable of performing precise semantic manipulations without the excessive rigidity of geometric locks. To robustly facilitate this propagation, we identify a powerful parallel between temporal consistency in videos and multi-view consistency in the rendered frames of a 3D scene. A camera trajectory moving around a static 3D object yields a sequence of frames that is structurally analogous to a video clip. This insight inspires us to leverage the robust spatiotemporal priors of pre-trained Video Diffusion Models (VDMs)~ wan2025wan, kong2024hunyuanvideo, blattmann2023stable, hong2022cogvideo, yang2024cogvideox . are to maintain object identity and semantic coherence across time, for 3D viewpoints. To transform sparse 3D renderings into a form compatible with video diffusion models, we introduce a Trajectory-Guided Rendering (TGR) strategy. To propagate edits from a key view to the rendered video clips, we develop Flow-Aligned Video Editing (FAVE), a training-free framework inspired by recent inversion-free editing methods~ kim2025flowalign, kulikov2025flowedit . Unlike prior methods that are primarily guided by text, our goal is to leverage the strong generative and editing capabilities of 2D image editing models to transfer a user-specified edit from one anchor view to the full 3D scene. In standard generation, classifier-free guidance (CFG)~ ho2022classifier evaluates the denoiser twice under different text conditions, while both evaluations typically share the same first-frame image as the temporal anchor. This design is effective for video synthesis, since a fixed first-frame condition helps preserve object identity and temporal coherence over time. In contrast, FAVE, as an inversion-free editing method, conceptually requires two distinct conditioning roles: one should follow the edited reference frame and target prompt, while the other should preserve the original scene structure under the source frame and source prompt. However, directly reusing the standard I2V conditioning scheme in our setting leads both evaluations to remain anchored to the same edited first frame, rather than forming the desired source-versus-target contrast. In I2V models, this mismatch is exacerbated by the strong first-frame anchoring effect: , the two evaluations similar image-conditioned components the intended guidance contrast To address this issue, we introduce Editing Consistency Guidance (ECG), a training-free inference-time guidance scheme that restores a meaningful source-versus-edit contrast in the guidance computation. , existing 3D editing methods~ chen2024gaussianeditor, wang2024view, chen2024dge, wu2024gaussctrl, lee2025editsplat suffer from global attribute leakage, where gradients intended for the target object erroneously update the entire scene. To address this issue, we introduce Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement (RS-GS), a method that explicitly constrains the refinement to the target region by back-projecting 2D segmentation masks into 3D space and using depth-guided filtering to select the corresponding Gaussians. By confining the optimization to these back-projected primitives while freezing all others, RS-GS ensures that geometric and appearance updates are confined to the edited regions. In summary, effectively reformulates 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. Our main contributions are: We design TGR to organize into smooth clips, improving their compatibility with pretrained I2V priors. We develop FAVE with ECG, a training-free mechanism that to enable precise edit propagation. We design RS-GS refinement to confine geometric and appearance updates to target primitives, background attribute leakage. Related Work sec:relatedwork A significant body of work has explored editing 3D scenes (NeRFs~ mildenhall2021nerf or 3DGS~ kerbl20233d ) through optimization or distillation strategies. Early implicit approaches relied on mesh scaffolds or interactive distillation~ yuan2022nerf, jambon2023nerfshop , while subsequent explicit methods utilize iterative optimization to distill 2D diffusion priors into 3D representations~ chen2024gaussianeditor, koo2024posterior, wang2024gaussianeditor . Recent advancements further enhance quality through identity-preserving noise estimation~ kim2024dreamcatalyst or task-specific optimization for style transfer and virtual try-on~ liu2024stylegaussian, cao2024gs . However, ensuring multi-view consistency remains a primary bottleneck. To address this, several methods geometric such as depth or epipolar alignment~ wu2024gaussctrl, chen2024dge, wang2024view, lee2025editsplat, gomel2024diffusion . SDEdit balances realism and fidelity through noising and denoising~ meng2021sdedit . With backbones and rectified flows~ peebles2023scalable,liu2022flow , preserve structure through attention and feature control~ hertz2022prompt,tumanyan2023plug,liu2024towards . MasaCtrl supports non-rigid edits with mutual self-attention~ cao2023masactrl , while KV-Edit and FreeFlux use DiT-specific key-value reuse for background-preserving, task-adaptive editing~ zhu2025kv,wei2025freeflux . Video editing adds temporal coherence: cross-frame attention control and fusion~ liu2024video,qi2023fatezero and space-time modulation~ yang2025videograin reduce drift and improve fine-grained control. I2V methods propagate first-frame edits using temporal features or motion--content alignment~ ku2024anyv2v,liu2025stablev2v , whereas FlowDirector uses inversion-free ODE steering~ li2025flowdirector . Complex motion and large appearance or shape changes remain challenging. title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
summary: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without any real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. We demonstrate that ZAP also generalizes to completely new objects, goals, strategies, and language by seating a test tube in a rack (and choosing a different hole in the rack when prompted), handing a test tube between arms mid-air, drawing an X on a tic-tac-toe board, and playing chess. These goals and types of manipulation don't appear in our training data. Furthermore, ZAP also transfers to an unseen embodiment. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.
