To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without any real-world robot data during training, reaches 96.7 success on real-world tasks, matching in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3 ), while running 3 faster and 17 cheaper than . We demonstrate that also generalizes to completely new objects, goals, strategies, and language by seating a test tube in a rack (and choosing a different hole in the rack when prompted), handing a test tube between arms mid-air, drawing an X on a tic-tac-toe board, and playing chess. These goals and types of manipulation don't appear in our training data. Furthermore, also transfers to an unseen embodiment. On a single-arm Franka, reaches 55.9 on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline. Introduction sec:intro A robot policy has to do two difficult things at once: it needs semantic reasoning to understand instructions in a potentially unfamiliar scene, and motion control to translate that understanding into precise physical actions. We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy ( ), which adds motion to a small pretrained vision-language model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), entirely in simulation. We evaluate how these skills carry over to new tasks, real hardware, and a new embodiment. Existing methods tend to trade off performance in one of these areas for the others, and broadly fall into three groups (Table~ tab:approaches ). Models that directly output robot actions. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) learn semantic reasoning motion control from robot action data~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,fang2026molmoact2 . Because diverse action data is scarce, both skills end up tied to the training distribution: the policy often generalizes poorly to new prompts, objects, scenes and goals, and a new task usually means training again. Code that directly drives the robot. In Code as Policies~ liang2022code,fu2026capx , a language model writes a program that composes perception and control APIs. This is quick and reliable when the situations it will face can be anticipated when the program is written, but struggles outside that script, for example with an unexpected failure, an unfamiliar object or an ambiguous instruction. Adapting to a new task or scene means rewriting the program. Large frontier models controlling the robot through tools. Frontier language models interacting with the robot via an agentic harness bring world understanding, reasoning and generalization ~ jia2026agentpolicy,robocurve2026inspect,li2026roboharness . But they are not explicitly trained to move a robot, and a trillion-parameter model is slow and costs dollars for a task that smaller policy models, when they can do them, do in seconds and cost pennies. combines semantic reasoning from vision-language pretraining with motion control learned entirely in simulation. We start with Qwen 3.6 27B~ qwen2026qwen36 , which contributes world understanding and reasoning. We then teach the model motion control in simulation - first SFT on its own mined successful traces, followed by RL across 40 pick-and-place, stacking, and reorientation tasks. Neither stage uses real-world robot demonstrations. At test time, the policy combines pretrained semantic reasoning with learned motion control to perform real-world tasks it was never trained to execute, generalizing to new objects, goals, and robot embodiments. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] Teacher-free training of an agent policy in simulation. We teach a pretrained vision-language model to control a robot with no frontier teacher and no real robot data. The model commands end-effector poses and gripper openings through a harness that is identical in simulation and on hardware. We seed it with successful traces mined from its own rollouts, then refine it with RL using a dense reward ladder that credits partial progress ( sec:method ). Transfer to hardware and new embodiment. With no real-world robot training data, matches on 10 real tasks at 3 the speed and 1/17 the cost. The same checkpoint transfers without retraining to a completely new embodiment (single-arm Franka) exceeding the performance of leading VLA/WAM baselines on RoboLab-120 ( sec:quant ). Generalization to new goals, language, and reasoning. combines pretrained semantic reasoning with learned motion control to execute real-world tasks unseen during robot training. The policy handles new objects and goals, follows instructions for manipulation strategies it never practiced, and applies complex reasoning to tasks such as chess and drawing ( sec:compose ). Related work sec:related_main Composing reasoning and motion. Task-and-motion planners compose symbolic operators that ground into geometric motion~ toussaint2015lgp,garrett2021tamp . Large language models then proved to be better high-level planners, sequencing a library of learned skills~ ahn2022saycan,huang2022innermonologue,lin2023text2motion or handing subgoals to low-level policies~ dalal2024psl,dalal2025manipgen . keeps the split between reasoning and motion but drops the fixed skill library. Motion is a skill the model learns itself, through a minimal harness that leaves scene reasoning and action sequencing to the model rather than imposing macros that simplify familiar tasks but limit generalization. End-to-end policies. VLAs and WAMs fold reasoning and motion into one network trained on robot actions~ brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0,ye2026dreamzero,fang2026molmoact2 . Several studies show that these policies keep the intent of an instruction but fail to execute it on new tasks, perturbations or skill combinations~ zhou2025agnostos,fang2025intact,zhou2025liberopro,park2026instructions . instead inherits the reasoning and language ability of a pretrained LLM and learns only motion, in simulation. It never has to learn language from action data, so it is not tied to the instructions that data happens to contain, and it follows what an instruction means rather than how it is worded. Foundation models as robot agents. Code as Policies and its successors compose perception and control APIs into programs~ liang2022code,huang2023voxposer , and frontier agents now act directly as closed-loop policies through tool harnesses~ jia2026agentpolicy,robocurve2026inspect,li2026roboharness . They bring reasoning for free, but they are slow, expensive and not trained to move a robot. The closest work trains compact tool-calling agents, mostly by distilling a frontier teacher: Guava into a 4B agent with object-referenced grasp and align tools, refined with GRPO on two tasks~ liu2026guava , RACaP into an 8B model over evolved policy APIs~ li2026racap , and Robo-Harness K1 into a 9B student evaluated in simulation~ li2026roboharness . uses no teacher: its fine-tuning data are its own successful rollouts, and RL trains it on all 40 tasks, so no teacher sets its ceiling. It commands complete end-effector poses rather than grasp macros. Guava's unseen tasks recombine the grasp, place and push primitives it was trained on; composes motions it never practiced, such as a mid-air handoff and a marker stroke, and runs on a different robot without retraining. Appendix~ sec:related gives a more detailed discussion. Method sec:method We first describe the harness, the tool interface through which the model perceives and acts, identical in simulation and on hardware ( sec:harness ). We then describe how we train the model to move entirely in simulation using GRPO and a dense reward ladder ( sec:training ), and how we initialize that run from successful traces gathered by a short GRPO warm-up and prefix-tree search ( sec:init ). One interface across simulation and hardware sec:harness controls two 6-DoF (degrees-of-freedom) YAM arms with parallel-jaw grippers~ i2rt_yam . It commands absolute end-effector poses and gripper openings, rather than joint angles, trajectories, or action chunks. We frame tasks as a conversation between the model and its environment through the harness: the model first writes a plan and names the objects to locate based on camera views of the environment, then repeatedly issues perception and movement tool calls to complete its task. The harness uses SAM~3.1~ meta2026sam31,carion2025sam3 to segment the objects named in the model's perception queries in each camera stream. These masks are combined with calibrated depth cameras to yield each object's 3D centroid, height, and principal axes. This process runs continuously and asynchronously in the background: the model steers perception by changing its queries, and receives object measurements and annotated camera images. The model controls the robot and manages the episode through five tools, two of which move the robot: move to sets a complete end-effector pose for one or both arms, and set gripper sets each jaw opening. change query sets what perception looks for, update todo keeps a short plan in view across turns, and done ends the episode. There are no grasp macros or motion primitives, so every approach, grasp, lift and release is a sequence of these two motion tools that the model plans itself. Appendix~ app:harness describes the rest of the harness: the pose and orientation parameterization, the observations, validation, the motion controller and its outcome reports, and how the same harness runs in simulation and on hardware. Appendix~ app:episode steps through a complete real-robot episode turn by turn. Learning to move in simulation sec:training We build our simulated tasks in Isaac Sim~ nvidia_isaacsim by adding simulated YAM arms with calibrated cameras and arm dynamics against real YAM arms. Learning motion control on simulated tasks. We design 40 simulated tasks, none of which appear in RoboLab-120, that exercise the same families of everyday object manipulation skills: grasping and lifting, single- and multi-object pick and place, stacking, and reorientation. The goals are deliberately simple, and none requires heavy reasoning. This lets us test whether motion control learned on simple tasks can combine with pretrained semantic reasoning to solve unseen tasks with new goals and strategies. GRPO with dense rewards. The GRPO run is initialized from the checkpoint detailed in sec:init and trains on all 40 tasks (hyperparameters in Appendix~ app:hparams ). Binary reward based on task success is inefficient since some tasks start with zero successes, and therefore a pass/fail reward would provide zero advantage and contribute no gradient. We instead shape a dense ladder of partial credit judged on the final state of the scene, manually designed per task type. For example, for pick and place tasks, approaching the object earns up to 0.2 in proportion to the gripper fingertip-to-object distance closed; grasping earns 0.2 and lifting up to a further 0.55, in proportion to height up to 8\,cm. Transport raises the total to at most 0.9, in proportion to the distance to the goal closed. Completing a task earns 5.0, minus a small length penalty which penalizes the model for taking too many turns to complete the task. The specific numbers for partial credit were not ablated and instead holistically chosen: our guiding principle was that final task success must have a much higher reward than partial reward; otherwise, the model settles for collecting partial credit. title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
summary: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Introduction sec:intro Transferring knowledge from large pretrained models to robotics has become a primary approach to general-purpose robot control~ firoozi2023foundation, ma2024vlasurvey, shen2026wamsurvey . Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt vision-language backbones for end-to-end visuomotor control~ kim2024openvla, black2025pi0, pi05, ma2026internvla, gigabrainteam2026gigabrain, yuan2026qwenrobotmanip , whereas world action models (WAMs) jointly model future visual dynamics and actions to utilize the physical and temporal priors of video generative models~ dreamzero, kim2026cosmos, li2026lingbotva, yuan2026fastwam, wang2026openwam, cai2026internw0 . Both approaches rely on post-training with robot manipulation trajectories: although effective within their training distributions, their generalization is bounded by the scale and diversity of collected robot data. By contrast, frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) acquire stronger emergent capabilities from massive-scale pretraining data, and this training scale remains costly to replicate with embodied data alone. Without robot-specific post-training, frontier MLLMs provide an alternative approach through their spatial understanding and embodied reasoning capabilities~ zhang2026robodojo, google2026argonrobotics . ~ openai2026astra , for example, can generate end-effector (EEF) commands directly from camera observations and language instructions~ zhang2026robodojo, liu2026roboicl, jia2026agent, lou2026knowbody . Combined with an agent harness that supplies its prompt, observation interface, and tools, the model serves as the core of an agent that controls the robot in closed loop, as formalized in Section~ sec:framework . Beyond direct control, recent studies explore a harness with policy in which the agent invokes a post-trained policy for action execution~ zhang2026harnessvla, baton, wang2026harnesspai . Such a harness combines the agent's task planning, progress monitoring, and error recovery with the closed-loop visuomotor control that the policy learns from robot demonstrations. Although prior studies have evaluated both direct control and a harness with policy, they have not comprehensively profiled these agent configurations against post-trained VLA and WAM policies across diverse manipulation demands. Specifically, two central questions remain to be addressed. First, under direct control, on which tasks does the agent outperform post-trained VLAs and WAMs, where does it fall short, and what limits its performance? Second, in a harness-with-policy setting, how does invoking a post-trained policy complement the agent's direct control, which limitations of direct control can it alleviate, and what new failure modes arise when the agent invokes a policy for execution and subsequently resumes decision-making? To further explore these questions, we evaluate as the core of an agent on EBench~ gao2026ebench . This diagnostic manipulation benchmark categorizes tasks by mobility, manipulation precision, and task horizon and evaluates robustness along the generalization dimensions of unseen objects, unseen backgrounds, paraphrased instructions, and their mixture. For a fair comparison, the agent operates under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, receiving only RGB camera images and proprioceptive robot states without depth, camera calibration, or simulator ground truth. For each task, the agent receives a task description annotated by from a single training episode as single-shot in-context learning (ICL). Across all 510 test episodes, we evaluate both direct control and a harness with policy invoking either the VLA or the WAM InternW0- , compare each configuration against the post-trained policies on the EBench leaderboard, and analyze execution trajectories across paired episodes. Under direct control, the -based agent achieves a 46.7 overall success rate and a 0.654 stage-completion score, outperforming post-trained policies such as Qwen-RobotManip and trained on 6 , 600 in-domain demonstrations. Among the compared post-trained policies, the agent ranks first on short-horizon tasks with a 73.2 success rate, shows the smallest success-rate variation across the four generalization dimensions, and completes a novel composite instruction zero-shot on which both compared post-trained policies fail. Conversely, its success rate drops to 27.3 on long-horizon tasks, 20.0 on tabletop manipulation, and 11.3 on high-precision contact-rich tasks. Trajectory analysis shows that while the agent performs well at visual grounding and in-episode error recovery, its physical execution is limited by long action chunks between observations and by contact geometry that it must infer explicitly from RGB views. Invoking a post-trained policy through the agent harness increases the overall success rate to 53.0 with and 56.0 with InternW0- and reduces the agent's token cost per success by more than half. With InternW0- , the harness surpasses all post-trained policies compared in Table~ tab:overall . The harness with policy retains the agent's high success rate on short-horizon tasks and improves performance on long-horizon and bimanual tasks where the post-trained policy is competent. At the same time, case analysis identifies two limitations of the current harness with policy. First, neither component resolves high-precision contact-rich manipulation. Second, agent and policy coordinate loosely in three respects: the agent invokes the policy for most execution steps even on tasks where that policy alone rarely succeeds, the policy follows the fixed task instruction instead of the agent's subgoal, and the agent often leaves a held grasp unmaintained when it resumes control after a policy invocation, which makes object drops more frequent. The main contributions of this report are as follows: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt] Paired evaluation across agent configurations and post-trained policies. Under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, we evaluate an -based agent under direct control and in a harness with policy across all 510 EBench test episodes. We compare both agent configurations against standalone post-trained VLA and WAM policies across all task groups and generalization dimensions. Characterization of agent capabilities under direct control. We locate where the -based agent leads or trails eight post-trained policies while using only a single annotated task demonstration and no parameter updates, trace its unsuccessful episodes to their failure mechanisms, and examine its in-episode adaptation, the safety of its execution, and its zero-shot composition of skills on a novel instruction. Together, these analyses show where the agent and the policies complement each other. Analysis of harness with policy and implications for agent harness design. We evaluate the harness with either policy against each of its components on every task, trace the episodes that newly fail under the harness and those that fail with both policies to their decisive incidents, and analyze the agent's policy invocation and the resulting token cost. These analyses locate the remaining gap to the better component in policy invocation, subgoal passing, and grasp maintenance when the agent resumes control, which informs the design of future agent harnesses. Related Work sec:related Robot manipulation with foundation models. Two lines of work apply foundation models to robot manipulation. Post-trained policies typically adapt foundation models on robot manipulation trajectories, including VLA models that fine-tune vision-language backbones for action prediction~ kim2024openvla, black2025pi0, pi05 and WAMs that jointly model future visual dynamics and actions~ dreamzero, kim2026cosmos, yuan2026fastwam, miao2026internw0deltaworldactionmodel . Direct control with frontier MLLMs, in contrast, uses frontier MLLMs as the cores of agents that control robots without parameter updates. Early approaches translate model predictions into robot motion through generated programs that call perception and control APIs~ codeaspolicies or through embodiment-specific semantic primitives~ chen2026showharness , whereas more recent studies prompt MLLMs to output EEF or joint commands directly~ jia2026agent, lou2026knowbody . On the RoboDojo benchmark, for example, generates robot actions directly from observations~ zhang2026robodojo , and providing in-context demonstration segments together with in-episode interaction history further improves task success~ liu2026roboicl, sensenova2026astra . Rather than evaluating direct control in isolation, our work systematically compares under direct control against post-trained VLA and WAM policies on EBench~ gao2026ebench by task group and generalization dimension, linking dimension-level performance to step-by-step execution trajectories. Harness with policy. Combining both lines, recent frameworks build hierarchical harnesses in which an agent with an MLLM core invokes post-trained policies for action execution~ qin2026towards, sensenova2026astra . For instance, Harness VLA invokes a frozen VLA alongside scripted or analytical primitives~ zhang2026harnessvla , BATON coordinates long-horizon VLA execution through a transition-aware memory that verifies subtask entry and exit conditions~ baton , and HarnessPAI synthesizes task-specific control programs that invoke post-trained policies without online deliberation~ wang2026harnesspai . Related frameworks also adapt harness coordination logic, policy interfaces, or recovery tools during deployment~ tang2026adahvla, li2026racap, ding2026zetta . However, existing studies primarily evaluate each proposed harness as a single integrated system. In contrast, we evaluate the agent both under direct control and in a harness with policy, and compare both agent configurations against standalone VLA and WAM policies across the same test scenes under a fixed in-context protocol. This paired evaluation quantifies how the agent's policy invocation decisions align with the standalone competence of the post-trained policy, and traces episode-level gains and losses to the agent's direct control, policy execution, or the transitions between them.
